ideas_up_v2.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex systems is key in numerous scientific fields. This strong interest is however hindered by modeling issues: often, the governing equations describing the physics of the system under consideration are not accessible or, if known, their solution might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints. Approximating complex systems in a generic functional format and informing it ex-nihilo from available observations has become common practice in the age of machine learning. Deep neural networks have provided numerous successful examples of this data-driven approach across diverse applications. Generalizability of the models, margins of guarantee and the impact of data are often overlooked in these approaches. These critical aspects are examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the physics when they are considered at all. We tackle these issues from a different viewpoint, by adopting a curriculum learning strategy. In curriculum learning, the dataset is structured such that the training process starts from simple samples towards more complex ones. This pedagogical ordering of training examples has been shown to favor convergence and generalization in machine learning tasks. The concept has been developed and successfully applied in robotics and control of systems. Here, we apply this concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems in a systematic way. First, leveraging insights from the ergodic theory, we assess the amount of data sufficient for a-priori guaranteeing a faithful model of the physical system. We thoroughly investigate the impact of the training set and its structure on the quality of long-term predictions through extensive numerical experiments. Based on that analysis, we consider entropy as a metric of complexity of the dataset. We show how an informed design of the training set based on the analysis of the entropy significantly improves the resulting models in terms of generalizability. Finally, we provide insights on the amount and the choice of data required for an effective data-driven modeling approach to dynamical systems.
ideas_up_v2.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7: The CII 158 microns line is the most important coolant of the interstellar medium in galaxies but substantial variations are seen from object to object. The main source of the emission at a galactic scale is still poorly understood. Previous studies of the CII emission in galaxies have a resolution of several kpc or more so the observed emission is an average of different ISM components. The aim of this work is to study, for the first time, the CII emission at the scale of a spiral arm. We want to investigate the origin of this line and its use as a tracer of star formation. We present CII and OI observations of a segment of a spiral arm of M~31 using the Infrared Space Observatory. The CII emission is compared with tracers of neutral gas (CO, HI) and star formation (H\alpha, Spitzer 24 mu). The similarity of the CII emission with the Ha and 24 mu images is striking when smoothed to the same resolution. The correlation with the neutral gas is much weaker than with star formation indicators. The CII cooling rate per H atom increases dramatically from ~2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom in the border of the map to ~1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom in the regions of star formation. The CII/FIR(42-122) ratio is almost constant at 2% across the observed region. This ratio is a factor 3 higher than typically quoted in the literature. However, we do not believe that M~31 is unusual. Whole-galaxy fluxes used for the comparisons include the central regions where the CII/FIR ratio is known to be lower. The resolved observations neither isolate a spiral arm nor include data as far out in the galactic disk as the observations presented here. A fit to published PDR models yields a plausible average solution of G_0~100 and n~3000 for the PDR emission in the regions of star formation. These parameters characterize the radiation field intensity and gas density in the arm of M31. Our results demonstrate that spatially resolved observations are essential for understanding CII emission mechanisms in galaxies.
ideas_up_v2.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: We study a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a topological crystalline insulator (TCI) protected by rotation symmetry. The model is built by stacking two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers which transform under conjugate representations of the rotation group, e.g. $p_\pm$ orbitals. Despite its apparent similarity to the Kane-Mele model, it does not host stable gapless surface states. The model exhibits topological responses including the appearance of quantized fractional charge bound to rotational defects (disclinations). Threading an elementary magnetic flux through the system pumps angular momentum. A mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field corresponding to the rotation symmetry describes these phenomena. The filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation. This obstruction is removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals, which implies fragile topology. The response of the model can be derived by representing it as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients. The model serves as a prototypical example of 2D TCIs protected by rotation. All TCIs protected by point group symmetries which do not have protected surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there is a stable Wannier obstruction. Dimensional reduction maps the problem of classifying 2D TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D) problem. This zero-dimensional formulation yields the complete non-interacting classification of such TCIs. Interactions reduce this classification, producing a different symmetry-protected topological ordering. The framework connects geometric defects to electronic structure topology through local symmetry properties. Rotational symmetries in two dimensions generate distinct topological invariants compared to time-reversal or mirror symmetries. Our results establish equivalences between band topology, defect responses, and the algebraic structure of orbitals in crystalline systems.
ideas_up_v2.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). The system extracts selected attributes from objects across multiple domains such as chess problems, classical music compositions, and renowned artworks. These attributes are then recombined algorithmically to generate novel characteristics applicable to creative object synthesis. The resulting framework enables machines to shoulder significant portions of creative content generation previously requiring human effort. Our experimental validation focused specifically on chess problem composition as the test domain. The system automatically composed numerous problem sets by processing attributes from diverse sources including human chess problems, tournament games, renowned paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, human photographs, and classical music recordings. We evaluated the generated chess problems using two distinct assessment methodologies. First, an existing computational chess aesthetics model, previously validated through experimental studies, provided automated quality measurements. Second, human experts with specialized domain knowledge conducted independent evaluations of the generated problems. The experimental findings indicate that cross-domain attribute extraction and recombination through DSNS successfully produces chess problems with reasonably high aesthetic merit. One particularly striking result emerged from combining low-quality chess sources with photograph data. Tournament game sequences between weak players, when merged with actual photographs of people, generated three-move problems matching or exceeding the quality of those derived from published expert compositions. This unexpected combination also demonstrated superior computational efficiency compared to high-quality chess sources alone. The mechanism by which foreign domain information integrates functionally into chess problem generation remains unexplained and presents an intriguing research question. The DSNS framework exhibits scalability potential extending beyond chess to any creative domain. The only technical requirement is that domain objects possess attributes expressible as real-number representations. This universality suggests broad applicability across artistic, musical, visual, and other creative fields where numerical attribute encoding proves feasible.
ideas_up_v2.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad: The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak, seen in the cosmic matter distribution at redshifts up to ~3.5, reflects the continued expansion of the sonic horizon first identified in temperature anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background. Current observational techniques enable measurement of the BAO peak position to better than ~1% accuracy using galaxies as tracers. Ly-alpha forests combined with quasar clustering statistics yield precision estimates in the range of ~1.4-1.6%. The Alcock-Paczyński (AP) effect exploits how the ratio of angular to spatial/redshift dimensions changes with distance for spherically-symmetric source distributions. Together with BAO measurements, this diagnostic represents one of the most powerful tools for constraining the geometry of the Universe. This paper analyzes five BAO peak measurements from the final release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV. These measurements span average redshifts <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33. We perform a direct head-to-head comparison of the standard Lambda-CDM model against one of its principal competitors, the R_h=ct universe. As a complementary diagnostic to the AP test, we employ a volume-averaged distance probe that assumes a constant comoving distance scale r_d. Both probes avoid dependence on uncertain parameters such as the Hubble constant, making them ideally suited for rigorous model selection. Our analysis reveals that R_h=ct is favored by measurements based solely on the AP effect, with a likelihood ~75% versus ~25% for the standard model. When using only the volume-averaged distance probe, Planck-Lambda-CDM receives preference over R_h=ct, with a likelihood ~80% versus ~20%. A joint analysis combining both probes produces an inconclusive outcome. The combined diagnostics yield comparable likelihoods to both models. Consequently, the BAO data alone cannot confirm the hypothesis of an accelerating Universe through this work.

Context. Filaments are ubiquitous in the Galaxy, and they host star formation. Detecting them in a reliable way is therefore key towards our understanding of the star formation process.

Aims. We explore whether supervised machine learning can identify filamentary structures on the whole Galactic plane.

Methods. We used two versions of UNet-based networks for image segmentation. H2 column density images of the Galactic plane obtained with Herschel Hi-GAL data served as input data. We trained the UNet-based networks with skeletons (spine plus branches) of filaments that were extracted from these images. Background masks and missing data masks that we produced were also incorporated into the training process. We tested eight training scenarios to determine the best scenario for our astrophysical purpose of classifying pixels as filaments. Each scenario varied in the combination of input features and network architecture parameters employed.

Results. The training of the UNets allows us to create a new image of the Galactic plane by segmentation in which pixels belonging to filamentary structures are identified. With this new method, we classify more pixels (more by a factor of 2 to 7, depending on the classification threshold used) as belonging to filaments than the spine plus branches structures we used as input. New structures are revealed, which are mainly low-contrast filaments that were not detected before. Standard metrics to evaluate the performances of the different training scenarios were applied systematically. The robustness of the method is demonstrated through cross-validation techniques. An optimal threshold value that maximizes the recovery of the input labelled pixel classification was determined through quantitative analysis.

Conclusions. This proof-of-concept study shows that supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures that are present throughout the Galactic plane. Low-density structures that have never been seen before now become accessible for scientific investigation. Important perspectives for the study of these filaments are offered by this detection capability.

Let me preface this by saying that I really do like Cowboy Bebop. The animation and designs are sublime, the soundtrack is fantastic, and the action sequences are expertly choreographed. When all three elements come together, the show can occasionally become a jaw dropping audiovisual masterpiece, particularly in the breathtaking finale. However, there are so many problems with it that I cannot in good faith call it a "masterpiece" or proclaim it to be one of the best of the medium as anything other than a gateway show.

I'll start off with the characters, which is where many of my problems lie. Spike and Jet are great characters with well-developed personalities and compelling backstories. Unfortunately, they represent only two-fifths of the entire Bebop Crew. Ein's introduction as a "data dog" or otherwise hyperintelligent canine goes nowhere, and this promising concept is never explored or utilized in any meaningful way. He spends the rest of the show just being the crew's pet without demonstrating any of the intelligence that made him valuable. Faye exhibits many of the worst characteristics that can be written about a female character in anime. She's bossy, greedy, and obsessed with her own beauty to the point of narcissism. She needs to either be rescued or serves as a hinderance to the group more often than functioning as an asset. Her wardrobe choices consist of revealing clothing for the sole purpose of fanservice rather than practical reasons. Ed is hit or miss, and walks the line between endearing and annoying throughout her appearances. The character hardly receives much development beyond her introductory episode, remaining static for the remainder of the series.

The main villain Vicious is especially bad and poorly constructed. He has very little character depth and motivation aside from a generic desire for more power. Even though the show goes a bit into his backstory through flashbacks, it never establishes clear motivation for his actions. At the end of the show, Vicious is little more than an evil guy in a black coat with exceptional fighting skills. His combat abilities make Spike struggle to land a bullet in him during their confrontations. The obvious fact remains that Vicious becomes a representation of the syndicate Spike ran away from rather than a fully realized antagonist. As a result, the five episodes that involve him don't leave me feeling as if they are as spectacular as the show wants me to feel like they are. These episodes include Sympathy for the Devil, Jupiter Jazz parts one and two, and Real Folk Blues parts one and two.

Aside from character issues, the quality of the episodes varies dramatically in both execution and storytelling. For an episodic show that only has about five episodes that build an overall story arc, that's saying a lot about inconsistency. Sure, there are fantastic episodes such as Waltz for Venus and Ganymede Elegy that showcase the series at its best. However, there are also fairly ho-hum episodes such as Bohemian Rhapsody, Speak Like a Child, and Boogie Woogie Feng Shui that feel like filler. The tonal shifts between episodes can be jarring and disrupt narrative momentum. Reddit, help me appreciate this show and tell me what I'm missing in my analysis of this celebrated series.

ideas_up_v2.coling::3bec38ad-9c98-4004-95a3-5b24858e: I live in New Zealand, and we are currently in the middle of "one of the most important elections in our country's history" according to politicians and media commentators. I am not planning to vote in this election. The electoral commission's campaigns to encourage universal voter turnout strike me as fundamentally misguided. Many politically engaged people in my social circle cannot comprehend that some citizens genuinely lack strong preferences between the available options. The transition from Helen Clark's government to John Key's administration produced no discernible changes in my daily existence. Labour winning the current election would similarly fail to alter my routine or personal circumstances in any meaningful way. I will continue my normal activities regardless of which party controls parliament. Citizens routinely express hatred toward whatever government holds power until the opposition eventually returns to office. This cyclical pattern of discontent occurs independently of which political faction temporarily governs. My informed assessment is that I genuinely lack investment in the outcome of this electoral contest. Conducting research to develop political opinions would represent an inefficient allocation of my limited time and attention. Leaving electoral decisions to informed, engaged citizens who understand policy nuances seems like the rational approach. This apathetic stance enjoys widespread acceptance in certain segments of New Zealand society. Recently, however, aggressive campaigns have emerged that attempt to shame non-voters into participating. One slogan declares "It's only democracy if you vote, idiot," combining civic messaging with personal insults. Another particularly extreme advertisement depicts Earth in ecological collapse, presumably referencing climate policy debates, alongside enormous letters spelling "VOTE." Revealing my non-voting intention to approximately half my friends would generate no reaction whatsoever. The other half would subject me to intense criticism and moral condemnation. These critics claim abstention represents a failure to "contribute to my country's future," as if voting were a civic obligation rather than a right. This guilt-based messaging pressures uninformed citizens into casting ballots despite lacking genuine political preferences. Such pressured voters become prime targets for manipulation by campaigns employing sophisticated persuasion techniques. A flyer distributed during one of my university lectures yesterday purported to provide neutral summaries of party platforms. The document actually employed colour-coding to designate certain policies as desirable or objectionable according to unstated criteria. This supposedly informative guide systematically portrayed right-wing positions as morally wrong and left-wing alternatives as virtuous. The Green Party recently visited campus offering free off-peak public transportation passes to university students. This policy represents transparent vote-buying with minimal societal benefit beyond securing electoral support from young adults. The initiative accomplishes essentially nothing regarding genuine transportation challenges or environmental objectives. Conservative parties undoubtedly engage in similar tactical pandering to their target demographics. Left-wing manipulation simply registers more prominently in my awareness due to my university environment. My central argument is that electoral commissions should discourage voting among uninformed citizens rather than promoting universal participation. Pressured voters frequently make choices based on trivial considerations or emotional manipulation rather than substantive policy analysis. Modern political campaigns exploit vulnerable, guilted voters through increasingly sophisticated manipulation techniques. Electoral officials push universal turnout because they personally find politics fascinating and project this interest onto the general population. These administrators fail to recognize that substantial portions of the electorate genuinely lack interest in political outcomes. Forcing political engagement on disinterested citizens resembles compelling the entire nation to watch rugby matches. Incidentally, the All Blacks losing an important game would genuinely affect my emotional state more than any governmental transition. This comparison illustrates how political significance varies dramatically across different population segments. Democratic participation should emerge from genuine engagement rather than social pressure or manufactured guilt. Universal suffrage represents a right to vote rather than an obligation to do so. Abstention by uninformed citizens arguably produces better electoral outcomes than pressured participation by those lacking genuine preferences. Electoral quality improves when decisions reflect the informed preferences of engaged citizens rather than the manipulated choices of guilted participants.
ideas_up_v2.coling::365ba259-c2eb-480e-84d9-eab251a4: Waterboarding strikes me as fundamentally trivial compared to genuine forms of physical abuse. The procedure cannot result in death when executed according to established protocols. Permanent bodily injury is medically impossible if the technique follows proper guidelines. The entire experience operates on psychological rather than physical mechanisms. I've watched demonstration videos showing the complete process from start to finish. Written accounts from various participants describe their subjective reactions during the event. These testimonials confirm that the suffering is primarily mental anguish rather than bodily harm. If psychological distress is the only consequence, this method represents the optimal interrogation tool for suspected terrorists. Intelligence agencies have extracted actionable information using this technique on numerous occasions. The willingness of journalists to undergo the experience demonstrates its relative safety. Medieval devices like thumb screws would never attract voluntary participants. The rack caused permanent skeletal damage that disabled victims for life. Waterboarding leaves no lasting physical marks or injuries on the body. Critics accuse America of hypocrisy regarding its stance on enhanced interrogation. The United States claims to oppose torture while simultaneously employing questionable methods. However, waterboarding arguably fulfills the goal of humane deterrence better than any alternative. The technique creates overwhelming terror through simulated drowning without actual danger. This simulation achieves all the coercive benefits while avoiding genuine physical destruction. My background includes no personal military service or firsthand experience with interrogation. Both my maternal and paternal relatives include multiple generations of armed forces veterans. Their experiences have educated me extensively about combat realities and military operations. My knowledge comes from extensive reading and family conversations rather than professional training. This perspective might overlook important ethical or practical considerations I haven't encountered. The contemporary world faces countless crises demanding immediate attention and resources. Geopolitical conflicts threaten millions of lives across multiple continents simultaneously. Climate change represents an existential threat to human civilization itself. Economic inequality destabilizes democratic institutions throughout the developed world. Given these pressing concerns, the waterboarding debate seems disproportionately prominent in public discourse. Conservative political circles rarely voice support for enhanced interrogation in mainstream forums. I'm curious whether this community shares my assessment or finds fundamental flaws in my reasoning. ideas_up_v2.coling::bd4df89c-701f-407b-9fc6-2c51aa5b: I'm talking about the type of condemnation voiced consistently by certain users of rpolitics, certain members of OWS, and Gawker's Hamilton Nolan. It is a viewpoint I will paraphrase roughly as follows: The mere fact that we live in a system where some people can amass vastly more money than others is, itself, immoral. Those who do accumulate significant wealth under this system are arguably bad people by virtue of that accumulation. Hedge fund managers spend tens of millions on embalmed sharks and similar extravagances. These wealthy individuals fail to recognize that a tiny fraction of their daily earnings would transform others' lives. Such amounts would be sufficient to eliminate the average redditor's student loan debt entirely. Every time I've encountered this argument, it has come from activists or internet commenters. These critics consistently hail from the middle-class tier of advanced Western economies, or occasionally from working-class backgrounds in such nations. Here's the critical counterpoint: you, too, possess vastly more resources than most people worldwide. You could save 100 dollars by declining to upgrade your smartphone this year. Walking home in the rain instead of taking a cab would preserve similar amounts. Eating lentils or beans for several weeks represents another cost-cutting option. Foregoing that new item of clothing you wanted would yield comparable savings. That 100 dollars could be donated to save the lives of dozens of children who would otherwise die of Malaria. Your comfort, convenience and entertainment are being prioritized over other peoples' survival. I will not tolerate deflections claiming that charities might not use donations responsibly. Similarly, arguments about charitable donations potentially harming local industry in the long run will not be entertained here. As a premise of this CMV, we must stipulate that wealth redistribution would genuinely benefit the recipients. We must further stipulate that the average American possesses the ability to donate in a genuinely-beneficial manner towards worthy causes. These assumptions strike me as quite reasonable given available evidence. My central thesis is that people who rail against "the rich" purely on grounds of their wealth are hypocrites. They overlook their own relative economic standing in the global context. Those who believe others' wealth should be redistributed to curb inequality are hypocrites if they refuse to redistribute their own wealth. I personally don't donate much to charity at present. However, I also don't regard people richer than me as innately evil human beings. I can acknowledge the preference revealed by my personal decision-making patterns. My choices indicate that I'd rather upgrade to business class than save 500 lives in a developing country. For this reason, billionaires who prefer upgrading their yachts to dissolving all assets for communism earn no condemnation from me. It seems quite a few people disagree with my position on this matter. I'm curious to see if anyone can change my view on this subject. Hello, users of CMV! ideas_up_v2.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: I find myself genuinely uncertain about this matter, though I'll begin by arguing against gay marriage. My reasoning for choosing this position stems from wanting to strengthen my debating abilities by defending the weaker stance. The burden of proof rests with those advocating for change to traditional institutions. A two-minute video I encountered presents an argument about institutional definitions that influenced my thinking. When someone responds to questions about gay marriage with "Why not?," they commit the teapot fallacy by reversing who must provide evidence. The equality argument fails to address the fundamental question at hand. Constitutional rights to life, liberty, freedom, and happiness apply universally regardless of sexual orientation. Marriage functions as an institution rather than a universal right that must accommodate every relationship type. The primary purpose of marriage historically centers on procreation and child-rearing. Homosexual unions, while potentially loving and committed, cannot produce biological offspring by their nature. Infertile heterosexual couples represent exceptions to marriage's procreative norm rather than a basis for expanding definitions. Exceptions do not logically require us to abandon the general rule they deviate from. This situation differs fundamentally from civil rights movements for voting rights or emancipation. People frequently propose "mutual love" as the sole criterion for marriage eligibility. Love has never served as the defining characteristic of marriage throughout history. Romantic attachment alone would permit incestuous marriages under such a standard. Critics claim incest differs because of power imbalances within families. Power dynamics exist in all relationship categories including heterosexual, homosexual, and familial connections. Legislation cannot practically address power imbalances as a distinguishing factor. Incestuous couples might choose adoption, face infertility, or themselves be homosexual. One could consistently argue for including both incest and homosexuality within marriage definitions. The burden remains on anyone making such arguments to provide compelling justification. Claiming that something causes no harm does not justify institutional restructuring. Utilitarianism provides no support for this position either. Long-term homosexual partnerships can flourish without requiring the marriage label. Accommodating one group's happiness by redefining institutions resembles yielding to special interest pressure. Emotional manipulation pervades much of the pro-gay-marriage discourse. The phrase "gay rights" creates false associations with historical injustices like internment. "Homophobe" was invented specifically to discredit opposition voices. Popularity within contemporary culture does not determine correctness. Religious fundamentalists often oppose gay marriage using fallacious reasoning. Their poor arguments do not validate the opposing position by default. A hypothetical movement supporting incestuous marriage could gain similar cultural momentum. Websites, videos, and media campaigns could romanticize such relationships just as effectively. Public opinion would likely shift if incest received the same sympathetic treatment. Sexual deviation is a neutral descriptive term I use without any negative connotation. Why should society grant marriage status to one form of sexual deviation but deny it to others? The procreative standard provides an objective criterion that love-based standards lack. Marriage evolved as a social structure for organizing reproduction and child-rearing responsibilities. Societies developed marriage to ensure children had stable environments with biological parents. Same-sex couples cannot fulfill this biological function regardless of their commitment levels. Adoption presents a separate issue from the core definition of marriage. The slippery slope argument has merit when criteria become subjective. Once we abandon procreation as a standard, no principle remains to limit marriage definitions. Polygamy becomes defensible under love-based or consent-based frameworks. The question remains what distinguishes acceptable relationship types from unacceptable ones. Cultural consensus shifts over time but does not constitute philosophical justification. My position evolved considerably even during the process of articulating these thoughts. I acknowledge entering this examination already inclined toward changing my view. Approximately seventy-five percent of my thinking had shifted before I began writing. Intellectual honesty requires admitting when arguments fail to convince even their own advocate. The exercise proved valuable for understanding both positions more thoroughly. Articulating weaker arguments reveals their limitations more clearly than passive consideration does. My ultimate conclusion moved away from my stated starting position.

Programs crash for numerous distinct reasons that stem from various types of errors. Division by zero represents one fundamental cause: mathematics defines division by zero as undefined, making it an impossible operation. When software instructs a computer to perform this invalid calculation, the system signals an error to the program. Programs lacking proper error-handling mechanisms for this scenario will terminate unexpectedly.

Memory access violations constitute another major crash category. Operating systems allocate specific memory regions to each running program for its exclusive use. Protected memory areas exist that no program should ever touch, as they belong to other processes or the system itself. Attempting to read from or write to these forbidden zones triggers a protective response from the operating system. The OS immediately notifies the offending program of its transgression through an error signal. Programs unprepared to handle such notifications will cease functioning.

Deadlock situations create a different kind of problem where programs freeze rather than terminate. Imagine two children each holding a toy the other wants, with both refusing to relinquish their possession until receiving the desired item first. This circular waiting pattern has no resolution without external intervention. Software experiences identical scenarios when two threads each lock a resource the other needs. The threads enter an infinite wait state, accomplishing nothing. The only remedy is forcibly terminating the frozen program and restarting it.

Unhandled exceptions represent sophisticated error conditions that programmers can anticipate and code for. Modern programming languages provide exception mechanisms where code detecting problems "throws" special error objects. Other code sections are designed to "catch" these thrown exceptions and execute recovery procedures. Exception objects can travel up through multiple layers of program code seeking a handler. When no handler exists anywhere in the call stack, the exception remains unhandled. Systems typically display error dialogs when this occurs, then shut down the malfunctioning program.

All these failure modes trace back to bugs—defects in the program's source code. Bugs are simply mistakes: incorrect logic, missing checks, or failure to anticipate certain conditions. Software quality varies dramatically across different applications and developers.

Time pressure during development contributes significantly to bug proliferation. Programmers rushing to meet deadlines may skip important validation steps or cut corners in implementation. Inadequate testing before release allows defects to reach end users instead of being caught during quality assurance. Complex software inherently contains more potential failure points than simple programs. When applications grow to millions of lines of code, tracking every possible execution path becomes humanly impossible.

Consider programs as procedural instructions analogous to making sandwiches. A basic algorithm might specify: obtain bread, acquire peanut butter, get jelly, fetch a knife, spread peanut butter on one slice, apply jelly to the other slice, combine the slices, then serve. Running out of peanut butter mid-process leaves the procedure stuck with no continuation path—that's a crash scenario. Pizza restaurants offer a more complex parallel: numerous ingredients require management, countless combination possibilities exist, multiple employees work simultaneously, and exponentially more failures can occur. Some problems admit solutions while others resist repair. Unfixable issues, plus those developers neglect to address, manifest as crashes that users experience in production environments. The restaurant analogy illustrates how scaling up operations multiplies potential failure modes geometrically rather than linearly.

ideas_up_v2.coling::1770be09-c92d-43e3-ab15-7b7318ca: Radiation encompasses the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from low-energy radio waves through visible light to high-energy X-rays and gamma rays. Ionizing radiation specifically refers to the high-energy forms capable of removing electrons from atoms, which includes the type produced by nuclear weapons and reactors. Teachers would make it a pretty fair and easy project that doesn't consume too much vacation time. Projects like these get kids more involved and excited to do them when the work is manageable. If teachers did a simple, and maybe even a little fun, project it would keep the kids thinking yet not stressed out. Some might argue that the students should design the project instead of teachers. This paper extends the work of Lenc&Vedaldi15 by examining CNN representations at the FC7 layer for equivariance properties. The original Lenc&Vedaldi15 study established that certain network layers exhibit equivariance to specific transformation classes. The current authors trained over 30 networks using different jittering strategies to investigate these properties. Data augmentation through jittering is already known to promote invariance in neural networks. The primary contribution here involves measuring equivariance at FC7 rather than at earlier layers previously studied. Unfortunately, the manuscript lacks a clear central thesis that distinguishes it from prior work.

The choice to focus exclusively on FC7 presents methodological concerns given its position in the network architecture. FC7 connects directly to FC8, which is merely a linear classification layer producing class probabilities. The equivalence mapping in this configuration essentially re-projects FC8 weights from the attached network back to the original network's weight space. Conducting similar analyses across multiple layers would provide more comprehensive insights into equivariance properties throughout the architecture. The networks have already been trained, making multi-layer analysis computationally feasible.

The representation distance experiments omit a critical evaluation metric: classification error on the test dataset. Without this information, readers cannot determine whether the representations are genuinely compatible under linear transformation. The K-NN experimental protocol lacks sufficient detail regarding whether measurements occur per test example or after training the equivalence map. A clearer demonstration would show that networks trained with similar jitter transformation groups exhibit greater compatibility on target tasks.

The proposed method fails to consistently improve equivariance across all evaluated tasks. The hyperparameters λ₁ and λ₂ take extremely small values in the experiments. With such small coefficients, the loss function effectively reduces to standard data jittering by simply summing losses from original and transformed images. The FC7 layer selection may be fundamentally problematic for achieving the authors' stated objectives.

The manuscript presents some intriguing results regarding FC7 equivariance characteristics. However, it does not extract sufficiently novel observations from the extensive experimental work conducted. The equivalence experiments contain design flaws that undermine their conclusions. The equivariance finetuning approach shows inconsistent benefits across different scenarios. These limitations prevent the work from making a compelling case for publication in its current form.

Reframing this manuscript as an investigative study rather than a methods paper could strengthen its contribution. Refining the experiments on pre-trained networks would address several methodological concerns. The field would benefit from a more systematic exploration of equivariance properties across network depths.

Several minor issues require correction before any resubmission. The new criterion for equivariance mapping lacks experimental validation showing improved results over baselines. Angular measurements on pages 1 and 5 do not specify units, leaving readers to assume degrees. Page three contains an error stating that M_g is maximized or minimized, when actually the loss over M_g undergoes optimization. Footnote 2 on page 4 incorrectly labels halving activations as dropout, since constant scaling factors can be absorbed into adjacent weight layers. The RVL-CDIP network architecture is never explicitly compared to AlexNet despite apparent similarities. Figure 3a and 3b on page 7 use white for diagonal elements, which misleads readers since same-representation distances should be zero. This visualization choice also prevents verification that experiments were executed correctly, as zero diagonal values serve as an important sanity check.
ideas_up_v2.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies IB to train deep networks (the original papers only presented the concept), but see below for the note of independent work claim.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference. The explanation of the IB principle is presented with good pedagogical clarity. Experimental results seem to be very promising. The benchmark comparisons demonstrate competitive performance across multiple datasets.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference/information maximisation, p usually denotes the model and q represents the "inference engine". This convention ensures that the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and approximated by the empirical distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). The authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case. This makes the two definitions contradict to each other! The notation switching between standard VI conventions and the proposed framework creates unnecessary cognitive load for readers.

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta). Even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in VAE (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in VIB is the variational approximation to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a component in the model). In VAE it is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similaly p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model. In VAE that is the approximate posterior and can be independently chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep NN but p(z|x) as a deep NN or a Gaussian process). These structural differences have implications for optimization dynamics and the learned representations.

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these point would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the VAE part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between VIB and VAE. Some intuitions explaining why the VIB interpretation is preferred would strengthen the exposition.

Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for independent work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. Nowadays deep learning research is very competitive that many people publish the same idea at the same time. I would trust this claim and commend the authors' honesty. However, should this turn out to be untrue, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.
ideas_up_v2.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection (e.g. sum of difference of cross-entropies).

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a text/sentence are more important than others and this is achieved by a CNN. The paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW or SEQ (or the combination of both) representation is more important and why. CNNs have the advantage of capturing local n-gram patterns through their convolutional filters. RNNs process sequences strictly left-to-right which may not be optimal for relevance scoring. The computational efficiency of CNNs compared to recurrent architectures makes them practical for large-scale data selection tasks.

The textual description of the CNN (one-hot or semi-supervised using pre-trained embeddings) is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects. However, a picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary (\citet vs. \citep) (e.g line 385).

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences (line 443) based on a separate validation set. What validation data is used here? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen. How sensitive are the models to this? Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected. As Figure 1 shows, the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this case.

Other comments: I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available, not just the development set. The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods to support the claims made in section 5.4. In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in 5.4, another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod, 2015, who replace some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity to see whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this. Using the sum of source and target classification scores is very similar to source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection: sum of difference of cross-entropies. A reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable. Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source & target classification scores by extending the CNN model to the bilingual/parallel setting.
ideas_up_v2.coling::4e7728dc-010d-47cb-95f2-16525a71:
In this submission, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output. However, the approach is not new, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the submission, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this submission by applying the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling, which I am missing here. The remaining novelty of the approach would be its application to machine translation. It remains somewhat unclear, inhowfar reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem. The translation-related part of the OVV problem should be elaborated in greater detail. Some of the claims of this submission seems somewhat exaggerated. The statement in Sec. 2.3 about "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete" appears overstated. The authors themselves express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity without an explicit output vocabulary. Modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144.

Sec. 2.3 claims that the objective requires a finite vocabulary. This statement only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. Using subwords and even individual characters, implicitly larger and even infinite vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. The corresponding statement should be qualified in this respect. The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified. The description in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view.

Concerning the configuration of NCE, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific configuration. The parameterization described in Sec. 3.4 lacks justification. Sec. 4.1 should mention that Kim et al. (2015) came to similar conclusions w.r.t. the performance of using character embeddings at the output. The suggestions for possible improvements given in Kim et al. deserve discussion. Sec. 4.2 overlooks that there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown words, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013). Sec. 4.4 and Table 4 fail to provide the size of the full training vocabulary.

Minor comments follow. Page 2, bottom: "three different input layer" should be "three different input layers" (plural). Fig. 1 uses fonts within the figure that are way too small. Page 3, first item below Fig. 1: "that we will note WE" should be "that we will denote WE". Sec. 2.3: "the parameters estimation" should be "the parameter estimation" (or: the parameters' estimation). Page 5, first paragraph: "in factored way" should be "in a factored way". Page 5, second paragraph: "a n-best list, a nk-best list" should be "an n-best list, an nk-best list". Sec. 4.2, last sentence: "Despite adaptive gradient," is missing both a verb and an article.
ideas_up_v2.coling::a0b0f9d5-62dc-4996-9de4-5e5f9b3b:
The paper introduces Edward, a probabilistic programming language built over TensorFlow and Python, and supporting a broad range of most popular contemporary methods in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:
The Edward library provides an extremely impressive collection of modern probabilistic inference methods in an easily usable form. The paper provides a brief review of the most important techniques especially from a representation learning perspective, combined with two experiments on implementing various modern variational inference methods and GPU-accelerated HMC. The first experiment (variational inference) would be more valuable if there was a clear link to complete code to reproduce the results provided. The HMC experiment looks OK, except the characterising Stan as a hand-optimised implementation seems unfair as the code is clearly not hand-optimised for this specific model and hardware configuration. I do not think anyone doubts the quality of your implementation, so please do not ruin the picture by unsubstantiated sensationalist claims. Instead of current drama, I would suggest comparing head-to-head against Stan on single core and separately reporting the extra speedups you gain from parallelisation and GPU. These numbers would also help the readers to estimate the performance of the method for other hardware configurations. A more balanced presentation would strengthen the overall credibility of the empirical evaluation.

Clarity:
The paper is in general clearly written and easy to read. The numerous code examples are helpful, but also difficult as it is sometimes unclear what is missing. It would be very helpful if the authors could provide and clearly link to a machine-readable companion with complete runnable code for all the examples. A Jupyter notebook would be ideal for this purpose. Even text or HTML would be easier to copy-paste from than a pdf like the paper.

Originality:
The Edward library is clearly a unique collection of probabilistic inference methods. In terms of the paper, the main threat to novelty comes from previous publications of the same group. The main paper refers to Tran et al. (2016a) which covers a lot of similar material, although from a different perspective. It is unclear if the other paper has been published or submitted somewhere and if so, where.

Significance:
It seems very likely Edward will have a profound impact on the field of Bayesian machine learning and deep learning.

Other comments:
In Sec. 2 you draw a clear distinction between specialised languages (including Stan) and Turing-complete languages such as Edward. This seems unfair as I believe Stan is also Turing complete. Additionally no proof is provided to support the Turing-completeness of Edward.
ideas_up_v2.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c:
First up, I want to point out that this paper is really long. It spans 17 pages without any supplementary material whatsoever. ICLR does not impose an official page limit on submissions. Reviewers must read and evaluate all submissions within tight deadlines. Exceeding the conventional 8-page limit by 1 or 2 pages is reasonable. More than doubling that standard length creates an unfair burden on the review process.

Now for the review: The paper proposes a new artificial dataset for sequence learning. The dataset was synthetically generated from the original MNIST dataset. MNIST contains real images of handwritten digits and is relatively small in scale. The authors also introduce a training method for recurrent networks based on a schedule over sequence length. They term this approach "incremental learning" throughout their work. Experiments demonstrate that their proposed schedule outperforms training without any schedule on this dataset. Additional experiments show superiority over several other intuitive scheduling approaches. Ablation studies on the proposed dataset verify these performance gains.

I have the following issues with this paper:

The proposed incremental learning schedule lacks novelty entirely. Training sequences with curriculum-based length scheduling is an obvious strategy. Bengio 2015 explored similar concepts in prior work. Ranzato 2015 also investigated related scheduling techniques. The ablation studies constitute the only original contribution. These studies isolate the curriculum's effect on performance improvements. However, ablation alone does not constitute sufficient novelty for publication.

The authors evaluate their hypothesis exclusively on their own artificial dataset. Real sequential datasets like language modeling benchmarks remain unexplored. Perhaps the technique fails on authentic data. Language modeling involves huge vocabulary sizes that differ fundamentally from digit recognition. The 74% improvement reported would likely vanish on language modeling tasks. Testing on established benchmarks would strengthen the claims considerably.

The value proposition of this artificial dataset remains unconvincing. Text, speech, finance, and many other domains already provide abundant real-world sequential datasets. The dataset's specific advantages over existing options are never clearly articulated. Creating new datasets can be valuable in principle. However, this dataset appears designed specifically to make the proposed method succeed. Demonstrating effectiveness on pre-existing benchmarks would have been far more persuasive. The lack of such validation raises serious concerns about generalizability.

The paper's excessive length compounds these substantive problems. Much content has no bearing on the central thesis. Section 6.2's experiment is completely unrelated to the main narrative. The transfer learning experiments in Section 6.4 similarly lack connection to the core story. These sections could be removed without losing any essential information. The remaining material would still communicate the authors' main contributions. Conciseness would have made the work more accessible and the arguments clearer. The current structure obscures rather than illuminates the key ideas.

In summary, the paper combines limited novelty with narrow experimental validation. The artificial dataset appears purpose-built rather than genuinely useful. Excessive length and tangential content further weaken the presentation. Stronger baselines, real-world datasets, and focused writing would be necessary for acceptance.
ideas_up_v2.coling::60e5cc06-240c-4ed3-80bd-353d0ba8:
Solar power represents a remarkable achievement in modern technology. The primary obstacle preventing its widespread adoption is economic rather than technical. Current solar installations remain costlier than conventional energy sources when considering residential applications. All renewable energy technologies face similar financial barriers to mass adoption.

Advocates frequently argue that utility-scale solar farms cost less to construct than new nuclear or coal facilities. This comparison holds validity only for industrial-scale projects involving hundreds of megawatts. Individual homeowners cannot build traditional power plants, making that comparison irrelevant to personal energy decisions. The crucial calculation involves panel cost divided by average electrical output over the system's lifetime.

Some propose government funding could replace existing nuclear facilities with solar arrays. California already provides substantial subsidies for residential solar purchases, demonstrating government investment in the sector. Private corporations own and operate nuclear power plants in the United States. Government agencies regulate these facilities but do not control their operations. Nuclear plant economics center on construction expenses and radioactive waste disposal rather than ongoing operational costs. Decommissioning a functional reactor wastes the capital already invested in building it.

Solar technology offers numerous advantages beyond simple energy production. Point-of-use generation eliminates transmission losses that occur when electricity travels through power lines over long distances. The generation process produces virtually no air pollution or greenhouse gases. Solar arrays operate without mechanical noise, providing acoustic benefits in residential areas. Peak solar production coincides with peak summer electricity demand during afternoon hours. This synchronization between supply and demand creates natural grid stability.

Air conditioning represents perhaps the ideal application for solar electricity. Summer heat that increases cooling requirements simultaneously maximizes solar panel output. Rooftop panels generate power for cooling systems installed in the same building. The physical presence of panels on roofs creates shade that reduces heat absorption by the structure below. This dual benefit lowers cooling requirements while generating electricity to meet remaining needs.

Pure economic analysis still favors fossil fuel generation for baseline electricity production. Natural gas plants provide the cheapest electricity in most markets. Coal remains competitive in regions with abundant coal deposits. Until manufacturing costs decline further or carbon pricing changes the equation, traditional sources maintain their cost advantage. Market forces alone have not yet made solar the economical choice for most applications.
ideas_up_v2.coling::ef4cca12-c45c-4b1b-9c67-8db766ad:
Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really love cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, you have to go to the middle east or India to get some of that fine stuff so it's *super-expensive*. Over there, however, it grows like a weed and costs very little money. If only you could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a lot of money!

Unfortunately, the only way to do that is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all wants nine months worth of pay), but it is also really risky. The boat could sink, after all. The cumin could spoil during the long voyage. Pirates might attack your vessel on the high seas. Storms could blow the ship off course, adding months to the journey. Disease might strike the crew, leaving no one to sail the ship home.

So how do you accomplish this? Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole nations, are that rich), how do you finance this? You could go to a bank or money-lender and take out a loan, a loan which would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of your profits. And what if the boat sank? You'd be completely bankrupt, and be thrown into prison, if the money-lender doesn't waste your broke ass first. 

So, you come up with an idea. You can't finance this trip alone. But you could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the cost of the trip. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also afford one tenth of the cost of the trip. So you all come to an agreement: you decide to each finance part of the cost for the trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the enterprise), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total enterprise. With this money, you pay for the boat and crew, send them off, and then nine months later, it comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin. The profits far and away compensate for the initial cost, and each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous profits.

But what happens if your boat sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew!), but you only payed for one tenth of the cost. This was a cost you could afford to eat without facing financial ruin. Since the risk was spread around to 10 people, no one landed in debtors prison. Everyone took a small hit, instead of one person taking an enormous hit. 

Think about this example, and all the people involved in it. The fancy ladies got their cumin and paid less than the previous monopoly prices. The shipwrights got work building a new ship. The captain and crew all got work and a salary. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin. The rope-makers sold their wares for the ship's rigging. The sailmakers found employment producing canvas for the voyage. Food suppliers provisioned the ship for nine months at sea. Amsterdam's port workers loaded and unloaded the cargo. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process. In short, *every single person is better off*.

This is the advantage of a stock market. It moves capital around from where it just lies around doing absolutely nothing to where it can be put to use, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer. It also distributes risk between lots of people, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time. Small investors can participate in large ventures that would otherwise be impossible. Entrepreneurs can pursue ambitious projects without gambling their entire fortunes.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of the stock market functions. Short-term speculation often replaces long-term investment thinking. High-frequency trading algorithms dominate many exchanges today. Executive compensation sometimes incentivizes stock price manipulation over genuine value creation. But the critique is that it stopped doing what it is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating capital so that it can be put into productive use). The basic concept of a stock market is a fantastic idea, and you'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose it. It is why we have railroads, cars, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful food, medicine, and all the other modern things we value so highly.

Depends on if your business is a sole proprietorship, single member LLC, multi member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Sole Proprietorship: All profits and losses pass to you individually. You're also personally liable for anything that goes wrong. Pro Tip: form an LLC or go get a free consultation with a business attorney. This structure requires no formal registration beyond basic business licenses in most jurisdictions.

Single Member LLC: Profits and losses pass through to you personally, but your liability is limited to the Company's assets. You also have to pay self employment tax. The LLC provides a legal shield separating your personal finances from business debts. Filing requirements vary significantly by state, with annual fees ranging from minimal to several hundred dollars.

Multi-Member LLC: Profits and losses are split in proportion to each members ownership interest in the company. You also pay self employment tax. An operating agreement should define each member's responsibilities and voting rights. Capital contributions don't have to match ownership percentages if the members agree otherwise.

LLC with "S" election: You pay yourself a reasonable salary, and that salary is not subject to the self employment tax. Remaining profits and losses are passed through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholders percentage interest in the corporation. Whether or not you get taxed on any distributions depends on your basis, but this is where is gets complicated and I can't ELI5 (just let the CPA worry about this). The IRS actively audits S corporations that pay suspiciously low salaries to owner-employees.

S Corporation: see above

C Corporation: The corporations profits are taxed at the corporate tax level and then any dividends made to shareholders are taxed as well. This is called double taxation and it's why C Corporations are not ideal for small business owners. However, C Corps can offer stock options and attract venture capital more easily than other structures.

Unethical Life Pro Tip: Want to live a lavish lifestyle, completely tax free, and without much hard work!? Start a non-profit seed faith mega church, go on TV, and convince all the sheeple to send your church money, because god will take the little "seed of faith" they send and will "sow" the seed into 10x the amount they sent.

It's about anonymity and vulnerability.

On the internet, you're anonymous and well outside the reach of the person you're talking to, so when people disagree, they tend to be a lot more confrontational and aggressive. Physical safety emboldens behavior because there's no chance of being punched in the face.

In the real world if you're 5" tall and weigh 90lbs soaking wet, you're probably not going to tell a 6"5 250lb guy that he's full of shit, even if that's what you think. Size disparities create natural restraints on hostile communication in face-to-face encounters. Online platforms eliminate these physical considerations entirely. Body language and tone of voice, which normally regulate human interaction, disappear in text-based exchanges.

The flip side is it's also much easier to be abusive or aggressive when the person you're communicating with is just words on a screen. The internet dehumanizes the person you're speaking to by removing their humanity and reducing them to pixels.

Basically, it's really easy to watch a bad youtube video and tell xXUsernameXx that they're a talentless piece of shit. Meeting that same content creator transforms the dynamic completely. Walking up to Jenny, the 14 year old girl who makes Minecraft videos to take her mind off her parent's divorce, and looking her in the eye changes everything. Her circumstances—her age, her coping mechanism, her family trauma—suddenly become visible and relevant.

Cars create similar conditions of anonymity and protection. You're in a big, locked metal box that's basically half suit of armor, half escape pod. Windows and metal panels serve as barriers that separate you from surrounding drivers. Lean on your horn, give the middle finger, because you're at your turning and will never see whoever's driving that car again. The vehicle becomes an object rather than a person—that stupid fucking Ford that cut you off. Jenny's Mom, who's distracted because she doesn't know how she's going to make rent that week, disappears behind the automobile.

Depends on your predictions, but the worst case is certainly bad. Projections of global average climate change exist and can be examined. The poles will experience the most dramatic temperature increases. Ocean temperatures will rise significantly alongside polar warming.

What does this sort of warming look like? The Cretaceous period represents the warmest geological era in the last few hundred million years. This period spanned from approximately 100 to 65 million years ago. Atmospheric CO2 concentrations during the Cretaceous reached about 1000 parts per million. Sea levels during the Cretaceous stood hundreds of meters above present-day measurements. A shallow inland sea covered the central portion of North America. Deciduous forests thrived in regions that are now polar ice. Hurricane and typhoon frequency increased dramatically under those temperature conditions. Extreme heat combined with oppressive humidity would render equatorial zones unlivable. Coastal flooding would displace hundreds of millions or possibly billions of people. All glacial ice would disappear completely, eliminating crucial freshwater sources. The Canadian wilderness territories would develop Mediterranean climates. Ocean salinity levels would undergo massive shifts. Marine pH would change drastically, threatening ocean chemistry. These chemical alterations would trigger mass extinctions of ocean wildlife. Fish populations that currently feed billions of humans would collapse. Terrestrial species unable to migrate quickly would face extinction. ideas_up_v2.coling::8e0f7cff-07ca-48c6-b381-34b577d1: Before babies start to use language, they form speech through babble. Basically they play with producing noise through open and closed mouths. ideas_up_v2.coling::ae050f0f-463e-4780-8638-108ef778: Alexander's victory resulted from multiple strategic and tactical advantages working in combination. ideas_up_v2.coling::f4f3b137-0da5-4cc5-a8e0-08f5a284: You cannot think of signals as digital in a wire when you transmit at high speed. Instead, you must conceptualize them as analog signals. A signal in a Cat 5 cable travels at 0.64 times the speed of light, which equals 4.8 to 5.3 nanoseconds per meter. For 100Mbit Ethernet, the data rate is 100 × 10^6 bits per second. This calculation means 100 bits are transmitted in 1000 nanoseconds. Therefore, 1 bit occupies 10 nanoseconds of transmission time. If an Ethernet cable exceeds 2 meters in length, more than one bit exists simultaneously within the cable. A standard cable can be 100 meters long, resulting in 50 bits present in the cable at any given moment. Clearly, the signal cannot be uniform throughout the entire length of the cable. The actual bitrate in the cable is higher in practice due to encoding schemes. An image of a 100Mbit Ethernet signal demonstrates this analog behavior (URL_1). Eye diagrams are created by overlapping different signal traces to show signal quality (URL_0). Wires must be twisted at specific rates relative to each other to minimize this interference. Standards are necessary to ensure cables have known parameters compatible with networking hardware. Proper cable design ensures that high-speed data transmission remains reliable over distance. Without standardized specifications, different cables would produce unpredictable results with networking equipment. The physics of electromagnetic wave propagation governs all these phenomena in data cables.
