ideas_up_v2.coling::9600c031-1ba2-4882-9aa0-8cb6b07d: Operation Claw () was a joint Swedish–American operation, with Norwegian support, that was carried out at Lillehammer shortly after the German capitulation by the end of World War II. Thirty-five German intelligence specialists were transferred along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied Germany through an agreement between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material from Operation Claw, among it a Soviet codebook, became very useful for the Americans during the Cold War. The operation proved controversial both when it happened and afterwards for multiple reasons involving sovereignty and alliance politics. In 1945, critics objected that the Americans operated in what was seen as a British controlled country. Additional controversy stemmed from the fact that they secured information about their ally the Soviet Union while cooperating with neutral Sweden. In later years, historians raised questions about the mysterious death of Norwegian resistance fighter Kai Holst in June 1945. The historian Tore Pryser has put forward the hypothesis that Holst's sudden demise was related to his involvement in Operation Claw. Even before the war in Europe ended the various allied states had begun the search for German scientists and other German expertise. Signals intelligence had been vital during World War II and especially the British work with breaking the German codes, from the Enigma had been of huge importance. The Yalta Conference in February 1945 had revealed conflicts of interest between the western allied nations on one side and the Soviet Union and the relation was severely strained. American intelligence organisations were very interested in German intelligence experts knowledge of the Soviet Union and immediately after the war in Europe ended they began to cooperate with the German Major General Reinhard Gehlen. Gehlen's organisation Fremde Heere Ost (FHO) had led German intelligence operations on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces. The Americans integrated Gehlen's network into their own intelligence apparatus in the emerging Cold War confrontation. It was part of an organized effort to obtain as much German intelligence information and personnel as possible; the operation had the name Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM). The war was however still fought in East-Asia, the US and the Soviet Union were still allies at this point. The Americans were counting on Soviet assistance in the war against Japan, making anti-Soviet operations particularly delicate. The allies had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence at international conferences. Both for the US and the neutral Sweden the operation was thus very sensitive and was conducted in great secrecy. In the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer a group of 35 German experts on signals intelligence were gathered. They had been working on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces and had an archive and extensive knowledge about Soviet affairs. This expertise included detailed understanding of Soviet military communications, cipher systems, and organizational structures. Western intelligence agencies believed this knowledge would prove invaluable in the emerging geopolitical confrontation with Moscow. In cooperation with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and support from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm agents for the Swedish intelligence organisation C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The German group of experts were taken out of the camp and transported to Sweden under cover of the chaotic immediate postwar period. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on June 12 flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany. The Germans were interned in an American military camp at Wiesbaden where they could be thoroughly debriefed. The transfer to Sweden of the German experts at Lillehammer, that OSS called Operation Claw, was directed from the highest level. From the U.S. side the leader of OSS, Major General William J. Donovan was involved, demonstrating the operation's strategic importance. From the Swedish side the chief of the Defense Staff, Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd coordinated the effort. The famous Swedish police director Harry Söderman was also involved from the Swedish side, lending his expertise in clandestine operations. More than a month after the German capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed in order to find people from Gestapo and other German key personnel that tried to hide among ordinary soldiers in German military camps. The search force that Kai Holst and other Norwegians were assisting were soon aware of that a number of German key personnel had been removed in the Swedish–American operation a month earlier. This discovery raised immediate questions about unauthorized operations in territory under British administrative control. Kai Holst had been working at the military office number 4 (Mi4) at the Norwegian legation in Stockholm during the war years. After the search he unexpectedly traveled right back to Stockholm without clear explanation for his sudden departure. The next day he was found shot at the top of the staircase in an apartment building at Rindögatan 42 on Gärdet. The official cause of death was stated as suicide by Swedish authorities investigating the incident. Neither Holst's family nor many of his colleagues from the resistance movement have accepted this conclusion. They are of the opinion that he was liquidated by parties unknown for reasons connected to his intelligence work. The historian Tore Pryser has put forward the hypothesis that Holst brought with him information from Lillehammer that could damage Operation Claw. To be able to damage the operation Kai Holst can not have been trusted as others were in the tight circle of those informed. He must have been considered a threat due to his contact with Alexandra Kollontaj who was ambassador in Stockholm representing Soviet Union. A possible reason for a murder of Kai Holst was thus not his knowledge as such but his connections to Soviet diplomatic personnel. Operation Claw was the beginning of the postwar era cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence services, in violation of Sweden's officially stated neutrality. From the American side the operation was viewed as a great success and the responsible within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations where the operation specifically were mentioned. For the Swedish C-byrån Operation Claw quickly became toxic when news began to spread within intelligence circles. Even though the operation was to be kept confidential, information leaked to the Swedish press creating political embarrassment. C-byrån were dissolved in February 1946 as a direct consequence of the scandal surrounding the operation. Information regarding Operation Claw continued to be classified as confidential in the post-war years and some of it still remains so today. A report about the operation in the British National Archives is restricted until 2020, suggesting sensitive diplomatic implications.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The short was released on February 17, 1934. Earl Duvall supervised the film's production. Jack King and Frank Tipper received animation credits for their character work. Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones, and Frank Tashlin animated without credit. Bernard Brown composed the music score and received sole credit for it. Norman Spencer also composed music but went uncredited. Bernard Brown recorded the sound without receiving credit for that role. The production number assigned was 6125.

The cartoon's plot follows a male and female bug who check into a hotel. During their stay, the hotel catches on fire. Al Dubin and Harry Warren wrote the song "Honeymoon Hotel." The 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade originally introduced this song. The DVD release of Footlight Parade includes this animated short.

The film holds significance as the first Warner Bros. cartoon produced in color. Walt Disney held exclusive rights to the Technicolor process at that time. Warner Bros. used Cinecolor as an alternative color technology. Beauty and the Beast became the only other Merrie Melodies cartoon produced in Cinecolor. The series returned briefly to black-and-white production after these two films. Merrie Melodies later adopted Technicolor for its productions. Looney Tunes continued black-and-white production until 1943. Several late 1940s Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts brought Cinecolor back.

The film is classified as a 1934 animated musical comedy. It features insects as its main characters. The setting takes place in a hotel. It belongs to the Merrie Melodies short film series. Warner Bros. produced it during the 1930s. The film is in the English language. BCDB and the Internet Archive provide external links to the film.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" is a short story by British author P. G. Wodehouse, which first appeared in the United States in the October 1923 issue of Cosmopolitan. The United Kingdom publication followed in the November 1923 issue of Strand magazine. The narrative centers on Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, a character known for his schemes and misadventures. The story was later collected in the book Ukridge, which appeared in 1924.

The plot begins when Ukridge and his companion Corky encounter one of Ukridge's acquaintances who works as a chauffeur. This friend is driving a gleaming new Daimler automobile and extends an invitation for a ride. During their journey, a man to whom Ukridge owes money spots them but they manage to evade him. The car nearly strikes a young girl pedestrian, prompting Ukridge to insist they escort her safely home. Her residence is located near Clapham Common in London. Ukridge ingratiates himself with the girl's family by displaying the impressive automobile. He also mentions his wealthy relative, Aunt Julia, to enhance his standing with them.

A week passes before Corky next sees Ukridge at the British Museum. On this occasion, Ukridge has two young children accompanying him. He confesses to making repeated visits to the Clapham household primarily to obtain complimentary meals. The family believes the Daimler belongs to Ukridge personally. He has made promises to take them on various excursions using what they assume is his vehicle. Additionally, he has offered to arrange introductions to his aunt, despite her having severed ties with him. A letter from her explicitly states "from now on, I have no nephew," ending their familial relationship.

Upon returning from a brief vacation, Corky learns surprising news from George Tupper about an engagement. Ukridge has apparently become betrothed to someone. When Corky visits to investigate, he discovers his friend sporting a black eye as evidence of recent violence. Ukridge explains how he became accidentally engaged to the girl from Clapham Common through a series of misunderstandings. A romantic competitor named Finch delivered the punch that caused the facial injury. While conversing on Ukridge's front steps, the creditor from their earlier car ride appears unexpectedly. Ukridge quickly conceals himself to avoid confrontation. A stranger passing by calms the angry creditor by claiming knowledge of where Ukridge can be found. This fortunate intervention works because Ukridge had prudently used the false name "Mr. Smallweed" in his dealings with this particular creditor. Consequently, Ukridge abandons his current residence to maintain the deception.

Ukridge and Corky devise a scheme to extricate Ukridge from the unwanted engagement through pretended illness. Corky visits the family to deliver rehearsed explanations about Ukridge's supposed poor health. However, the helpful passer-by from the earlier creditor incident makes an unexpected appearance at the house. This man is actually George Finch, the romantic rival who had previously punched Ukridge. Finch exposes Ukridge as a penniless fraud actually named Smallweed rather than his claimed identity. He brings the creditor along as concrete proof of Ukridge's deceptions and debts. Finch also presents the letter from Aunt Julia denying any nephew exists in her family. After Corky settles the outstanding debt owed to the creditor, both he and Ukridge face expulsion from the premises.

T. D. Skidmore created illustrations for the Cosmopolitan publication. Reginald Cleaver provided different artwork for the Strand magazine version. The 1932 anthology Nothing But Wodehouse, edited by Ogden Nash, included this story among its selections. Doubleday, Doran & Company served as the publisher for that collection. Week-End Wodehouse, a British edition from Herbert Jenkins Limited, first appeared in 1939 containing this tale. The World of Ukridge, published by Barrie & Jenkins in October 1975, also featured the story.

A 1956 radio adaptation featured Michael Shepley voicing Ukridge in the leading role. Other cast members included Hubert Gregg as Corcoran and Olaf Pooley as the chauffeur Frederick. The television series The World of Wodehouse presented an adapted episode in 1968 under the title "The Wedding Bells." This television version incorporated Looney Coote, a character borrowed from another Wodehouse story entirely.

Modern Greek art encompasses artistic production from the establishment of the independent Greek state through the end of the 19th century. The Ottoman Empire controlled mainland Greece for four hundred years, preventing participation in the Renaissance. Crete and the Ionian islands experienced Venetian and other European governance, enabling absorption of European artistic innovations from the 14th through 18th centuries. The Cretan School developed as one significant artistic movement paralleling Western European trends. The Heptanese School emerged as another important artistic current following comparable trajectories to those in Western Europe. Greece's specific socioeconomic circumstances fundamentally determined the character of its modern artistic production. A substantial Greek diaspora spread throughout Europe contributed to artistic development. An emerging Greek social elite patronized and influenced artistic creation. Germany and France provided the predominant external artistic influences shaping Greek artistic practice.

The era of Romanticism marked the beginning of modern Greek artistic development in sculpture and painting during the 19th century. Greek artists incorporated numerous elements from European contemporaries into their work. A distinctive Greek Romantic style emerged, drawing inspiration from revolutionary ideals. The country's unique geography and historical legacy also informed this artistic style. The newly independent Greek state offered limited opportunities for formal arts education. Studying abroad became essential for aspiring Greek artists. Munich functioned as a major international arts center during this period. The majority of 19th-century Greek artists selected Munich for their training. Karl von Piloty led the Munich school where students learned true fresco techniques. Mural paintings on fresh wet lime plaster constituted a key component of the curriculum. Emotional intensity and theatrical presentation characterized much artwork from this era. Urban life emerged as one prominent thematic focus of Munich School artists. Rural life provided another major subject for artistic representation. Still life compositions attracted significant artistic attention. Landscape painting developed as an important genre within the school.

Greek artists eventually returned home to transmit their acquired knowledge. Some chose to remain in Munich, which Germans called "Athens on the Isar." Academic relationships formed between Greek painters and Munich artistic circles. Personal friendships also developed between these artistic communities. The Greek "Munich School" of painting emerged from these interconnections. Nikolaos Gysis taught at the Munich Academy while producing important artworks. He became a leading figure commanding respect among Greek artistic circles. Academism dominated early Munich School approaches to painting. Realism characterized much of the artistic production from this movement. Genre painting depicting everyday scenes gained popularity. Upper middle class portraiture served as a significant source of commissions. Landscape painting frequently exhibited impressionist characteristics. Symbolism began replacing earlier styles near the century's end. Jugendstil influences appeared in works by certain Greek artists. Art Nouveau elements became traceable primarily in Nikolaos Gysis's later production. Aristeas and other artists also incorporated these newer stylistic tendencies. Early-20th-century modernism found representation among significant Greek artists working in Munich. Everyday Greek life provided subject matter for numerous Munich School painters. Local customs and traditions inspired many artistic compositions. Living conditions of ordinary Greeks became documented through these artworks.

Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in creating historical paintings for Greek audiences. The 1821 Greek War of Independence particularly inspired his artistic imagination. Nikiphoros Lytras focused his efforts on realistic depictions of contemporary Greek existence. Georgios Jakobides devoted special attention to portraying infants and young children. He later assumed the position of first Director at the new National Gallery of Athens. Georgios Roilos emerged as another leading painter closely connected with Munich School principles. His early career especially demonstrated strong Munich School associations. Konstantinos Volanakis drew primary inspiration from the Greek maritime environment. Symeon Sabbides maintained association with the Munich School artistic community. Yannoulis Chalepas worked as both painter and sculptor within this movement. Leonidas Drosis contributed to Munich School artistic production. Theofrastos Triantafyllidis represented modernist artists who received Munich training. Jorgos Busianis studied in Munich while developing modernist approaches. Giorgio de Chirico also received education in Munich despite later developing different artistic directions.

Sculptural arts flourished in the new Greek Kingdom alongside painting. Leonidas Drosis created extensive neo-classical architectural ornament for the Academy of Athens building. Lazaros Sochos produced notable sculptural works during this formative period. Georgios Vitalis contributed significant sculptures to Greek artistic heritage. Dimitrios Filippotis worked as an important sculptor of this era. Ioannis Kossos created sculptural pieces for the developing nation. Georgios Bonanos produced works reflecting neoclassical sculptural ideals. Lazaros Fytalis completed the roster of notable sculptors from this generation.

A smaller number of Greek painters pursued studies in Paris rather than Munich. These artists resided in the French capital while following French Art Academy guidelines. Their work invariably reflected personal interpretations despite academic training. Jacob Rizos concentrated on rendering female grace in his compositions. Theodoros Rallis depicted scenes from the Orthodox East. Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos practiced portraiture, still life, and genre painting. The avant-garde Impressionist movement developed in Paris during this same period. Most Greek painters maintained fidelity to traditional academic precepts despite exposure to impressionism. Only tentative movements toward impressionist techniques appeared in most Greek painters' work. Périclès Pantazis became the first Greek artist fully embracing impressionist methods. After studying in Paris, he settled in Belgium permanently. He joined the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte as an active member.

El Greco's distinctive style provided inspiration for many Greek artists of this period. Religious themes particularly prompted artists to reference El Greco's approach. Modern secular Greek art referenced classical styles in its visual vocabulary. Religious art drew upon Byzantine traditions and Byzantine-inspired imagery. Grace Files The Department Break-Room is always a fun place. Its employees, like me, all share one little gift from the Chief Executive: Immortality. So long as we continue to do our jobs, we're given all the time we could ever want or need. A large chunk, usually a bit less than three quarters of it, is spent working. The sheer volume of deaths occurring simultaneously across the planet demands constant attention from our workforce. Even with the advantage of existing outside of Time and Space, we Reapers still have a bit of trouble processing all the people who are dying. Management has tried hiring more staff, but training new Reapers takes centuries of careful mentorship. Of course, we can all still take off a quarter of our infinity to chill out on Earth or around the Department's Campus. This vacation time is mandatory after particularly difficult assignments involving children or mass casualty events. That policy leads to another fun thing that being immortal causes: you get people from everywhere and everywhen you can think of. One of the older reapers was around when the Aztec Empire was basically a handful of guys with an insane idea involving a cactus, a snake, and an eagle. Another of us was on the Senate Floor when Gaius Julius Caesar was killed. A third Reaper claims to have witnessed the actual construction of Stonehenge, though nobody believes that story. You get a lot of weird interactions when you mix in so many people. For example, you get Roman sitting in front of a big screen TV watching a Chariot Race from back when the Empire was at its height. The Aztec is chatting with a Norseman about the merits of hanging as opposed to cutting the heart out as a method of ritual sacrifice. A medieval plague doctor argues with a modern epidemiologist about disease transmission theories near the coffee station. Some of the Americans, such as myself, are chatting about college sports around a water cooler. The younger members of our staff are setup in the region we call "The Arcade." That area contains gaming systems from every era, including some that won't be invented on Earth for another two hundred years.

After all those people... there's the guy at the bar. He's the oldest of the Reapers. We don't even know the guy's name, since he hasn't bothered telling anyone and his records are covered up. The classification level on his file requires clearance that even senior management doesn't possess. He doesn't get out much, but we've all seen him milling around the Department. His shift assignments come directly from the Chief Executive's office, bypassing all normal scheduling protocols. Never seen him in the Break Room though, much less at the bar. We've got every drink imagined, at least up until the present day out on Earth. The bar automatically updates its inventory whenever someone somewhere invents a new cocktail or discovers a new brewing technique.

I took a seat next to him. "Evening," I said without thinking too much about the guy understanding me since Language barriers don't exist for Reapers, we hear everything in our native language. Everyone hears us in their native language as well, which leads to all kinds of insanity in the modern world. The translation effect works on written text too, making ancient scrolls perfectly readable to modern Reapers. We once had an incident where two Reapers argued for hours before realizing they were actually agreeing in different languages.

"Evening," the Eldest said. His voice sounded deep, and ancient. The words seemed to carry weight beyond their simple meaning, like stones dropped into still water. "What are you drinking to," I asked. "Death," the Eldest said. The bartender, a former speakeasy owner from Chicago, didn't even blink at the answer. I didn't laugh, and neither did he. "Whose?" I asked. "Millions," he said. The number hung in the air between us like a physical presence. I nodded in reply.

Reapers may be immortal, and we may have a lot of not-quite-natural abilities, but we're all still human at our core. Our minds are just like the minds of the people we reap, and doing our job is rough. I'd honestly call it the hardest job in the world... having to be there when someone's dying. Seeing the grieving families of those who slip away to cancer, or other diseases, and having to deliver a bitter mercy to spare someone the pain. The moment of death itself involves complex rituals that must be performed with absolute precision. That's not even thinking about the horrors you get when you walk into a combat zone to retrieve the deceased. War zones require special protective equipment since we can still feel physical sensations even though we can't truly be harmed. Some assignments involve retrieving those who succumbed to despair, which carries its own unique emotional burden.

Anyway, there isn't a Reaper on staff who hasn't gotten depressed over that, over not being able to help the dying beyond giving them the bitter mercy that is death. We're all human, and we all still have our empathy. The Department considers compassion fatigue a workplace hazard worthy of extensive mental health resources. I figured that the Eldest had managed to experience that. "You talked to the Councilors about it?" I asked.

The Councilors aren't Reapers for the most part. They're among the Dead, the people who live in whatever comes next. Their perspective on mortality gives them unique insight into our psychological struggles. They're also volunteers who come into the Department to help us out with our mental hang-ups. I know I spend a lot of time talking to 'em. My regular Councilor served as a therapist during her mortal life, bringing professional expertise to our sessions.

"No..." the guy said, "at least... not this century." His last documented counseling session occurred in 1847 according to departmental gossip. "Which deaths have you down?" I asked. "Fratricide..." the Reaper said, "It... it reminds me of myself a bit too much." His hands trembled slightly as he lifted his glass. I nodded.

Reapers come in all forms. Some of us are like me, and we took the job offer to get someone else a better afterlife than they would have had otherwise. My younger brother received immediate entry to paradise because I agreed to serve a minimum term of ten thousand years. Some are here serving to get themselves into something halfway decent. The Eldest was apparently among the latter.

"So," I said, "You thought about requesting that those assignments be diverted to other Reapers?" "Can't..." he said, "It's part of my... my sentence." The word carried implications of guilt that stretched back millennia. "Ouch," I said, and I genuinely meant it.

When it comes to Reapers like the Eldest, they have something called a Sentence which is designed to reform them to a state where they would be acceptable in the Afterlife they're due to be sent to. It's a set of obligations they must fulfil, or be sent on ahead of schedule to one of the... less desirable final rests. If they're lucky, they just get reincarnated. If they're unlucky, they're supposed to get thrown into Torment. The specifics of Torment remain classified, but rumors suggest it involves experiencing every death you ever caused from the victim's perspective.

"It's just..." He said, "I've seen so many of them." His voice cracked with centuries of accumulated grief. "Every time I go out... I don't see the person I'm sent for." The psychological condition has a clinical name in our training materials: Projection Trauma Disorder. "I see someone... someone I knew back before I was a Reaper... and I see myself standing over them." I saw a tear roll down the Eldest's cheek at those words, and I remained silent.

"Damn it..." the Eldest said, "I need to get back to work... need to get out of here..." "Luck," I said, "and consider scheduling an appointment." Professional help could prevent a complete mental breakdown that would affect the entire Department. "We don't need you going renegade." The last Reaper who went rogue caused a temporal paradox that took three decades to untangle. "That generally results in a lot of paperwork for the rest of us."

The Eldest scoffed at that, and nodded in my direction as he got up to leave. It was only once he'd left the room that I realized that I still didn't have his name.

Usually the low advertised rates are for term life insurance. This type of life insurance has an expiration date, unlike permanent policies that last a lifetime. Term insurance is typically used to protect during periods of higher expenses when dependents need financial support. For example, one might buy a term policy that expires when the kids graduate college or the house mortgage is paid off. An untimely death during the coverage period would provide funds so kids can attend college or prevent a surviving spouse from selling the house. If you live until the expiration point, the policy terminates without any payout to you. The average buyer purchases coverage in their 30's and maintains it into their 50's or 60's. Most policyholders survive the term, so only a small fraction of policies result in death benefits. The premiums from policies that don't pay out help cover the costs of the ones that do.

The probability of any individual claim remains extremely low compared to the total number of premium payers. Consider 100 people each buying a $100,000 life insurance plan for $10 monthly. If one person dies during that month, the insurance company collects $1,000 in premiums. The company pays $100,000 to the deceased person's estate, leaving them with a loss on that transaction. However, this simplified example doesn't account for years of premium collection before a claim occurs. Insurance companies invest the premiums they collect in stocks, bonds, and other financial instruments. These investment returns generate substantial additional revenue beyond premium income. Scaling up to millions of policyholders while maintaining low claim rates creates enormous profit potential. Insurance companies carefully screen applicants to exclude high-risk individuals who are statistically more likely to file claims. People with life-threatening medical conditions find life insurance difficult or impossible to obtain. Vehicle insurance becomes progressively more expensive or unavailable as driving records worsen with accidents and violations.

The pricing models rely entirely on actuarial probability and statistical odds. Term length significantly affects premium calculations, as do age, health status, occupation, and lifestyle factors. The insurance industry operates fundamentally as a profit-driven business. Casinos provide an apt comparison: putting a quarter in a slot machine occasionally yields thousand-dollar jackpots, but the house always wins overall.

Section 51(xxxi) is a subclause of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia.

It empowers the Commonwealth to make laws regarding the acquisition of property, but stipulates that such acquisitions must be on just terms.

The provision is sometimes referred to in shorthand as the 'just terms' clause.

Aside from its importance to Australian Constitutional Law and Property Law, the section is notable for its role as a plot device in The Castle, an iconic Australian film.

Text 
Section 51(xxxi) reads as follows in the constitutional document:

Jurisprudence 
While s51(xxxi) was adapted from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, it has many differences in operation and scope.

The 'just terms' requirement has been held not to affect the State Parliaments in their legislative functions.

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon stated that the inclusion of the condition was to "prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject."

The interpretation of the terms "acquisition" and "just terms" by the High Court of Australia have had the effect of limiting its protection of property rights.

The provision operates at any time the Commonwealth makes a compulsory acquisition of property.

As such, it is a contingent guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy property rights.

The Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws".

This requirement means that every law supported by s 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other additional legislative power.

Property
The High Court of Australia has taken a wide view of the concept of "property" under this provision.

Several members of the court took the opportunity to consider the meaning of the term property in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944).

Justice Starke said the term includes "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action."

Justice McTiernan confirmed the term property extends to tangible and intangible property.

An example of the breadth of the concept of property in section 51(xxxi) is provided by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth, known as the Bank Nationalisation Case.

In that case, Federal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banks through vesting of shares in private banks in the Commonwealth.

The legislation also provided for the appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank.

Justice Dixon characterised the provisions as removing effective control over the property of the private banks.

He concluded that this was, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right.

While statutory licences have sometimes been equated with proprietary interests, the removal of rights enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property within section 51(xxxi).

Licence conditions are inherently susceptible to change, which distinguishes them from more permanent property rights.

Acquisition
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody.

The acquisition must be for a Commonwealth purpose to fall within the scope of the provision.

This is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the destination does not matter and it is enough that the holder of property has been deprived of it.

In JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which restricted the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property.

Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass for retired members of Parliament were not an acquisition of property.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court held that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just.

The validity of a grant in the absence of a requirement to acquire property was upheld in the later case of Pye v Renshaw.

Just terms
Typically, a determination of just terms based on the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will be sufficient to satisfy the requirement of just terms.

Unlike the "just compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, "just terms" imports no equivalence of market value.

The arrangements offered must be "fair", or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair".

This judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected, not just those of the dispossessed owner.

The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily require that a compensation package be presented as part of the acquisition scheme.

It is sufficient that the scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair compensation.

The Court may scrutinise such procedures closely to ensure their adequacy.

There may be some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution.

Section 51(xxxi) is an exception to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" another.

In this case, the Court will not allow another grant of power to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi).

Related legislation
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, largely drafted by Littleton Groom, was the first to deal with the compulsory acquisition of land by the federal government.

Its most contentious provision was a clause authorising the federal government to grant mining leases and regulate mining on Commonwealth land.

Responsibility for compulsory acquisition was initially placed with the Department of Home Affairs.

The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act 1945 compulsorily acquired a substantial area of land owned by Chinese-Australians in Darwin.

This acquisition led to the end of the local Chinatown community.

The legislation was suggested in 1943 by the Northern Territory's administrator Aubrey Abbott.

Abbott proposed a combination of compulsory acquisition and conversion of the land to leasehold in order to effect "the elimination of undesirable elements which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past".

He stated that he hoped to "entirely prevent the Chinese quarter forming again".

Abbott further observed that "if land is acquired from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other assets".

The territory's civilian population had mostly been evacuated during the war.

The former Chinatown residents returned to find their homes and businesses reduced to rubble by bombing and subsequent demolition.

The Act represented one of the most controversial uses of federal acquisition powers in Australian history.

Contemporary scholars have criticized the legislation as racially motivated.

Canada and the United States have roughly comparable quality of life rather than one being dramatically superior. Online forums like rworldnews and rpolitics sometimes paint an exaggerated picture of American dysfunction. The United States actually offers decent living standards for most residents.

Relocating to another country means abandoning your entire social network, career connections, and familiar surroundings. Such drastic action only makes sense when current circumstances are truly unbearable. Most Americans don't perceive enough potential improvement to warrant the massive disruption of emigration.

Immigration to developed nations involves lengthy bureaucratic procedures and substantial financial costs. Canada specifically maintains selective entry requirements rather than accepting all applicants. The application process itself can take years to complete with no guarantee of approval.

Housing and general expenses run higher in Canada than in most American regions. Winter temperatures across much of Canada are significantly more severe than what most Americans experience. A large wave of newcomers would saturate the Canadian job market, leaving many unable to find employment.

Strong labor protections become meaningless when unemployment is high and positions are scarce. The Canadian economy is considerably smaller than America's and cannot absorb unlimited workers. Population density in Canada is already concentrated in specific corridors due to climate constraints.

Neither country faces active military conflict within its borders that would trigger refugee movements. The vast majority of citizens in both nations enjoy stable, peaceful family lives. These two nations share the world's longest undefended border and maintain deep alliance bonds.

No systematic persecution exists in either direction across this border. Governmental structures differ only in details while fundamental values remain aligned. Cultural similarities between the countries far outweigh their differences.

Currency exchange rates favor Americans, with Canadian dollars valued around 76 cents USD. This financial reality makes moving north less economically attractive. The climate factor cannot be overstated for those accustomed to warmer American states.

Claims of American societal collapse largely originate from young people with limited perspective on hardship. European commentators sometimes engage in online exaggeration about American problems. These critics often mistake ordinary challenges for existential crises.

Life across Canada, America, and Europe offers broadly similar experiences for middle-class residents. Professionals with marketable skills often earn higher salaries in American markets. Geographic mobility comes with emotional costs that outweigh marginal quality-of-life improvements.

Affordable Canadian regions tend to be extremely cold and remote from services. Every nation struggles with distinct problems rather than some being problem-free. The United States functions adequately for the majority despite legitimate criticisms of specific policies.

Neither service is genuinely cost-free despite appearances. Both participants in a Skype conversation must maintain active internet connections to communicate. Public WiFi networks are installed by businesses as customer acquisition tools, with operational expenses built into their broader budgets. The illusion of zero cost stems from internet infrastructure operating without national boundaries or borders. Traditional telephony requires your carrier to compensate the foreign network operator for completing international calls and messages. These interconnection fees typically exceed actual delivery costs by substantial margins. Consumers ultimately bear expenses regardless, though payment mechanisms differ between technologies.

Telephone networks originated during an era when cross-border communication demanded enormous capital investment and technical resources. This historical context established pricing expectations that persisted for decades. Most telephone companies operated as government-sanctioned monopolies with legal barriers preventing competitive entry. These dominant carriers imposed steep termination charges on foreign telecommunications companies routing calls into their territories. Alternative routing options simply did not exist for international traffic. The general public rarely made overseas calls, so interconnection fees remained largely invisible to everyday consumers. These charges functioned as premium revenue streams that subsidized affordable domestic calling infrastructure nationwide.

The internet's emergence disrupted this established model fundamentally. Early Internet Service Providers typically launched as nimble startups rather than entrenched monopolies. These companies delivered connectivity through existing copper telephone infrastructure using dial-up modem technology. Their competitive strategy emphasized open peering relationships with content networks and other providers. Distance between networks mattered little because telecommunication hotels concentrated numerous carriers in shared facilities. Multiple companies competed aggressively to provide inter-city data transmission, driving prices downward. Internet connectivity costs plummeted as competition intensified across the sector. Meanwhile, traditional telephone carriers failed to modernize their pricing structures accordingly.

This historical analysis illuminates ongoing net neutrality debates effectively. American broadband infrastructure has consolidated into monopolistic arrangements mirroring old telephony patterns. Consumers could previously dial any ISP through standard phone lines for internet access. Contemporary Americans typically face merely one or two cable providers offering high-speed connections. These providers are reverting to previous business models granting them pricing leverage over consumers. Nations maintaining competitive infrastructure policies avoid these concentrated power dynamics. New Zealand exemplifies open-access frameworks where residents select among dozens of fiber providers at local exchanges. Such structural competition prevents the monopolistic behaviors that net neutrality regulations attempt to constrain.

Established phone carriers view you as existing revenue to maximize through additional charges. Skype regards you as a prospective customer they must attract from zero baseline.

If there is an available syllabus for the Biology class, read it carefully to know the rules, materials needed, and any other important information before going to the first Biology class. Review it before going to class each day to make sure nothing is forgotten. One way of remembering the syllabus is to highlight, underline, and take notes on it.

Use different note-taking methods such as underlining, highlighting, drawing a symbol such as a star next to something important, drawing a box around important sentences, and taking notes either on a separate sheet of paper or the back of the syllabus. Always check with the teacher before marking up the syllabus to ensure this practice is acceptable. If needed, make a copy with a scanner so there are multiple copies. Keeping one unmarked version and another with annotations allows for updates when changes occur.

Students without scanners at home have a few different options for scanning the syllabus. One is to go to the nearest library that has a scanner and bring the syllabus along. Usually it costs no more than $0.20 per page to scan. Another option is for students with smartphones or tablets with a camera built into the device. Install an app made for scanning documents. These apps allow users to take a picture of a document and convert it to PDF, DOC, and other various document formats. The school office may also have a scanner available for student use. Biology teachers can often scan the syllabus themselves if students request assistance.

Usually the teacher will give students at least the first week of class to pay this fee. Most of the time it is refundable, meaning when students have completed the course the money is refunded back to them. If anything has been damaged by a student, most likely this fee will not be refunded to them. Lab materials require careful handling regardless of whether they are dangerous substances or safe equipment. Some schools allow payment plans for students who cannot afford the full lab fee upfront. The exact amount of the lab fee varies by school district and the specific Biology course level.

Usually pencils or pens and paper to take notes are required in most classes. Even if note-taking is not required by the teacher, it is an excellent idea to bring supplies and take notes anyways. This will help retain information and allow students to review what they learned in class. Good note-taking skills contribute significantly to academic success. Refer to "Part 2 of 3: Taking Notes" for more information on effective techniques. Colored pens can help organize notes by topic or importance level. Digital note-taking on laptops or tablets is becoming increasingly common in Biology classrooms.

Taking supplies out before class begins gets students ready faster. This prevents students from digging around in their school bag when it is actually time to use them. Only skip this if the teacher instructs the students not to take anything out until they say so. This is also a good time to quickly review yesterday's homework and notes. Checking for missing assignments during this pre-class period allows time to address problems before instruction begins.
ideas_up_v2.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f: Judith Scott (May 1, 1943 – March 15, 2005) was an American fiber sculptor, born with Down Syndrome and deaf. She was internationally renowned for her art. In 1987, Judith was enrolled at the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, California which supports people with developmental disabilities. There, Judith discovered her passion and talent for abstract fiber art and she was able to communicate in a new form. An account of Scott's life, Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott (2016) has been written by her twin sister. Judith was born into a middle-class family in Cincinnati, Ohio in May 1, 1943 along with her fraternal twin sister Joyce. Unlike Joyce, Judith was born with Down Syndrome. During her infancy, Judith suffered from Scarlet Fever, which caused her to lose her hearing, a fact that remained unknown until much later on in her life. Judith Scott spent her first seven and a half years at home with her parents, twin sister and older brothers. Although the developmental gap between the two girls was apparent, "the parents consciously sought to treat these youngest members of the family alike." However, when it was time for the girls to start attending school, Judith was found to be "ineducable." There was only one classroom for children with disabilities, and Judith was not able to pass the verbally-based entrance tests, due to her still undiagnosed deafness. Consequently, on medical advice, her parents placed Judith in the Columbus State Institution (formerly the Columbus State School), an institution for the mentally disabled, on October 18, 1950. This separation had a profound effect on both twins. The records from Judith Scott's first few years at the Institution indicate that she had an IQ of 30 (based upon oral testing before her deafness was recognized). For this reason she was denied any training opportunities. Deprived of her twin, Judith became severely alienated, and behavioral problems soon surfaced. Her Clinical Record states that "She does not seem to be in good contact with her environment. She does not get along well with other children, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats other children. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Soon after, she was moved to a smaller state institution at Gallipolis, Ohio. In 1985, after 35 years of complete separation and lengthy and difficult negotiations, Joyce Scott became her sister's legal guardian, and brought Judith to live with her in California, a state where all mentally disabled citizens are entitled to an ongoing education. Judith Scott died of natural causes at her sister's home in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks short of her 62nd birthday. She outlived her life expectancy at birth by almost fifty years. On April 1, 1987, Judith Scott began attending the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the first organizations in the world to provide studio space for artists with disabilities. For almost two years, Judith showed little interest in any artistic activity. She was unexceptional with paint. She scribbled loops and circles, but her work contained no representational imagery. The staff was considering ending her involvement with the program due to her lack of engagement with traditional materials. It wasn't until Judith casually observed a fiber art class conducted by visiting artist Sylvia Seventy, that she had her artistic breakthrough. Using the materials at hand, Judith spontaneously invented her own unique and radically different form of artistic expression. While other students were stitching, she was sculpting with an unprecedented zeal and concentration. Her creative gifts and absolute focus were quickly recognized, and she was given complete freedom to choose her own materials. Taking whatever objects she found, regardless of ownership, she would wrap them in carefully selected colored yarns to create diverse sculptures of many different shapes. Some resemble cocoons or body parts, while others are elongated totemic poles. Many of her works also feature pairs, reflecting Scott's experience as a twin. Judith worked on her art five days a week for eighteen years, producing over 200 pieces in total. Judith had her first exhibition in 1999, which coincided with the publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott. Together, these events helped propel her to worldwide recognition. Scott's work has become immensely popular in the world of outsider art, and her pieces sell for substantial sums. Scott is now hailed as a contemporary artist, no longer just an outsider. Her art is held in the permanent collections of many museums, including: Museum of Modern Art (Manhattan, New York), the American Visionary Art Museum (Baltimore, Maryland), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Museum of American Folk Art (Manhattan, New York), Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art (Chicago, Illinois), Irish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin, The Oakland Museum, Oakland, CA. L'Aracine Musee D'Art Brut (Paris, France), Art Brut Connaissance & Diffusion Collection (Paris and Prague), Collection de l'art brut (Lausanne, Switzerland). Below is a list of select notable exhibitions for Judith Scott. 2018 – Judith Scott: Touchdown, Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California 2014-15 – Bound and Unbound, Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn, New York 2009 – Judith Scott: Retrospective, Ricco Maresca Gallery, New York City, New York 2002 – Cocoon: Judith Scott, Ricco-Maresca Gallery, New York City, New York 2019 – Memory Palaces: Inside the Collection of Audrey B. Heckler, American Folk Art Museum, New York City, New York 2019 – The Doors of Perception, Curated by Javier Téllez in collaboration with the Outsider Art Fair, Frieze Art Fair, New York City, New York 2019 – Flying High: Women Artists of Art Brut, Bank Austria Kunstforum, Vienna 2018 – Outliers and American Vanguard Art, National Gallery of Art, Washington DC 2017 – Forget Me Not: Judith Scott, Zuckerman Museum of Art, Kennesaw, Georgia 2017 – Viva Arte Viva, the 57th Venice Biennale, Venice, Italy 2015 – Collection ABCD, La Maison Rouge, Paris, France 2013 – Create, Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California 2013 – Create, Boca Raton Museum of Art, Boca Raton, Florida 2013 – Extreme Art, The Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, Ridgefield, Connecticut 2012 – Rosemarie Trockel: A Cosmos, New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York City, New York 2011 – World Transformers, Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt, Frankfurt, Germany 2000 – Visions, American Visionary Art Museum, Baltimore, Maryland 2005 – Creative Growth, The Ricky Jay Broadside Collection, Yerba Buena Center for the Arts, San Francisco, California

After the discussion below, I examined the authors' previous MUS-ROVER system on which this paper builds. This background reading clarified several aspects of the current methodology.

The paper addresses JSB chorales using probabilistic approaches and n-gram models, topics with which I have professional familiarity. Despite my expertise in these areas, I struggled to follow significant portions of the manuscript. The notation density obscured rather than illuminated the underlying concepts.

The core ideas demonstrate originality and merit dissemination to the research community. However, ICLR may not provide the optimal forum for this work in its present state. Music applications legitimately belong at major machine learning venues when properly contextualized. The technical approach itself shows promise and theoretical soundness.

My recommendation stems from structural rather than conceptual concerns about the submission. A journal format would accommodate the comprehensive treatment this research demands. Such venues typically allow 15-20 pages instead of the 8-10 page conference constraint. The authors could then include worked examples that walk readers through complex operations step by step. 

Background material on the predecessor system belongs in the main text rather than forcing readers to hunt through citations. Multiple datasets would demonstrate that the technique generalizes beyond a single corpus. The JSB chorales represent only one musical tradition and computational challenge. Evaluation on folk melodies, pop music, or non-Western musical systems would strengthen validity claims.

Focusing the conference paper on a single subsystem might resolve the compression problem, though I cannot identify which component to highlight. The interconnected nature of the architecture resists such modular presentation. Each piece depends on understanding how other pieces function and interact.

Substantial revision could prompt me to increase my rating if executed successfully. That said, I believe the authors' time would yield better returns if invested in a journal manuscript. Such publications reach wider audiences, receive more thorough review, and remain accessible longer than conference proceedings.

Based on the authors' responses to reviewer questions and their manuscript revisions, I have adjusted my evaluation upward from my initial assessment.

Energy is not a substance that travels through space like a physical object. Rather, it represents a property belonging to a system or object at any given moment. When work is performed on an object, its energy can transform from one type to another. In the example of pushing a ball uphill, muscular chemical energy first converts to kinetic energy, then gravitational potential energy. Work is defined as applying a force over a distance, which serves as the mechanism for energy transfer.

Different materials store and transfer energy through distinct physical mechanisms. Gases hold energy in vibrational motion between molecular bonds, then pass momentum to neighboring gas molecules, creating thermal energy flow. Metals conduct energy through oscillations that propagate along their crystalline lattice structures. Perovskite materials can generate electrical charges when mechanical strain causes shifts in their atomic arrangement at AB crystallographic sites.

The broader thermodynamic principle is that energy flows from states of high enthalpy, or order, toward states of high entropy, or disorder. This directional flow occurs because disordered states are statistically more probable than ordered ones as time progresses. When you decide to move a stationary ball, your conscious intent overcomes the ball's stable equilibrium position. Chemical signals in your nervous system trigger muscle fibers to contract, which in turn pushes your rigid skeletal bones forward through space.

The contact interaction between your solid arm and the ball causes the ball to absorb energy at the atomic level. Strong nuclear forces between atoms in the ball's material create repulsion against your hand's atoms during contact. The ball begins rolling forward because the force from chemical energy in your arm exceeds the combined resistance forces from the table surface and air friction. Chemical energy itself derives from electrons seeking stable orbital configurations, governed ultimately by fundamental electromagnetic and nuclear forces.

To explain this more simply: energy is like having an abundance of something that naturally spreads to other things upon contact. If you possess ten cookies worth of energy to run one mile, you must expend three of those cookies sharing energy with your muscles, the ground, and your surroundings. Alternatively, you could spend two cookies bribing a friend to complete household chores like washing dishes or removing trash. This cookie analogy illustrates how energy represents a currency that gets exchanged whenever actions occur or tasks get accomplished in the physical world.

The relationship between US nuclear policy and international law exemplifies the principle of "do as I say, not as I do." The United States positions itself as a global enforcer of nuclear non-proliferation norms. This self-appointed role grants America the authority to intervene in other nations' weapons programs. International consensus holds that unstable dictatorships should not possess nuclear capabilities. Most nations tacitly accept American enforcement actions because challenging them proves futile.

The concept of "allowing" US actions misrepresents the actual power dynamics at play. American nuclear interventions occur regardless of international approval or disapproval. Sanctions against the United States would lack sufficient force to alter its behavior. The US developed atomic weapons before any international regulatory framework existed. No entity possessed the capability to prevent the Manhattan Project's completion in 1945. Once America had assembled a substantial nuclear arsenal, reversing this reality became impossible. Arguing against established nuclear powers wastes diplomatic capital on unchangeable circumstances.

American nuclear dominance actually reduces global weapons proliferation in practical terms. NATO allies rely on the US nuclear umbrella for their strategic defense needs. This arrangement eliminates the motivation for allied nations to pursue independent weapons programs. Japan, Germany, and South Korea forgo nuclear development because American protection makes it unnecessary. The umbrella effect has prevented dozens of countries from acquiring their own arsenals.

Universal agreement exists that nuclear, biological, and chemical weapons require strict international controls. The United States does not stand alone in advocating for non-proliferation measures. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty establishes a legal framework for weapons management. This treaty permits existing nuclear states to maintain their arsenals while prohibiting new entrants. The United States provides nuclear weapons to select NATO partners under treaty provisions. These sharing arrangements comply with international law despite their controversial nature.

The UN Security Council designated America as a primary enforcement mechanism for weapons treaties. This official role legitimizes US interventions against suspected proliferators. Member states regularly criticize this arrangement through diplomatic channels. The peacekeeping mandate creates inherent conflicts of interest within the international system.

Military supremacy determines which nations can ignore international norms with impunity. The United States commands more combat power than all other militaries combined. Opposing American military actions presents three realistic options for other countries. Direct military confrontation guarantees catastrophic defeat and regime change. Public criticism results in diplomatic isolation and economic retaliation. Silent acquiescence preserves national interests and maintains working relationships. Historical evidence demonstrates that surviving nations consistently choose the third option. Pragmatism trumps principle when facing overwhelming force disparities in international relations.

The core issue centers on anonymity paired with physical safety from consequences.

Digital communication creates distance and namelessness that shields you from retaliation, which is why interactions online become hostile and combative so readily... since aggression flows easily when there's zero risk of physical punishment or confrontation.

Face-to-face encounters impose natural restraints because vulnerability is real—if you're small and physically weak, you won't mouth off to someone large and powerful, even when you disagree completely. The internet erases that vulnerability entirely. Who's threatened when separated by distance and screens?

This same protective distance makes cruelty easier because you're not facing an actual human being, just text and usernames. Remoteness strips away the humanity of whoever receives your words, turning people into abstractions.

Basically, safety from consequences transforms behavior: insulting an anonymous account feels simple and harmless, but confronting that same person directly—seeing their face, knowing their story, recognizing their humanity—makes the identical insult far harder to deliver because consequence and empathy suddenly become real.

The automobile situation parallels this exactly. You're encased in metal and glass, protected and mobile, which creates the same emotional distance and safety. Honking aggressively or gesturing obscenely feels justified because you're shielded inside your vehicle and will vanish from this stranger's life in seconds. That other car becomes an object to hate rather than a human being with context and struggles, an annoying obstacle instead of another vulnerable person having difficulties you cannot see.

In both cases—online exchanges and road rage—the fundamental dynamic is identical: separation creates safety, safety permits aggression, and distance prevents empathy. When consequences disappear and other people become abstractions instead of individuals, hostility replaces restraint. The common thread is always insulation from retaliation combined with the dehumanization that remoteness provides, whether that remoteness comes from digital anonymity or automotive isolation.

topics_down_v2.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex dynamical systems is key in numerous scientific fields. This strong interest in dynamical systems is however hindered by modeling issues: often, the governing equations describing the dynamics of the system under consideration are not accessible or, if known, their solution might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints for these systems. Not surprisingly, approximating complex dynamical systems in a generic functional format and informing it ex-nihilo from available observations of system behavior has become common practice in the age of machine learning, as illustrated by the numerous successful examples of learned dynamical system models based on deep neural networks. However, generalizability of the dynamical system models, margins of guarantee and the impact of data are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the system dynamics. We tackle these issues in dynamical system learning from a different viewpoint, by adopting a curriculum learning strategy for training system models. In curriculum learning for dynamical systems, the dataset is structured such that the training process starts from simple dynamical samples towards more complex system trajectories in order to favor convergence and generalization of the learned dynamics. The concept has been developed and successfully applied for learning control of dynamical systems. Here, we apply this concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems in a systematic way. First, leveraging insights from the ergodic theory of dynamical systems, we assess the amount of trajectory data sufficient for a-priori guaranteeing a faithful model of the dynamical system and thoroughly investigate the impact of the training set structure on the quality of long-term predictions of system evolution. Based on that analysis of system data, we consider entropy as a metric of complexity of the dynamical dataset; we show how an informed design of the training set based on the analysis of the entropy of system trajectories significantly improves the resulting dynamical models in terms of generalizability, and provide insights on the amount and the choice of trajectory data required for effective data-driven modeling of dynamical systems.

Context. Filaments are ubiquitous in the Galaxy, and they host star formation. Detecting filaments in a reliable way is therefore key towards our understanding of how filaments contribute to the star formation process within our Galaxy.

Aims. We explore whether supervised machine learning can identify filamentary structures across the whole Galactic plane where filaments are distributed.

Methods. We used two versions of UNet-based networks for filament segmentation. We used H2 column density images of the Galactic plane obtained with Herschel Hi-GAL data as input data showing filament candidates. We trained the UNet-based networks with skeletons, comprising the spine plus branches of filaments that were extracted from these images of filamentary structure, together with background and missing data masks for filaments that we produced. We tested eight training scenarios to determine the best scenario for our astrophysical purpose of classifying pixels as filaments in the Galactic plane.

Results. The training of the UNets allows us to create a new image of the Galactic plane by segmentation in which pixels belonging to filamentary structures are identified as filament components. With this new method, we classify more pixels, more by a factor of two to seven depending on the classification threshold used, as belonging to filaments than the spine plus branches structures of filaments we used as input. New filamentary structures are revealed, which are mainly low-contrast filaments that were not detected before in previous filament surveys. We use standard metrics to evaluate the performances of different training scenarios for filament detection. This allows us to demonstrate the robustness of the filament identification method and to determine an optimal threshold value that maximizes the recovery of the input labelled pixel classification for filaments.

Conclusions. This proof-of-concept study shows that supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures that are present throughout the Galactic plane. The detection of these filamentary structures, including low-density and low-contrast filaments that have never been seen before, offers important perspectives for studying these filaments.

topics_down_v2.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: The truth is that I am actually undecided on the question of gay marriage, but I will start on the side against gay marriage for two reasons: 1. I lean less towards my starting side and it seems much more fragile and unpopular, so advocating for a weaker position I feel less strongly about helps to practice my argument articulation skills. 2. I believe that the burden of proof is on the side in favor of gay marriage (as I will explain), so I started on the other side. First, please watch [this video] (it's only two minutes). Due to this argument, I feel that the burden of proof is on the people that wish to redefine the criteria for the institution of marriage (I do not have problems with redefinition itself, but I am just saying that redefinition requires compelling reason). When people answer the question "Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?" with "Why not?," this is really just the teapot fallacy (attempting to shift the burden of proof). I do not believe equality is a good argument for gay marriage. Marriage is not a kind of privilege or a right that must be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around procreation, and homosexual relationships, which may be loving and committed, by definition are non-procreational. There are also heterosexual marriages which are non-procreational, such as old or infertile couples, but if you watched the video, you'll understand why it's not analogous to gay marriage; just because there are exceptions to the norm in marriage, doesn't mean you can extend the definition of marriage to a non-norm, as the norms of marriage are not defined by their exceptions. Many times the criteria for gay marriage is presented as (a posed question): "If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?" Marriage criteria have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love for that matter. If your criteria for marriage are two individuals who have romantic or sexual love, then the question of gay marriage opens other questions about marriage criteria. The "why would you care?" argument is invalid regarding gay marriage; Just because a proposition does not affect anyone adversely, doesn't mean we can change institutions like marriage at whim. Even under utilitarianism, this argument doesn't work for gay marriage. Gay people can have fulfilling long-term romantic and sexual relationships without calling it marriage. Redefining marriage for the happiness of a group raises questions about what marriage fundamentally is and what purposes it serves. Most arguments for gay marriage are appeals to emotion or popularity. The term "gay rights" was designed to make it sound like we have internment camps for them. Even the term "homophobe" was coined to stigmatize the opposition to gay marriage. Just because the issue of gay marriage is popular in our zeitgeist, and many of the opponents of gay marriage are religious fundamentalists who use straw man arguments, doesn't make the "more reasonable side" correct about gay marriage. Why is one approach to marriage relationships more valid than another when we discuss gay marriage? The debate over gay marriage ultimately comes down to what we believe marriage is for and whether gay marriage fits that definition. If marriage exists primarily for procreation, then gay marriage doesn't fit. If marriage exists for other purposes, then gay marriage might fit those purposes. The question of gay marriage forces us to articulate what marriage means and why society recognizes marriage at all. Those who support gay marriage must explain why the traditional definition of marriage should be expanded. Those who oppose gay marriage must explain why the traditional definition should be maintained. The gay marriage debate is fundamentally about the nature and purpose of marriage itself. View changed. In all fairness, I was already 75 percent there when I wrote this about gay marriage.
topics_down_v2.coling::bd4df89c-701f-407b-9fc6-2c51aa5b: I'm talking about the type of condemnation voiced consistently by certain users of rpolitics, certain members of OWS, and Gawker's Hamilton Nolan. It is a viewpoint I will paraphrase roughly as follows: The mere fact that we live in a system where some people can amass vastly more money than others is, itself, immoral; if you do amass wealth under this system, you are quite arguably a bad person. Hedge fund managers are sitting around spending tens of millions on embalmed sharks...don't they know that a tiny fraction of their daily earnings would make a huge difference in others' lives? Would be enough to pay off the average redditor's student loans, for example? Every time I've heard this shitty argument, I've heard it from activists or internet commenters who hail from the middle- or perhaps working-class tier of an advanced Western economy. Here's the thing, though: you, too, have vastly more resources than most people worldwide. If you could save 100 by not upgrading your smartphone, by walking home in the rain instead of taking a cab, by eating lentils or beans for a few weeks or by foregoing that new item of clothing you wanted, you could donate that 100 to improve the lives of people less fortunate than yourself. Is your comfort, convenience and entertainment more important than addressing global economic inequality? And, btw, I will not tolerate deflections to the effect of: "but charities might not use the money responsibly; charitable donations could have negative effects on local industry in the long run..." As a premise of this CMV, we must stipulate that if wealth could be redistributed, that redistribution would, indeed, benefit the recipients. We must further stipulate that if the average American wanted to donate in a genuinely-beneficial manner towards addressing wealth inequality, he'd be able to do so. I don't think these are crazy assumptions to make when discussing wealth redistribution principles. So, my view is that people who rail against "the rich," purely on the ground that they're rich, are hypocrites for overlooking their own relative economic standing in the world. If they believe others' wealth should be redistributed to curb inequality, they are hypocrites for not redistributing their own wealth to curb inequality. These critics of wealth accumulation apply different standards to billionaires than they apply to themselves, despite occupying analogous positions in the global wealth hierarchy. Now, I don't donate much to charity myself. But nor do I regard people richer than me as innately evil human beings simply because they possess greater wealth. I can acknowledge the preference revealed by my decision-making, which is: I'd rather upgrade to business class than donate that money to reduce global inequality. For this reason, if some billionaire would rather upgrade his yacht than dissolve all his assets to reduce economic disparity, I don't really blame him for making the same calculation I make. The billionaire's choice to retain wealth rather than redistribute it mirrors my own choice to retain wealth rather than redistribute it, just at different scales of magnitude. It seems quite a few people disagree with me about this analysis of wealth inequality criticism, so I'm curious to see if anyone can CMV on whether criticizing the wealthy while retaining one's own comparative wealth constitutes hypocrisy. The fundamental question remains whether those who condemn wealth accumulation are obligated to practice the wealth redistribution they preach, or whether there exists some principled distinction between their own economic position and that of the wealthy they criticize.
