topics_down_v2.coling::49a2d576-81e8-4b16-889d-beb4a986: A teenager has died after falling off the roof of a six-story Bronx building while fleeing police officers. Hakeem Kuta, 17, was on life support and passed away Saturday morning after succumbing to injuries from the fall that happened on Thursday night, said the New York Police Department. Police said Kuta, a junior at Bronx Envision Academy, appeared to have misjudged a ledge while backing away from approaching cops on the rooftop. Kuta plunged six stories from the roof of the Bronx building on Thursday evening during the incident. The 17-year-old jumped over a three-foot high wall before he fell six stories from the building located on Valentine Avenue in Mott Haven. Officers had chased Kuta and five other teenagers up the stairs to the roof of the apartment building, said spokesman Stephen Davis. When the officers got to the roof, some teens jumped to another roof and ran away, however Kuta and his 14-year-old companion, who has not been named, were pinned in by a dividing wall on the rooftop. Police said Kuta then jumped over a three-foot high wall without realizing there was a gap between the buildings below. His friend tried to help by desperately holding onto his jacket as Kuta dangled 60 feet from the ground above an alleyway between the buildings. When officers reached the roof, some teens had already jumped and run away to safety. However, Kuta and his 14-year-old companion were trapped and pinned in by a dividing wall that blocked their escape route. Officer Edmundo Rivera grabbed onto the companion to keep him from falling over the edge of the building, but the friend lost his grip on Kuta who fell from the roof, plunging six stories down to the pavement below. Police officers ran to where he fell in the courtyard of the building and Kuta was then taken to St. Barnabas Hospital where he was listed in critical condition with severe injuries. He died around 11am on Saturday morning from the injuries sustained in the fall. His father Munir Kuta, 42, said his son stayed out of trouble, according to the New York Daily News. 'It's not so easy,' he said about losing his son. 'He was a nice kid.' Kuta's father, Munir, said his son was a good teenager who avoided getting into trouble. The fall occurred at the building on Valentine Avenue in the Mott Haven section of the Bronx. Kuta had been a student at Bronx Envision Academy where he was enrolled as a junior. The teenager fell approximately sixty feet from the rooftop to the courtyard pavement. Officer Rivera attempted to prevent the tragedy by grabbing Kuta's companion on the roof. The 14-year-old friend held desperately onto Kuta's jacket trying to save him from falling. Despite these efforts, Kuta slipped from his friend's grasp and plummeted from the building. The incident happened on Thursday night and Kuta remained on life support until Saturday morning when he succumbed to his injuries at St. Barnabas Hospital.

There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common ones: Division by zero: When a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. The program should have been written to check for zero before attempting division, but if that check is missing, a crash occurs. Some programming languages will automatically catch this error and allow the program to continue, but others will simply terminate the program immediately when division by zero is attempted.

Access violation: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts are off-limits. If a program tries to access part of memory that is off-limits, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. Access violations often happen when a program tries to use memory that has already been freed, or when it attempts to write to memory locations that belong to other programs or to the operating system itself.

Deadlock: When a program has multiple parts running at the same time, those parts sometimes need to wait for each other to finish certain tasks. A deadlock happens when part of the program is waiting for another part to finish, but that other part is also waiting for the first part to finish. Both parts will sit there forever waiting for the other to complete, and the program freezes up. When this happens inside a program, there is nothing you can do except kill the program and start it again.

Unhandled exception: Sometimes a program will have a special sort of error checking built into it. When an error is detected, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with it. If an exception gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting you know that a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will terminate.

All of these situations are caused by bugs in the program. Bugs are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more bugs than other programs. Maybe the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test it as well as they should have. Maybe the program is so complicated that it is difficult to deal with every possible situation that might arise during execution. Testing can catch many bugs before a program is released, but some bugs only appear under very specific conditions that weren't tested. When programs interact with user input, network connections, or file systems, there are countless combinations of states that the program might encounter, and programmers cannot always predict every scenario. Programs also crash when they run out of memory, when they encounter corrupted data they cannot parse, or when the underlying system resources they depend on become unavailable.
topics_down_v2.coling::37e384a6-d2b8-444e-ac7f-d4288c17: Paralympic classification systems group athletes based on the functional impact of their disabilities rather than the specific medical diagnoses. The classification process examines how a disability affects an athlete's ability to perform in their particular sport. Each sport has developed its own classification system that reflects the specific physical demands of that sport. Cycling classifications, for example, divide athletes according to functional capacity: athletes with upper body limitations compete in one category, while athletes with single-limb disabilities who retain bilateral leg function compete in another category. Athletes who can pedal with only one leg due to unilateral lower limb impairment form a separate classification group. Athletes with bilateral lower limb involvement, regardless of whether that involvement stems from cerebral palsy, amputation, or another condition, compete together in yet another classification category. The classification process requires international certification through formal evaluation procedures. These evaluations assess the functional limitations that result from each athlete's disability. Trained classifiers conduct physical examinations and functional assessments to determine the appropriate competition category for each athlete. The classification system aims to ensure fair competition by grouping athletes with similar functional abilities together. The system also prevents athletes from misrepresenting their capabilities to gain competitive advantages by entering categories designed for athletes with more significant impairments. When athlete numbers are insufficient to fill separate races for each classification, organizers sometimes combine similar classifications in the same event while maintaining separate scoring within each category. This consolidation practice allows competitions to proceed even with limited participant numbers in individual classifications. The approach ensures that athletes with comparable functional abilities compete against one another for medals and rankings despite sharing the track or course with athletes from adjacent classification categories. Paralympic classification ultimately seeks to balance the goals of fair competition, adequate participation numbers, and practical event management within the Paralympic sports system.

Playing dead operates through predator psychology rather than any conscious deception. When prey animals cease movement, they trigger a shift in predator instincts that governs whether the predator continues its attack or disengages entirely. The predator's response depends fundamentally on what type of threat response initially motivated its aggression toward the prey.

Predators attacking from territorial or defensive instincts lose interest once movement stops because movement itself signals the presence of a threat requiring neutralization. When the prey goes still, the predator's brain registers that the immediate crisis has passed, and the defensive drive that powered the attack diminishes rapidly. The predator experiences a reduction in the physiological arousal that accompanied its defensive state, and without continued movement to sustain that arousal, the predator's attention shifts away from the now-motionless prey. This explains why playing dead proves effective against predators like bears, which typically attack humans defensively rather than as prey items.

Predators hunting for food, however, respond to stillness differently because their motivation centers on obtaining a meal rather than eliminating a perceived threat. These predators possess instincts calibrated to movement as a trigger for chase and capture behaviors, but once capture occurs, stillness does not signal safety to the predator. Instead, the predator transitions from pursuit mode into feeding mode. The prey's immobility actually facilitates consumption rather than discouraging it. Pack hunters like wolves exemplify this pattern: they attack to eat, and when struggling ceases, they interpret this as the appropriate moment to begin feeding rather than as a reason to withdraw.

The effectiveness of death feigning therefore depends entirely on correctly assessing the predator's underlying motivation. Against a predator defending territory or reacting to perceived danger, immobility can deactivate the aggressive response by removing the movement cues that maintain defensive arousal. Against a predator hunting for sustenance, immobility fails because the predator's instinctive sequence proceeds directly from successful capture to consumption, with stillness serving as the signal to transition between these phases rather than to abandon the interaction entirely.
topics_down_v2.coling::a9b058a8-5ce8-448f-820a-6ffba640: Because of the camera's field of view (FOV). The field of view represents the angular extent of the observable area that a camera can capture at any given moment. If we consider what a camera can see as a cone starting at the lens and expanding outward, then FOV is the angle between the two boundary lines of that cone. The field of view fundamentally determines how much of a scene the camera will include in its frame. A camera with a narrow field of view captures a smaller angular portion of the scene, while a camera with a wide field of view captures a much larger angular portion. When you adjust the field of view setting on a camera, you change the relationship between object size and distance in the resulting image. As you increase the FOV, you cause the camera to see more area on the left and right sides of the frame. But you'll also notice that objects in the frame appear to be farther away even though the camera position hasn't changed - that's because as you increase the FOV you also change how the light from distant objects converges on the camera's sensor or film surface. Essentially a larger FOV means that objects seem to decrease in size faster as they recede into the distance. The field of view creates a compression effect where the rate of size change with distance becomes exaggerated. The opposite is also true: if you decrease the FOV then it increases the apparent size of far away objects since they now converge on a larger portion of the image area. A narrower field of view makes distant objects appear closer together and more similar in size regardless of their actual separation. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61 degrees. This extremely narrow field of view makes it very effective at capturing objects across vast distances because the camera focuses on a very small cone of light. The restricted field of view also means that the distance between the Earth and the Moon doesn't have the same effect on their relative size as it would when taken with a camera having a wider field of view. In a camera, the focal length of the lens determines the field of view that will be captured. A longer focal length creates a narrower field of view, while a shorter focal length creates a wider field of view. The physical size of the camera's sensor also influences the field of view for any given focal length. A larger sensor will produce a wider field of view than a smaller sensor when using the same lens. The EPIC camera on the spacecraft that took these images is specifically designed with a particular field of view optimized for observing the Earth from a great distance. The field of view was deliberately constrained to provide the appropriate level of magnification for Earth observation from DSCOVR's orbital position. Different cameras have different fields of view depending on their intended purpose and optical design. The field of view determines not just what appears in frame, but also how spatial relationships between objects at different distances are rendered in the final image.
topics_down_v2.coling::1770be09-c92d-43e3-ab15-7b7318ca: Radioactive atoms are unstable atoms that change over time by releasing particles and energy in order to become more stable. An atom is the basic building block of all matter in the physical world. Atoms are made of protons, neutrons, and electrons. Different numbers or combinations of these particles result in different types of atoms, which we call elements. Most atoms are stable, meaning they don't change their structure over time, but some atoms aren't stable at all. The unstable atoms are what we call radioactive atoms. These radioactive atoms will seek stability by offloading protons, neutrons, and electrons as time passes. This process of releasing particles happens because there are too many particles packed into the radioactive atom for it to remain stable in its current configuration. When a radioactive atom has too many particles, it becomes uncomfortable in a sense, much like an overcrowded space. Some particles will leave the atom instead of staying bound together with all the others. The radioactive atom keeps releasing particles until it eventually transforms into a stable atom that can hold together without losing any more particles. This is actually how lead is formed in nature; lead is simply uranium that has released enough particles over a very long time to make itself stable enough for the remaining particles to stay together permanently without losing anyone else. When radioactive atoms release these particles, the particles are sent away very quickly at high speeds, which is what makes radioactive atoms potentially dangerous to living things. The released particles are like tiny little bullets that hit other things at the atomic level with tremendous force. If these fast-moving particles collide with another atom nearby, they hit that atom with enough force to send that atom's protons, neutrons, and electrons scattering in different directions like pool balls. Different radioactive atoms release different types of particles at different rates, which is why some radioactive atoms are more dangerous than others. Some radioactive atoms take millions of years to become stable, while other radioactive atoms become stable much more quickly. The rate at which a radioactive atom releases particles and transforms into a stable atom is called its half-life, and understanding the half-life of different radioactive atoms helps scientists predict how long radioactive materials will remain dangerous.
topics_down_v2.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1: Wealth taxes, which may also be called capital taxes, represent levies imposed on what you own rather than what you earn. These taxes assess the total value of your assets or property holdings at a particular point in time. The fundamental principle behind wealth taxes is that they target accumulated wealth itself, measuring your net worth or specific categories of assets you possess. Various nations implement wealth taxes differently, but all versions share the common feature of taxing ownership rather than income flows. Some wealth tax systems apply only when your total assets exceed a specified threshold, while others tax particular categories of wealth regardless of your overall net worth. The threshold amounts vary considerably between jurisdictions that employ wealth taxes, ranging from relatively modest levels to quite substantial minimums before taxation begins. Switzerland operates a wealth tax system where taxation occurs once your assets surpass certain levels, and these levels differ by canton. Italy implements a wealth tax specifically targeting foreign real estate owned by its residents, making ownership of property abroad subject to annual taxation. Canada formerly imposed wealth taxes on corporate assets, though these corporate capital taxes were phased out across different provinces during the past fifteen years. The United States applies a wealth tax concept through its estate tax, which taxes the total wealth a person possesses at death. Estate tax thresholds have fluctuated dramatically, but currently the exemption sits around five million dollars in total assets. Wealth taxes differ fundamentally from taxes on investment income such as interest, dividends, or rental earnings from property you own. Those investment earnings face taxation as income, added to your wage income for tax calculation purposes. A wealth tax operates separately and additionally, assessing the underlying assets themselves rather than any income those assets generate. The distinction matters because you could owe wealth taxes even when your assets produce no income during a given year, since the tax applies to ownership itself rather than to any earnings that ownership produces.
topics_down_v2.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe: You could have both options exercised and assigned to you on the same day, but I don't think you could lose money on both options on the same day. The reason is that while option exercises are immediate, option assignments are processed after the markets close at the end of each day. See http://www.888options.com/help/faq/assignment.jsp for details. So you would get both option assignments at the same time, that night. The net effect should be that you don't own any stock position (someone would put you the stock through the put option, then the stock would be called away through the call option) and you don't have the options anymore. You should have incoming cash of $1500 selling the stock to the call option exerciser and outgoing cash of $1300 buying from the put option exerciser, right? So you would have no more options but $200 more cash in your account in the morning from this options transaction. You bought at 13 and sold at 15 through your options position. This options position is an agreement to buy at 13 and sell at 15 at someone else's option. The way you lose money on these options is if one of the options isn't exercised while the other option is exercised, meaning if the stock is below 13 so nobody is going to opt to buy the stock from you at 15, but they'll sell the stock to you at 13 through the put option; or the stock is above 15 so nobody is going to opt to sell the stock to you at 13, but they'll buy the stock from you at 15 through the call option. You make money on the options if neither option is exercised (you keep the options premium you sold for) or both options are exercised (you keep the gap between the two options strikes, plus the premium collected). Having both options exercised is surely rare, since early option exercise is rare to begin with, and early exercise tends to happen when options are deep in the money; so you'd expect both options to be exercised if both options are deep in the money at some point. Having both options be exercised on the same day cannot be common, but such dual option exercise is maybe most likely just before option expiration with minimal time value remaining, particularly if the underlying stock moves around quickly so both options move in and out of the money at different points during that trading day.
topics_down_v2.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96: The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how they will apply the payments when you have multiple interest rates on the same card. As noted previously, payment allocation rules vary, and in some cases they will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must apply the rest above the minimum to the higher rate balance. In other jurisdictions, payment allocation on credit cards will vary by law and custom regarding how payments are distributed across different rate balances on your card. Do not assume your credit card will pay off the higher balance, or proportionally, without asking your card issuer about their specific payment allocation policy. Let's take the following credit card example. You owe $6000 on your card. $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate on the card) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate on the same card). If your bank applies payments on your credit card to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500 and your cash advance balance by $100. The average APR on your card, then, is simply sum of the product of the APR times balance for each portion of your card debt. So here, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15% for the card's weighted average rate. This is called a weighted average for credit card interest. If the bank applies the payment on your card differently - such as to the lower rate first, or some specified part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate on your card - then this weighted average will be misleading if you enter it into a credit card calculator, because your average APR on the card will rise over time as you pay off the purchase balance but don't pay off the cash advance balance on your card, or the card's average rate may decrease if the opposite payment pattern happens. The weighted average for your card is probably reasonably close in the circumstance that you describe, even if you have rules applying the balance differently on your card, so long as they don't 100% pay down the lower rate portion - so it may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations for your card's effective rate.

I cannot stress this enough, so I'll just repeat it: Don't plan your finances around your credit score. Don't even think about your credit score at all. Your credit score is not a goal in itself; it's merely a byproduct of sound financial behavior. Don't try to plan your finances around raising your credit score. Don't make purchasing decisions based on what might happen to your credit score. Don't take out loans you don't need just to improve your credit score. Don't carry balances on credit cards for the sake of your credit score. Don't open new accounts specifically to optimize your credit score. Don't close old accounts out of worry about your credit score. All of these actions treat your credit score as the primary objective, when it should never be more than a secondary consequence of responsible money management.

One rule you shouldn't have is "do whatever will optimize your credit score" because, again, you shouldn't plan your finances around your credit score. The right approach is to focus on the fundamentals of personal finance and let your credit score follow naturally. When you pay your bills on time, your credit score benefits. When you use credit responsibly and avoid overextending yourself, your credit score improves. When you maintain a reasonable mix of credit types and keep your utilization low, your credit score rises. But these actions should be taken because they represent sound financial practice, not because of their effect on your credit score.

Your credit score will take care of itself when you handle money properly. It will reflect your financial discipline without requiring your direct attention or manipulation. The score exists to summarize your creditworthiness for lenders, not to serve as a target for you to game or manipulate. Chasing your credit score is like chasing your shadow—the harder you run directly at it, the more it eludes you, but when you move forward naturally, it follows along automatically.

In closing, let me repeat one final time: Don't plan your finances around your credit score.
topics_down_v2.coling::b21c6524-7e1a-4589-933c-d0152005: The assumption that companies listed OTC are not serious is far from the truth. Many companies on the OTC are just starting off there because they don't meet the requirements to be listed on the NASDAQ or NYSE. The OTC market structure itself includes multiple tiers that reflect different levels of company development and regulatory compliance. The OTC market offers three distinct tiers for company listings: OTCQX, OTCQB, and OTC Pink. Each tier within the OTC market has specific requirements that companies must satisfy. While the OTC market doesn't require minimum levels of revenue, profits or assets for listing, this doesn't mean the OTC market lacks standards entirely. Companies trading on the OTC market must provide audited financial statements and maintain ongoing filing and reporting to the SEC and NASD. The OTCQX tier represents the highest standard within the OTC market, requiring companies to meet stringent financial standards and undergo annual verification and management certification. Companies on the OTCQX level of the OTC market must also have a professional third-party sponsor. The OTCQB tier of the OTC market serves as a venture marketplace for entrepreneurial and development stage companies. Companies listed on OTCQB within the OTC market must be current in their reporting to the SEC or a banking regulator and undergo an annual verification and management certification process. The OTC Pink tier is the most open marketplace within the OTC market structure. Companies on OTC Pink may include those that provide current information to investors and those that provide limited or no information. The OTC market's reputation has suffered due to promotional schemes targeting OTC-listed stocks. Some promoters create hype around particular OTC market stocks, encouraging investors to buy shares without proper research. When investors lose money on poorly researched OTC market investments, they often blame the OTC market itself rather than their own lack of due diligence. A company deciding to trade on the OTC market is making a serious commitment to going public. The fees for getting listed on the OTC market range from thirty thousand to one hundred fifty thousand dollars depending on the firm handling the listing and the services included in their package. These substantial costs demonstrate that companies entering the OTC market are making significant financial commitments. When evaluating OTC market opportunities, investors should focus on thorough company research rather than dismissing all OTC market listings as inferior. The tier system within the OTC market provides useful information about different companies' regulatory compliance and reporting standards. Understanding how the OTC market operates and the different requirements for each OTC market tier helps investors make better decisions about OTC market investments.

topics_down_v2.coling::a3c20aed-e22b-4f5a-ac3a-784b5d94: This soap is worse than bad: it's poisonous. Of the many television shows that have had a corrosive influence on British society over the past twenty years, Eastenders is the prime example. For two decades this show has celebrated the oaf, the thug, the wide-boy, the tart, the gobby, the violent, the sexually-incontinent, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious. How many times has someone or other remarked that Eastenders "mirrors life"? Life on which planet, exactly? It's written about "working-class" characters, as imagined by middle-class people who have taken a course in creative writing. Eager to show to their middle-class peers how familiar they are with the "working-class" they dream up the lumpen rabble that is the citizenry of Eastenders. This has a toxic effect on some minds less well-equipped than others to handle fiction, and so we find members of the real population assuming the attitudes and demeanour of the inhabitants of Walford. Thus, it came to pass that Eastenders mirrors life; but only after life had been hoodwinked into mirroring Eastenders. The show's writers manufacture conflict after tedious conflict, ensuring that every character slouches through Albert Square embodying some variation of confrontation, aggression, or moral turpitude. Eastenders has become a factory for producing scenes of misery, where the scriptwriters concoct an endless parade of family betrayals, public humiliations, and sordid entanglements. The programme's creators seem convinced that authenticity resides solely in depicting working-class life as an unrelenting cavalcade of dysfunction and despair. Every storyline reinforces the same dreary template: Eastenders presents its characters as perpetually angry, perpetually scheming, perpetually embroiled in some tawdry drama that the programme makers mistake for gritty realism. The writers will grow rich on the proceeds of such output, and will go on to enjoy the finer things of life in their rarified enclaves. Meanwhile, the burgeoning number of new, Eastenders-induced drones will proceed inexorably toward cultural bankruptcy. And there you have the creators and creatures of this pernicious programme, architect and victim alike of Eastenders' twenty-year assault on British television.

topics_down_v2.coling::019875e1-f507-4de8-a2a7-1f1dffeb: Every time the supposed explorers and we, the audience, is primed to set its first sights on one of the wondrous new worlds, for some ungodly reason, the filmmakers decided to distract with an "emergency" or some false alarm or some bit of artificial dramatic suspense related to the mission itself. This paper is an extension of Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN representations at FC7 layer are to certain extent equivariant to various classes of transformations and that training with a certain group of transformation makes the representations more equivalent.

Authors performed a large amount of experiments, training over 30 networks with different forms of jitter on FC7 representations, which is quite impressive. However it is rather difficult to find a main message of this work concerning FC7 layer properties. Yes, authors measured the properties on FC7 layer specifically, however it is hard to find some novel insights about FC7 beyond confirming that jitter helps FC7 achieve invariance. The evaluation of FC7 seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the FC7 analysis task advertised in its title really well.

Major issues are in the experiments with the FC7 representation distances:
* The selection of only FC7 is a bit controversial since FC7 is followed only by a single classification layer (FC8) to the common output. Because the FC8 is just a linear projection from FC7, what the equivalence map does is just to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network based on FC7 alignment. Probably performing similar experiments but examining FC7 alongside other layers may be more useful to understand FC7's role, given that the networks are already trained and FC7 can be compared to earlier representations.
* The experiment with FC7 representation distance is missing what is the classification error on the testing dataset when using FC7 features. This would answer whether the FC7 representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all, and whether FC7 maintains discriminative power.
* It is not clear for the experiment measuring FC7 compatibility with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example using FC7 features. Is this after training the equivalence map on FC7? More clear would be to show that networks trained on similar group of jitter transformations produce more compatible FC7 representations on the target task.
* The proposed method does not seem to improve FC7 equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss applied to FC7 is basically equal to simple data jitter as it just adds up the loss of the original and transformed image flowing through FC7. Maybe the issue is in the selection of specifically the FC7 layer for applying this equivariance objective.

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 equivariance properties, but it does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations about FC7 out of these experiments. Due to some issues with the FC7 equivalence experiments and the finetuning of FC7 equivariance, I would not recommend acceptance of this manuscript. However, refining the experiments on FC7 in already trained networks and restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work about FC7 may lead to interesting contribution to the field.

There are also few minor issues regarding FC7 analysis:
* It is not experimentally verified that the new criterion for FC7 equivariance mapping helps to gain better results at the FC7 level.
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult... ", it is not M_g operating on FC7 which is maximised/minimised, but the loss over the M_g applied to FC7 features.
* On page 7, Figure 3a+3b showing FC7 distances - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements representing same FC7 representations to white is really misleading, and probably even incorrect, as the distance between the same FC7 representations should be zero, which is also a way how to verify that the FC7 distance experiments are performed correctly.

Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies IB to train deep networks, though the original information bottleneck papers only presented the theoretical concept without practical implementation for neural network training.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound for the information bottleneck is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference approaches to the information bottleneck. Also the explanation of the IB principle itself is clear and well-motivated within the information bottleneck framework. Experimental results using the information bottleneck seem to be very promising for demonstrating the utility of this principle.

I found the presentation for the information bottleneck model a bit confusing. In variational inference approaches to information bottleneck and information maximisation, p usually denotes the model component and q represents the variational inference component. This means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure in information bottleneck formulations. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the underlying data distribution for the information bottleneck problem, thus here the information bottleneck model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the predictive distribution in the information bottleneck formulation in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense within the information bottleneck framework? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz for the information bottleneck in this case, but this makes the two definitions of the information bottleneck contradict to each other!

The authors have made an interesting connection between the information bottleneck and variational auto-encoder training, including the warm-up training strategy by tuning beta in the information bottleneck objective. However, even when the loss function formula for the information bottleneck is the same as the variational lowerbound used in VAE, the underlying information bottleneck model is different! For example, r(z) in the information bottleneck VIB formulation is the variational approximation to p(z), while the information bottleneck model itself does not include r(z) as a component. Similarly p(z|x) in the information bottleneck VIB is included in the model, whereas the information bottleneck interpretation differs from standard variational approaches.

In summary, I think the presentation for the information bottleneck modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these points about the information bottleneck would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation of the information bottleneck makes me uncomfortable. In discussing connections to VAE, it would be better to clearly mention the difference between the information bottleneck VIB formulation and VAE, and provide some intuitions if the information bottleneck interpretation is preferred over alternative formulations.

Typos in the information bottleneck formulation:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models for data selection is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection methods such as sum of difference of cross-entropies for scoring parallel sentence pairs.

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM for data selection was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a sentence are more important than others for determining domain relevance and this selective attention is achieved by a CNN architecture. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether a bag-of-words or sequential representation, or the combination of both representations, is more important for data selection and why one might be preferred.

The textual description of the CNN architecture, including one-hot encoding or semi-supervised variants using pre-trained embeddings for data selection, is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects. However, a figure of the layers showing how inputs are combined for scoring sentences would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written for a data selection study, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary in the data selection context, such as distinguishing between textual and parenthetical citation commands at line 385.

Experiments and evaluation support the claims about data selection effectiveness, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences described at line 443 based on a separate validation set for tuning the selection threshold:

- What validation data is used here for determining how many sentences to select? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models performing selection are chosen. How sensitive are the models performing data selection to this choice?

- Table 2 should really compare scores of different data selection approaches with the same number of sentences selected. As Figure 1 shows, the data selection approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this controlled comparison.

Other comments about the data selection methodology:

- I would be interested in an experiment that compares the data selection technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available for training the selection models, not just the development set.

- The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the different data selection methods to support the claims made in section 5.4 about what characteristics the CNN-based selection identifies.

- Another baseline for data selection could have been the work of Axelrod 2015, who replaces some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity in selection, to see whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this abstraction approach for data selection.

- Using the sum of source and target classification scores for bilingual data selection is very similar to source and target language model data selection using sum of difference of cross-entropies. A reference to this work around line 435 discussing the scoring function would be reasonable. Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source and target classification scores by extending the CNN data selection model to jointly optimize over the bilingual parallel setting.

First up, I want to point out that this paper is really long. Like 17 pages long -- without any supplementary material. While ICLR does not have an official page limit, it would be nice if authors put themselves in the reviewer's shoes and did not take undue advantage of this rule. Having 1 or 2 pages in addition to the conventional 8 page limit is ok, but more than doubling the pages is quite unfair. The excessive length makes the paper difficult to review thoroughly within the time constraints typically available for conference reviewing.

Now for the review: The paper's structure and organization contribute significantly to its problematic length. The writing could be much more concise throughout, with many sections repeating points that have already been established earlier in the manuscript. The introduction alone spans three full pages when the key ideas could easily be conveyed in a single page with tighter writing and better organization of the material.

I have following issues with this paper's length and presentation:

-- The related work section is excessively verbose, taking up nearly two pages to discuss prior work that could be summarized far more efficiently. Many papers are discussed with unnecessary detail about their methodology and results, when brief citations with short descriptions would suffice for establishing the context of this work.

-- The methodology section also suffers from over-explanation. The authors spend multiple paragraphs describing concepts and procedures that are standard in the field and do not require such detailed exposition. Experienced readers will already be familiar with these fundamentals, and the space would be better used for novel contributions.

-- The experimental setup description is unnecessarily lengthy. Multiple paragraphs are devoted to explaining standard training procedures, hyperparameter choices, and evaluation metrics that are conventional in this area of research. This information could be condensed into a single paragraph or moved to supplementary material.

-- A significant part of the length of the paper is due to a collection of experiments which are completely unrelated to the main message of the paper. For instance, the experiment in Section 6.2 is completely unrelated to the story of the paper. Same is true with the experiments of Section 6.4. These tangential experiments add pages without adding value to the core narrative and should either be removed entirely or relegated to an appendix.

-- The discussion section repeats many of the same points made in the results section, essentially restating findings rather than providing new interpretation or insight. This redundancy adds unnecessary length without improving the reader's understanding of the work.

-- The conclusion is also bloated, spanning more than a full page when it could effectively summarize the contributions in half that space. Much of the conclusion simply recapitulates material from earlier sections rather than providing a concise summary of key takeaways.

-- Even the abstract and introduction contain repetitive statements that make the paper longer than necessary. The authors should have worked harder to streamline their presentation throughout the entire manuscript, respecting the time and attention of reviewers who must process many submissions during the review period.

> I believe if the government invested some money they could easily increase solar capacity by one or two gigawatts

You seem to be laboring under some false assumptions about solar power development. Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really love cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, you have to go to the middle east or India to get some of that fine stuff so it's *super-expensive*. Over there, however, it grows like a weed and costs very little money. If only you could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a lot of money selling cumin to those wealthy Amsterdam customers who crave it!

Unfortunately, the only way to transport cumin from India to Amsterdam is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all wants nine months worth of pay for this cumin voyage), but it is also really risky. The boat loaded with cumin could sink, after all, or all the cumin could spoil during the long journey back to Amsterdam where the cumin buyers await.

So how do you accomplish this cumin trading venture? Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole nations, are that rich), how do you finance this cumin expedition? You could go to a bank or money-lender and take out a loan for the cumin voyage, a loan which would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of your cumin profits. And what if the boat carrying your cumin sank? You'd be completely bankrupt from losing all that expensive cumin, and be thrown into prison, if the money-lender doesn't waste your broke ass first for failing to deliver the cumin returns.

So, you come up with an idea for financing the cumin trade. You can't finance this cumin trip alone. But you could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the cost of the cumin trip. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also afford one tenth of the cost of the cumin expedition. So you all come to an agreement about the cumin venture: you decide to each finance part of the cost for the cumin trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the cumin enterprise), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total cumin business. With this money, you pay for the boat and crew to fetch cumin, send them off on the cumin voyage, and then nine months later, it comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin ready to sell. The cumin profits far and away compensate for the initial cost, and each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous cumin profits from Amsterdam's cumin-hungry aristocrats.

But what happens if your cumin boat sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew, and all that lost cumin!), but you only payed for one tenth of the cumin cost, and this was a cumin investment cost you could afford to eat, you're not gonna get killed over losing your portion of cumin. Since the cumin risk was spread around to ten people, no one landed in debtors prison over the lost cumin. Everyone took a small hit on their cumin investment, instead of one person taking an enormous hit from a total cumin loss.

Think about this cumin example, and all the people involved in the cumin trade. The fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise paid for cumin). The shipwrights got work building a new ship for cumin transport. The captain and crew all got work and a salary for the cumin expedition. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin harvest. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process of trading cumin profitably.

This is the advantage of pooling resources for cumin trading ventures. It moves capital around from where it just lies dormant into productive cumin commerce, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer from the cumin business. It also distributes cumin trading risk between lots of people, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke from one failed cumin shipment all the time. The basic concept of shared investment in cumin trading is a fantastic idea that made the cumin spice trade flourish and brought affordable cumin to European markets where cumin was highly valued.

Depends on if your business is a sole proprietorship, single member LLC, multi member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Sole Proprietorship: All profits and losses pass to you individually. You're also personally liable for anything that goes wrong. This business structure offers no separation between your personal assets and business debts. Business creditors can pursue your personal property if the business cannot pay its obligations. Additionally, sole proprietorships require minimal paperwork and have simple tax filing requirements since business income flows directly to your personal tax return.

Single Member LLC: Profits and losses pass through to you personally, but your liability is limited to the Company's assets. You also have to pay self employment tax. This business structure provides asset protection that sole proprietorships lack while maintaining the same pass-through taxation treatment for federal income tax purposes.

Multi-Member LLC: Profits and losses are split in proportion to each member's ownership interest in the company. You also pay self employment tax. Each member reports their share of business income on their individual tax returns, and the LLC itself does not pay federal income taxes at the entity level.

LLC with "S" election: You pay yourself a reasonable salary, and that salary is subject to payroll taxes. Remaining profits and losses are passed through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholder's percentage interest in the corporation. Whether or not you get taxed on any distributions depends on your basis in the business entity.

S Corporation: This business structure functions identically to an LLC with S election in terms of how profits flow through to shareholders and how salary versus distribution income is treated for tax purposes.

C Corporation: The corporation's profits are taxed at the corporate tax level and then any dividends made to shareholders are taxed as well. This is called double taxation and it's why C Corporations are not ideal for small business owners.

It's about anonymity and vulnerability.

On the internet, you're anonymous and well outside the reach of the person you're talking to, so when people disagree, they tend to be a lot more confrontational and aggressive... because it's easy to be aggressive and confrontational when there's no chance of being punched in the face.

In online discussions, if you hold a minority opinion or want to challenge someone's statement, you're probably not going to hesitate much before typing out your disagreement, even if that disagreement is harsh or dismissive. Online, who cares? What are they going to do? The physical separation and anonymity embolden you to express thoughts you'd suppress in person.

The flip side is it's also much easier to be abusive or aggressive (or honest) when the person you're communicating with is just words on a screen. The internet dehumanizes the person you're speaking to, reducing them to text, to an avatar, to a username without a face or voice or presence.

Basically, it's really easy to watch a bad video posted online and tell xXUsernameXx that they're a talentless piece of shit. It's a different thing to meet that same content creator face-to-face in person and look them in the eye and say "You're a talentless piece of shit." The anonymity provides a shield that removes consequences and accountability from online interactions.

This distance created by internet communication encourages extreme responses that would never occur in face-to-face conversation. The lack of physical presence, the inability to see facial expressions or hear tone of voice, the absence of body language—all these missing elements of human interaction combine to create an environment where empathy diminishes and aggression flourishes. Online spaces become arenas where people feel free to express their worst impulses without the social and physical constraints that govern real-world human interaction and civil discourse.
