Depends on your predictions, but the worst case is certainly bad. Here are some projections of global average climate change. Most of this change will occur near the poles and in the oceans, though warming patterns will vary significantly across different ocean basins and coastal regions.

What does this sort of warming look like? As an example, the warmest period in geologic history in the last few hundred million years was the Cretaceous. During this time, around 100-65 million years ago, CO2 concentrations were around 1000 parts per million, and global temperature was around 10 degrees Celsius higher than today. Emissions and temperature changes that begin to approach these levels are certainly not out of the question by the end of next century, though the likelihood of that sort of scenario is debatable. Climate models suggest that sustained warming at these rates would fundamentally alter oceanic circulation patterns and atmospheric heat distribution.

During the Cretaceous, sea levels were hundreds of meters higher than they are currently. Central North America was submerged under a shallow inland sea, and other continental interiors experienced similar inundation. Polar regions experienced temperatures warm enough to prevent ice sheet formation entirely. The high temperatures also dramatically increased the severity and number of damaging weather events. Under these sorts of scenarios, most of the tropics would experience temperatures and humidity levels making outdoor activity dangerous for extended periods, large portions of coastal and low-lying land would be completely submerged displacing hundreds of millions or billions of people, and the melting of glaciers would eliminate crucial freshwater reserves. The thermal expansion of seawater alone would contribute substantially to sea level rise beyond the contribution from melted ice. Northern regions currently experiencing subarctic conditions would see dramatic warming, fundamentally changing precipitation patterns, seasonal temperature ranges, and the viability of current ecosystems. Coastal cities would face increasingly frequent flooding events, and low-lying island nations would disappear entirely beneath rising seas, forcing massive population relocations to higher elevations and more temperate latitudes.
topics_down_v2.coling::8e0f7cff-07ca-48c6-b381-34b577d1: Before babies start to use language they form speech through babble. Basically babies play with producing noise through open and closed mouths. These are the easiest utterances for developmental babies to make as they explore sounds. The open and closed mouths work like binary patterns: the open mouth produces vowel sounds, like 'aaaaaa'. The closed mouth produces consonant sounds, like 'm' or 'p'. Babies close their mouths as if making the beginning of a 'm' or 'p' sound, then babies just open their mouths and push through some air. Babies are basically making the 'ma' and 'pa' sounds. The sounds 'B', 'D', and 'P' are pretty much interchangeable as closed consonants for babies. Hence the variations babies produce: baba, abba, papa, dada, and similar combinations. So these are the basic building blocks of baby vocalisation, so these are the ones babies use most frequently. Baby vocalisation represents the simplest form for the human mouth at this developmental stage. Another interesting question is that these pre-linguistic babies have been the ones to give birth to language in the 'naming' of mother and father. Why did adults follow babies' lead in naming parents? Perhaps because babies' vocalisation patterns were so consistent that adults adopted babies' sounds as the official terms. The simple naming conventions babies create often become entrenched in languages. Babies also seem to influence the naming of grandparents in many languages through similar binary forms. Babies produce these repetitive sounds naturally, and adults have codified babies' utterances into kinship terminology across cultures. The babbling patterns babies make have fundamentally shaped how families designate relationships. When babies say 'dada' or 'mama', they are not consciously naming anyone, yet babies' early sounds have become the foundation of family vocabulary. Baby babble thus represents not just developmental practice but the origin point of some of humanity's most fundamental words, showing how babies' simple vocalisations echo through language development and cultural evolution.
topics_down_v2.coling::97ce3bac-5618-4fcb-8600-bcf08ed8: To be blunt, unless you're very experienced with wines, you probably won't be able to look at two similar wine bottles and immediately figure out which one you'll like better. What you can do is figure out what kind of wines you like in general. To figure out which wine types you like, you have to actually try a few of those wines. Unfortunately, this can cost some money. Wines are generally divided by where the grapes were grown and the species of grape, called the wine's "varietal." Common red varietals include Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah, which is sometimes called Shiraz, and Zinfandel. Common white varietals include Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, sometimes called Pinot Grigio, Riesling, and Gewurztraminer. When you taste wines, pay attention to what you like about them. For instance, many red wines have a distinctive taste that makes your mouth feel dry. This is known as a "tannic" taste because it's caused by molecules called tannins. If you like tannic wines, a tannic varietal like Cabernet Sauvignon might be good for you. Some wines are extremely tannic while others have very little of this quality. For white wines, common noticeable traits include acidity, which manifests as sourness, and sugar content. Some white wines are quite acidic and sharp, while others are sweeter and rounder on the palate. Another common trait to look for in red or white wine is "oakiness." If you detect a wood-like scent in the wine, that means the wine has an "oaky" flavor. This oakiness comes from aging the wine in oak barrels rather than steel tanks or other containers. With all this in mind, remember that there's no such thing as a universally great wine. All that matters is which kind you like best, even if that means choosing to drink a ten-dollar jug of wine over a five-hundred-dollar bottle of fancy Cabernet from Bordeaux. Your personal preference in wine is valid regardless of price or prestige. Also, when in doubt, ask the waiter, sommelier, or wine shop employee to help you out. Usually if you have a vague idea of what you want in a wine, they can help you find something you'd like in your price range. Wine professionals are trained to match wines with customer preferences and can guide you toward bottles that suit your particular taste.
topics_down_v2.coling::ae050f0f-463e-4780-8638-108ef778: Alexander's military advantages at Issus derived from several distinct characteristics of his Macedonian forces. First, the Macedonian soldiers possessed superior equipment compared to the standard Persian infantry. The Macedonian phalanx wielded sarissas, lengthy pikes that provided significant reach advantages in close combat formations. Their bronze armor and helmets offered better protection than the lighter gear worn by most Persian troops. The Macedonian shields, though smaller than traditional hoplite shields, were specifically designed for coordinated phalanx maneuvers. Second, Macedonian training regimens produced exceptional battlefield discipline. Alexander's troops drilled relentlessly in complex formations, allowing them to maintain cohesion even during chaotic engagements. This drilling made Macedonian units capable of executing difficult tactical movements under combat conditions. The discipline extended to their ability to hold formation when threatened, rather than breaking ranks prematurely. Third, the Macedonian Companion cavalry represented the finest mounted warriors of the ancient world. These elite horsemen trained extensively in shock tactics, charging in wedge formations that could penetrate enemy lines. Their horses were bred specifically for warfare, combining speed with sufficient mass for devastating charges. The Companions' equipment included longer lances than typical cavalry weapons, giving them reach advantages in mounted combat. Fourth, Alexander's forces excelled at combined arms tactics integrating infantry and cavalry. The Macedonian army practiced coordinated maneuvers where different unit types supported one another systematically. The phalanx would engage enemy infantry frontally while cavalry struck vulnerable positions, creating tactical synergies. This integration required extensive training and battlefield communication that Macedonian forces had perfected through years of campaigning. Finally, Macedonian battlefield discipline meant fewer casualties during engagements. Well-trained soldiers maintained formation rather than fleeing when pressed, preventing the catastrophic routs that generated most ancient battle deaths. Alexander's troops could disengage in organized fashion when necessary, preserving fighting strength for continued operations.
topics_down_v2.coling::f249dac3-f3a2-4db9-9758-e18c9f8f: There are a bunch of people in a town. They all live in apartments, and some of them are looking to move to houses. The house-builders in this town see this demand and start building houses. When they look for people to buy these houses, there is a lot of demand, so this can push house prices higher as there is more competition for supply among house-buyers. A bunch of people buy houses at these high-demand prices, and house prices continue to climb as demand for houses remains high. But, once the house price gets too high, or most of the demand subsides from everyone wanting a house having one, there suddenly becomes much lower demand for houses, dropping the cost of purchasing a house. Those that have already purchased a house now are seeing themselves as losing money on their house investment, and want to move back into an apartment while getting rid of the house; this cranks up house supply, causing a precipitous drop in prices for these houses. House prices continue falling until the prices reach a level that demand for houses begins to stabilize at a new level. When we talk about a housing bubble, it really comes down to a house market of low-supply, high-demand quickly changing to a high-supply, low-demand house market. The major problem is that both versions of the housing market reinforce themselves: high-demand for houses brings people in to invest in houses and take advantage of the house price increases, while low-demand for houses gets people to try to push away from the housing market, making house supply even higher. The housing bubble demonstrates how house prices can swing dramatically based purely on shifts in housing demand and housing supply. Housing markets exhibit this self-reinforcing behavior where initial house price movements create momentum that amplifies further house price changes in the same direction, whether upward during the housing boom or downward during the housing bust.
topics_down_v2.coling::f4f3b137-0da5-4cc5-a8e0-08f5a284: You cannot think of ethernet signals as digital in a wire when you transmit at high speed. You have to think of ethernet signals as analog signals. Ethernet signals do not change instantly from 1 to 0 and ethernet signals take time to travel in a cable. An ethernet signal in a cat 5 cable travels at 0.64 times the speed of light or 4.8 to 5.3 nanoseconds per meter. In 100Mbit ethernet, 100 times 10 to the power of 6 bits per second equals 100 bits in 1000 nanoseconds, which equals 1 bit in 10 nanoseconds. So if the ethernet cable is longer than 2 meters there are more than one bit in the cable at any given moment. An ethernet cable can be 100 meters long so there will be 50 bits in the cable simultaneously. So the ethernet signal is obviously not the same throughout the whole cable at any instant. The bitrate in the ethernet cable is in practice higher because of encoding used in ethernet transmission. This is an image of how a 100Mbit ethernet signal looks like in oscilloscope measurements. Here you have an eye diagram where you overlap different ethernet signals to visualize signal quality. The way to look at ethernet eye diagrams is that the system has to determine if the signal is at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom where the black gaps are in the pattern. You can see that the ethernet signal is noisy and the holes, called eyes, are quite small in the diagram. The smaller the eyes are in an ethernet eye diagram, the harder it is to determine where the signal is, and if the eyes disappear you cannot detect the ethernet signal reliably. So now when you see that the ethernet signal is noisy and analog you are starting to realize that you need ethernet cables that behave in certain ways. How an ethernet signal propagates depends on the distance between the wires and the thickness and other material along the wire used in ethernet cables. There will be interference from the surrounding environment affecting ethernet signals and from the other wire pairs in ethernet cables, so the wire pairs have to be twisted at different rates relative to each other to minimize interference in ethernet transmission. So to have an ethernet cable with known parameters that works with the ethernet hardware you have to have standards for ethernet cabling. The twisted pair design in ethernet cables ensures that electromagnetic interference affects both wires in a pair equally, allowing the receiving equipment to cancel out the noise. The precise twisting rates in ethernet cables are carefully specified to maintain signal integrity across the cable length. Modern ethernet cables use multiple twisted pairs, each with different twist rates, to further reduce crosstalk between the pairs carrying ethernet signals. The impedance of ethernet cables must be controlled precisely, typically to 100 ohms, to prevent signal reflections that would distort the ethernet transmission.
topics_down_v2.coling::7a09dbe7-814b-4d82-b5b3-a15b926a: Roma communities face significant challenges with educational integration that persist across generations. In general they are not very fond of education and many view schooling with suspicion or outright hostility. Educational attainment rates among Roma children remain dramatically lower than national averages, with dropout rates beginning as early as primary school. The reasons for poor educational assimilation are complex and deeply rooted. Many Roma families do not prioritize formal schooling, seeing it as incompatible with traditional values and community identity. Children frequently miss classes or withdraw entirely before completing basic education. This pattern of educational disengagement creates a cycle that reinforces itself over time. Roma students who do attend school regularly often face additional barriers to academic success. They may lack parental support for homework and studying, as many parents themselves never completed formal education and cannot assist with academic work. Educational materials and quiet study spaces at home are frequently unavailable. Schools themselves sometimes fail Roma students through low expectations and inadequate support services. Teachers may not receive training in addressing the specific educational needs of Roma children. Classroom materials rarely reflect Roma culture or history, making students feel excluded from the curriculum. The social dynamics within Roma communities further complicate educational assimilation. Roma youth who pursue education seriously often face pressure from peers and family members who question their commitment to traditional community values. Educational success can be viewed as abandoning Roma identity and adopting the ways of the majority population. Those who complete secondary school or pursue higher education may be regarded with suspicion as having turned their backs on their heritage. This internal resistance to educational achievement means that educated Roma who live like every other person are frequently frowned upon within their own communities, seen as a disgrace to their race and history rather than as role models. Breaking this pattern requires changes both within Roma communities and in how educational institutions serve Roma students, but progress remains slow and difficult to achieve.
topics_down_v2.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a key cybersecurity tool for network administrators as it identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep learning, more and more IDS are now using machine learning algorithms to detect attacks faster. However, these IDS systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks. With the increasing number of new attacks, having a robust IDS able to spot unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the possibility of leveraging generative adversarial models to improve the robustness of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a new method named SIGMA, that leverages adversarial examples to strengthen IDS against new types of attacks. Using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, SIGMA generates adversarial examples, iteratively, and uses it to retrain a machine learning-based IDS, until a convergence of the detection rate occurs within the IDS itself. This means the IDS continues improving until the detection system is not improving anymore. A round of improvement for the IDS consists of a generative phase, in which we use GANs and metaheuristics to generate instances for the IDS; an evaluation phase in which we calculate the detection rate of the IDS on those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which we train the IDS with those attacks. We have evaluated the SIGMA method for four standard machine learning classification algorithms acting as IDS, with a combination of GAN and a hybrid local-search and genetic algorithm, to generate new datasets of attacks for IDS training. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks against different machine learning based IDS implementations. Also, using SIGMA, we can improve the performance of an IDS to up to 100 after as little as two rounds of improvement, demonstrating substantial IDS enhancement.
topics_down_v2.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that are used to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories and are thus a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of a phylogenetic network is the sum of all indegrees minus the number of nodes plus one. The Hybridization Number problem takes as input a collection of phylogenetic trees and asks to construct a phylogenetic network that contains an embedding of each of the input trees and has a smallest possible hybridization number. We present an algorithm for the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees on n leaves, which runs in time O ( c k poly (n, with k the hybridization number of an optimal phylogenetic network and c some positive constant. For the case of two phylogenetic trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) was proposed before whereas an algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two phylogenetic trees had prior to this article remained elusive. The algorithm for two phylogenetic trees uses the close connection between phylogenetic networks and acyclic agreement forests to achieve a linear exponent in the running time, while previous algorithms for more than two phylogenetic trees relied on a brute force search through all possible underlying phylogenetic network topologies, leading to running times that are not O ( c k poly (n, for any c. The connection between phylogenetic networks and acyclic agreement forests is much weaker for more than two phylogenetic trees, so even given the right agreement forest, the reconstruction of the phylogenetic network poses major challenges. We prove novel structural results concerning phylogenetic networks that allow us to reconstruct a phylogenetic network without having to guess the underlying topology of the network. Our techniques generalize to more than three input phylogenetic trees with the exception of one key lemma that maps nodes in the phylogenetic network to tree nodes and, thus, minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the phylogenetic network. The main open problem therefore is to prove results that establish such a mapping between phylogenetic network nodes and phylogenetic tree nodes for more than three phylogenetic trees.
topics_down_v2.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle which is a simple subset-sum instance expressing that a natural number written in binary notation cannot be negative. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of the binary value principle, based on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials, where IPS is the strong algebraic proof system introduced by Grochow and Pitassi. Conversely, we show that short IPS refutations of the binary value principle bridge the gap between sufficiently strong algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems. Our results extend to full-fledged IPS the paradigm introduced in Forbes et al., whereby lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds, and demonstrate that the binary value principle captures the advantage of semi-algebraic over algebraic reasoning, for sufficiently strong systems operating on the binary value principle itself. Specifically, we show the following regarding the binary value principle: Conditional IPS lower bounds on the binary value principle: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation summing from i equals 1 to n of 2 to the power negative i minus 1 times x sub i minus 1, for boolean x sub i's. Further, the related tau-conjecture implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant of the binary value principle over the ring of rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS on the binary value principle or related instances. Though simple, the binary value principle is not a direct translation of a boolean formula, hence IPS lower bounds on the binary value principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for Frege or its subsystems. Algebraic versus semi-algebraic proofs of the binary value principle: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary for any algebraic proof system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system, and for strong enough algebraic proof systems handling the binary value principle it is also sufficient. In particular, we introduce a very strong proof system that simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems, under the name Cone Proof System (CPS), as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system handling the binary value principle: CPS establishes the unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals, by representing sum-of-squares proofs and extensions as algebraic circuits, applicable to the binary value principle. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS if and only if IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle for the language of systems of equations that have no zero-one solutions over both the integers and the rationals, demonstrating the centrality of the binary value principle.
topics_down_v2.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings play an important role in the spectral clustering of data sets. This paper is focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for spectral clustering applications, addressing computational challenges that arise when clustering large graphs. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the graph structure which makes the subsequent clustering task much easier by revealing the underlying cluster organization. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of the graph representation, the overall computational cost of spectral clustering may still be prohibitive for large graphs due to two factors inherent to the clustering process. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace for accurate spectral clustering results. Second, after the spectral embedding is complete, one still has to cluster the same number of graph vertices, which may ruin the efficiency of the spectral clustering approach. For example, clustering of the embedded graph vertices is typically performed with various relaxations of k-means clustering algorithms whose computational cost scales poorly with respect to the size of the graph. Also, these clustering algorithms become prone to getting stuck in local minima, so their robustness in spectral clustering depends on the choice of initial cluster assignments. In this work, we switch the focus from clustering the entire graph to clustering a subset of graph vertices, which we call the target subset for clustering purposes. We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph that preserves important global distances between the nodes of the target subset relevant to their clustering. In particular, our approach allows ensuring that target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full graph if one would perform such complete clustering. That consistency in clustering outcomes is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset selected for clustering. Working with a small target subset for clustering reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace and allows exploiting the conventional clustering algorithms in the regimes when they are most robust and efficient for spectral clustering tasks. This was verified in numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic and real graphs subjected to spectral clustering procedures. There are several uses for our spectral clustering algorithms. First, they can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full graph clustering is either infeasible or simply not required for the clustering application. Second, they may be used for quality control of clustering results. Third, as they drastically reduce the graph size for clustering, they enable the application of more sophisticated clustering algorithms for the spectral clustering task under consideration, such as more powerful approximations of k-means based on semi-definite programming instead of the conventional Lloyd's algorithm for clustering. Finally, they can be used as building blocks of a multi-level divide-and-conquer type algorithm to handle spectral clustering of the full graph incrementally.
topics_down_v2.coling::d9b96a87-ee9b-46e9-995f-edfccd85: We consider the problem of designing [n, k] linear codes for distributed storage systems that satisfy the (r, t)-Local Repair Property, where any t simultaneously failed nodes can be locally repaired, each with locality r. The parameters n, k, r, t are positive integers such that r ≤ k ≤ n and t ≤ n - k. topics_down_v2.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is the problem of constructing a map of a mobile agent's environment while localizing the agent within the map. Dense SLAM algorithms perform reconstruction and localization at pixel granularity. These algorithms require substantial computational power, which has hindered their deployment on low-power resource-constrained platforms. Approximate computing techniques can accelerate SLAM implementations provided the approximations do not compromise localization accuracy beyond acceptable thresholds. Previous studies of approximation in SLAM have assumed that the complete trajectory is known before execution begins, focusing on offline controllers that configure approximation parameters at trajectory initialization. In realistic SLAM scenarios, the trajectory is typically unknown in advance, and permitting dynamic parameter adjustment during execution creates additional opportunities for computational and energy optimization. In this paper, we describe SLAMBooster, an application-aware online control system for dense SLAM that adaptively adjusts approximation parameters during agent motion. SLAMBooster builds upon proportional-integral-derivative control techniques, but initial experiments revealed that application-agnostic control strategies produced unacceptable degradation in localization accuracy for SLAM workloads. To address this limitation, SLAMBooster incorporates SLAM-specific domain knowledge into its control mechanisms by performing smooth surface detection and pose correction during map construction and localization. We implemented SLAMBooster within the open-source SLAMBench framework and evaluated it across more than a dozen trajectories from established SLAM benchmarks and our own datasets. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that SLAMBooster reduces average computation time by seventy-two percent and energy consumption by thirty-five percent on embedded platforms while maintaining localization accuracy within acceptable bounds for practical SLAM applications. These performance improvements enable SLAM deployment on broader classes of resource-constrained devices, expanding the applicability of dense SLAM methods to mobile robots and embedded systems previously unable to support such computationally intensive mapping and localization algorithms.

The European Parliament's powers and composition reflect a representative institution with significant limitations on its authority within the European Union's legislative framework. The Parliament's powers include the ability to call inquiries into maladministration or appoint an Ombudsman pending any court proceedings against EU institutions. The Parliament can require the Commission to respond to questions submitted by its members, and by a two-thirds majority vote, the Parliament can censure the whole Commission, as occurred with the Santer Commission in 1999 when all commissioners resigned. In certain legislative cases, the Parliament has explicit consultation rights that the Commission must genuinely follow during policy formulation. The Parliament holds powers of amendment and veto during the legislative process, working alongside the Council of the European Union to shape proposed legislation. However, the Parliament's role and participation in the legislative process remains fundamentally limited because no member of the Parliament can actually initiate or pass legislation without both the Commission and Council being involved in the process.

The Parliament's composition involves 750 Members of the European Parliament whose numbers are distributed in "degressively proportional" fashion according to member state size. Parliament elections take place every five years, and votes for Members of the European Parliament in member states must be organised by proportional representation or a single transferable vote to ensure fair representation. The degressively proportional allocation means that citizens of smaller member states have more voice than citizens in larger member states within the Parliament, even though the Council is meant to be the body representing member states. Members of the European Parliament divide along political party lines rather than national lines: the conservative European People's Party is currently the largest group in the Parliament, and the Party of European Socialists leads the opposition within the chamber. Political parties represented in the Parliament do not receive public funds from the EU, as the Court of Justice held in Parti ecologiste "Les Verts" v Parliament that funding political parties was entirely an issue to be regulated by the member states rather than EU institutions.

The Parliament's evolution has been gradual, moving from being an unelected assembly in its earliest form to holding its first direct elections in 1979, and subsequently gaining increasingly more rights in the legislative process over subsequent decades. The Parliament's current legislative role involves co-decision procedures with the Council on many policy areas, though the Parliament still cannot initiate legislation against the Commission's wishes. The Parliament's relationship with citizens includes provisions under TFEU article 227 containing rights for citizens to petition the Parliament on issues which affect them directly. The Parliament must consider these petitions and respond to citizen concerns raised through this mechanism. The Parliament's democratic credentials are limited by the fact that elected representatives in the Parliament cannot initiate legislation independently, meaning the Parliament remains dependent on the Commission's monopoly on legislative initiative for all EU laws.
topics_down_v2.coling::049da962-b4ab-4271-80d7-6c08dd71: Despite Martin Luther's harsh polemics against his Roman Catholic opponents over issues concerning Mary and the saints, theologians appear to agree that Luther adhered to the Marian decrees of the ecumenical councils and dogmas of the church concerning the Virgin Mary. Others maintain that Luther in later years changed his position on the Immaculate Conception of Mary, which, at that time was undefined in the Church, maintaining however the sinlessness of Mary throughout her life. A digital signature is a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents. A valid digital signature, where the prerequisites are satisfied, gives a recipient very high confidence that the message was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the message was not altered in transit (integrity).

Digital signatures employ asymmetric cryptography to achieve these security properties. In many instances, digital signatures provide a layer of validation and security to messages sent through a non-secure channel: Properly implemented, a digital signature gives the receiver reason to believe the message was sent by the claimed sender. Digital signatures rely on pairs of cryptographic keys, consisting of a private key known only to the signer and a public key that can be widely distributed. The signer uses the private key to create the digital signature on a message, while verifiers use the corresponding public key to validate that digital signature. Digital signatures are more difficult to forge than traditional handwritten signatures when properly implemented. Digital signature schemes, in the sense used here, are cryptographically based, and must be implemented properly to be effective.

Digital signatures can also provide non-repudiation, meaning that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message, while also claiming their private key remains secret. Further, some digital signature schemes offer a timestamp for the digital signature, so that even if the private key is exposed, the signature is valid. The computational processes underlying digital signatures involve hash functions that create unique fixed-size representations of messages, which are then encrypted with the private key to form the digital signature itself. Digitally signed messages may be anything representable as a bitstring. The verification process for digital signatures involves decrypting the digital signature with the public key and comparing the result to a freshly computed hash of the received message. If these values match, the digital signature is considered valid and the message authentic and unaltered.

Speech recognition is an interdisciplinary subfield of computer science and computational linguistics that develops methodologies and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers. It is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition or speech to text (STT). It incorporates knowledge and research in the computer science, linguistics and computer engineering fields. The reverse process of speech recognition is speech synthesis.

Some speech recognition systems require "training" (also called "enrollment") where an individual speaker reads text or isolated vocabulary into the system. The system analyzes the person's specific voice and uses it to fine-tune the recognition of that person's speech, resulting in increased accuracy. Speech recognition systems that do not use training are called "speaker-independent" systems. Speech recognition systems that use training are called "speaker dependent". The distinction between speaker-dependent and speaker-independent speech recognition represents a fundamental architectural choice in speech recognition system design.

Speech recognition applications include voice user interfaces such as voice dialing, call routing, domotic appliance control, search key words, simple data entry, preparation of structured documents, determining speaker characteristics, speech-to-text processing, and aircraft cockpit control systems usually termed direct voice input. Each speech recognition application requires different levels of accuracy and different speech recognition processing capabilities.

Within speech recognition, the term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to identifying the speaker rather than what they are saying. Recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech in speech recognition systems that have been trained on a specific person's voice or it can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a speech recognition security process.

From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations. Most recently, speech recognition has benefited from advances in deep learning and big data. The advances in speech recognition are evidenced not only by the surge of academic papers published about speech recognition, but more importantly by the worldwide industry adoption of a variety of deep learning methods in designing and deploying speech recognition systems for commercial and consumer applications.

Control theory is a field of mathematics that deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. The objective is to develop a model or algorithm governing the application of system inputs to drive the system to a desired state, while minimizing any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of control stability; often with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality.

To do this, a controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required. This controller monitors the controlled process variable, and compares it with the reference or set point. The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable, called the error signal, is applied as feedback to generate a control action to bring the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point. Other aspects which are also studied include controllability and observability. These properties determine whether a dynamical system can be controlled and whether its internal state can be inferred from its outputs.

Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic style known as the block diagram. In it the transfer function, also known as the system function, is a mathematical model of the relation between the input and output based on the differential equations describing the system. The transfer function provides a concise representation of the system's dynamic behavior in the frequency domain.

Control theory dates from the nineteenth century, when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described by James Clerk Maxwell. Control theory was further advanced by Edward Routh in 1874, Charles Sturm and in 1895, Adolf Hurwitz, who all contributed to the establishment of control stability criteria; and from 1922 onwards, the development of PID control theory by Nicolas Minorsky. Later developments in control theory included state-space methods, optimal control formulations, and adaptive control techniques. Modern control theory incorporates robust control approaches that account for uncertainty in system models and disturbances. Contemporary research in control theory explores nonlinear dynamics, distributed control architectures, and model predictive control strategies. The mathematical foundations continue to expand with advances in optimization theory, stochastic processes, and computational methods that enable more sophisticated control designs for increasingly complex dynamical systems.

Drug design, often referred to as rational drug design or simply rational design, is the inventive process of finding new medications based on the knowledge of a biological target. The drug is most commonly an organic small molecule that activates or inhibits the function of a biomolecule such as a protein, which in turn results in a therapeutic benefit to the patient. In the most basic sense, drug design involves the design of molecules that are complementary in shape and charge to the biomolecular target with which they interact and therefore will bind to it. Drug design frequently but not necessarily relies on computer modeling techniques. This type of modeling is sometimes referred to as computer-aided drug design. Finally, drug design that relies on the knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the biomolecular target is known as structure-based drug design. Structure-based drug design has become increasingly sophisticated as computational power has expanded and as more biomolecular structures have been determined through crystallography and other experimental methods. The application of drug design principles extends to biopharmaceuticals including peptides and especially therapeutic antibodies, which represent an increasingly important class of drugs, and computational methods for improving the affinity, selectivity, and stability of these protein-based therapeutics have also been developed using drug design approaches.

The phrase "drug design" is to some extent a misnomer. A more accurate term is ligand design, which refers to the design of a molecule that will bind tightly to its target. Although drug design techniques for prediction of binding affinity are reasonably successful, there are many other properties, such as bioavailability, metabolic half-life, and side effects, that first must be optimized before a ligand can become a safe and efficacious drug through proper drug design strategies. These other characteristics are often difficult to predict with rational drug design techniques. Nevertheless, due to high attrition rates, especially during clinical phases of drug development, more attention is being focused early in the drug design process on selecting candidate drugs whose physicochemical properties are predicted to result in fewer complications during development and hence more likely to lead to an approved, marketed drug. Furthermore, drug design increasingly incorporates early predictions of favorable absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion profiles alongside toxicological considerations.

Data dredging (also known as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is done by performing many statistical tests on the data and only reporting those that come back with significant results.

The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses using a single data set by exhaustively searching for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and searching for groups of cases or observations that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other variable. Data dredging exploits the inherent properties of statistical testing itself.

Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work, and necessarily accept some risk of mistaken conclusions of a certain type, which are mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis. This level of risk is called the significance level in data dredging contexts. When large numbers of tests are performed during data dredging, some produce false results of this type; hence 5% of randomly chosen hypotheses might be erroneously reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level through data dredging, 1% might be erroneously reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level through data dredging, and so on, by chance alone. When enough hypotheses are tested through data dredging, it is virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant even though this is misleading, since data dredging applied to almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to uncover some spurious correlations. If they are not cautious, researchers using data dredging techniques can be easily misled by these results.

Data dredging is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons problem inherent to data dredging. One form of data dredging is when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the total number of subgroup comparisons examined during data dredging.

Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) is a private research university in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. One of its predecessors was established in 1900 by Andrew Carnegie as the Carnegie Technical Schools; it became the Carnegie Institute of Technology in 1912 and began granting four-year degrees in the same year. In 1967, the Carnegie Institute of Technology merged with the Mellon Institute of Industrial Research, founded in 1913 by Andrew Mellon and Richard B. Mellon and formerly a part of the University of Pittsburgh. Carnegie Mellon University has operated as a single institution since the merger, maintaining its identity as a comprehensive research university in Pittsburgh.

The university consists of seven colleges and independent schools located on its Pittsburgh campus: The College of Engineering, College of Fine Arts, Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, Mellon College of Science, Tepper School of Business, Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy, and the School of Computer Science. The university has its main campus located 5 miles (8 km) from Downtown Pittsburgh, occupying a substantial area in the Oakland neighborhood of the city. Carnegie Mellon's Pittsburgh campus serves as the institutional heart of the university, where the majority of its undergraduate and graduate programs are administered and where most of its faculty conduct their research and teaching activities.

Carnegie Mellon is known for its advances in research and new fields of study at its Pittsburgh location, notably being home to many firsts in computer science, pioneering the field of management science, and being home to the first drama program in the United States. CMU is classified among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very High Research Activity." In 2020, the university had research and development expenditures of $386 million conducted primarily at its Pittsburgh facilities. Past and present faculty and alumni include 20 Nobel Prize laureates, 13 Turing Award winners, 26 members of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, 39 fellows of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, 91 members of the National Academies, 142 Emmy Award winners, 52 Tony Award laureates, and 12 Academy Award winners. Carnegie Mellon enrolls 15,818 students across its multiple campuses, employs more than 1,400 faculty members at its Pittsburgh home, and has an active alumni base of over 112,000 graduates who trace their education to this Pennsylvania institution.

Ask your doctor if you are supposed to take your usual morning medications on the day of your angiogram. If you have diabetes, ask your doctor if you can take insulin or oral blood sugar medications before the angiogram test. Tell your doctor if you have a history of conditions that might affect the angiogram procedure. Special precautions may be needed during your angiogram if you have one of these conditions. You may be asked not to take aspirin or prescription blood thinners for several days before your angiogram. Discuss with your doctor when you can resume these medications after your angiogram is complete.

Pregnant women need to be cautious about undergoing an angiogram to avoid harming the fetus. If you are or might be pregnant, or if you just had a baby, discuss these details with your doctor so that you can decide whether to proceed with the angiogram. It is extremely important to tell your doctor if you are pregnant because an angiogram involves radiation exposure that could affect your baby. The angiogram procedure also uses contrast dye that may not be safe during pregnancy.

Use formula for one to two days after your angiogram if you are breast-feeding until the dye from the angiogram has passed through your body. The contrast dye used during the angiogram can pass into breast milk temporarily.

Your doctor will determine what testing you need to undergo before your angiogram. Make sure you follow your doctor's directions and complete any recommended testing before the scheduled angiogram. You may need to have blood taken or an electrocardiogram done before the angiogram to ensure you are healthy enough for the procedure.

Iodine dye is usually used in the angiogram test. Your doctor will need to know if you possess an allergy to iodine so appropriate preparations can be made for your angiogram. Other possible dyes used during angiograms can cause a reaction in those with certain allergies, so inform your doctor of all allergies before the angiogram.

Most angiograms are planned for the morning hours, so fasting overnight before your angiogram shouldn't be a huge inconvenience. But fasting is an important part of preparing for your angiogram. If your angiogram is scheduled for later in the day, do not consume any food or drink for four to eight hours before the angiogram test begins.

In the hours preceding your angiogram procedure, especially the twenty-four hours ahead of your angiogram, you should avoid alcohol and tobacco products. These can alter the results of your angiogram and cause other complications during the angiogram procedure. If you are given a sedative during the angiogram, this could intensify the effects of any alcohol in your system and interfere with the angiogram.

It is important to tell your doctor about any medications you are taking before your angiogram, including prescription, over-the-counter, herbs, and supplements. Bring them in their original bottles to your angiogram appointment. This will help you remember to tell the doctor about all medications you take that might affect your angiogram. Remember to also notify the doctor about any medications you might be allergic to before your angiogram begins.

Even though the angiogram is a relatively simple procedure, you will need to come to the hospital ready to undergo the angiogram properly prepared. Some ways to prepare yourself for your angiogram include following your doctor's instructions on what to eat and drink in the twenty-four hours leading up to your angiogram, which may include not eating or drinking anything in the six to eight hours leading up to your angiogram. Remove your contact lenses, eyeglasses, hair clips, nail polish, and jewelry before the angiogram test. Leave your jewelry at home before coming for your angiogram, if possible. Empty your bladder before the angiogram begins because the angiogram procedure can take several hours to complete.

At the hospital you'll need to check in and meet with your medical team to discuss exactly what will happen during your angiogram so that you feel prepared for the angiogram. They will let you know about any possible complications or risks associated with your specific angiogram. You'll be taken to a room where you can change into a hospital gown before your angiogram procedure begins.

After your angiogram, you will stay at the facility for four to six hours following the angiogram procedure. This is so that the staff can observe you after your angiogram and make sure there are no postoperative complications from the angiogram. During this recovery time after your angiogram, try to relax. Don't let yourself stress about the angiogram results.

You may be given a sedative during the angiogram procedure or immediately before your angiogram begins. This sedative will impair your ability to function after the angiogram and to operate a motor vehicle following your angiogram. You'll need someone to give you a ride home after your angiogram and help you get settled in after your angiogram procedure. Try to find someone you trust who can stay with you for a couple hours, preferably overnight, after your angiogram in case you need help. Most medical facilities will refuse to perform an angiogram on you if you do not have a responsible adult with you who has agreed to take you home after the angiogram.

One of the best ways to help your body recover from an angiogram is to get as much rest as possible after the angiogram. This will help your body heal after the angiogram and avoid any potential complications from the angiogram. After the angiogram procedure, you'll probably feel discomfort where the catheter was inserted during the angiogram. Bed rest will help that area heal properly after your angiogram. You should plan on staying home for a few days after the angiogram to help you take it easy and recover from the angiogram.

Talk to your doctor about any questions or concerns about your angiogram. Ask your doctor about the outcome of the angiogram and what the angiogram results mean for you.
topics_down_v2.coling::8df379b4-a387-496d-947d-b224f86b: Bear spray is a critical defensive tool designed specifically for deterring charging bears in close-range encounters. It is a type of pepper spray that creates a 30-foot (9 m) cone of spray when discharged. The spray is formulated with capsaicin and related compounds that cause temporary but intense irritation to a bear's eyes, nose, and respiratory system. Bear spray is only to be used when a bear is charging at you to change its direction and stop the attack. The canister should be kept within arms reach at all times when you are in bear country so you can access it immediately if needed. Learn where the trigger is in advance by familiarizing yourself with the canister before you venture into the wilderness. Practice removing the safety clip quickly so the motion becomes automatic under stress. Pull the trigger when the bear is within 40 feet (12 m) of you to ensure the spray reaches the animal effectively. Deploying bear spray at greater distances wastes the product and leaves you vulnerable if the bear continues approaching. Never use bear spray as a preventative measure by spraying it around your campsite or on the perimeter of your tent. It is extremely potent and should not be sprayed on equipment, clothing, or gear because the residual capsaicin can actually attract bears rather than repel them. The spray loses effectiveness over time, so check the expiration date on your canister regularly and replace it when necessary. Store bear spray at moderate temperatures, avoiding extreme heat or cold that can compromise the pressure system. When carrying bear spray, use a holster that keeps the canister accessible on your hip or chest strap rather than buried in your backpack. Wind direction matters significantly when deploying bear spray, as spraying into the wind can blow the irritant back into your own face. After using bear spray, leave the area immediately because the bear may recover and become aggressive again. Dispose of used or expired bear spray canisters properly according to local regulations, as they are pressurized containers. Bear spray has proven highly effective in stopping aggressive bear behavior in numerous documented encounters, making it an essential item for anyone traveling through bear habitat.

Pick a time when they are in a good mood. Avoid approaching them right after a hard day at work. Try to figure out their mood by asking, "How was your day?" You want to select a moment when they seem relaxed and open to conversation, not distracted or preoccupied with other concerns. If they seem tense or worried, it might be better to wait for another opportunity when they appear more receptive.

This works best if you know your mom, for example, is a bit more lenient or if you feel closer to her. Consider which parent might be more understanding or easier to talk to initially, and use that relationship as a starting point.

Staying honest and straightforward during your conversation with them is just one way to show your maturity. So, don't tell lies, even white lies, when you talk with them about this matter. If they ask you direct questions, answer them truthfully and completely. If you are caught in a lie you will lose any ground that you've gained with them. Your credibility is essential to maintaining their trust throughout this discussion and beyond.

Another part of honesty in your conversation with them is your being open to their concerns so you can respond to them thoughtfully. Listen carefully when they express worries or reservations about what you're asking. Acknowledge their perspective and show that you understand why they might have these concerns. This demonstrates emotional maturity and respect for their point of view.

Avoid comparing yourself with others during your talk with them if it involves exaggeration. For example, don't tell your parents that your best friend has been in a similar situation for the past two years, unless it is really true. Your parents will sense that you are not being honest and can easily check the facts. Stick to discussing your own situation and your own readiness rather than trying to justify your position by pointing to what others are doing.

These are all expectations that show you understand the gravity of what you're asking and that you're willing to meet them halfway. Your parents will most likely have quite a bit to say back to you, so make sure to pay close attention to what they are saying. Look into their eyes when they are talking. This will help to show that you are not embarrassed or ashamed to talk about your request. Nod your head when they make good points and even smile if you really agree with something. Show them through your body language that you respect their input and value their wisdom.

A big part of active listening to them is asking questions. If they say no to you, respond by asking, "Why not?" Tell them that you honestly want to understand their perspective in this situation. This will help you to figure out what is bothering them so you can work on addressing their concerns. Press them gently for specifics so you know exactly what you need to do to earn their approval.

If you just can't talk to your parents face-to-face, you may need to write down your feelings and thoughts via a letter to them. This is also a good idea if you think your parents may have an extreme reaction to your request. Make sure that your letter to them is well written and calm. Do not write anything that you will regret. Instead of writing something confrontational, frame your letter in respectful, measured terms. It may be helpful to show your letter to a trusted friend or family member for feedback before presenting it to your parents.

Trapdoor spiders are approximately 0.79 to 1.26 inches (1 to 3 cm) long, which means roughly between the size of your pinky nail and your thumbnail. Trapdoor spiders are black or brown, with stout bodies and legs. Some trapdoor spider species have paler color markings, or they may have a silky covering of hair on their bodies. Trapdoor spider bodies are divided into two sections: the thorax (containing the head and legs) and the abdomen. The abdomen of a trapdoor spider is typically lighter and a slightly different color from the thorax.

Though they may be difficult to see because of the small size, a trapdoor spider will have 6 eyes arranged in 3 groups, whereas most other spider species have 8 eyes. Trapdoor spiders are relatives of tarantulas, but trapdoor spiders are less hairy, and trapdoor spiders have smaller, shinier bodies compared to tarantulas. The jaws of a trapdoor spider are attached to the front of its head. Trapdoor spider jaws move up and down, unlike most other spider species, whose jaws move side to side instead.

Female trapdoor spiders are larger than the male trapdoor spiders, but you will seldom see female trapdoor spiders because they rarely leave their burrows. Therefore, if you see a trapdoor spider, it is most likely a male trapdoor spider. Look for these characteristics that identify male trapdoor spiders: short and blunt spinnerets, which produce silk and are located at the tip of the abdomen of trapdoor spiders; a double spur about halfway along their front legs; a dusty or dull carapace (a harder area covering much of the thorax of trapdoor spiders) that is lightly covered in bristles; and pedipalps (small appendages near the jaws of trapdoor spiders) that resemble boxing gloves.

There are numerous varieties of trapdoor spiders, each trapdoor spider variety with slightly different physical characteristics. More varieties of trapdoor spiders are still being discovered by researchers studying trapdoor spiders. If you think you have seen a trapdoor spider, look up the specific varieties of trapdoor spiders that live in your area, so that you know what kind of specific markings to expect on trapdoor spiders.

Trapdoor spiders favor warm environments. Throughout the world, trapdoor spiders are found in temperate forests and deserts. Trapdoor spiders will burrow in grassy areas, hillsides, and dirt embankments. Trapdoor spiders burrow in the ground, creating holes about 0.75 inches wide and up to 8 inches deep. Trapdoor spiders cover their burrow with a silken hinged "trapdoor" camouflaged by sticks, pebbles, and other natural material. Because the burrows of trapdoor spiders are camouflaged, trapdoor spider burrows can be very hard to see. Larger trapdoor spider burrows may have multiple trapdoors. Usually, the burrow of a trapdoor spider faces sunlight and will be found near vegetation.

Trapdoor spiders are shy and are rarely seen far from their burrows. Male trapdoor spiders may wander during mating season, however. Trapdoor spiders may be nocturnal. You might be able to spy a trapdoor spider when it eats. Trapdoor spiders will wait in their burrows until they sense vibrations in the ground. Then, trapdoor spiders will leap out of the trapdoor, grab prey, and drag it back into the burrow. Trapdoor spiders are solitary creatures that spend most of their lives within their carefully constructed underground homes.

Wipe your knee with a damp washcloth and, if necessary, a mild soap. Wash away grease, sweat, and any soap residue, then dry your knee thoroughly. Making sure your knee is clean and dry will help prevent irritation under the tape and ensure proper adhesion to the knee surface. You can also shave the knee area twelve hours prior to taping if your knee will be taped repeatedly. This will help reduce pain when the tape is removed from your knee and make the taping process more comfortable for your knee joint.

Lie with your back propped up or supported and legs outstretched in front of you, positioning your knees for optimal tape application. Your knees should be completely relaxed and slightly bent to ensure the kneecap sits in its natural resting position. To help keep your knee bent and relaxed during the taping procedure, place a rolled towel under your knee to maintain this comfortable knee position throughout the entire process.

You'll use rigid sports tape to perform the actual McConnell knee taping technique on your kneecap. However, sports tape can be irritating and uncomfortable directly on knee skin, so you should first cover your entire knee with a strip of low irritant, hypoallergenic underwrap tape designed specifically for protecting the knee. A permeable, breathable white cotton tape is a good underwrap option for your knee because it protects the knee skin while still allowing the outer tape to grip the knee area effectively.

Use a marker or pen to gently trace all four sides of your kneecap, creating clear boundaries on your knee. This will define your work surface on the underwrap layer covering your knee and make the entire knee taping procedure more precise. It'll be easier to apply the sports tape properly to your knee if you can actually see the kneecap's boundaries clearly marked on your knee surface.

Use non-stretch adhesive sports tape specifically designed for knee applications when performing the McConnell knee technique. Cut a two to three inch strip of knee tape, or enough tape to cover your knee from the outer to inner edges of your kneecap completely. Sports tape with a width of thirty-eight millimeters is the best size for knee taping procedures because it covers the kneecap surface area appropriately.

Apply one end of the tape to the outer edge of your kneecap so the tape is vertically centered with your knee joint. Adhere the tape to your knee skin in a downward direction toward the lower inside corner of your knee, and use your thumb to gently push the kneecap toward the inside of your knee while securing the tape across your knee.

While moving the kneecap and applying the tape to your knee, use your fingers to carefully pull the knee skin on the inside of your knee toward the kneecap itself. Your goal is to push the kneecap toward the inside of your knee, wrinkle the skin there on your knee so it meets the kneecap, and use the tape to hold your knee skin and kneecap tightly together in this corrected knee position.

Place one edge of the second strip of knee tape on the outer edge of your knee and, again, make sure it's vertically centered with your kneecap position. Secure the tape to your knee skin in a straight, horizontal motion across your knee. The tape should make a straight line from the outside of your knee to the inside edge of your knee. Apply one to three more layers of tape to your knee until you feel your desired level of tightness and support for your kneecap.

Make sure you've created skin wrinkles on the inside part of your knee during this knee taping process. These knee wrinkles should run vertically, or up and down along your knee, and you should be able to see them through the underlay on your knee. Wrinkling of the knee skin results when you pull the kneecap inward and secure it to the skin on the inside of your knee.

Wear the knee tape during physical activity as directed for your knee condition. In general, you should remove the knee tape within forty-eight hours of application to your knee.

Hold your kneecap as you slowly peel off the tape from your knee to prevent worsening a knee injury. Remove the knee tape immediately if it worsens your knee pain or causes knee discoloration, pins and needles, or swelling in your knee area.

Corfe Castle railway station is a railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally an intermediate station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Wareham to Swanage, the line and station were closed by British Rail in 1972. It has since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, a heritage railway that runs from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station. The station serves as an important stopping point on this heritage line and provides access to the historic village of Corfe Castle.

Corfe Castle station is on a railway line connecting Wareham and Norden, providing essential rail service through this section of the Isle of Purbeck.

History
The position of Corfe Castle station, commanding the only relatively low level route across the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that the railway line passed close to the centre of the village. Corfe Castle station was built for the opening of the Swanage Railway line on 20 May 1885, following the receipt of its Act in 1881. From its opening, the railway line and Corfe Castle station were operated by the L&SWR, and the line was absorbed into that railway company in 1886. 

Corfe Castle station was the only intermediate station on the Swanage branch line, a status it retained throughout its operational history until closure by British Rail. The station possessed the only passing loop between the junction with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage station, making it a crucial operational point on the branch line. At least one camping coach was positioned at Corfe Castle station by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967, and probably from 1948 to 1953. From 1960, the allocated coach at the station was a camping coach converted from a Pullman car, which was fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping compartments and a room with two single beds. From 1962 until 1967 there were two of these camping coaches stationed here at Corfe Castle.

Closure of Corfe Castle station was first proposed in 1967, and despite local opposition the station and line finally closed on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of Corfe Castle station's operation under British Rail, passenger train services calling at the station were operated by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units, also known as type 2H.

From the time of the first proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen Corfe Castle station and the railway as a steam locomotive operated heritage railway developed. Most of the track bed, including Corfe Castle station site, was bought by Dorset County Council. Proposals to use the railway route through Corfe Castle as a road bypass for the village were eventually rejected by the county council in 1986, preserving the station site for potential railway use. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the line in 1982, gradually working toward reopening Corfe Castle station.

There were concerns that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern terminus for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village surrounding the station. It was therefore decided to extend the line a further half a mile north from Corfe Castle station to a new Park and Ride site. Here the new Norden station was built and most trains terminate there rather than at Corfe Castle station. Corfe Castle station itself reopened on 12 August 1995, although the official opening of the restored station was not until February of the following year.

A 5-year project by Swanage Railway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle station was completed in April 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening of this new station facility. The footbridge installed at Corfe Castle station was originally built in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, the footbridge spent its previous life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, before being removed by Swanage Railway volunteers and relocated to Corfe Castle station. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now use Corfe Castle station, and is safer and more convenient for passengers at the station than crossing over the track via the gated and locked foot crossing that previously served Corfe Castle station. The footbridge project at Corfe Castle station won the National Railway Heritage Awards in December 2007, with a plaque presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of volunteers who worked on the Corfe Castle station footbridge.

In summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway operated two trains per day to and from Corfe Castle station, connecting it to Wareham, with one service continuing to Poole and the other to London Waterloo via Weymouth. There were also National Rail services on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage calling at Corfe Castle station in summer 2018 and 2019, operated by West Coast Railway Company with three trains per day in each direction stopping at the station. However, in July 2019 these National Rail services calling at Corfe Castle station were stopped and there are currently no National Rail services to Corfe Castle station.

Services at Corfe Castle station
Services at Corfe Castle station run every day from the beginning of April to late October, with weekend only operation at the station in March, November and December. The level of service at Corfe Castle station varies from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction, depending on the season and the day of the week. Southbound from Corfe Castle station, trains operate to stations at Harman's Cross (10 minutes from Corfe Castle), Herston (where trains stop only on request), and Swanage (21 minutes from Corfe Castle station). Northbound from Corfe Castle station, trains operate to Norden station, reached in just 3 minutes from Corfe Castle.

Museum at Corfe Castle station
Corfe Castle station is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum, which is housed in the old goods shed at Corfe Castle station and an adjacent rail van located at the station. The museum at Corfe Castle station is open on most operating days when trains are running through the station. The museum at Corfe Castle station includes a narrow gauge steam locomotive called Secundus, built in 1874, which is displayed at the station and forms part of the collection housed at Corfe Castle station.
