Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former second for the Mike McEwen team which curled out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the new Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk as fellow members of the curling team. For the 2006-07 curling season, Richter and Melnuk left the curling team and were replaced with curlers Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The curling team disbanded after just one season of competitive curling together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007 to form a new competitive curling team. In their first curling season together, they were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's provincial curling championship. Their first Grand Slam curling event as a team was at the end of the curling season, at the 2008 Players' Championships curling event. The curling team won two games at the curling event, before being eliminated from the curling competition.

At the conclusion of the 2008-09 curling season the McEwen curling team was ranked 7th on the Canadian Curling Association rankings. The curling team had made it to three Grand Slam curling playoffs, and finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship curling event.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Olympic Qualifier curling event, the McEwen curling team just lost out to fellow Manitoba curlers on the Jason Gunnlaugson curling team in the semi-finals of the curling competition. The McEwen curling team thus missed out on the 2009 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials final despite being the favourite in that particular curling matchup versus the Gunnlaugson curling team.

McEwen's curling rink made it to his first provincial curling final in 2010, when the curling team lost to Jeff Stoughton's curling team in the 2010 Manitoba provincial curling final. The curling game was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba and as the Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach, the McEwen curling team were treated very much as the home team and crowd favourites at the curling event.

2010-2015: Grand Slam curling success and perennial provincial curling runner-up
The McEwen curling team started the 2010-11 curling season off well by defeating provincial curling rival Jeff Stoughton's curling team to win the World Cup of Curling and his first ever Grand Slam curling title in November, 2010. In part because of the curling team's runner-up result in the provincial curling finals of 2010 and in part because of his 4 curling victories and leading the overall money winnings in the World Curling Tour season as of November 2010, the McEwen curling team was named as a nominee for the provincial curling team of the year by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters Association.

The curling team continued their strong curling season that year by defeating provincial curling rival Stoughton's curling team in the semi-final of the 2011 Canadian Open curling event. The curling team would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard curling team in the extra end of the final, thus winning their second career Grand Slam curling event and their second curling championship of that season.

Wozniak's curling rink once again made it to the Manitoba provincial curling championship this time, being the top seed curling team (also ranked 1st in Canada for curling). However, the curling team once again lost to Stoughton's curling team in the final of the 2011 Safeway Championship curling event, losing by one point in the final end. The McEwen curling team then lost their third straight provincial curling final game at the 2012 Safeway Championship, this time losing to Rob Fowler's curling team, thus tying a provincial curling record for consecutive curling final losses previously set by curler Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This dubious curling record was avoided in 2013, when the McEwen curling rink failed to reach the curling final, but again losing to the rival Stoughton curling rink in the 2013 Safeway Championship curling semi-final. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship curling event, the curling team lost the final to Stoughton's curling team.

Despite being ranked first in the world on both the World Curling Tour Order of Merit rankings and on the WCT money list for curling, Wozniak lost his fifth provincial curling final in six years in 2015, losing to Reid Carruthers' curling team.

Three Briers and curling team breakup 
Wozniak's curling rink won their first provincial curling title in 2016, sending the curling team to their first Brier curling championship. The Matt Dunstone curling rink had committed themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships, which occurred at the same time as the 2016 Tim Hortons Brier, so when the Dunstone curling rink beat Reid Carruthers' curling team in the semi-final, McEwen's curling team would go to the Brier, even if the curling team had lost to Dunstone's curling rink.

In 2017, Wozniak defended his Manitoba curling Championship by beating Reid Carruthers' curling team in the final. Wozniak would then better his 2016 Brier curling showing, going 9–2 in the curling round robin to enter the curling playoffs in first place and with hammer and choice of curling rocks (Brad Gushue's curling team was also 9–2 but lost first place due to losing his curling round robin meeting with the Manitoba curling team). Wozniak's curling team then lost 7–5 to Brad Gushue's curling team in the 1 vs. 2 curling game. In the curling semi finals against reigning Brier and World curling Champion Kevin Koe's curling team, Wozniak's curling team was in control for most of the curling game, being up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end, but Koe's curling team made a comeback with a steal in the eighth end, two points in the tenth end, and another steal in the extra end, dropping the Manitoba curling team to the bronze medal curling game. The curling team recovered to win their first Brier curling medal, defeating Brad Jacobs' curling team in their curling rematch of the 2016 bronze medal curling game, 7–6 in an extra end.

While competing at the 2018 Viterra Championship curling event, skip McEwen came down with chickenpox and was unable to play curling after the first curling game. B. J. Neufeld skipped the curling team, until a surprise appearance by McEwen in the curling final, where the curling team lost to Carruthers' curling team. Despite the curling setback, the curling team still had a chance to qualify for the 2018 Tim Hortons Brier through the wildcard curling game, which the curling team won over Jason Gunnlaugson's curling team. The McEwen curling team had a difficult Brier and alongside Carruthers' curling team was unable to qualify for the curling playoffs. Following the Brier curling championship, the McEwen curling team announced the curling team would be breaking up at the end of the 2017–18 curling season. Just days after the curling announcement, the McEwen curling team won the 2018 Elite 10 Grand Slam of Curling event, winning the top $28,000 prize money, and was the first curling team to go through the entire curling event undefeated. The Grand Slam curling victory was the curling team's seventh overall.

Wozniak took a few years off from men's curling play after the McEwen curling team broke up. However, Wozniak played mixed doubles curling with his current girlfriend Marlene Albrecht and spared for McEwen's new curling team. After Alex Forrest stepped away from competitive curling after the 2019–20 curling season, Wozniak joined the Jason Gunnlaugson curling rink. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial curling championship was cancelled. As the Gunnlaugson curling team were the reigning provincial curling champions, the curling team was chosen to represent Manitoba

Operation Claw was a joint Swedish–American intelligence operation, with Norwegian support, that was carried out at Lillehammer shortly after the German capitulation by the end of World War II. The operation involved transferring thirty-five German intelligence specialists along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied Germany through an agreement between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material secured through Operation Claw, including a Soviet codebook and extensive signals intelligence archives, became very useful for the Americans during the early Cold War period. Operation Claw was controversial both when it happened and afterwards, raising questions about sovereignty, alliance obligations, and the boundaries of acceptable intelligence gathering in the immediate postwar period. The operation was particularly sensitive because the Americans were operating in what was seen as a British controlled country, and because they were securing information about their wartime ally the Soviet Union, doing so in cooperation with neutral Sweden.

The planning and execution of Operation Claw began even before the war in Europe ended, as American intelligence organisations sought German intelligence experts with knowledge of the Soviet Union. American officials immediately after the war in Europe ended began to cooperate with German Major General Reinhard Gehlen and his organisation Fremde Heere Ost (FHO) which had led German intelligence on the Eastern Front. Operation Claw was part of an organized effort to obtain as much German intelligence information and personnel as possible, an effort that had the name Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM). The operation was conducted with great secrecy because the war was still being fought in East-Asia, the US and the Soviet Union were still officially allies, and the allies had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence. Both for the US and the neutral Sweden, Operation Claw was thus diplomatically very sensitive and required careful concealment from both the British and the Soviets.

At the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer, a group of 35 German experts on signals intelligence had been gathered who possessed extensive knowledge about Soviet affairs. In cooperation with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and support from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, agents for the Swedish intelligence organisation C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The German group of experts were taken out of the camp and transported to Sweden as part of Operation Claw. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on June 12 flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany and were interned in an American military camp at Wiesbaden. The transfer of the German experts at Lillehammer through Operation Claw was directed from the highest level, with Major General William J. Donovan leading from the U.S. side and Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd serving as chief of the Defense Staff from the Swedish side.

More than a month after the German capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed to find people from Gestapo and other German key personnel hiding in German military camps. The search force soon became aware that a number of German key personnel had been removed in Operation Claw a month earlier. Operation Claw had successfully extracted these valuable intelligence assets before the British-led search could locate them. This discovery raised questions about the propriety of Operation Claw and whether it had undermined the broader allied effort to account for German intelligence personnel. The secrecy surrounding Operation Claw meant that even allied personnel conducting subsequent searches were unaware that key German intelligence specialists had already been removed. This lack of coordination highlighted the tensions that Operation Claw both reflected and exacerbated among the wartime allies.

Operation Claw was the beginning of postwar era cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence services, marking a significant shift in violation of Sweden's officially stated neutrality. From the American side Operation Claw was viewed as a great success and the responsible officers within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations where Operation Claw specifically was mentioned. The success of Operation Claw from the American perspective was measured both by the intelligence materials obtained and by the successful recruitment of German experts who could provide ongoing assistance in understanding Soviet capabilities. For the Swedish C-byrån, however, Operation Claw quickly became toxic and problematic. Even though Operation Claw was to be kept confidential, information about the operation leaked to the Swedish press, creating a political scandal. The exposure of Operation Claw and Sweden's violation of neutrality led to C-byrån being dissolved in February 1946. The dissolution of C-byrån demonstrated the high political costs that Operation Claw carried for Sweden, even as it brought intelligence benefits.

Information regarding Operation Claw continued to be classified as confidential in the post-war years and some of it still remains classified today. A report about Operation Claw in the British National Archives was restricted until 2020, demonstrating the lasting sensitivity of the operation. The continued classification of materials related to Operation Claw decades after its execution suggests that the operation involved methods, sources, or outcomes that governments still consider too sensitive for public disclosure. Operation Claw thus remains partially obscured from historical scrutiny, with its full dimensions and consequences still not entirely known to researchers and the public.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The short was released on February 17, 1934 and received production number 6125.

The film was supervised by Earl Duvall, who handled the directorial responsibilities for this Merrie Melodies entry. The characters were animated by Jack King and Frank Tipper, both of whom received credit for their animation work on Honeymoon Hotel, as well as Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, whose contributions to the cartoon went uncredited. The music score was composed by Bernard Brown, who received sole credit, and Norman Spencer, who composed music but remained uncredited for his work on Honeymoon Hotel. The sound was recorded by Bernard Brown, though he went uncredited for this particular contribution to the cartoon.

The plot of Honeymoon Hotel follows a male and female bug who check into a hotel which subsequently catches on fire during their stay at the establishment.

The film is notable for being the first Warner Bros. cartoon produced in color, marking a significant milestone in the studio's animation history. Honeymoon Hotel used the Cinecolor process since Walt Disney held exclusive rights to the superior Technicolor process at that time. Only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon, Beauty and the Beast, was produced in Cinecolor before the Merrie Melodies series briefly returned to black-and-white production. Eventually, the Merrie Melodies series transitioned to Technicolor for its color cartoons, though the Looney Tunes series continued being produced in black-and-white until 1943. The Cinecolor process made a return appearance in several late 1940s Looney Tunes shorts and Merrie Melodies shorts before being phased out permanently from Warner Bros. animation production.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" is a short story by British author P. G. Wodehouse, which first appeared in the United States in the October 1923 issue of Cosmopolitan, and in the United Kingdom in the November 1923 Strand. The story features the irrepressible Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, and was included in the collection Ukridge, published in 1924.

The story opens with Ukridge and Corky running into a friend of Ukridge's, a chauffeur driving a shiny new Daimler, and he offers to take them for a ride. Along the way they are seen by a creditor of Ukridge's, who they shake off, and almost hit a young girl, who Ukridge insists they drive to her home near Clapham Common. Ukridge befriends her family, who are impressed by the car and Ukridge's famous Aunt Julia.

When Corky meets Ukridge a week later in the British Museum, Ukridge is accompanied by two children. Ukridge reveals he has been visiting the house, mainly for the free food, and promising to take the family out on trips in his friend's car, which they believe to be his, and to introduce them to his aunt, who, he reveals, has disowned him, in a letter which states "from now on, I have no nephew".

Returning from short holiday, Corky hears from George Tupper that Ukridge is engaged. Visiting his friend, Corky finds Ukridge with a black eye, and hears the tale of how Ukridge found himself inadvertently engaged to the girl from Clapham Common, and got punched by a rival suitor named Finch. As they talk on Ukridge's doorstep, the creditor from the car ride arrives, and Ukridge hides. A friendly passer-by soothes the enraged creditor, arguing that he knows where Ukridge lives; Ukridge moves out of his house, remarking on the good fortune that led him to use the pseudonym "Mr. Smallweed" when dealing with the man.

Ukridge and Corky form a plot to get Ukridge out of the engagement by feigning ill-health, but as Corky is delivering his speech to the family, the passer-by arrives. The passer-by is George Finch, Ukridge's rival for the girl; he reveals that Ukridge is an impoverished imposter, in fact called Smallweed, and produces the creditor to prove it. George Finch also bears a letter from Ukridge's aunt, claiming that she has no nephew. Once Corky has paid off the debt to the creditor, Corky and Ukridge are chased from the house.

The story's main characters include Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, the irrepressible entrepreneur; Julia Ukridge, his haughty writer aunt; Jimmy Corcoran, Ukridge's writer friend; George Tupper, an old schoolfriend of Ukridge and Corcoran; Frederick, a chauffeur, a friend of Ukridge; Mabel Price, a girl Ukridge meets on the road; Mr Price, her doting father; Ernie Finch, her admirer, a resourceful man; and Mr Grindlay, a man Ukridge owes money to, who knows him only as "Mr Smallweed".

The story was illustrated by T. D. Skidmore in Cosmopolitan. The story was illustrated by Reginald Cleaver in the Strand.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" was included in the 1932 collection Nothing But Wodehouse, edited by Ogden Nash and published by Doubleday, Doran & Company. The story was included in Week-End Wodehouse (UK edition), first published by Herbert Jenkins Limited in 1939. The story was also collected in The World of Ukridge, published in October 1975 by Barrie & Jenkins.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" was adapted for radio in 1956, with Michael Shepley as Ukridge, Hubert Gregg as Corcoran, Olaf Pooley as Frederick, Jeffrey Segal as Mr Grindley, Mairhi Russell as Mabel Price, and Brewster Mason as Tupper.

Modern Greek art is art from the period between the emergence of the new independent Greek state and the 20th century. As Mainland Greece was under Ottoman rule for all four centuries, Greek artistic development was hindered and Greek creative expression was suppressed, preventing Greek artists from participating in the Renaissance and artistic movements that transformed other European nations. Greek islands such as Crete and the Ionian islands experienced different conditions that allowed Greek artistic traditions to persist and evolve, as these Greek territories were under Venetian or other European powers' rule, enabling Greek painters and sculptors in those regions to assimilate radical artistic changes while maintaining Greek cultural identity. The Cretan School represents an important Greek artistic movement that developed distinctive Greek visual language, and the Heptanese School of art represents another important Greek artistic movement that cultivated Greek aesthetic sensibilities through techniques absorbed from broader European culture.

Modern Greek art developed its distinctive character through the particular socioeconomic conditions of Greece itself, shaped fundamentally by Greek historical circumstances and Greek cultural aspirations. The large Greek diaspora across Europe influenced Greek artistic development, as Greek artists abroad maintained connections to Greek themes and Greek subject matter. The new Greek social elite patronized Greek artists and supported Greek artistic institutions, fostering Greek cultural revival through visual arts. External artistic influences affected Greek painting and Greek sculpture, predominantly from Germany and France, yet Greek artists transformed these influences into distinctively Greek expressions.

Modern Greek art began to develop around the time of Romanticism, when Greek artists absorbed many elements from European colleagues while creating a distinctive style of Greek Romantic art. Greek revolutionary ideals inspired Greek painters, as did Greece's geography and Greece's history, providing Greek artists with profound subject matter rooted in Greek experience. After centuries of Ottoman rule, few opportunities for education in the arts existed in newly independent Greece, so Greek artists studied abroad while maintaining Greek cultural consciousness. Munich became an important international center where the majority of Greek artists of the 19th century chose to study, and the school of Munich, led by Karl von Piloty, taught Greek students true fresco techniques for Greek mural paintings on fresh wet lime plaster. During this period much Greek art was emotional and theatrical in tone, reflecting Greek aspirations and Greek struggles. The most prominent themes of Greek artists studying in Munich included Greek urban life, Greek rural life, Greek still life subjects, and Greek landscape painting.

Greek artists would return to Greece and pass on their knowledge to younger Greek students, establishing Greek artistic institutions and Greek educational frameworks. Some Greek artists remained in Munich, developing the Greek "Munich School" of painting through academic and personal bonds between Greek painters and Munich artistry. Nikolaos Gysis became an important Greek teacher and Greek artist at the Munich Academy, soon becoming a leading figure among Greek artists and Greek cultural ambassadors. Greek academism, Greek realism, Greek genre painting, Greek upper middle class portraiture, Greek still life and Greek landscape painting often represented impressionist features within Greek aesthetic frameworks. These Greek artistic modes would be replaced by Greek interpretations of Symbolism, Greek versions of Jugendstil, and Greek applications of Art Nouveau, mainly traced in work by Greek artists like Nikolaos Gysis and other Greek modernists. Early-twentieth-century Greek modernism developed through significant Greek artists in Munich who explored Greek themes through contemporary techniques.

Many Greek artists of the Munich School chose subjects depicting Greek everyday life, Greek local customs, and Greek living conditions, documenting Greek society through visual representation. Several important Greek painters emerged during this formative period of Greek art. Theodoros Vryzakis, a prominent Greek painter, specialized in Greek historical painting especially inspired by the 1821 Greek War of Independence, creating powerful images of Greek heroism and Greek sacrifice. Nikiphoros Lytras, another significant Greek artist, concentrated on realistic depictions of Greek life, portraying Greek people in Greek settings with Greek authenticity. Georgios Jakobides, an accomplished Greek painter, devoted his attention to Greek infants and Greek children, later becoming the first Director of the new National Gallery of Athens, a crucial Greek cultural institution. Georgios Roilos was another leading Greek painter of the period closely associated with Greek interpretations of Munich School principles. Konstantinos Volanakis, a celebrated Greek maritime painter, was inspired by the Greek sea, capturing Greek coastal scenes and Greek nautical traditions.

Other Greek artists associated with the School of Munich included Symeon Sabbides, whose Greek subjects reflected Greek sensibilities, and Yannoulis Chalepas, a Greek sculptor of exceptional talent. Leonidas Drosis contributed to Greek sculpture and Greek architectural ornament, along with several Greek modernist artists who studied in Munich, including Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, who brought Greek perspectives to modernist movements, and Jorgos Busianis, who explored Greek themes through contemporary Greek visual language. Even Giorgio de Chirico, though developing an international reputation, maintained Greek cultural connections.

Notable Greek sculptors of the new Greek Kingdom included Leonidas Drosis, whose major work was extensive neo-classical Greek architectural ornament at the Academy of Athens, a defining Greek institution. Lazaros Sochos created important Greek public monuments, while Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis all contributed to Greek sculptural traditions, developing Greek three-dimensional art through both Greek classical references and contemporary Greek innovations. These Greek sculptors established foundations for Greek plastic arts that would inspire subsequent generations of Greek artists.

A few Greek painters studied in Paris rather than Munich, developing Greek artistic perspectives within French cultural contexts. Despite residing in the French capital and following French Art Academy guidelines, Greek painters invariably maintained Greek interpretations and Greek thematic concerns. Jacob Rizos, a Greek painter, involved himself with rendering female grace through Greek aesthetic lenses, while Theodoros Rallis, another Greek artist, focused on Greek Orthodox Eastern scenes. Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos, a Greek portraitist, worked with Greek portraiture, Greek still life and Greek genre painting. During this period the avant-garde Impressionist movement developed in Paris, but most Greek painters remained faithful to academic precepts, with only some Greek artists making tentative thrusts toward impressionism. The first Greek impressionist was Périclès Pantazis, a Greek painter who settled in Belgium after Paris, becoming part of the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte while maintaining Greek identity.

Many Greek artists of this period drew upon El Greco's style for inspiration, particularly when creating Greek religious art based on Greek Orthodox themes. This approach tied in with modern secular Greek art referencing Greek classical styles, while Greek religious art referenced Byzantine Greek
topics_down_v2.coling::f3328e08-1b91-430d-bea9-e5b836b0: "Wait. You can see me?" she stared at me confused. "Yeah" I said. Dragging out the end of the word unsure of where she was going with this. "Hmmm" she mused back, cocking her head to one side. "What are you?" "Dead" I grinned. Been dead for years now, wandering these same stretches of road. This is the first time I've seen another ghost out here, let alone one trying to hitch a ride from the living. Don't you know the rules yet? The newly dead always think they're still breathing. "Are you certain?" she asked. "I'm not ready to accept this and I'd really rather not be stood in the middle of a freezing wood in a sundress on an October evening as a corpse." "Fair enough" I shrugged, gesturing toward the phantom impression of my car. As she slumped into the passenger seat putting her feet up on the dash, my suspicions were confirmed. There was enough ethereal light from the spectral interior to show the bruises on her ankles, and the faded pale skin of scar tissue where she had bled out. This woman wasn't living anymore. She didn't have the right to be complaining about being dead when she was leaving ghostly muddy bootprints on the inside of my phantom car, when those boots were probably in an evidence locker next to her body in the morgue. "The boots?" I nodded. "Were you killed up here?" "Something like that" she nodded. "I've been wandering away from my body too long though." "My husband thought we needed to get away." "We had been growing apart and I think he wanted to end things permanently." "Errr" I mumbled. I haven't had the best death myself and the last thing I needed was to anger a newly dead woman who had obviously been murdered by her husband on their so-called 'reconnection' outing in these woods. "And you're leaving your death site without closure?" "He left me here to rot!" she glared at me. "Why do you think I was trying to hitch?" "He took everything from me, even my chance to say goodbye." "I guess that makes sense" I replied, watching the phantom road unroll before my spectral vehicle. "So how long have we been dead?" she asked turning back to me. "About twenty years for me, obviously much less for you" "Not long in death terms" "What do you mean, not long in death terms?" As she said it she turned away from me and looked out of the ghostly windscreen. She stared ahead as the memory replayed itself, the moment of my own death cycling again. The phantom car imploded around us exactly as it had two decades before. Shattered glass sprayed across the seats and my head spun round with that familiar crack. The air filled with the eternal hissing of my death scene and the drone of the truck's horn as that driver remained slumped across his wheel forever. "Hey" she prodded me. "You've seen this before?" I turned my head to her, my neck still broken from that original impact. "You're new to being dead, aren't you" I said. "Huh?" she replied. "You asked why I could see you." "That's the thing about death." "We see each other."

topics_down_v2.coling::7a28bc6c-3b1e-4ac2-a169-10374ef5: Kevin could hear the front door unlocking from his perch in the master bathroom. Perhaps "master" was an overly generous adjective for the much abused and only toilet in the two room urban squat, but it did connect to the bedroom, and that was by virtue of being the only bedroom in the house the master. The toilet seat snagged Kevin's right cheek as he leaned toward the bathroom door, straining to follow the steps that were now almost certainly moving through the entryway. He tried to remember who had a spare key to his apartment. His girlfriend had one, which she kept on a keychain with a small rubber duck. The cleaning woman he had hired once who vowed never to return again had taken a key, supposedly to return it by mail, but Kevin had never received it back. His mom had a key on her main ring, the one with the library card holder attached. His pet sitter had been given a key last summer, though Kevin no longer had a pet and had forgotten to ask for it back. After a moment of quiet review, Kevin decided that the steps in the hallway belonged to none of these key holders. There was a stranger in the house, someone who had obtained a key through means Kevin couldn't immediately determine. Perhaps one of the key holders had lost their copy, and this intruder had found it with his address still attached. Perhaps the landlord had made an extra copy without telling Kevin, and that copy had been stolen or sold. Perhaps someone had picked the lock, which was old and probably easy to manipulate with the right tools. Kevin wondered if he should have installed a deadbolt when he first moved into the apartment. He wondered if he should have changed the locks after the cleaning woman incident. He wondered if his girlfriend had made a copy for someone else without mentioning it to him. He wondered if the pet sitter had duplicated the key before eventually returning the original. The footsteps were in the kitchen now, accompanied by a percussion section of opening drawers and cupboards. The thunderstorm of slamming drawers moved boldly toward the bedroom. Kevin tried not to tense. But it wasn't long before the thundering abated. A stagnant quiet began to build in the house. The stranger's voice: "Ummm..... hello?" Kevin: " ..... hi." And then, quickly. "Please don't come in here." Hesitation hung heavy. "I didn't think there was anyone home." "Yeah." Kevin squeaked. "Are you okay, man? This isn't how it usually works." "I'm just..... if you could not take my stuff." "So uh..... good bye?" "Wait!" The steps had begun to move away, back toward the door. "Wait! Wait!" "What?" "Can you leave the bottle opener? Please? It's just the one thing. It's in the kitchen drawer, the one by the sink. The bottle opener with the wooden handle. Just leave that one thing, please. Everything else, I don't care, but leave that." "Ummm..... sure. Yeah. No problem, man." "Thanks." The door clicked shut.

topics_down_v2.coling::bb048a1e-39f8-4c80-9db0-70176b1c: Grace Files The Department Break-Room is always a fun place. Its employees, like me, all share one little gift from the Chief Executive: Immortality. So long as we continue to do our jobs, we're given all the time we could ever want or need. A large chunk, usually a bit less than three quarters of it, is spent working. Mostly because there are so many people running around the world dying at any given moment. Even with the advantage of existing outside of Time and Space, we Reapers still have a bit of trouble processing all the people who are dying. Of course, we can all still take off a quarter of our infinity to chill out on Earth or around the Department's Campus. The Campus itself is massive, sprawling across what appears to be an endless expanse when you first arrive. New Reapers often get lost trying to find their assigned wings during their first few centuries on the job. The architecture shifts depending on which era's Reapers designed each particular section, so you'll walk from baroque corridors into minimalist modern hallways without any real transition. The Break-Room sits at the center of the entire Campus, accessible from every wing through doors that somehow always appear exactly when you need them. It's the largest room in the Department, designed to accommodate every Reaper who might want to take their break at the same time, though that's never actually happened in all the time I've been here. The ceiling stretches up so high that you can't actually see it, just a kind of gentle glow that provides light without any visible source. The bar runs along one entire wall, stocked with every drink that's ever been conceived by human imagination up until the present moment on Earth. The Department keeps it updated in real-time, so new cocktails and beverages appear on the shelves almost as soon as they're invented down below. Behind the bar, there's no bartender—you just reach for what you want and it appears in your hand, already prepared exactly how you'd prefer it. Some of the younger Reapers find this disconcerting at first, but you get used to the Department's way of handling things. Near the bar, there are clusters of tables and chairs, also in varying styles from different eras, where Reapers can sit and talk during their breaks. The furniture never runs out, never needs replacing, and always seems to be clean no matter how much use it gets. Along another wall, someone installed a massive screen for watching recorded events from Earth's history, and the selection available is comprehensive—every moment that's ever been observed by human eyes, plus plenty that weren't. The screen responds to whoever's standing in front of it, showing whatever they want to see. Sometimes Reapers watch their own former lives, though the Department's counselors generally advise against that particular practice. There's also a game area that the younger Reapers have claimed, filled with entertainment options from various time periods. The Department doesn't discriminate—there are ancient board games sitting next to modern video game consoles, all of them functional, all of them available for anyone who wants to use them during their downtime. The Break-Room never closes because time doesn't really work the same way here as it does on Earth. Reapers come and go according to their own schedules, taking breaks between assignments whenever they feel the need. Some Reapers spend most of their free time here, finding comfort in the presence of others who understand the weight of the work. Others rarely visit, preferring to take their breaks elsewhere on the Campus or down on Earth itself. The atmosphere in the Break-Room shifts constantly depending on who's present. Sometimes it's loud and energetic, filled with conversation and laughter as Reapers share stories and blow off steam. Other times it's quiet and contemplative, with just a few individuals scattered around, lost in their own thoughts. The room seems to adapt to whatever mood prevails at any given moment, the ambient sound and lighting shifting subtly to match. There are quiet corners for those who want solitude while still being around others, and there are central gathering spaces for those who want to socialize. One section has comfortable chairs arranged in circles, perfect for group discussions or the informal support sessions that happen spontaneously when someone's having a hard time with a particularly difficult assignment. The Department encourages Reapers to use the Break-Room, to take advantage of the community it provides. Working as a Reaper can be isolating despite the constant contact with the dying. You're present at someone's most intimate moment, but you're not really there for them in the way their loved ones are. You're there to facilitate a transition, to guide them from life to whatever comes after. It's meaningful work, essential work, but it takes a toll. The Break-Room helps with that toll by providing a space where Reapers can decompress, where they can talk to others who truly understand what they're going through. The Department also uses the Break-Room for occasional mandatory meetings, though those are rare. Usually it's just a space for Reapers to exist without the weight of their duties pressing down on them. You can be yourself here, not Death's representative but just another employee trying to cope with an impossible job. The Break-Room represents a kind of sanctuary within the Department, a reminder that even immortal Reapers need rest and community. New arrivals often find the Break-Room overwhelming at first, with its impossible size and its mix of beings from every era of human history. But eventually, it becomes a second home, a place where you know you can always find someone who understands, someone who's been through what you're going through. The Department designed it that way deliberately, understanding that even those who serve Death need comfort and connection to continue their eternal work.

topics_down_v2.coling::7426cf8e-20e5-4e81-bfbb-380b1547: The vote held on Friday was for 68 seats out of the 290 in parliament. It meant that nervous Iranians woke up on Saturday morning to an all new political landscape within parliament. For the first time in 13 years moderates and reformists now have a majority in parliament. While it was not a sweeping victory for the supporters of President Hassan Rouhani, it was still a surprise win, especially given the months of heavy campaigning against the government's policies within parliament. Hardliners had a majority in the outgoing parliament. In the three years since Hassan Rouhani took office, they have bitterly opposed most of government's plans in parliament, organising a fierce attack on the government's legislative agenda through parliamentary procedures. Some MPs have even gone so far as to block ministerial appointments through parliamentary votes. The popular moderate ministers have regularly been subject to harsh criticism in parliament and are under constant threat of impeachment by fundamentalist MPs who control key parliamentary committees. Now almost all those MPs have been unseated by moderate or reformist counterparts, and those who remain either supported the government or at least never attacked it as vociferously as their unseated comrades in parliamentary debates. Many observers argue the parliamentary composition not only determined legislative outcomes but was also the deal-breaker in future parliamentary sessions. The people were saying no to those who had promised to obstruct parliament. What puts this victory in a more meaningful context is the fact that it was achieved despite almost all well-known reformists being banned from running in the parliamentary elections and a complete lack of coverage of their parliamentary campaigns. topics_down_v2.coling::8d68dd4d-1de2-4490-8a68-ccd52f7f: Usually the low advertised rates are for term life insurance. This type of life insurance has an expiration date, and is typically used to protect during periods when death benefit needs are highest. One might buy a term policy that expires after twenty years, or one that expires after thirty years, to ensure beneficiaries receive a payout if death occurs during the coverage period. But if the policyholder lives until that point in time, the policy expires without payout. So say the average term life insurance buyer purchases coverage in their thirties and maintains it into their fifties or sixties. Most policyholders will survive the term, so only a small fraction of term life insurance policies pay out death benefits, and the premiums collected from policies that don't pay out help cover the death benefits for policies that do pay out. The chances of a term life insurance payout are relatively small compared to the number of policyholders paying premiums. For example, if one hundred people each buy term life insurance coverage with a hundred thousand dollar death benefit for ten dollars per month, and one policyholder dies during the term, the life insurance company collects one thousand dollars in total premiums. The life insurance company pays one hundred thousand dollars to the deceased policyholder's beneficiaries. The life insurance company can also invest the premium dollars collected and earn additional money from those investments before any death claims are paid. When the numbers of people buying term life insurance policies increase and the percentage of policyholders dying during the term decreases, the potential profits for the life insurance company grow substantially. The life insurance company is also very careful to screen out applicants who are more likely to die during the policy term. Term life insurance is difficult or expensive to obtain if the applicant has health conditions that shorten life expectancy. The life insurance premiums aren't arbitrary numbers. The death benefit payouts are calculated based on mortality tables, probability statistics, and actuarial odds. The length of the term life insurance coverage period and many other underwriting factors come into play when setting premium rates.
topics_down_v2.coling::4622a5f2-c96d-4ea1-9629-b734e976: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey now extends over a large enough region that galaxies in low density environments can be detected. Rojas et al. have developed a technique to extract more than 1000 void galaxies with delta rho/rho < -0.6 on scales r>7 h^{-1} Mpc from the SDSS. In this paper, we present the luminosity function of these void galaxies and compare it to that of void galaxies in different subsamples within the survey. We obtain a measurement of the void galaxy luminosity function over the range -21.5<M_r*<-14.5 in the SDSS r-band. The void galaxy luminosity function is well fit by a Schechter function with values of Phi*=(0.19 +- 0.04)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-19.74 +- 0.11 and alpha=-1.18 +- 0.13. The value of M_r* for void galaxies is consistent with previous work by Rojas et al. who found that void galaxies were intrinsically fainter objects distributed throughout these underdense regions. To investigate the void galaxy luminosity function further, we consider how the luminosity function of void galaxies varies as a function of their local density within the voids themselves. Even within voids, void galaxies in slightly denser regions show marginally different faint end slopes. The luminosity function of the void galaxies is also compared across different morphological types among the void galaxy population. The luminosity function of the bluest void galaxies, void galaxies with Sersic index n<2, and void galaxies with EW(Halpha)>5A all show very similar shapes, with only slightly different M_r* values and similar values of alpha across these void galaxy subsamples. The value of alpha ~ -1.2 found from the void galaxy luminosity function is shallower than that predicted for void galaxies from CDM models, suggesting that voids are not filled with a large population of dwarf void galaxies as some simulations of void galaxy formation have proposed. This result indicates that void galaxy formation processes may differ from theoretical expectations regarding low-mass void galaxy populations.

topics_down_v2.coling::da2d8730-7c13-4b32-befb-c2bbe666:
Section 51(xxxi) is a subclause of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia.

Section 51(xxxi) empowers the Commonwealth to make laws regarding the acquisition of property, but stipulates that such acquisitions must be on just terms.

Section 51(xxxi) is sometimes referred to in shorthand as the 'just terms' provision.

Section 51(xxxi) is notable for its importance to Australian Constitutional Law, and particularly for its role in protecting property rights from arbitrary Commonwealth acquisition.

Text of Section 51(xxxi)
Section 51(xxxi) reads as follows within the broader framework of section 51 of the Constitution.

Jurisprudence concerning Section 51(xxxi)
While section 51(xxxi) was adapted from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, section 51(xxxi) has many differences from its American counterpart.

The 'just terms' requirement contained in section 51(xxxi) has been held not to affect the State Parliaments.

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon stated that the inclusion of the condition in section 51(xxxi) was to "prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject."

The interpretation of the terms "acquisition" and "just terms" in section 51(xxxi) by the High Court of Australia have had the effect, however, of limiting section 51(xxxi)'s protection of property rights. Moreover, section 51(xxxi) operates at any time the Commonwealth makes a compulsory acquisition of property. As such, section 51(xxxi) is a contingent guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy property rights.

Under section 51(xxxi), the Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws". This means that every law supported by section 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other additional legislative power.

Property under Section 51(xxxi)
The High Court of Australia has taken a wide view of the concept of "property" under section 51(xxxi). Several members of the court took the opportunity to consider the meaning of the term property in section 51(xxxi) in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke said the term in section 51(xxxi) includes: "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action." Justice McTiernan confirmed the term property in section 51(xxxi) extends to tangible and intangible property.

An example of the breadth of the concept of property in section 51(xxxi) is provided by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisation Case). In that case concerning section 51(xxxi), Federal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banks through vesting of shares in private banks in the Commonwealth, and later the appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised the provisions as removing effective control over the property of the private banks. He concluded that this was, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right under section 51(xxxi).

While statutory licences have sometimes been equated with proprietary interests under section 51(xxxi), the removal of rights enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property within section 51(xxxi), as licence conditions are inherently susceptible to change.

Acquisition under Section 51(xxxi)
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody, and the acquisition must be for a Commonwealth purpose. This aspect of section 51(xxxi) is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the destination does not matter – it is enough that the holder of property has been deprived of it. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which restricted the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property under section 51(xxxi). Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass for retired members of Parliament were not an acquisition of property under section 51(xxxi).

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court held that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW compulsorily acquiring property was invalid under section 51(xxxi) as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just. The validity of a grant in the absence of a requirement to acquire property was upheld under section 51(xxxi) principles in the later case of Pye v Renshaw.

Just terms under Section 51(xxxi)
Typically, a determination of just terms under section 51(xxxi) based on the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will be sufficient to satisfy the requirement of just terms. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" under section 51(xxxi) imports no equivalence of market value. The arrangements offered under section 51(xxxi) must be "fair", or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair". However, this judgment of "fairness" under section 51(xxxi) must take account of all the interests affected, not just those of the dispossessed owner.

The requirement of "just terms" under section 51(xxxi) does not necessarily require that a compensation package be presented as part of the acquisition scheme. Under section 51(xxxi), it is sufficient that the scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair compensation. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures under section 51(xxxi) closely to ensure their adequacy.

There may be some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution.

Section 51(xxxi) is an exception to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" another. In this case, however, the Court will not allow another grant of power to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi). This interpretive principle ensures that section 51(xxxi) maintains its force as a protection against unjust acquisitions. The operation of section 51(xxxi) thus requires careful consideration of how it interacts with other constitutional powers. Courts interpreting section 51(xxxi) must balance the Commonwealth's need to acquire property with the constitutional mandate for just terms. Section 51(xxxi) thereby serves as a crucial limitation on Commonwealth power while still permitting necessary acquisitions.

Phone companies charge fees because they're trying to maximize revenue from their existing customer base who are already locked into their service. Traditional telecommunications providers have you as a customer and they structure their pricing to extract as much money as possible from that established relationship. When you make an international call through a phone company, they're charging you premium rates because you're already their customer and they know you'll pay. The phone company billing system is designed around getting more money from people who have already signed up for their service.

Skype and similar services price differently because they're attempting to acquire you as a customer in the first place. These internet-based calling services are fighting for market share and need to attract users away from traditional phone companies. Skype's business model centers on converting non-customers into customers, so they offer lower rates or even free calling between users to make their service appealing. They're willing to provide inexpensive or no-cost calling because acquiring customers is their primary goal.

The fundamental difference is where each type of company sits in the customer acquisition cycle. Phone companies have already acquired you - you're paying them monthly fees, you've signed a contract, and switching providers involves hassle and potential costs. They've moved past the acquisition phase into the retention and revenue maximization phase. Their pricing reflects the fact that they already have you locked in as a customer.

Internet calling services are still in customer acquisition mode. They haven't locked you in yet, so they need to offer compelling pricing to get you to sign up and start using their platform. These services are pursuing customers rather than already possessing them. Their entire pricing strategy revolves around being attractive enough that people will switch from traditional phone services or adopt their platform for internet calling.

Traditional phone providers can charge higher fees because customer switching costs protect them. You're already integrated into their billing system, your number is established, and changing providers requires effort. Phone companies exploit this incumbent advantage by maintaining higher prices for services like international calling. They've got existing customers and they're working to maximize what they earn from those customers.

Meanwhile, internet-based calling platforms must remain price-competitive to pull customers away from established phone services. They're still trying to earn anything at all from potential customers, while phone companies are trying to earn more from the customers they already have. This difference in customer relationship status drives the pricing gap between traditional phone services and internet calling platforms completely.

If there is an available syllabus for the Biology class, read it carefully to know the rules, materials needed, and any other important information before going to the first Biology class. It is a good idea to review the syllabus before going to class each day to make sure nothing is forgotten. One way of remembering the syllabus is to highlight, underline, and take notes on it directly so the most crucial syllabus information stands out immediately.

Use different note-taking methods on the syllabus such as underlining, highlighting, drawing a symbol such as a star next to something important in the syllabus, drawing a box around important sentences or paragraphs in the syllabus, and taking notes either on a separate sheet of paper or the back of the syllabus itself. These tips will ensure every detail in the syllabus is remembered when needed throughout the semester.

Make sure it is okay with the teacher before marking up the syllabus document. If needed, make a copy of the syllabus with a scanner so there are multiple copies of the syllabus available. It is a good idea to keep one unmarked syllabus and the other syllabus with notes so if anything in the syllabus changes, new notes can be made on the second copy of the syllabus without losing the original syllabus information.

Students without scanners at home have a few different options for scanning the syllabus to create backup copies. One option is to go to the nearest library that has a scanner and bring the syllabus along to make copies there. Usually it costs no more than twenty cents per page to scan the syllabus at a public library. Another option for making copies of the syllabus is for students with smartphones or tablets with a camera built into the device to use that technology. Install an app made for scanning documents like the syllabus. These types of apps allow users to take a picture of a document such as the syllabus and the app will convert the syllabus to PDF, DOC, and other various document formats that preserve the syllabus text. If these options for copying the syllabus are not available, do not hesitate to ask the school if they have a scanner available for students to copy their syllabus, or ask if the Biology teacher can scan the syllabus for students who need copies. Teachers will be happy to help students get copies of the syllabus.

Most Biology teachers will give students the syllabus on the first day and expect them to refer to it regularly. The syllabus typically includes the grading policy, attendance requirements, and assignment due dates that students need to track. Keeping the syllabus organized and accessible helps students stay on top of syllabus requirements throughout the course. Students should check the syllabus weekly to confirm upcoming syllabus deadlines and expectations.

Some syllabi are posted online where students can access the syllabus digitally whenever needed. Digital syllabi can be bookmarked on computers or phones for quick reference to syllabus details. Whether the syllabus is physical or digital, students must familiarize themselves thoroughly with the syllabus content to succeed in Biology class and meet all syllabus expectations outlined by the instructor at the semester's beginning.
topics_down_v2.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f: Judith Scott (May 1, 1943 – March 15, 2005) was an American fiber sculptor, born with Down Syndrome and deaf. She was internationally renowned for her fiber art creations. In 1987, Judith was enrolled at the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, California, where she discovered her passion and talent for abstract fiber art sculpture. An account of Scott's fiber art practice, Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott (2016) has been written by her twin sister. Judith was born into a middle-class family in Cincinnati, Ohio on May 1, 1943 along with her fraternal twin sister Joyce. Unlike Joyce, Judith was born with Down Syndrome. During her infancy, Judith suffered from Scarlet Fever, which caused her to lose her hearing, a fact that remained unknown until much later in her life and significantly affected her eventual artistic development. Judith Scott spent her first seven and a half years at home with her parents, twin sister and older brothers. Although the developmental gap between the two girls was apparent, the parents consciously sought to treat these youngest members of the family alike during those early formative years. However, when it was time for the girls to start attending school, Judith was found to be "ineducable" by the standards of the time. There was only one classroom for children with disabilities, and Judith was not able to pass the verbally-based entrance tests, due to her still undiagnosed deafness which prevented proper assessment of her capabilities. Consequently, on medical advice, her parents placed Judith in the Columbus State Institution (formerly the Columbus State School), an institution for the mentally disabled, on October 18, 1950. This separation had a profound effect on both twins and would influence Judith's later artistic expression. The records from Judith Scott's first few years at the Institution indicate that she had an IQ of 30 (based upon oral testing before her deafness was recognized). For this reason she was denied any training opportunities that might have developed her creative potential earlier. Deprived of her twin, Judith became severely alienated, and behavioral problems soon surfaced during her institutional confinement. Her Clinical Record states that "She does not seem to be in good contact with her environment. She does not get along well with other children, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats other children. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Soon after, she was moved to a smaller state institution at Gallipolis, Ohio, where she remained institutionalized and separated from family. In 1985, after 35 years of complete separation and lengthy and difficult negotiations, Joyce Scott became her sister's legal guardian, and brought Judith to live with her in California, a state where all mentally disabled citizens are entitled to an ongoing education and opportunities for personal development. Judith Scott died of natural causes at her sister's home in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks short of her 62nd birthday. She outlived her life expectancy at birth by almost fifty years, having spent the final decades creating her remarkable fiber sculptures. On April 1, 1987, Judith Scott began attending the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the first organizations in the world to provide studio space for artists with disabilities to explore creative expression. For almost two years, Judith showed little interest in any artistic activity at the center. She was unexceptional with paint and other conventional media. She scribbled loops and circles, but her work contained no representational imagery, and she was so uninterested in creating that the staff was considering ending her involvement with the program and discontinuing her artistic instruction. It wasn't until Judith casually observed a fiber art class conducted by visiting artist Sylvia Seventy, that she had her artistic breakthrough and discovered her true creative medium. Using the fiber materials at hand, Judith spontaneously invented her own unique and radically different form of artistic expression through sculptural wrapping techniques. While other students were stitching fabric in conventional ways, she was sculpting with fiber materials with an unprecedented zeal and concentration that astonished instructors. Her creative gifts and absolute focus on fiber sculpture were quickly recognized, and she was given complete freedom to choose her own materials for herWrapping practice. Taking whatever objects she found, regardless of ownership, she would wrap them in carefully selected colored yarns and threads to create diverse fiber sculptures of many different shapes and textures. Some fiber pieces resemble cocoons or body parts, while others are elongated totemic poles wrapped in layers of yarn. Many of her fiber works also feature pairs of wrapped forms, reflecting Scott's experience as a twin and her deep connection to pairing and duality in her sculptural practice. Judith worked on her fiber art five days a week for eighteen years, producing over 200 wrapped fiber sculpture pieces in total at Creative Growth. Judith had her first fiber art exhibition in 1999, which coincided with the publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott, an extensive study of her sculptural output. Together, these events helped propel her fiber sculpture to worldwide recognition in contemporary art circles. Scott's fiber work has become immensely popular in the world of outsider art and contemporary fiber art, and her wrapped sculpture pieces sell for substantial sums at galleries and auctions. Scott is now hailed as a contemporary fiber artist, no longer just an outsider creating wrapped objects. Her fiber art is held in the permanent collections of many museums, including: Museum of Modern Art (Manhattan, New York), the American Visionary Art Museum (Baltimore, Maryland), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Museum of American Folk Art (Manhattan, New York), Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art (Chicago, Illinois), Irish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin, The Oakland Museum, Oakland, CA. L'Aracine Musee D'Art Brut (Paris, France), Art Brut Connaissance & Diffusion Collection (Paris and Prague), Collection de l'art brut (Lausanne, Switzerland). Her fiber sculptures continue to be exhibited posthumously in major international exhibitions celebrating her innovative wrapped forms. Scott's fiber art has been featured in numerous notable exhibitions since 1999, showcasing her wrapped sculptural creations to growing audiences. In 2018, Judith Scott: Touchdown presented her fiber work at Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California. From 2014-15, Bound and Unbound at Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn, New York featured her binding techniques. In 2009, Judith Scott: Retrospective at Ricco Maresca Gallery, New York City showed the breadth of her fiber sculpture practice. In 2002, Cocoon: Judith Scott at Ricco-Maresca Gallery, New York City focused on her cocoon-like wrapped forms.

topics_down_v2.coling::ce094fc2-a215-4a99-a6f1-dc2a198d: Well, energy isn't a thing that gets literally transferred through space. Instead, it's a property of an object. It can be converted into other forms of energy by performing work on that object. In your example, the energy stored in your muscles gets converted to kinetic and subsequently to potential energy of the ball as you push it up a hill. You "give" the energy to the ball by performing work on it, which just means by applying a force on it over a distance. The ball gains energy precisely equal to the force you apply multiplied by the distance over which you apply that force. When you stop pushing the ball, it has acquired all the energy you transferred to it through your work. The ball's new energy state reflects the work done upon it. If you push the ball harder, you apply more force, and the ball gains more energy. If you push the ball over a longer distance, you do more work, and again the ball gains more energy. The relationship between force, distance, and energy transfer to the ball remains constant. The ball cannot gain energy without work being performed on it. Similarly, the ball cannot lose energy without performing work on something else. When the ball rolls back down the hill, it performs work on the air molecules it pushes aside, on the ground it rolls across, and potentially on your hand if you catch it. The ball transfers its energy by doing work on these other objects. The total energy of the ball before rolling down equals the work it can perform while rolling down. If the ball has more potential energy at the top of the hill, it can do more work on its way down. If the ball has less potential energy, it does less work. The ball's energy determines how much work the ball can accomplish. Work and energy represent two sides of the same physical process involving the ball. You cannot separate the ball's energy from the work done on the ball or by the ball. Every change in the ball's energy corresponds to work, and every instance of work corresponds to a change in the ball's energy. I hope my answer about the ball's energy is kinda helpful to you.

Under these treaties, the US retained its nuclear arsenal while other nations agreed to forego nuclear weapons development. The US extended its nuclear umbrella over numerous allied countries, promising nuclear retaliation against any nuclear attack on these allies, which theoretically eliminated their need for independent nuclear arsenals. This arrangement means the US maintains thousands of nuclear weapons while simultaneously working to prevent other countries from acquiring nuclear weapons. The US enforces non-proliferation agreements through diplomatic pressure, economic sanctions, and occasionally military action against countries attempting to develop nuclear weapons programs. The US positions itself as enforcing international consensus against nuclear proliferation, even though the US itself maintains a massive nuclear stockpile. The US argues this role is legitimate because the US operates within the framework of international treaties that explicitly permit the US to retain nuclear weapons as a recognized nuclear power. The US also points to its record of reducing its nuclear arsenal from Cold War peaks, though the US still possesses thousands of nuclear warheads. Critics argue the US applies a double standard by maintaining its own nuclear weapons while demanding other nations forsake nuclear programs entirely. The US responds that early nuclear powers like the US have different obligations under international law than nations that developed or sought to develop nuclear weapons after non-proliferation treaties took effect. We examine a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding framework for a topological
crystalline insulator (TCI) safeguarded by rotational symmetry. This construction is assembled
by layering two Chern insulators having opposite numerical values transforming
under conjugate representations of the rotational group, e.g. $p_\pm$ orbitals.
Despite apparent similarities to the Kane-Mele framework, it does not host stable
gapless boundary modes. Nevertheless this system exhibits nontrivial responses
including the emergence of quantized fractional charges bound to rotational
defects (disclinations) and the pumping of orbital momentum in reaction to
threading an elementary magnetic flux, described by a mutual
Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective
field corresponding to the rotational symmetry. Additionally, we demonstrate that
although filled bands of this construction do not admit a symmetric Wannier
representation, such obstruction is removed upon adding appropriate
atomic orbitals, implying fragile topology. Consequently, the reaction of
this system can be derived by representing it as a superposition of localized
orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients. Following the
analysis of this framework, which serves as a prototypical example of 2D TCIs
safeguarded by rotation, we demonstrate that all such insulators protected by point group
symmetries lacking protected boundary modes are either atomic
phases or fragile varieties. Remarkably, this implies gapless boundary
modes exist in free electron configurations if and only if there is a stable localized-orbital
obstruction. We then employ dimensional reduction to map the challenge of
classifying 2D TCIs safeguarded by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D) challenge
subsequently used to obtain the complete non-interacting classification of

The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) signature, observed within cosmic matter
distribution at redshifts reaching approximately 3.5, represents continued expansion of the
sonic horizon initially detected in temperature anisotropies of primordial
microwave radiation. The BAO feature location can currently be determined to better than
roughly 1% accuracy employing galaxies, and approximately 1.4-1.6% precision utilizing Ly-alpha forests plus
quasar clustering. Combined with the Alcock-Paczyński (AP)
phenomenon, arising from changing ratios of angular versus spatial/redshift
dimensions for (presumed) spherically-symmetric source arrangements at varying distances,
BAO determination is regarded as among the most powerful instruments for
assessing Universe geometry. Within this paper, we employ five such BAO signature
determinations from the final release of Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, at
average redshifts <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33, conducting a direct
head-to-head evaluation of the standard framework, Lambda-CDM, alongside one principal
competitor, designated the R_h=ct universe. For completeness, we
supplement the AP diagnostic via a volume-averaged distance method assuming
a constant comoving scale r_d. Both diagnostics are free from uncertain
quantities, such as Hubble's parameter, thus ideally suited for
this variety of framework selection. We find that R_h=ct is preferred by these
observations over conventional theory based solely on AP effects, with a
likelihood approximately 75% versus roughly 25%, while Planck-Lambda-CDM is favored over R_h=ct
relying solely upon volume-averaged distance methods, with likelihood around 80%
versus about 20%. A joint analysis combining both techniques produces an inconclusive
result, yielding comparable likelihoods favoring both frameworks. We are therefore unable
to confirm through this work that BAO evidence, independently, supports an
accelerating Universe.

objects across the entire Galactic plane.

that we generated. Eight training scenarios underwent testing to determine
optimal approaches for our astrophysical goal of classifying pixels as
filamentary.

segmentation identifying pixels belonging to filamentary architecture. This

I'm discussing the variety of criticism expressed repeatedly by particular participants within rpolitics, specific individuals from OWS, and [Gawker's Hamilton Nolan]. This represents a perspective I will summarize approximately as follows: The simple reality that we exist within a framework where certain humans can accumulate vastly greater resources than their neighbors is, inherently, unethical; if you do gather riches under such arrangements, you are quite arguably a reprehensible individual. Hedge fund managers are sitting around spending tens of millions on embalmed sharks...don't they recognize that a tiny portion of their daily income would make a huge impact in other peoples' existences? Would suffice to eliminate the average redditor's student debt, for instance? Every occasion I've encountered this terrible reasoning, I've witnessed it from activists or internet commentators who originate from the middle- (or, perhaps, working-class) segment of an advanced Western economy.

Here's the thing, though: you, too, possess vastly greater assets than most humans worldwide. If you could save 100 by not upgrading your smartphone, by walking home in the rain rather than taking a cab, by eating lentils or beans for several weeks or by foregoing that fresh garment you desired, you could donate those 100 dollars to rescue the existence of dozens of children who would otherwise perish from Malaria. Is your comfort, convenience and entertainment more significant than other individuals' survival?

As a premise of this CMV, we must stipulate that if prosperity could be redistributed, that redistribution would, indeed, benefit the recipients. We must further stipulate that if the average American wanted to contribute in a genuinely-beneficial manner towards a worthy cause, he'd be capable of doing so. I don't think these are crazy assumptions to accept.

So, my perspective is that those who rail against "the wealthy," purely on the ground that they're affluent, are hypocrites for overlooking their own relative economic standing in the world. If they believe other peoples' fortunes should be redistributed to curb inequality, they are hypocrites for not redistributing their own holdings to reduce disparity.

I can acknowledge the preference revealed by my decision-making, which is: I'd rather upgrade to business class than save 500 existences in a developing nation. I cannot stress this enough, so I'll just repeat it: Don't organize your finances around your credit score. Don't even think about your credit rating at all. Create a budget and stick to it. Make sure you include short and long term savings in your spending plan. Pay your bills on time. Use credit responsibly. Do all of these things, and your credit standing will take care of itself. Don't try to arrange your finances around raising it.

On the subject of 0% financing specifically, my rule of thumb is to only ever utilize it when I have enough money saved up to buy the thing outright, and even then only if my household ledger will still balance with the added cost of repaying the loan. One regulation you shouldn't follow is "do whatever will optimize your credit rating" because you shouldn't structure your finances around your numerical standing.

You're not really getting free money; you're just shifting around the time frame for payment, and only within a limited window at that. Also, be sure to read the fine print in the agreement; they can be filled with gotchas and pitfalls. In particular, if you don't clear the balance by the end of the introductory period, you can sometimes incur interest charges retroactively to the date of purchase. Make sure you know your terms and conditions cold.

It sounds like you're just getting started, so best of luck, and remember that Rome wasn't built in a day. Patience can be the most effective tool in your personal finance arsenal. This program is worse than terrible: it's toxic. Among the numerous television broadcasts that have exerted a corrosive influence on British society during the past two decades, Eastenders stands as the prime example. For twenty years this series has celebrated the oaf, the thug, the wide-boy, the tart, the gobby, the violent, the sexually-incontinent, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious...How often has someone or other remarked that Eastenders "mirrors existence"? Eager to demonstrate to their bourgeois peers how familiar they are with the "proletariat" they dream up the lumpen rabble that comprises the citizenry of Walford.

This has a poisonous effect on certain minds less well-equipped than others to handle fiction, and so we find members of the real population assuming the attitudes and demeanour of the inhabitants depicted in this soap opera.

Thus, it came to pass that Eastenders mirrors reality; but only after reality had been hoodwinked into mirroring such programming.

Meanwhile, the burgeoning number of new, TV-induced drones will proceed inexorably toward cultural bankruptcy.

And there you have the new priests and the new creatures of the early twenty-first century. Much of this results from the immeasurable power of that illuminated boxful of dancing pixels in the corner of your sitting-room. It's your fault, gentle reader: that's what you chose as the only window through which to look out from your prison.
