Educational institutions offering online attendance options or video-conference participation demonstrate greater likelihood of enhancing pupil achievement. Beginning in 2009, educational facilities commenced providing such programming to communities. Numerous households within the vicinity considered these initiatives worthless, while families residing at considerable distances regarded this as a brilliant concept. Such programming debuted at Generic_School, involving approximately ninety-two pupils. The inaugural year proved successful, as did the subsequent one.

Afterward, enrollment figures began declining. Why were fewer participants engaging with programming? What solutions could address this challenge? Why did local residents deem these offerings worthless? Why did distant households regard this as brilliant thinking? When programming enabling learners to participate via digital means or video-conference launched at Generic_School on September 2, 2009, ninety-two enrollees participated initially. All appreciated the offering, yet merely 70% returned for a subsequent term. The following period saw only sixty-five joining web-based instruction. Feedback received stated: "Being home while taking web-based courses is pleasant, and not worrying about tardiness is awesome, yet as a learner I'd love sharing thoughts and perspectives with fellow enrollees." By the third year, participation dropped to 10%. Beginning in 2011, approximately twenty learners enrolled in digital programming. Numbers decreased because remaining home constantly became boring for participants. Not sharing perspectives with fellow learners or engaging with peers proved problematic. Learners believed they required additional activities rather than remaining stationary in singular locations.

Several approaches could restore participant interest in programming. Digital instruction provides choices before joining any course. Such options include whether she/he wishes to venture out completing projects with fellow participants taking identical coursework. They can chat with peers and obtain information, selecting meeting dates. Alternatively, they could conduct video chats with fellow learners or utilize voice communication exclusively. Another possibility involves permitting participants to visit educational facilities weekly or monthly. Should these alternatives succeed, increasingly more enrollees will participate. Numerous local folks in 2009 believed digital coursework was worthless, fearing that opening enrollment broadly would reduce physical attendance at educational institutions. Several households approached the principal, stating "For many years our objective has been getting learners to physically attend educational facilities, and with such programming our objective will fail." Responding, the principal said "Certainly, we desire maximum possible physical attendance, but for various reasons not everyone can reach our facility, and as a benefit and opportunity for others seeking education we decided creating this offering." The principal conducted numerous meetings with parents disagreeing with this concept. After a month, most accepted and understood programming objectives. Distant residents thought this was brilliant thinking, since they wouldn't need traveling lengthy periods daily reaching educational facilities. Money would be saved, representing a tremendous opportunity for their children learning from residences. Distant households assembled and, as an act of appreciation, made donations supporting activities such as soccer, track or other pursuits. The educational institution recognized they genuinely pleased households, which was their objective: happiness and making everyone comfortable during their learning journey.

This manuscript extends Lenc&Vedaldi15's publication, demonstrating convolutional neural network encodings at the FC7 stage exhibit partial equivariance towards various categories of transformations, and that instruction utilizing particular groups of modifications renders encodings increasingly equivalent.

The researchers conducted an extensive quantity of trials, instructing over thirty architectures incorporating different forms of augmentation, which proves quite impressive. Nevertheless, identifying the central contribution of this investigation remains rather challenging. Indeed, the scientists measured properties on a distinct stage compared to Lenc&Vedaldi15's study; however, discovering novel insights beyond the established fact that augmentation assists in achieving invariance proves difficult. The assessment appears mostly accurate, yet the manuscript does not adequately address the problem advertised in its heading.

Primary concerns exist within the trials involving encoding distances:
* Selecting exclusively FC7 appears somewhat controversial—it precedes merely a single classification stage (FC8) leading to the standard output—class probabilities. Since FC8 constitutes just linear projection, what the equivariance mapping accomplishes is simply re-projecting the FC8 parameters of the attached architecture onto the parameters of the original architecture. Conducting comparable trials across additional stages might prove more beneficial (given that architectures are already instructed).
* The trial examining encoding distance omits reporting classification errors on validation datasets. This information would clarify whether encodings are genuinely compatible up to linear transformation whatsoever...
* For the K-NN trial, whether this measurement occurs per individual validation set instance remains unclear. Following instruction of the equivariance mapping? More transparent would be demonstrating that architectures instructed on comparable groups of augmentation modifications are more compatible regarding the target objective.
* The suggested approach does not consistently enhance equivariance across every objective. Particularly with λ₁ and λ₂ possessing such minimal values, the objective function basically equals simple data augmentation since it merely sums up the objective of the unmodified and modified image. Perhaps the concern lies in selecting the FC7 stage?

Overall, this manuscript presents some intriguing findings regarding FC7 equivariance, but fails to extract numerous intriguing fresh observations from these trials. Given several concerns regarding the equivalence trials and the fine-tuning of equivariance, I cannot recommend acceptance of this submission. Nevertheless, refining the trials on previously instructed architectures and restructuring this submission into more investigative scholarship might yield intriguing contributions to the discipline.

Several additional minor concerns exist:
* Experimental verification that the novel criterion for equivariance mapping produces superior outcomes is absent.
* The angles mentioned on pages one and five lack units (degrees?).
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult...", the component being maximised/minimised is not M_g itself, but rather the objective function over M_g.
* Page four, footnote two—if you are merely halving the activations, characterizing it as dropout seems inappropriate since this constant multiplier can be transferred to the subsequent/preceding parameters.
* Is the architecture for RVL-CDIP identical to Alexnet's structure?
* On page seven, Figures 3a+3b—in my view, converting diagonal elements to white appears genuinely misleading, and possibly even erroneous, since the distance between identical encodings should be zero (which also provides a method to verify that trials are conducted correctly).

Thank you for an intriguing contribution. I personally appreciate the information bottleneck principle and am delighted to observe its application toward deep neural architectures. To my understanding, this represents the inaugural manuscript applying IB for training multilayer networks (the original publications only introduced the concept), but see below regarding the notation of concurrent research claims.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound appears exceptionally transparent, even for readers who are not particularly familiar with variational inference methodologies. Additionally, the explanation of the IB framework is lucid. Experimental outcomes appear remarkably promising and demonstrate considerable potential.

I discovered the exposition concerning the architecture somewhat perplexing. In variational inference/information maximisation, p typically denotes the generative model whereas q represents the "inference engine". This implies the selection of inference techniques remains independent from the modelling procedure. However, the introduced VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and approximated by the empirical distribution), thus here the actual model becomes q(y|z)p(z|x). Subsequently, the authors introduced p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what manner? I suspect you intended p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this instance, but this renders the two definitions contradictory!

The authors have established an intriguing connection toward variational auto-encoders and the warm-up optimization (by tuning beta). Nevertheless, even when the loss function formula remains identical to the variational lowerbound employed in VAE (in this scenario beta equals 1), the underlying architecture differs substantially! For illustration, r(z) in VIB constitutes the variational approximation toward p(z) (which indicates r(z) is not a component within the architecture), whereas in VAE it represents the prior probability which is genuinely defined during the modelling procedure. Similarly, p(z|x) in VIB gets included within the architecture, whereas in VAE that becomes the approximate posterior and can be independently selected (e.g. you might employ p(x|z) as a multilayer NN but p(z|x) as a multilayer NN or a Gaussian process framework).

In summary, I believe the exposition regarding the modelling methodology remains unclear. I hope these points would receive clarification during revision since the current exposition leaves me uncomfortable as a Bayesian practitioner. In the VAE portion, it's preferable to explicitly mention distinctions between VIB and VAE, and supply intuitions if the VIB interpretation receives preference.

Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you intend q(y|z) rather than q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you intend "larger"?

**claim regarding concurrent research**
The authors asserted that the submission constituted an independent effort relative to Chalk et al. 2016 which appeared online since May 2016. It appears to me that contemporary deep learning scholarship is extremely competitive that numerous researchers publish identical ideas simultaneously. So I would trust this assertion and commend the authors' honesty, but should this prove untrue, I would not recommend the submission for acceptance. The competitive landscape makes simultaneous discoveries increasingly common.

This manuscript presents an MT training corpus selection methodology that evaluates and
prioritizes general-domain utterances utilizing a CNN classifier. Comparisons against previous research
employing continuous or n-gram based language modeling approaches are executed well, although it
remains ambiguous whether the study also contrasted with bilingual corpus selection techniques (e.g.
summation of cross-entropy differences).
The rationale for employing a CNN rather than an RNN/LSTM was initially unclear to me, but
it constitutes a merit of the manuscript to argue that certain segments of a text/sentence
carry greater significance than others and this is accomplished by a CNN. Nevertheless, the
manuscript fails to experimentally demonstrate whether a BOW or SEQ (or their combination)
representation proves more valuable and why.
The textual characterization of the CNN (one-hot or semi-supervised utilizing
pre-trained embeddings) 
appears lucid, comprehensive, and highlights the crucial aspects. Nevertheless, a diagram of
the layers illustrating how inputs are merged would be worth a thousand utterances.
The manuscript is generally well crafted, but some parentheses for citations prove
unnecessary (\citet vs. \citep) (e.g line 385).
Experiments and evaluation substantiate the assertions of the manuscript, but I am slightly
concerned regarding the procedure for determining the quantity of selected in-domain
utterances (line 443) relying on a separate validation corpus:
- What validation material is utilized here? It also remains ambiguous on what material
hyperparameters of the CNN architectures are chosen. How sensitive are these architectures to
this?
- Table 2 should genuinely contrast performance of different methodologies with identical
quantity of utterances selected. As Figure 1 demonstrates, the methodology of the manuscript
still appears to surpass the baselines in this scenario. 
Additional comments:
- I would be interested in an experiment that contrasts the technique of the
manuscript against baselines when additional in-domain material is available, not just the
development corpus.
- The findings or discussion segment could feature some example utterances
selected by the different techniques to substantiate the assertions made in section 5.4.
- Regarding the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in 5.4:
Another baseline to contrast against could have been the research of Axelrod, 2015,
who replaces some terms with POS tags to reduce LM corpus sparsity to determine whether
the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this.
- Utilizing the summation of source and target classification performance is very similar to
source & target Lewis-Moore LM corpus selection: summation of cross-entropy differences. A reference to this research around line 435 would be reasonable.
Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the summation of both source &
target classification performance by extending the CNN architecture to the
bilingual/parallel setting.

Within this manuscript, an intriguing methodology toward character-based language modeling is pursued that maintains word-level representations both within the context, and optionally also inside the output. Nevertheless, the technique is not novel, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the paper, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this contribution by applying the strategy using RNNs/LSTMs. Also, Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion of different methodologies to character-level modeling, which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing research. The remaining novelty of the proposal then would be its application to machine translation, although it remains somewhat unclear, in how far reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem - the translation-related part of the out-of-vocabulary issue should be elaborated here. That said, some of the claims of this manuscript seem somewhat exaggerated, like the statement in Sec. 2.3: "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete", whereas the authors e.g. express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity w/o an explicit output lexicon. For example modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144

Sec. 2.3: You claim that the objective requires a finite lexicon. This assertion only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. However, using subwords and even individual characters, implicitly larger and even infinite vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. Even though this requires a model different from the one proposed here, the corresponding statement should be qualified in this respect, making clear the boundaries of what was actually achieved and demonstrated.

The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified further. The description in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view and requires expansion.

Concerning the configuration of NCE, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific setup and parameterization described in Sec. 3.4 through experimentation.

Sec. 4.1: you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar conclusions w.r.t. the performance of using character embeddings at the output, and discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given therein rather than omitting relevant comparisons entirely.

Sec. 4.2: there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown tokens, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013), addressing measurement concerns raised previously.

Sec. 4.4 and Table 4: the size of the full training lexicon should be provided here for completeness and reproducibility purposes overall.

Minor comments:
p. 2, bottom: three different input layer -> three different input layers (plural form needed)
Fig. 1: fonts within the figure are way too small (readability compromised)
p. 3, first item below Fig. 1: that we will note WE -> that we will denote WE (proper verb choice)
Sec. 2.3: the parameters estimation -> the parameter estimation (or: the parameters' estimation with possessive)
p. 5, first paragraph: in factored way -> in a factored manner (article required)
p. 5, second paragraph: a n-best list, a nk-best list -> an n-best listing, an nk-best listing (article correction)
Sec. 4.2, last sentence: Despite adaptive gradient, -> verb and article missing (incomplete syntax).

The manuscript presents Edward, a probabilistic programming framework constructed atop TensorFlow and Python, accommodating an extensive array of widely-utilized contemporary approaches in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:

The Edward toolkit offers an exceptionally remarkable compilation of modern probabilistic inference techniques in an readily accessible format. The manuscript delivers a concise overview of crucial methodologies, particularly from a representation learning viewpoint, coupled with two experiments implementing various recent variational inference procedures and GPU-accelerated HMC.

The initial experiment (variational inference) would prove more beneficial if there existed an explicit connection to comprehensive code enabling reproduction of reported outcomes. The HMC investigation appears satisfactory, although characterizing Stan as a hand-optimized implementation feels unjust since the program is obviously not manually-optimized for this particular model and hardware setup. I doubt anybody questions the caliber of your system, so please avoid spoiling the presentation by unverified sensationalist assertions. Rather than current theatrics, I recommend comparing head-to-head versus Stan on a single processor and independently documenting the additional accelerations you obtain from parallelization and GPU. Such figures would furthermore assist readers in estimating the performance of the technique for alternative hardware setups.

Clarity:

The manuscript is generally lucidly composed and straightforward to comprehend. The multiple code illustrations are beneficial, but also challenging as it remains occasionally ambiguous what is absent. It would prove extremely valuable if the authors could supply and explicitly link to a machine-readable supplement (a Jupyter notebook would be excellent, but even plain text or HTML would be simpler to copy-paste from than a PDF like the manuscript) containing complete executable code for every illustration.

Originality:

The Edward toolkit is undeniably a distinctive compilation of probabilistic inference approaches. Regarding the manuscript, the primary challenge to novelty originates from prior publications of the identical research group. The principal manuscript references Tran et al. (2016a) which addresses substantial similar content, albeit from a different angle. It remains vague whether the other manuscript has been published or submitted elsewhere and if affirmative, where.

Significance:

It appears highly probable Edward will exert a substantial influence on the domain of Bayesian machine learning and deep learning.

Additional remarks:

In Section 2 you establish a sharp distinction between specialized frameworks (including Stan) and Turing-complete frameworks such as Edward. This appears unjust as I understand Stan is also Turing-complete. Furthermore, no demonstration is furnished to substantiate the Turing-completeness of Edward.
lexical_diversity_up_s.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c:
Initially, I want to mention that this manuscript is extremely lengthy. Approximately 17 pages extended -- without any supplementary materials. While ICLR does not impose an official page limitation, it would be considerate if researchers positioned themselves in the evaluator's perspective and avoided taking undue advantage of this regulation. Having 1 or 2 additional pages beyond the conventional 8-page restriction is acceptable, but more than doubling the count is quite unreasonable.

Now for the assessment: This submission proposes a novel synthetic corpus for sequential training. I characterize it as synthetic because it was artificially constructed from the original MNIST collection which is a relatively small repository of authentic photographs of handwritten numerical characters. In addition to the corpus, the researchers propose to train recurrent architectures using a curriculum over the duration of the input, which they term "incremental training". The experiments demonstrate that their suggested curriculum is superior to not having any scheduling on this collection. Furthermore, they also establish that their recommended approach is stronger than a few other intuitive curricula. The researchers verify this by performing some ablation investigations over the architecture on the suggested corpus.

I have following concerns with this submission:

-- I did not find anything innovative in this manuscript. The suggested incremental training curriculum is nothing original and is a natural thing to attempt when training sequences. Similar concepts have already been explored by a number of researchers, including Bengio 2015, and Ranzato 2015. The only fresh piece of contribution is the ablation investigations which the researchers conduct to tease out and confirm that indeed the enhancement in results is due to the scheduling used.

-- Furthermore, the researchers only test their hypothesis on a single collection which they suggest and is synthetically constructed. Why not use it on a genuine sequential corpus, such as, language modeling. Does the technique not succeed in that scenario? In fact I am quite confident that for language modeling where the vocabulary magnitude is enormous, the improvement gains will be nowhere close to the 74% reported in the manuscript.

-- I'm not persuaded about the merit of having this synthetic corpus. Already there are so many authentic world sequential collections available, including in text, speech, finance and other domains. What exactly does this collection contribute to the discussion is not super obvious to me. While having another corpus may not be a negative thing in itself, I almost felt that this collection was constructed for the sole intention of making the suggested concepts succeed. It would have been so much superior had the researchers shown evaluations on other collections.

-- As I mentioned, the manuscript is excessively lengthy. A significant portion of the duration of the submission is due to a compilation of evaluations which are completely unrelated to the main theme of the manuscript. For instance, the evaluation in Section 6.2 is completely disconnected from the narrative of the submission. Identical is accurate with the transfer training evaluations of Section 6.4.

Solar energy represents a miracle of modern science. There exists one tiny little problem, however. It remains more expensive than utilizing alternative forms of electricity generation. If cost weren't an issue, photovoltaic technology would be a superior choice, but that applies to all renewable sources.

Many individuals will point out that installing photovoltaic systems is on par with or even cheaper than constructing new electrical facilities, like atomic or fossil-fuel stations. While this holds true on a very large scale, you probably won't be building your own generating plant, and therefore don't face that expense to contend with.

Examine the price of a photovoltaic panel versus how much electricity *on average* it can produce. Do the math.

> I believe if the government invested some money they could easily shut down one or two nuclear power plants

You seem to be laboring under some false assumptions. Firstly, governmental agencies are subsidizing photovoltaic purchases in California in a huge way - so they *are* investing funds. Secondly, authorities do not operate atomic facilities - those are run by private corporations. They remain *regulated* by officials. Also, the primary expense of an atomic facility involves construction and radioactive waste disposal - not daily operations. Shutting functioning reactors wastes resources rather than saving them.

Like I said, I love photovoltaic energy for numerous reasons. It's "point of use," meaning there exists minimal loss due to long-distance transmission. Emissions are practically zero. Operation is silent (that's important for me). Photovoltaics provide greatest benefit when demand peaks highest, during summer, in daytime.

Possibly the best application of photovoltaics might involve running air conditioning. During warm months when sunshine is strong, cooling needs are intense. Employ radiation captured by panels to help chill buildings. Additionally, if collectors are mounted on roofs, they provide shade for structures. Win/win.

Still, on a pure expense versus benefit analysis, however, fossil fuels like coal or natural gas remain cheaper for providing electricity. Traditional methods continue dominating because financial considerations outweigh environmental advantages. Until pricing shifts dramatically, conventional generation will persist as the dominant approach despite ecological drawbacks inherent in burning hydrocarbons for residential and commercial consumption.

Imagine you're a trader residing in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a group of wealthy women who absolutely adore cumin (as in, the seasoning). Unfortunately, this spice doesn't flourish anywhere near your city; you must travel to the Middle East or India to obtain some of that excellent product, making it *extraordinarily costly*. Over there, however, the plant thrives like weeds and requires very little payment. If only you could transport some of that inexpensive seasoning over to your hometown, you could earn substantial profits!

Unfortunately, the sole method to accomplish that is dispatching a massive vessel for approximately nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you require a ship, plus a captain and sailors who all demand nine months' compensation), but it also carries tremendous danger. The vessel could sink, after all, or all the spices could rot.

So how do you achieve this goal? Assuming you're not fabulously wealthy yourself (and very few individuals or organizations, aside from perhaps entire nations, possess such riches), how do you fund this venture? You could approach a bank or lender and secure a loan, borrowing which would carry a very steep interest rate that could almost consume all of your earnings. And what if the boat sank? You'd be completely bankrupt, thrown into prison, if the creditor doesn't waste your broke ass first.

So, you devise a solution. You can't fund this voyage alone. But you could rather easily cover, say, one tenth of the expedition's price. And look at that—you have nine friends, each of whom could also afford one tenth of the journey's expense. So you all reach an agreement: you decide to each sponsor part of the voyage's expenditure (i.e. you "purchase shares" in the enterprise), each receiving portions worth one tenth of the total venture. With this capital, you cover the vessel and sailors, dispatch them, and then nine months later, they return with a cargo-hold brimming with delicious, extraordinarily expensive seasoning. The earnings far and away compensate for the initial investment, and each of you and your companions receives one tenth of the enormous returns.

But what happens if your vessel sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the sailors!), but you only paid for one tenth of the expenditure, and this was an amount you could afford to absorb; you're not gonna get killed over it. Since the danger was distributed around to 10 individuals, nobody landed in debtors prison. Everyone took a small hit, instead of one individual taking an enormous blow.

Consider this example, and all the participants involved in it. The fancy women obtained their seasoning (and for less than they would have otherwise). The shipwrights received work constructing a new vessel. The captain and sailors all secured employment and wages. The merchant in India gained a new customer for his spices. And obviously, you and your companions became really wealthy in the process. In short, *every single participant is better off*, and it wouldn't have occurred if this notion of "purchasing and selling shares" didn't exist.

This is the advantage of a stock market. It moves capital around from where it just lies idle doing absolutely nothing to where it can be put to use, and in the meantime, everybody becomes richer. It also distributes danger between lots of participants, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of the stock exchange functions. But the critique is that it stopped doing what it is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating resources so that they can be put into productive use) and stopped being a means to an end, becoming an end unto itself. The basic concept of a stock exchange is a fantastic notion, and you'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose it. It is why we have railroads, automobiles, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful food, medicine, and all the other contemporary things we value so highly.

To be blunt, unless you're very experienced with vintages, you probably won't be able to look at 2 similar bottles and immediately figure out which one you'll like better. What you can do is determine what kind of selections you prefer in general. To discover which types you enjoy, you have to actually sample a few of those options. Unfortunately, this can cost some money. Additionally, if you're actually 5, then it's illegal to purchase alcohol in the US.

Vintages are generally divided by where the grapes were grown and the species of grape (called the selection's "varietal"). Common Red Varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah (sometimes called Shiraz), Zinfandel. Common White Varietals: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris (sometimes called Pinot Grigio), Riesling, Gewurztraminer.

When you taste offerings, pay attention to what you appreciate about them. For example, many red selections have a distinctive flavor that makes your mouth feel dry. This is known as a "tannic" characteristic (because it's caused by molecules called tannins). If you appreciate tannic beverages, a tannic varietal, like Cabernet Sauvignon, might be good for you.

For white options, common noticeable traits include acidity (sourness) and sugar content. You probably don't need an explanation of what qualifies as sour or sugary. Another common trait to look for in red or white beverages is "oakiness". If you detect a wood-like scent in the vintage, that means that the drink has an "oaky" profile.

With all this in mind, remember that there's no such thing as a universally great bottle. All that matters is which kind you prefer best, even if that means choosing to consume a $10 jug of selection over a $500 container of fancy Cabernet from Bordeaux.

Also, when in doubt, ask the waiter, sommelier, or shop employee to help you out. Usually if you have a vague idea of what you want, they can assist you in finding something you'd appreciate in your price range. These professionals understand the nuances and can guide your decision effectively, ensuring you discover beverages that match your preferences without overspending or feeling overwhelmed by choices.

lexical_diversity_up_s.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) represents a crucial cybersecurity instrument for network administrators as it identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep neural networks, increasingly more IDS now employ automated algorithms to detect threats faster. However, these systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen categories of intrusions. With the growing number of novel exploits, especially against Internet of Things devices, having a resilient IDS able to spot unusual and emerging threats becomes necessary. This work explores possibilities of leveraging generative adversarial models to improve the strength of algorithm-based intrusion detection. More specifically, we propose a fresh method named SIGMA, that leverages hostile examples to strengthen defenses against emerging categories of breaches. Using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, SIGMA produces adversarial instances, iteratively, and uses them to retrain an algorithm-driven IDS, until convergence of the recognition rate occurs (i.e. until the defensive system stops improving). A round of enhancement consists of a generative stage, in which we use GANs and metaheuristic approaches to produce samples; an evaluation stage in which we calculate the recognition percentage of those newly produced intrusions; and a retraining stage, in which we coach the IDS with those breaches. We have assessed the SIGMA approach for four standard automated classification techniques acting as defenders, with a combination of GAN and a hybrid local-search plus genetic strategy, to create fresh datasets of exploits. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully produce hostile intrusions against different algorithm-driven IDS implementations. Also, using SIGMA, we can enhance the performance of an intrusion detector to up to 100 after as little as two cycles of refinement, demonstrating substantial improvements in defensive capabilities.
lexical_diversity_up_s.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks constitute leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs employed to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories, representing thus a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization value for such a network equals the sum totaling all indegrees minus node quantity plus one. The Hybridization Number challenge accepts as input a collection comprising phylogenetic trees, asking to construct a phylogenetic network containing an embedding for each supplied tree while possessing a smallest possible hybridization value. We present an algorithm addressing the Hybridization Number challenge on three binary phylogenetic trees over n leaves, operating in time O(c^k poly(n)), where k denotes the hybridization figure of an optimal network and c some positive constant. For scenarios involving two trees, an algorithm with running duration O(3.18^k n) was proposed previously, whereas an algorithm with running duration O(c^k poly(n)) for more than two trees had prior to this article remained elusive. The algorithm for two trees exploits the close connection to acyclic agreement forests to achieve a linear exponent in the running duration, while previous algorithms addressing more than two trees (explicitly or implicitly) relied on a brute force search through all possible underlying network topologies, leading to running durations that are not O(c^k poly(n)), for any c. The connection to acyclic agreement forests is much weaker when handling more than two trees, so even given the right agreement forest, the reconstruction of the network poses major challenges. We prove novel structural results allowing us to reconstruct a network without having to guess the underlying topology. Our techniques generalize to more than three input trees with the exception of one key lemma that maps nodes in the network to tree nodes and, thus, minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the network. The main open problem therefore is to prove results establishing such a mapping for more than three trees, which remains an outstanding theoretical question requiring further investigation and analysis to resolve completely.
lexical_diversity_up_s.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle which constitutes a simple subset-sum instance expressing that natural numbers written using binary representation cannot be negative, relating this to central problems in proof and algebraic complexity. Graph-Laplacians alongside their spectral embeddings serve crucial functions across numerous machine-learning domains. This paper concentrates on graph-Laplacian dimensionality reduction for clustering purposes as a primary application, though the methodology also finds utility in mining, manifold exploration, etc. Spectral representation yields low-dimensional parametrization of underlying structures, simplifying subsequent operations (e.g., partitioning via k-means or related approximations). Nevertheless, despite diminishing dimensionality, overall computational expense may remain prohibitive for large-scale datasets owing to two factors. First, calculating partial eigendecomposition of graph-Laplacians typically necessitates extensive Krylov subspaces. Second, following spectral transformation, one must still manipulate identical quantities of samples, potentially undermining efficiency. For instance, partitioning embedded observations usually employs various k-means relaxations whose computational burden scales poorly relative to dataset magnitude. Additionally, such methods become susceptible to entrapment in local minima, making robustness dependent upon initial selection.

In this work, we redirect attention from entire collections toward subsets of vertices (target collections). We develop two novel procedures for achieving low-dimensional representations of original structures while preserving significant global distances among nodes within target collections. Particularly, this permits ensuring target-collection partitioning remains consistent with spectral partitioning of complete datasets should one execute such operations. This achievement stems from properly parametrized reduced-order models (ROM) of graph-Laplacians approximating accurately diffusion transfer functions of original structures for inputs and outputs restricted to target collections. Operating with small target collections reduces substantially the required Krylov-subspace dimension while permitting exploitation of conventional procedures (like k-means approximations) in regimes where they demonstrate maximum robustness and efficiency. This received verification through numerical experiments involving both synthetic and authentic observations. We additionally note that ROM approaches can function in purely transfer-function-data-driven fashions, becoming the sole feasible option for extremely large-scale structures inaccessible directly.

Several applications exist for these procedures. First, they can serve independently for representative-subset partitioning in situations where handling full structures proves either infeasible or simply unnecessary. Second, they may provide quality-control mechanisms. Third, by drastically reducing problem scale, they enable deployment of more sophisticated procedures for tasks under consideration (like more powerful k-means approximations relying on semi-definite programming (SDP) rather than conventional Lloyd's methodology). Finally, they can function as building blocks of multi-level divide-and-conquer type strategies to handle complete structures. The latter will receive treatment in separate articles.

Our contribution addresses fundamental challenges in large-scale spectral analysis by providing computationally tractable alternatives that maintain essential geometric properties. The developed framework demonstrates versatility across various scenarios while preserving accuracy guarantees necessary for reliable downstream processing. Experimental validation confirms practical benefits across diverse settings, establishing the viability of our approach for real-world deployments.

The parameters n , k , r , t are positive integers satisfying r k n and t - n k . By functional restoration, we mean that the packet stored in each newcomer is not necessarily an exact replica of the vanished data but a symbol preserving the (r , t) -local restoration property. By the sequential methodology, we indicate that the t newcomers are ordered in a proper sequence enabling each newcomer to be restored from the live nodes and the newcomers that are ordered before it. lexical_diversity_up_s.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) involves constructing spatial representations of a mobile robot's surroundings while determining the robot's position within those representations. Dense SLAM methods perform reconstruction plus positioning at pixel granularity. These approaches require substantial computational resources, hindering their deployment on low-power resource-constrained hardware. Approximate computing can accelerate SLAM implementations provided the approximations don't prevent the robot from navigating correctly through its surroundings. Previous investigations of approximation in SLAM assumed that the entire trajectory was known before the robot starts, focusing on offline controllers setting approximation parameters at the trajectory's beginning. In practice, trajectories are usually unknown ahead of time, and allowing parameter settings to change dynamically opens more opportunities for reducing computation duration plus energy. In this paper, we describe SLAMBooster, an application-aware, online control mechanism for dense SLAM that adaptively manages approximation parameters during the robot's motion. SLAMBooster relies on a control technique called proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller but our experiments showed this application-agnostic approach led to unacceptable reductions in positioning accuracy. To address this issue, SLAMBooster also exploits domain expertise for managing approximation by performing smooth surface detection alongside pose correction. We implemented SLAMBooster in the open-source SLAMBench framework and evaluated it on more than a dozen trajectories from both published literature and our own investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that on average, SLAMBooster reduces computation duration by 72 percent and energy consumption by 35 percent on an embedded platform, while maintaining positioning accuracy within reasonable bounds. These improvements make deploying SLAM feasible across a wider range of hardware configurations, enabling broader adoption of these technologies on devices previously considered too resource-limited for such sophisticated mapping and localization tasks.
lexical_diversity_up_s.coling::6b54ef51-f42e-4ac2-840e-6b536faa: While the Commission possesses a monopoly on proposing legislation, the European Parliament and Council of the European Union wield powers of amendment plus veto throughout the lawmaking process. According to Treaty on European Union articles 9 and 10, the EU observes "the principle of equality of its citizens" and is meant to be founded on "representative democracy." In practice, parity and democratic governance are deficient because elected representatives in Parliament cannot propose laws against the Commission's wishes, inhabitants of smallest countries possess ten times the voting weight in Parliament as residents of largest nations, and "qualified majorities" or consensus of the Council are required to legislate. The justification for this "democratic deficit" under the Treaties is usually thought to be that completion integration of the European economy and political institutions required technical coordination of experts, while popular understanding of the EU developed and nationalist sentiments declined post-war. Over time, this has meant Parliament gradually assumed more voice: from being an unelected assembly, to its first direct elections in 1979, to having increasingly greater rights in the lawmaking process. Citizens' rights are therefore limited compared to the democratic polities within all European member states: under TEU article 11 inhabitants and associations possess rights such as publicising their views and submit an initiative that must be considered by the Commission with one million signatures. TFEU article 227 contains a further right for people to petition Parliament on issues which affect them. Parliamentary elections take place every five years, and votes for Members of the European Parliament in member states must be organised by proportional representation or a single transferable vote. There are 750 MEPs and their numbers are "degressively proportional" according to member state size. This means - although Council is meant to be the body representing member states - in Parliament citizens of smaller nations have more voice than inhabitants in larger countries. MEPs divide, as they do in national Parliaments, along political party lines: the conservative European People's Party is currently the largest, and the Party of European Socialists leads the opposition. Parties do not receive public funds from the EU, as the Court of Justice held in Parti ecologiste "Les Verts" v Parliament that this was entirely an issue to be regulated by member states. Parliament's powers include calling inquiries into maladministration or appoint an Ombudsman pending any court proceedings. It can require the Commission respond to questions and by a two-thirds majority can censure the whole Commission (as happened to the Santer Commission in 1999). In some cases, Parliament has explicit consultation rights, which the Commission must genuinely follow. However its role participation in the legislative process still remains limited because no member can actually propose or pass legislation without the Commission and Council, meaning power kratia is not in the hands of directly elected representatives of the people demos: in the EU it is not yet true that "the administration is in the hands of the many and not of the few."

A digital signature constitutes a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of electronic messages or documents. A valid cryptographic signature, where prerequisites are satisfied, gives a recipient very high confidence that content was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that transmitted information was not altered in transit (integrity).

Such signatures are a standard element of most cryptographic protocol suites, and are commonly employed for software distribution, financial transactions, contract management applications, and in other cases where detecting forgery or tampering is important.

These cryptographic tools are often utilized to implement electronic signatures, which includes any electronic data that carries the intent of a handwritten mark, but not all such electronic authentication uses cryptographic validation. Electronic signing has legal significance in some countries, including Canada, South Africa, the United States, Algeria, Turkey, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Saudi Arabia,[10] Uruguay,[11] Switzerland, Chile[12] and nations of the European Union.[13][14]

Cryptographic signatures employ asymmetric encryption. In many instances, they provide a layer of validation and security to communications sent through a non-secure channel: Properly implemented, such authentication gives the receiver reason to believe transmitted content originated from the claimed originator. These methods are equivalent to traditional handwritten marks in many respects, but properly implemented cryptographic authentication is more difficult to forge than the handwritten type. Signature schemes, in the sense used here, are cryptographically based, and must be correctly applied to be effective. They can also provide non-repudiation, meaning that signers cannot successfully claim they did not authorize correspondence, while also claiming their private key remains secret.[15] Further, some non-repudiation approaches offer a timestamp for the cryptographic mark, so that even if the private key is exposed, the authentication remains valid.[16][17] Cryptographically signed communications may be anything representable as a bitstring: examples include email, contracts, or correspondence sent via some other encryption protocol.

Voice pattern identification represents an interdisciplinary subfield within computing sciences and computational linguistics, developing methodologies plus technologies enabling recognition alongside translation of spoken language into written form via machines, with primary advantages including searchability. This discipline is additionally termed automatic vocal recognition (ASR), machine utterance identification, or talk-to-writing (STT). The area incorporates knowledge from informatics, philology, and electronic engineering domains. The inverse procedure involves synthesis.

Certain vocal identification platforms require "training" (alternatively labeled "enrollment") whereby individual users read passages or isolated vocabulary aloud for processing. Such systems analyze that particular person's distinctive timbre, utilizing these characteristics to refine detection capabilities regarding their articulations, yielding enhanced precision. Platforms eschewing such preparation are designated "speaker-independent" arrangements. Conversely, those employing calibration bear the designation "speaker dependent" configurations.

Applications for utterance detection encompass auditory user interfaces like telephone dialing through commands (for instance, "contact residence"), routing incoming communications (such as "I desire placing a reverse-charge telephone connection"), home automation device management, locating keywords during searches (for example, discovering podcasts containing specific terminology), basic information input tasks (including entering payment card digits), creating organized documentation (like radiological reports), ascertaining vocalization characteristics, converting oral communication into written format (within word processing programs or electronic correspondence), plus aviation contexts (commonly called direct auditory input).

The expression vocal recognition or speaker identification denotes determining who is speaking instead of deciphering their message content. Identifying the individual vocalizing can streamline translation tasks within platforms calibrated for particular persons' timbres, or serve authentication purposes, verifying someone's identity during security protocols.

Regarding technological evolution, vocal pattern detection possesses extensive historical development featuring multiple waves of significant breakthroughs. Recently, this domain has gained from progressions in neural networks and massive datasets. These developments manifest through surging quantities of scholarly publications appearing within the discipline, but more significantly through global commercial implementation of diverse neural network techniques when designing and launching voice pattern identification platforms across industries worldwide, demonstrating practical adoption beyond theoretical advancement.

Control theory represents a mathematical discipline addressing the regulation of dynamical systems within engineered processes plus machinery. Its objective involves developing models or algorithms governing how inputs are applied for driving these arrangements toward desired states, while minimizing delays, overshoot, plus steady-state errors and ensuring stability; often aiming to achieve optimality.

Accomplishing this requires controllers with requisite corrective behavior. Such controllers monitor controlled process variables (PV), comparing them against references or set points (SP). The difference between actual and target values, termed the error signal or SP-PV discrepancy, gets applied as feedback for generating corrective actions bringing the monitored variable to match the setpoint. Additional aspects studied include controllability plus observability. This discipline finds application in system engineering for designing automation that has revolutionized manufacturing, aircraft, communications, and other industries, creating new domains like robotics.

Extensive utilization is typically made of diagrammatic styles known as block diagrams. Within these, transfer functions—also called system or network functions—constitute mathematical models representing relations between inputs and outputs based on differential equations describing the arrangement.

The discipline dates from the nineteenth century, when theoretical bases for governor operation were first described by James Clerk Maxwell. The field was further advanced by Edward Routh in 1874, Charles Sturm, and in 1895, Adolf Hurwitz, who all contributed toward establishing stability criteria; and from 1922 onwards, development of PID methodology by Nicolas Minorsky.

Although a major application of mathematical regulation involves process management systems for industry, other applications range far beyond. As the general study of feedback arrangements, this discipline proves useful wherever feedback occurs—thus having applications in life sciences, computer engineering, sociology, and operations research. The widespread relevance stems from fundamental principles governing how information about outcomes influences subsequent actions, making the framework applicable across diverse domains. Whether managing industrial operations, understanding biological homeostasis, optimizing computational algorithms, analyzing social dynamics, or improving operational efficiency, the underlying concepts provide valuable analytical tools for understanding and improving complex interactive systems across multiple disciplines and practical contexts.

Pharmaceutical design, frequently termed rational medication development or simply rational creation, is the inventive procedure of discovering novel therapeutics grounded in understanding a biological target. The compound is typically an organic small molecule activating or inhibiting biomolecular function, such as proteins, which consequently produces therapeutic benefits for patients. In the most fundamental sense, pharmaceutical development involves creating molecules complementary in structure and electrical properties to the biomolecular targets with which they interact and therefore bind. Medicinal development often but not necessarily relies on computer modeling approaches. This category of simulation is sometimes called computer-aided pharmaceutical creation. Finally, therapeutic development relying on understanding three-dimensional structures of biomolecular targets is termed structure-based medicinal creation. Beyond small molecules, biopharmaceuticals including peptides and especially therapeutic antibodies represent an increasingly significant category of therapeutics, and computational techniques for improving affinity, selectivity, and stability of these protein-based treatments have also been created.

The phrase "pharmaceutical design" is somewhat a misnomer. A more accurate expression is ligand creation (i.e., developing a compound binding tightly to its target). Although development approaches for predicting binding affinity prove reasonably successful, many additional properties, such as bioavailability, metabolic half-life, adverse effects, etc., must first be optimized before a ligand becomes a safe and efficacious medication. These additional characteristics are frequently difficult to forecast with rational development strategies. Nevertheless, due to high attrition rates, especially during clinical stages of pharmaceutical development, greater attention is being focused early in the medicinal creation procedure on selecting candidate compounds whose physicochemical attributes are predicted to yield fewer complications during advancement and hence prove more likely to result in an approved, marketed therapeutic. Data dredging (also known as snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of analysis to find patterns in information that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is done by performing many statistical tests on observations and only reporting those that come back with noteworthy results.

The process of dataset dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses using a single collection by exhaustively searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and perhaps for groups of cases or records that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other measure.

Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular outcome would arise if chance alone were at work, and necessarily accept some risk of mistaken conclusions of a certain type (erroneous rejections of the null hypothesis). This level of danger is called the significance threshold. When large numbers of evaluations are performed, some produce false findings of this sort; hence 5% of randomly chosen conjectures might be (incorrectly) reported to be statistically meaningful at the 5% level, 1% might be (wrongly) declared statistically important at the 1% threshold, and so on, by chance alone. When enough propositions are examined, it is virtually certain that some will be announced as statistically relevant (even though this is misleading), since almost every dataset with any degree of randomness is likely to contain (for example) some spurious associations. If they are not cautious, researchers using mining techniques can be easily deceived by these outcomes.

Dataset snooping is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons challenge. One form occurs when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the total number of subgroup analyses examined, creating an illusion of discovery where none exists in reality.

Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) represents a private research institution situated within Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. During 1967, the Carnegie Institute of Technology merged alongside the Mellon Institute of Industrial Research, founded during 1913 by Andrew Mellon plus Richard B. Mellon and formerly part of the University of Pittsburgh.[10] Carnegie Mellon University has operated as a single consolidated institution since that merger occurred.

This university consists of seven colleges plus independent schools: The College of Engineering, College of Fine Arts, Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, Mellon College of Science, Tepper School of Business, Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy, alongside the School of Computer Science.[11][12] The institution possesses its main campus situated 5 miles (8 kilometers) from Downtown Pittsburgh. It also maintains over a dozen degree-granting locations across six continents, including degree-granting facilities within Qatar, Silicon Valley, and Kigali, Rwanda (Carnegie Mellon University Africa) plus partnerships alongside universities throughout the United States and within the United Kingdom, Portugal, Japan, China, Mexico, and Italy.[13]

Carnegie Mellon remains known for advances in investigation and novel fields of study, notably being home to many firsts in computer science (including the first computer science, machine learning, and robotics departments), pioneering the field of management science,[14] and housing the first drama program in the United States. Trapdoor spiders measure approximately 0.79 inches to 1.26 (1 to 3 cm) in length. That means roughly between the dimension of your pinky nail and your thumbnail.

These arachnids are black or brown, possessing stout bodies and limbs. Certain species display paler markings, or they might possess a silky covering of hair. Their anatomy is divided into two sections: the cephalothorax (containing the cranium and appendages) and the posterior segment. The posterior portion is typically lighter and a somewhat different shade.

Though they may prove difficult to observe because of their diminutive stature, a trapdoor arachnid will possess 6 visual organs arranged in 3 clusters, whereas most other spiders possess 8 ocular structures. Trapdoor varieties are relatives of tarantulas, but are less hairy, and have smaller, shinier physiques.

The mandibles of a trapdoor specimen are attached to the front of its cranium. They move up and down, unlike most other arachnids, whose jaws shift side to side.

Female trapdoor creatures are larger than the males, but you will seldom encounter females because they rarely leave their underground dwellings. Therefore, if you observe a trapdoor arachnid, it is most likely a male specimen. Look for these characteristics that identify masculine trapdoor individuals:

Short and blunt spinnerets. These produce silk, and are located at the tip of the abdomen. A double projection about halfway along their front limbs.

A dusty or dull shield (a harder area covering much of the cephalothorax) that is lightly covered in bristles. Pedipalps (small appendages near the mandibles) that resemble boxing mitts.

There are numerous varieties of trapdoor arachnids, each with somewhat different physical attributes. More variations of trapdoor specimens are still being discovered. If you think you have encountered a trapdoor creature, research the specific kinds that inhabit your region, so that you know can what sort of particular features to expect.

The geographic distribution of trapdoor creatures is erratic and is attributed to continental drift. Various forms of trapdoor arachnids can be found all over the planet. Search for trapdoor examples in: North America: Canada, The United States (southeastern and pacific regions, and north to Colorado)

Central America (Guatemala, Mexico, etc.)

Asia (China, Japan, Thailand, etc.)

South Africa and Madagascar

Australia

Throughout the globe, trapdoor specimens favor warm environments, such as temperate woodlands and arid landscapes. They will excavate in grassy terrain, hillsides, and dirt embankments.

Trapdoor arachnids excavate in the soil (about 0.75 inches wide and up to 8 inches deep) and conceal their tunnel with a silken hinged "lid" camouflaged by sticks, pebbles, and other natural material. Because the tunnels are camouflaged, they can prove very hard to detect.

Larger excavations may have multiple lids.

Usually, the tunnel faces sunlight and will be found near vegetation.

Trapdoor creatures are shy, may be nocturnal, and are rarely observed far from their excavations (males may wander during breeding season, however). You might be able to spy one, however, when it feeds. The arachnids will wait in their tunnels until they sense vibrations in the earth caused by insects (including crickets, moths, beetles, and grasshoppers) and other arthropods. Then, the creatures will leap out of the entrance, grab one of these prey animals, and drag it back into the underground dwelling.

Cleanse your kneecap using a moistened cloth and, if needed, gentle cleanser. Remove grease, perspiration, and any lathering agent remnants, then pat the area completely moisture-free. Ensuring the kneecap surface remains pristine and without dampness will help prevent irritation. Consider shaving this region 12 hours before applying adhesive if wrapping will occur repeatedly. This step helps reduce discomfort when removing the binding material.

Recline with your back propped upward or supported while legs extend outward before you. Kneecaps should remain completely relaxed and slightly flexed. To maintain this bent, calm position, place a rolled towel beneath the joint.

You'll utilize rigid athletic adhesive to perform the actual McConnell method. However, such binding material can prove irritating and uncomfortable, so first cover your entire kneecap with low-irritant, hypoallergenic wrapping. A permeable, breathable white cotton strip serves as an excellent underwrap option.

Utilize a marker or pen to gently trace all four borders of your patella. This action defines your working surface on the underwrap layer. Applying the athletic adhesive properly becomes easier when you can actually observe the patella's boundaries.

Employ non-stretch sticky athletic binding for the McConnell method. Cut a two-to-three-inch (five-to-eight-centimeter) section, or sufficient length to span from outer to inner edges. Athletic adhesive with a width measuring 38 millimeters (1.5 inches) works best for patella wrapping.

Position one end of the strip along the outer border of your patella so the binding remains vertically centered with the joint. Attach the adhesive to skin in a downward direction toward the lower inside corner, and utilize your thumb to gently nudge the patella toward the inside of the limb.

While moving the patella and positioning the binding, utilize fingers to carefully draw the flesh on the interior of your limb toward the kneecap. Your objective involves pushing the patella toward the inside of your extremity, wrinkling the flesh there so it meets the kneecap, and employing the adhesive to hold them tightly together.

Position one border of the second section along the outer margin of your joint and, again, ensure it's vertically centered with your patella. Attach the binding to flesh in a straight, horizontal motion. The strip should form a straight line from the outside of your joint to the interior. Add one to three additional layers until you feel your desired level of firmness and stability.

Ensure you've created flesh wrinkles on the interior portion of your joint. These creases should run vertically, or upward and downward, and you should observe them through the underlay. Wrinkling of the flesh results when you draw the patella inward and fasten it to the tissue on the interior of the limb.

Wear the binding during physical exertion as directed by your rehabilitation specialist or another healthcare professional. Generally, you should eliminate the adhesive within 48 hours of placement. As strength, range of mobility, and equilibrium improve, maintain the joint wrapped for shorter durations during general activities. Progress toward wrapping it only for higher-risk endeavors, like athletics.

Hold your patella as you slowly peel away the binding to avoid worsening an injury. Position your fingers as close as possible to the adhesive's attachment line, or where it contacts your flesh. Follow this line with your digits as you draw the section away to guide it off your skin. Removing too quickly can cause dermal irritation or abruptly force the patella out of alignment.

Eliminate the binding immediately if it worsens your discomfort. Remove the wrapping if you experience discoloration, tingling sensations, or inflammation after positioning the adhesive. Inform your rehabilitation specialist or other healthcare professional about these or any other adverse symptoms resulting from wrapping. It's best to consult a healthcare professional before wrapping, especially if you have circulatory complications, a joint fracture, or are allergic to athletic adhesive.

Corfe Castle railway station is a railroad depot located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally an intermediate stop on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch route from Wareham to Swanage, the track and facility were closed by British Rail in 1972. It has since reopened as a terminal on the Swanage Railway, a heritage line that runs from Norden depot just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage terminus.

Corfe Castle sits on a railroad connection linking Wareham and Norden.

History
Corfe Castle lies in the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, a peninsula bordered by the English Channel to the south, and by the marshy lands of the River Frome and Poole Harbour to the north and east. At the beginning of the 19th century, the area around Corfe Castle was known for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay, which at that time was shipped by a pair of horse-drawn tramways (the Middlebere Plateway and the Furzebrook Railway) to wharves on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage at the tip of the Isle was equally well recognised for the Purbeck Marble that was mined locally and transported out by sea.

The presence of these industries attracted railroad promoters once the L&SWR main track reached Wareham in 1847. Several schemes were promoted and failed, but eventually the Swanage Railway received its Act in 1881 and commenced operations on 20 May 1885. The position of Corfe Castle, commanding the only relatively low level route across the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that the connection passed close to the centre of the village, and Corfe Castle depot was constructed for the inaugural service. From its beginning, the route was operated by the L&SWR, and absorbed into that company in 1886. Corfe Castle facility was the only intermediate stop on the Swanage branch, a status it retained until closure by British Rail, and possessed the sole passing loop between the junction with the main artery at Worgret Junction and Swanage. At least one camping coach was positioned here by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967, and probably from 1948 to 1953. From 1960, the allocated carriage was a camping vehicle converted from a Pullman car, which was fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping compartments and a room with twin single beds, from 1962 until 1967 there were two of these vehicles here.

While the development of Swanage as a tourist resort brought additional passenger traffic to the route, the collapse of both the clay and marble extraction businesses, and the increase in private automobile ownership in the second half of the 20th century made the branch unprofitable. Shutting down was first proposed in 1967, and despite local opposition the railroad finally ceased operations on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of operation under British Rail, passenger train services were handled by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units (also known as type 2H).

From the time of the first proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen the railway as a steam locomotive operated heritage attraction developed. Most of the trackbed, including Corfe Castle terminal, was bought by Dorset County Council. Proposals to use the corridor through the Corfe Castle gap as a road bypass for the village were eventually rejected by the county authorities in 1986. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the artery in 1982.

There were concerns that reopening Corfe Castle facility as a northern endpoint for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the settlement. It was therefore decided to extend the connection a further half a mile north to a new Park and Ride site built on the former location of the exchange sidings between the Swanage branch and the clay tramways. Here the new Norden terminus was constructed and most trains stop here. Corfe Castle depot reopened on 12 August 1995, although the official ceremony was not until February of the following year.

A 5-year project by Swanage Railway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running tracks between the platforms at Corfe Castle was completed in April, 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official unveiling. The overpass was originally constructed in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, the structure spent its life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon corridor until removed by Swanage Railway supporters. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now use Corfe Castle facility, and is safer and more convenient for the public than crossing over the rails via the gated and locked foot crossing. The endeavor won the National Railway Heritage Awards in December 2007, with a plaque presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of helpers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee.

In summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway operated two trains per day to/from Wareham, one of which continued to Poole and the other to London Waterloo via Weymouth. There were also National Rail journeys on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage in summer 2018 and 2019 operated by West Coast Railway Company with three locomotives per day in each direction. However, in July 2019 these schedules were stopped and there are currently no National Rail connections to Corfe Castle.

Services
Services run every day from the beginning of April to late October, with weekend only operation in March, November and December. The level of provision varies from 6 to 17 departures a day in each direction, depending the season and the day of the week. Southbound, locomotives operate to stations at Harman's Cross (10 mins), Herston (vehicles stop only on request), and Swanage (21 mins). Northbound, engines operate to Norden depot (3 mins).

Museum
Corfe Castle facility is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railroad Museum, which is housed in the old goods shed and an adjacent rail van. The exhibition is open on most operating days.

The collection includes Secundus, a narrow gauge steam engine built by Bellis and Seeking in 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway. This machine was in use until 1955, and then displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000. It is planned that the equipment will eventually be transferred to a new home at the Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum, currently being developed adjacent to Norden railway terminal.
