Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former vice for the Mike McEwen squad which competed out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the newly formed Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk. For the 2006-07 campaign, Richter and Melnuk departed the foursome and were replaced with Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The lineup disbanded after just one year together.

Wozniak and McEwen united with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007. In their inaugural season as teammates, they were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's provincial competition. Their debut Grand Slam event as a unit was at the conclusion of the campaign, at the 2008 Players' Championships. The quartet won two games, before being eliminated.

At the end of the 2008-09 season the McEwen foursome was ranked 7th on the CCA rankings. They had advanced to three Grand Slam playoffs, and finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Olympic Qualifier, the McEwen squad just lost out to fellow Manitobans the Jason Gunnlaugson rink in the semi-finals. Team McEwen thus missed out on the 2009 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials final despite being the favourite in that particular matchup versus Gunnlaugson.

McEwen's lineup made it to his first provincial championship match in 2010, when he fell to Jeff Stoughton in the 2010 Manitoba title bout. The contest was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba and as the Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach, were treated very much as the home squad and crowd favourites.

2010-2015: Grand Slam success and perennial provincial runner-up
Team McEwen started the 2010-11 campaign off well by defeating regional rival Jeff Stoughton to capture the World Cup of Curling and his inaugural ever Grand Slam victory in November, 2010. In part of the teams runner-up result in the provincial finals of 2010 and in part because of his 4 triumphs and leading the overall money winnings in the World Curling Tour season as of November 2010, the McEwen ensemble was named as a nominee for the provincial squad of the year by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters Association.

The ensemble continued their strong season that year by vanquishing territorial rival Stoughton in the semi-final of the 2011 Canadian Open. They would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard foursome in the extra end of the championship, thus winning their second career Grand Slam and their second of that campaign.

Wozniak's rink once again advanced to the Manitoba provincial this time, being the top seed (also ranked 1st in Canada). However, once again fell to Stoughton in the finale of the 2011 Safeway Championship, dropping by one point in the concluding end. The McEwen lineup then dropped their third straight provincial title contest at the 2012 Safeway Championship, this time falling to Rob Fowler, thus tying a provincial record for consecutive championship defeats previously set by Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This dubious record was avoided in 2013, when the McEwen rink failed to reach the finale, but again dropping to the rival Stoughton ensemble in the 2013 Safeway Championship semi-final. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship, the unit dropped the title match to Stoughton.

Despite being ranked first in the world on both the World Curling Tour Order of Merit rankings and on the WCT money list, Wozniak dropped his fifth provincial championship in six years in 2015, falling to Reid Carruthers.

Three Briers and team breakup
Wozniak's rink captured their inaugural provincial crown in 2016, sending them to their debut Brier. The Matt Dunstone ensemble had committed themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships, which occurred at the same time as the 2016 Tim Hortons Brier, so when the Dunstone outfit beat Reid Carruthers in the semi-final, McEwen's squad would go to the Brier, even if they had dropped to Dunstone.

In 2017, Wozniak defended his Manitoba Championship by defeating Reid Carruthers in the finale. He would then better his 2016 Brier showing, going 9–2 in the round robin to enter the playoffs in first place and with hammer and choice of rocks (Brad Gushue was also 9–2 but dropped first place due to dropping his round robin meeting with Manitoba). He then dropped 7–5 to Brad Gushue in the 1 versus 2 contest. In the semi-finals against reigning Brier and World Champion Kevin Koe, they were in control for most of the encounter, being up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end, but Koe made a comeback with a steal in the eighth end, two points in the tenth end, and another steal in the extra end, dropping Manitoba to the bronze medal encounter. They recovered to capture their inaugural Brier medal, vanquishing Brad Jacobs in their rematch of the 2016 bronze medal encounter, 7–6 in an extra end.

While competing at the 2018 Viterra Championship, skip McEwen came down with chickenpox and was unable to participate after the opening contest. B. J. Neufeld skipped the unit, until a surprise appearance by McEwen in the championship, where they dropped to Carruthers. Despite the setback, they still had a chance to qualify for the 2018 Tim Hortons Brier through the wildcard encounter, which they captured over Jason Gunnlaugson. Team McEwen had a difficult Brier and alongside Carruthers was unable to qualify for the playoffs. Following the Brier, the McEwen ensemble announced they would be breaking up at the conclusion of the 2017–18 campaign. Just days after the announcement, the McEwen foursome captured the 2018 Elite 10 Grand Slam of Curling tournament, capturing the top $28,000 prize money, and was the initial outfit to go through the entire competition undefeated. The Grand Slam triumph was the ensemble's seventh overall.

Wozniak took a few years off from men's play after Team McEwen broke up. However, he participated in mixed doubles with his current girlfriend Marlene Albrecht and spared for McEwen's newly formed outfit. After Alex Forrest stepped away from competitive curling after the 2019–20 campaign, Wozniak joined the Jason Gunnlaugson rink. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial championship was cancelled. As Team Gunnlaugson were the reigning provincial champions, they were chosen to represent Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons Brier. Because of the pandemic situation affecting Manitoba, the 2021 regional title event was called off. As the defending titleholders, Team Gunnlaugson was selected to represent Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons Brier. At the Brier, they finished with a 6–6 record.

Personal life
Wozniak is employed as a mortgage broker for Vertuity Mortgage. He is currently in a relationship with Swiss curler Marlene Albrecht and has two children.

Operation Claw () was a joint Swedish–American operation, with Norwegian support, that was carried out at Lillehammer shortly after the German capitulation by the end of World War II. Thirty-five Reich intelligence specialists were transferred along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied territories through an agreement between the Americans and the Wehrmacht's High Command in Norway. The espionage material from this undertaking, among it a Soviet codebook, became very useful for the United States during the Cold War.

This mission was controversial both when it happened and afterwards. In 1945, controversy arose because the United States operated in what was seen as a British controlled country, and that they secured information about its ally Russia, in cooperation with neutral Sweden. In later years, a hypothesis that the Norwegian resistance fighter Kai Holst's sudden death in June 1945 was related to his involvement in the affair has been put forward by among others the historian Tore Pryser.

Even before the European conflict ended the various allied states had begun searching for Reich scientists and other Third Reich expertise. Signals intelligence had been vital during World War II and especially the British work breaking codes, including deciphering Enigma transmissions, had been of huge importance. The Yalta Conference in February 1945 had revealed conflicts of interest between the western allied nations on one side and Moscow on the other, and relations were severely strained. U.S. intelligence organisations were very interested in Third Reich espionage experts' knowledge of Russia and immediately after hostilities in Europe ended they began cooperating with Major General Reinhard Gehlen and his organisation Fremde Heere Ost (FHO) which had led military intelligence on the Eastern Front. It was part of an organized effort to obtain as much Reich espionage information and personnel as possible; the initiative had the name Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM).

The conflict was however still fought in East-Asia, Washington and Moscow were still allies and the United States were counting on Russian assistance in the struggle against Japan. The victors had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence. Both for Washington and neutral Sweden the undertaking was thus very sensitive and was conducted in great secrecy.

In the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer a group of 35 Reich experts on signals intelligence were gathered. They had been working on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces and had an archive and extensive knowledge about Russian affairs. This was expertise the Western Allies, and especially America, wanted and that probably also proved useful during the subsequent confrontation between East and West. In cooperation with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and support from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm agents for the Swedish intelligence organisation C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The assembled group of specialists were taken out of the camp and transported to Sweden. After a few weeks there they were on June 12 flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to U.S. occupied territory and were interned in an American military facility at Wiesbaden.

The transfer to Sweden of the Reich specialists at Lillehammer, that OSS called Operation Claw, was directed from the highest level. From the U.S. side the leader of OSS, Major General William J. Donovan was involved, from the Swedish side the chief of the Defense Staff, Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd. The famous Swedish police director Harry Söderman was also involved from Stockholm's perspective.

More than a month after the Reich capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed in order to find people from Gestapo and other key individuals that tried to hide among ordinary soldiers in military camps. The search force that Kai Holst and other Norwegians were assisting soon became aware that a number of crucial individuals had been removed in the Swedish–American extraction a month earlier. Kai Holst had been working at the military office number 4 (Mi4) at the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, and after the investigation he unexpectedly traveled right back there. The next day he was found shot at the top of the staircase in an apartment building at Rindögatan 42 on Gärdet. The official cause of death was stated as suicide, but neither Holst's family nor many of his colleagues from the resistance movement have accepted this verdict and are of the opinion that he was liquidated.

The historian Tore Pryser has put forward the hypothesis that Holst brought with him details from Lillehammer that could damage the entire mission and thus was killed. To be able to sabotage it Kai Holst cannot have been trusted as others were. He must have been considered a threat due to his contact with Alexandra Kollontaj who was ambassador in Stockholm representing Moscow. A possible reason for a murder of this resistance member was thus not his knowledge as such but his connections to Soviet representatives.

This undertaking was the beginning of postwar era cooperation between Swedish and U.S. espionage services, in violation of Stockholm's officially stated neutrality. From Washington's side the mission was viewed as a great success and the responsible individuals within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations where the endeavor specifically were mentioned. For the Swedish C-byrån this enterprise quickly became toxic. Even though the affair was to be kept confidential, details leaked to the press and C-byrån were dissolved in February 1946. Documentation regarding this joint effort continued to be classified as confidential in subsequent years and some of it still remains so today. A report about the incident in the British National Archives is restricted until 2020.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The short was released on February 17, 1934.

The production was supervised by Duvall. The characters received animation from Jack King, Frank Tipper, both credited, Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, final four uncredited. The music score was composed by Bernard Brown (solely credited) and Norman Spencer (solely uncredited). The sound was exclusively recorded by Brown in the uncredited capacity. Production number 6125.

Plot

The cartoon follows a male and female bug/insect who check into a hotel which catches on fire during their stay.

Music

The song "Honeymoon Hotel" (by Al Dubin and Harry Warren) was originally introduced in the 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade. This short appears on the DVD release of that picture.

Color process

The production is notable for being the first Warner Bros. cartoon manufactured in color. It used Cinecolor since Walt Disney had exclusive rights to the Technicolor process. There was only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon manufactured in Cinecolor (Beauty and the Beast) before the series went briefly back to black-and-white. Later, the Merrie Melodies moved to Technicolor, though the Looney Tunes continued to be produced in black-and-white until 1943. Cinecolor would make a return in several late 1940s Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" is a short story by British author P. G. Wodehouse, which first appeared in the United States in the October 1923 issue of Cosmopolitan, and in the United Kingdom in the November 1923 Strand. It features the irrepressible Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, and was included in the collection bearing his name, published in 1924.

Plot
Stanley and Corky run into an acquaintance of the protagonist's, a chauffeur driving a shiny new Daimler, and he offers to take them for a ride. Along the way they are seen by a creditor demanding payment, who they shake off, and almost hit a young girl, whom Stanley insists they drive to her home near Clapham Common. He befriends her family, who are impressed by the car and Stanley's famous Aunt Julia.

When Corky meets Stanley a week later in the British Museum, he is accompanied by two children. He reveals he has been visiting the house, mainly for the free food, and promising to take the family out on trips in his companion's automobile, which they believe to be his own, and to introduce them to his aunt, who, he discloses, has disowned him, in a letter which states "from now on, I have no nephew".

Returning from a short holiday, Corky hears from George Tupper that Stanley is engaged. Visiting his comrade, he finds him with a black eye, and hears the tale of how the protagonist found himself inadvertently betrothed to the girl from Clapham Common, and got punched by a rival suitor named Finch. As they talk on the doorstep, the creditor from the earlier ride arrives, and Stanley hides. A friendly passer-by soothes the enraged moneylender, arguing that he knows where the debtor lives; Stanley moves out of his lodgings, remarking on the good fortune that led him to use the pseudonym "Mr. Smallweed" when dealing with the man.

The pair form a plot to extricate Stanley from the engagement by feigning ill-health, but as Corky is delivering his speech to the relatives, the passer-by arrives. He is George Finch, Stanley's rival for the lady; he reveals that the protagonist is an impoverished imposter, in fact called Smallweed, and produces the moneylender to prove it. He also bears a letter from Stanley's aunt, claiming that she has no nephew. Once Corky has paid off the debt to the moneylender, the two are chased from the residence.

Main characters
Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, the irrepressible entrepreneur
Julia, his haughty writer aunt
Jimmy Corcoran, Stanley's writer friend
George Tupper, an old schoolfriend of both protagonists
Frederick, a chauffeur, an acquaintance of Stanley's
Mabel Price, a girl Stanley meets on the road
Mr. Price, her doting father
Ernie Finch, her admirer, a resourceful man
Mr. Grindlay, a creditor Stanley owes money to, who knows him only as "Mr. Smallweed"

Publication history
The story was illustrated by T. D. Skidmore in Cosmopolitan. It was illustrated by Reginald Cleaver in the Strand magazine.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" was included in the 1932 collection Nothing But Wodehouse, edited by Ogden Nash and published by Doubleday, Doran & Company. The narrative was also featured in Week-End Wodehouse (UK edition), first released by Herbert Jenkins Limited in 1939. The tale was also collected in The World of Stanley Featherstonehaugh, released in October 1975 by Barrie & Jenkins.

Adaptations
"No Wedding Bells for Him" was adapted for radio in 1956, with Michael Shepley as Stanley, Hubert Gregg as Corcoran, Olaf Pooley as Frederick, Jeffrey Segal as Mr. Grindley, Mairhi Russell as Mabel Price, and Brewster Mason as Tupper.

The narrative was adapted for the television series The World of Wodehouse. The episode, titled "The Wedding Bells", aired in 1968, and included the character Looney Coote (from "The Long Arm of Looney Coote").

Following centuries under Ottoman dominion, limited opportunities for artistic education existed within the recently independent nation, making foreign study essential for aspiring creators. As endeavors continued with fresh directions alongside objectives, Hellenic creators emerging globally throughout the nineteenth century's initial decades reconnected Greek creativity with its ancient heritage, plus with the pursuits of European workshops, especially those of Munich's Academy, with defining illustrations of the Hellenic contemporary creativity from the interval including productions by Theodoros Vryzakis alongside Nikiphoros Lytras.

"Evening," I said without considering whether the fellow understood me since Language barriers don't exist for Reapers, we hear everything in our native tongue. Everyone hears us in their native dialect as well, creating all kinds of insanity in the contemporary world... or when we communicate with folks in Ancient Greece or Rome. "Evening," the Eldest stated. His voice sounded deep, and ancient. "What are you drinking to," I inquired. "Death," the Eldest responded. I didn't laugh, and neither did he. "Whose?" I queried. "Millions," he replied. I nodded in acknowledgment. Reapers may be immortal, possessing a lot of not-quite-natural abilities, but we're all still human at our core. Our minds resemble the minds of the individuals we reap, making our job rough. I'd honestly call it the hardest occupation in existence... having to be present when someone's expiring. Witnessing the grieving families of those who slip away to cancer, or other diseases, and delivering a bitter mercy to spare someone the pain. "No..." the fellow stated, "at least... not this century." "Which deaths have you down?" I asked. "Fratricide..." the Reaper said, "It... it reminds me of myself excessively." I nodded. "So," I said, "You thought about requesting that those assignments be diverted to other Reapers?" "Can't..." he stated, "It's part of my... my sentence." "Ouch," I said, genuinely meaning it. When it concerns Reapers like the Eldest, they have something called a Sentence designed to reform them to a state where they would be acceptable in the Afterlife they're due to be transferred to. "Damn it..." the Eldest uttered, "I need to get back to work... need to depart from here..." "Luck," I said, "and consider scheduling an appointment. We don't need you going renegade. That generally results in substantial paperwork for the rest of us." The Eldest scoffed at that, nodding in my direction as he got up to leave. It was only once he'd departed the room that I realized that I still didn't have his name or any identifying information about the mysterious ancient figure.

This variety of protection has an expiration date, and is generally used to safeguard during periods of higher expenses.... for example, one might purchase a temporary policy that lapses when the children graduate university or home mortgage is repaid, to ensure that an untimely demise doesn't prevent the offspring from attending college or forcing a surviving partner to sell the residence. But if you survive until that point in time, the contract lapses without payout. The chances of a distribution are so minimal and the number of individuals paying is so large. For example let's say one hundred people acquire a hundred-dollar protection plan for ten dollars and one person perishes. The insurer receives one hundred times ten equaling one thousand dollars. The carrier pays one hundred to the deceased individual's estate leaving them with nine hundred. The provider can also invest the nine hundred and earn revenue from the investment. Now raise the quantities of people buying coverage and lower the percentage of individuals making claims and the potential profits for the carrier are huge. The insurer is also very careful to screen out people who are more likely to file a claim. Protection is difficult or impossible to obtain if you have a threatening condition, vehicle coverage becomes harder the worse your driving record is, etc. It isn't cheap by accident. The payouts are calculated based on probability and odds. Also the length of the term and a myriad of other factors come into play. Make no mistake; the industry is in it for profit. Section 51(xxxi) is a subclause of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia.

It empowers the Commonwealth to make laws regarding the acquisition of property, but stipulates that such acquisitions must be on just terms.

The provision is sometimes referred to in shorthand as the 'just terms' clause.

Aside from its importance to Australian Constitutional Law, and Property Law; this subsection is notable for its role as a plot device in The Castle, an iconic Australian film.

Text
Section 51(xxxi) reads:

Jurisprudence
While s51(xxxi) was adapted from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, it has many differences.

The 'just terms' requirement has been held not to affect the State Parliaments.

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon stated that the inclusion of this condition was to "prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject."

The interpretation of the concepts "acquisition" and "just terms" by the High Court of Australia have had the effect, however, of limiting its protection of property rights. Moreover, it operates at any time the Commonwealth makes a compulsory acquisition of property. As such, it is a contingent guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy proprietary entitlements.

The Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws". This means that every statute supported by s 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other additional legislative authority.

Property
The High Court of Australia has taken a wide view of the concept of "property". Several members of the court took the opportunity to consider the meaning of this expression in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke said the term includes: "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action. Justice McTiernan confirmed that this terminology extends to tangible and intangible assets.

An example of the breadth of how "property" operates in section 51(xxxi) is provided by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisation Case). In that case, Federal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banks through vesting of shares in private banking institutions within the Commonwealth, and later the appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised these provisions as removing effective control over the holdings of the private banking entities. He concluded that this was, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary entitlement.

While statutory licences have sometimes been equated with proprietary interests, the removal of privileges enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property within section 51(xxxi), as licence conditions are inherently susceptible to change.

Acquisition
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody, and the acquisition must be for a Commonwealth purpose. This is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the destination does not matter – it is enough that the holder of property has been deprived of it. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which restricted the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property. Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass for retired members of Parliament were not an acquisition of property.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court held that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just. The validity of a grant in the absence of a requirement to acquire property was upheld in the later case of Pye v Renshaw.

Just terms
Typically, a determination of just terms based on the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will be sufficient to satisfy the requirement of just terms. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" imports no equivalence of market value. The arrangements offered must be "fair", or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair". However, this judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected, not just those of the dispossessed owner.

The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily require that a compensation package be presented as part of the acquisition scheme. It is sufficient that the program provides adequate procedures for determining fair recompense. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures closely to ensure their adequacy.

There may be some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution.

Section 51(xxxi) is an exception to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" another. In this instance, however, the Court will not allow another delegation of authority to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi).

Related legislation
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, largely drafted by Littleton Groom, was the first to deal with the compulsory acquisition of land by the federal government. Its most contentious provision was a clause authorising the federal government to grant mining leases and regulate mining on Commonwealth land. Responsibility for compulsory acquisition was initially placed with the Department of Home Affairs.

The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act 1945 compulsorily acquired land owned by Chinese-Australians in Darwin, leading to the end of the local Chinatown. The legislation was suggested in 1943 by the Northern Territory's administrator Aubrey Abbott, who proposed a combination of compulsory acquisition and conversion of the land to leasehold in order to effect "the elimination of undesirable elements which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past" and stated that he hoped to "entirely prevent the Chinese quarter forming again". He further observed that "if land is acquired from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other assets". The territory's civilian population had mostly been evacuated during the war and the former Chinatown residents returned to find their homes and businesses reduced to rubble. This forced appropriation resulted in significant displacement and permanent loss for these community members, who discovered devastation where their enterprises once stood.

They're not free though are they. Both users regardless of location require an internet connection. Even if you both utilized complimentary wifi the wireless network is gratis to entice business and is still being paid for. The fact that it appears costless is down to it using the web which is borderless. For traditional voice and text it requires your provider paying the carrier in the other country for their service to deliver the call or message. Although usually the fees are massively inflated. Bottom line you pay either way just in a different manner.

Telephone systems were built a long time ago, when international communication was really expensive - that set a precedent. Generally telephony companies were national monopolies, often with legal protection from competition. So they would charge high rates to other telecoms trying to hand conversations into their nation. They could do this because there was no alternative option and overseas dialing charges weren't worried about by most people (in effect these payments were like the cream that the corporation was allowed in exchange for providing affordable domestic calling infrastructure). Then the internet arrived. Many ISPs started as small competitive startups offering access over landlines (dial up). That meant they were keen to freely interconnect with content distributors as it made them more competitive (by providing better service to their customers), even when they were far apart they could obtain cheap links as they'd have entry to a "telecom hotel" with lots of enterprises competing to offer connections between cities, towns, regions, etcetera. So online connectivity has become very inexpensive, telephone carriers haven't kept pace.

NB: this should also supply you with good background on net neutrality. As the US shifts toward monopolised infrastructure (you could dial into any provider but most Americans only have one or two high speed cable choices) ISPs are attempting to shift toward the old framework where they possessed much greater power over what they billed consumers. In nations with more open systems (eg in NZ you can choose any fibre supplier in your local exchange, normally several dozen alternatives) this isn't such an issue.

You're already a telephone company subscriber (trying to earn more revenue). Skype is still hoping to convert you into a customer (earn anything whatsoever from selling services to new adopters who might generate income).

lexical_diversity_up_s.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f: Judith Scott (May 1, 1943 – March 15, 2005) was an American fiber sculptor, born with Down Syndrome and deaf. She was internationally renowned for her artwork. In 1987, Judith enrolled at the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, California which supports people with developmental disabilities. There, this remarkable individual discovered her passion and talent for abstract textural creations and she could communicate through a novel medium. An account of Scott's existence, Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott (2016) has been written by her fraternal twin sibling. Judith entered the world within a middle-class household in Cincinnati, Ohio on May 1, 1943 alongside her non-identical companion Joyce. Unlike Joyce, this child arrived with Down Syndrome. During infancy, young Judith suffered from Scarlet Fever, which caused hearing loss, a medical fact that remained unknown until much later during her lifetime. The girl spent her initial seven and a half years residing at home with parents, twin companion and older male siblings. Although the developmental gap between these two daughters proved apparent, "the parents consciously sought to treat these youngest members of the household alike." However, when time came for the girls to start attending school, one child was found to be "ineducable." There existed only one classroom for youngsters with disabilities, and this particular student couldn't pass verbally-based entrance tests, due to her still undiagnosed deafness. Consequently, on medical advice, her mother and father placed young Judith into the Columbus State Institution (formerly the Columbus State School), an establishment for the mentally disabled, on October 18, 1950. This separation had a profound effect on both twins. The records from this person's first few years at the facility indicate she possessed an IQ of 30 (based upon oral testing before her hearing impairment was recognized). For this reason she was denied any training opportunities. Deprived of her companion, the isolated individual became severely alienated, and behavioral problems soon surfaced. Her Clinical Record states that "She does not seem to be in good contact with her environment. She doesn't get along well with other youngsters, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats fellow residents. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Soon after, she was moved to a smaller governmental institution at Gallipolis, Ohio. In 1985, after thirty-five years of complete separation and lengthy, difficult negotiations, Joyce became her sibling's legal guardian, and brought the long-institutionalized woman to reside with her in California, a jurisdiction where all mentally challenged citizens are entitled to ongoing education. This remarkable sculptor died of natural causes at her sister's residence in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks short of her sixty-second birthday. She outlived her predicted lifespan at birth by almost fifty years. On April 1, 1987, this future artist began attending the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the first organizations worldwide to provide studio space for creators with disabilities. For almost two years, the newcomer showed little enthusiasm for any artistic activity. She proved unexceptional with paint. She scribbled loops and circles, but her efforts contained no representational imagery, and she remained so uninterested in creating that the staff considered ending her involvement with the program. It wasn't until this potential talent casually observed a fiber workshop conducted by visiting instructor Sylvia Seventy that she had her artistic breakthrough. Using the materials at hand, the inspired woman spontaneously invented her own unique and radically different form of aesthetic expression. While other students were stitching, she was sculpting with unprecedented zeal and concentration. Her creative gifts and absolute focus were quickly recognized, and she was given complete freedom to choose her own supplies. Taking whatever objects she found, regardless of ownership, this determined creator would wrap them in carefully selected colored yarns to produce diverse sculptures of many different shapes. Some resemble cocoons or body parts, while others are elongated totemic poles. Many of her pieces also feature pairs, reflecting Scott's experience as a twin. The dedicated artist worked on her creations five days weekly for eighteen years, producing over two hundred pieces in total. This sculptor had her inaugural exhibition in 1999, which coincided with the publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott. Together, these events helped propel her to worldwide recognition. Scott's creations have become immensely popular in the realm of outsider artwork, and her pieces sell for substantial sums. This creator is now hailed as a contemporary master, no longer just an outsider. Her sculptures are held in the permanent collections of many museums, including: Museum of Modern Art (Manhattan, New York), the American Visionary Art Museum (Baltimore, Maryland), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Museum of American Folk Art (Manhattan, New York), Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art (Chicago, Illinois), Irish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin, The Oakland Museum, Oakland, CA. L'Aracine Musee D'Art Brut (Paris, France), Art Brut Connaissance & Diffusion Collection (Paris and Prague), Collection de l'art brut (Lausanne, Switzerland). Below is a list of select notable exhibitions for Judith Scott. 2018 – Judith Scott: Touchdown, Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California 2014-15 – Bound and Unbound, Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn, New York 2009 – Judith Scott: Retrospective, Ricco Maresca Gallery, New York City, New York 2002 – Cocoon: Judith Scott, Ricco-Maresca Gallery, New York City, New York 2019 – Memory Palaces: Inside the Collection of Audrey B. Heckler, American Folk Art Museum, New York City, New York 2019 – The Doors of Perception, Curated by Javier Téllez in collaboration with the Outsider Art Fair, Frieze Art Fair, New York City, New York 2019 – Flying High: Women Artists of Art Brut, Bank Austria Kunstforum, Vienna 2018 – Outliers and American Vanguard Art, National Gallery of Art, Washington DC 2017 – Forget Me Not: Judith Scott, Zuckerman Museum of Art, Kennesaw, Georgia 2017 – Viva Arte Viva, the 57th Venice Biennale, Venice, Italy 2015 – Collection ABCD, La Maison Rouge, Paris, France 2013 – Create, Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California 2013 – Create, Boca Raton Museum of Art, Boca Raton, Florida 2013 – Extreme Art, The Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, Ridgefield, Connecticut 2012 – Rosemarie Trockel: A Cosmos, New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York City, New York 2011 – World Transformers, Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt, Frankfurt, Germany 2000 – Visions, American Visionary Art Museum, Baltimore, Maryland 2005 – Creative Growth, The Ricky Jay Broadside Collection, Yerba Buena Center for the Arts, San Francisco, California

lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The prediction of the behavior of systems is key in scientific fields. This interest is however hindered by issues: often, the equations describing the physics of the system under study are not accessible or, if accessible, their solution might require a time incompatible with the prediction time constraints. Not surprisingly, approximating systems in a format and informing it from available observations has become practice in the age of learning, as illustrated by the examples based on networks. However, generalizability of the models, margins of guarantee and the impact of data are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on knowledge of the physics. We tackle these issues from a viewpoint, by adopting a learning strategy. In learning, the dataset is structured such that the process starts from simple samples towards more samples in order to favor convergence and generalization. The concept has been developed and applied in robotics and control of systems. Here, we apply this concept for the learning of systems in a way. First, leveraging insights from the theory, we assess the amount of data sufficient for guaranteeing a model of the system and investigate the impact of the set and its structure on the quality of predictions. Based on that, we consider entropy as a metric of the dataset; we show how an informed design of the set based on the analysis of the entropy improves the models in terms of generalizability, and provide insights on the amount and the choice of data required for modeling. The prediction of behavior of systems relies on understanding how systems evolve, and our approach demonstrates that structured learning using entropy analysis of the dataset enables better prediction of system behavior over time through informed selection of data for learning.

The CII 158 microns line is the most important coolant of the interstellar
medium in galaxies but substantial variations are seen from galaxy to galaxy.
The main source of the CII emission at a galactic scale is still poorly understood.
Previous studies of the CII emission in galaxies have a resolution of several
kpc or more so the observed CII emission is an average of different ISM components.
The aim of this work is to study, for the first time, the CII emission at the
scale of a spiral arm. We want to investigate the origin of this CII line and its
use as a tracer of star formation. We present CII observations and OI observations of a
segment of a spiral arm of M~31 using the Infrared Space Observatory. The CII
emission is compared with tracers of neutral gas (CO, HI) and star formation
(H\alpha, Spitzer 24 mu.) The similarity of the CII emission with the Ha and 24
mu images is striking when smoothed to the same resolution, whereas the
correlation with the neutral gas is much weaker. The CII cooling rate per H
atom increases dramatically from ~2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom in the border of the map
to ~ 1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom in the regions of star formation. The CII/FIR(42-122)
ratio is almost constant at 2%, a factor 3 higher than typically quoted.
However, we do not believe that M~31 is unusual. Rather, the whole-galaxy
fluxes used for the comparisons include the central regions where the CII/FIR
ratio is known to be lower and the resolved observations neither isolate a
spiral arm nor include observations as far out in the galactic disk as the observations
presented here. A fit to published PDR models yields a plausible average
solution of G_0~100 and n~3000 for the PDR emission in the regions of star
formation in the arm of M31. The CII emission in the arm of M31 shows that CII emission studies at the scale of the spiral arm reveal details about the CII emission not visible in whole-galaxy studies of CII emission.

We study a two-dimensional (2D) model of a topological crystalline
insulator (TCI) protected by rotation symmetry. The model is built by stacking
two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers which transform under
conjugate representations of the rotation group, e.g. $p_\pm$ orbitals. Despite
its apparent similarity to the Kane-Mele model, it does not host stable gapless
surface states. Nevertheless the model exhibits topological responses including
the appearance of quantized fractional charge bound to rotational defects
(disclinations) and the pumping of angular momentum in response to threading an
elementary magnetic flux, which are described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling
between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field
corresponding to the rotation symmetry. In addition, we show that although the
filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, this
obstruction is removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals, which
implies fragile topology. As a result, the response of the model can be derived
by representing it as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and
negative integer coefficients. Following the analysis of the model, which
serves as a prototypical model of 2D TCIs protected by rotation, we show that
all TCIs protected by point group symmetries which do not have protected
surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Remarkably, this
implies that gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only
if there is a stable Wannier obstruction. We then use reduction to map the
problem of classifying 2D TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D)
problem which is then used to obtain the complete classification of such TCIs
as well as the reduction of this classification in the presence of interactions.
The reduction provides the classification of the model and the classification of
all such models with rotation symmetry.
lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). This approach uses selected attributes from objects in various domains (e.g. chess problems, classical music, renowned artworks) and recombines these attributes in such a way as to generate new attributes that can then, in principle, be used to create novel objects of creative value to humans relating to any one of the source domains. This approach allows some of the burden of creative content generation to be passed from humans to machines. The approach was tested in the domain of chess problems. We used this approach to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems based on attributes extracted and recombined from chess problems and chess games by humans, renowned paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, photographs of people, and classical music. The quality of these generated chess problems was then assessed automatically using an existing and experimentally-validated computational chess aesthetics model. These chess problems were also assessed by human experts in the domain. The results suggest that attributes collected and recombined from chess and other domains using the DSNS approach can indeed be used to automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality. In particular, a low quality chess source (i.e. chess sequences between weak players) used in combination with actual photographs of people was able to produce three-move chess problems of comparable quality or better to chess problems generated using a high quality chess source (i.e. published chess compositions by human experts), and more efficiently as well. Why information from a foreign domain can be integrated and functional in this way remains an open question for now. The DSNS approach is, in principle, scalable and applicable to any domain in which objects have attributes that can be represented using real numbers.

Context. Filaments are present throughout the Galaxy, and these filaments host star formation. Detecting these filaments in a reliable way is therefore important towards our understanding of the star formation process.
  Aims. We explore whether supervised machine learning can identify filamentary structures on the whole Galactic plane.
  Methods. We used two versions of UNet-based networks for image segmentation. We used H2 column density images of the Galactic plane obtained with Herschel Hi-GAL data as input data. We trained the UNet-based networks with skeletons (spine plus branches) of filaments that were extracted from these images, together with background and missing data masks that we produced. We tested eight training scenarios to determine the best scenario for our purpose of classifying pixels as filaments.
  Results. The training of the UNets allows us to create a new image of the Galactic plane by segmentation in which pixels belonging to filamentary structures are identified. With this new method, we classify more pixels (more by a factor of 2 to 7, depending on the classification threshold used) as belonging to filaments than the spine plus branches structures we used as input. New structures are revealed, which are mainly filaments that were not detected before. These filaments are filaments with properties that made detection difficult previously. We use metrics to evaluate the performances of the different training scenarios. This allows us to demonstrate the robustness of the method and to determine a threshold value that maximizes the recovery of the input labelled pixel classification.
  Conclusions. This study shows that supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures that are present throughout the Galactic plane. The detection of these structures, including structures that have never been detected before, offers important perspectives for the study of these filaments and for the study of star formation in these filaments.

lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: The truth is that I am actually undecided on this issue, but I will start on the side against marriage for gay people for two reasons: 1. I lean less towards my starting side and it seems much more fragile and unpopular, so arguing for a weaker side I feel less strongly about helps to practice my argument skills. 2. I believe that the burden is on the side in favor of marriage for gay people (as I will explain), so I started on the other side. First, please watch this video (it's only two minutes). Due to this argument, I feel that the burden is on the people that wish to redefine the criteria for the institution of marriage (I do not have problems with redefining itself, but I am just saying that redefining requires compelling reason). When people answer the question "Do you think marriage for gay people is a good idea?" with "Why not?," this is really just the teapot fallacy (attempting to shift the burden). I do not believe equality is a good argument. It is true that people with different orientation deserve equal rights to life, liberty, freedom, and the pursuit of happiness as detailed by the constitution. However, the whole equality thing is a red herring in this particular instance. Marriage is not a kind of privilege or a right that must be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around procreation, and relationships between gay people, which may be loving and committed, by definition are non-procreational relationships. There are also marriages between heterosexual people which are non-procreational relationships, such as old or infertile people, but if you watched the video, you'll understand why it's not analogous; just because there are exceptions to the norm, doesn't mean you can extend the definition to a non-norm, as the norms are not defined by their exceptions. This equality argument is not the same as women voting or black people being free. Many times the criteria is presented as (a posed question): "If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?" Marriage criteria have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love for that matter. If your criteria are two people who have romantic or sexual love, then incest is fair game. Some will argue that incest is different because within the family, there are power issues, and also genetic defects. There can be power issues within any relationship, whether between heterosexual people, between gay people, or incestuous people. There is no reason to base marriage legislation on this. Also, incestuous people don't have to have children, can adopt, or may be infertile or gay. One may argue that incest should be a valid form of marriage as well as marriage for gay people. You can try to argue this point if you want, but please include valid reasoning as the burden is on you. The "why would you care?" argument is invalid; Just because a proposition does not affect anyone adversely, doesn't mean we can change institutions at whim. Even under utilitarianism, this argument doesn't work. Gay people can have fulfilling long-term romantic and sexual relationships without calling it marriage. Redefining marriage for the happiness of a group is akin (logically, not emotionally) to giving in to lobbyist demands so that they will be happier with this redefining. Most arguments for marriage for gay people are appeals to emotion or popularity. The term "gay rights" was designed to make it sound like we have internment camps for gay people. Even the term "homophobe" was coined to stigmatize the opposition to marriage for gay people. Just because this issue is popular in our zeitgeist, and many of the opponents are religious fundamentalists who use straw man arguments, doesn't make the "more reasonable side" correct. If there was a movement to legalize incestuous marriage and it was popular, with videos and websites online that glorified the struggle of such people seeking incestuous marriage, most people would be for that as well. Why is one sexual deviation (and I mean to use that term with complete respect and absolutely no stigma, connotation, or implication) more "marriageable" than another deviation? Why should marriage apply to one deviation but not another deviation? View changed. In all fairness, I was already 75 there when I wrote this argument.

lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418: There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common reasons: Division by zero: You may remember from math that you can't divide a number by zero. The result of dividing by zero is undefined. Well, if a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that the program is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation where the program is dividing by zero, the program may crash. Access violation: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts of memory are off-limits. If a program tries to access part of memory that is off-limits, the computer will tell the program that the program is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation where the program is accessing off-limits memory, the program may crash. Deadlock: Let's say you and Billy are playing with blocks. You have the red block, and Billy has the blue block. You want to switch blocks, so you tell Billy that you will give Billy the red block after Billy gives you the blue block. Billy tells you that Billy will give you the blue block after you give Billy the red block. Both of you will sit there waiting for the other person to hand over the block, and you will never get anything done. That is a deadlock situation, and when deadlock happens inside a program, the program freezes up and there is nothing you can do except kill the program and start the program again. Unhandled exception: Sometimes a program will have error checking built into the program. When an error is detected in the program, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with the exception. If an exception gets thrown and the exception is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting you know that a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will terminate. All of these situations are caused by bugs in the program. Bugs are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or bugs don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more bugs than other programs. Why do some programs have more bugs? Maybe because the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test the program as well as they should have, or because the program is so complicated that dealing with every possible situation that might happen is difficult. Think of a program as a way to do things - a common example given is how to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. Your first program might read: get bread get peanut butter get jelly get knife put peanut butter on one slice put jelly on other slice put bread together SERVE If you run out of peanut butter, you're stuck halfway through the program without anywhere left to go - that's a crash. A more complicated program would describe how a pizza restaurant works - there's more ingredients in the program, more ways to combine ingredients, you have workers coming and going at the same time and a bunch more things that can go wrong. There's things that can go wrong you can fix and things that can't be fixed - things that can't be fixed are crashes.

lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::a9b058a8-5ce8-448f-820a-6ffba640: Because of the camera's field of view (FOV). If you're a big first person shooter game player (or you know about cameras) you're probably familiar with FOV. If we consider what we can see as a cone starting at our eye and expanding out like [this] (URL0) then FOV is the angle between the two boundary lines of the cone. In shooter games FOV is often expanded by pros to gain an advantage, since expanding FOV lets you see more of your surroundings in the game. [Here] (URL1) is a quick example of increasing a game's FOV I googled up. The image on the left has the FOV expanded to 65 degrees compared to the FOV of 45 degrees on the left. With the larger FOV you can see more on the left and right in the image. But you'll also notice that the 2 trailer things look like they're farther away even though the player is standing in the same place in the game - that's because as you increase the FOV you also change how the light from distant objects is going to converge on your 2D surface. Essentially a larger FOV means that objects seem to decrease in size faster as the objects get farther away. The opposite is also true with FOV, if you decrease the FOV then decreasing FOV increases the apparent size of far away objects since the objects now converge on a larger portion of the view area. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61deg. The small FOV makes the camera very effective at collecting light from far away objects because the camera is focused on a very small cone. The small FOV also means that the distance between the Earth and the Moon doesn't have the same effect on relative size as the distance does when taken with a regular camera or human eyes.," "Hold your hand in front of your face. Your hand is probably about as big as your monitor. Keep your hand in the same spot and move your head backwards. Your hand now appears smaller than the monitor appears. There's a certain distance where your hand and the monitor get smaller together, at the same rate. This is because the distance between you and those two things becomes a lot greater than the distance between those two things. Angular diameter depends on distance, and ratio of distances. Basically, the first image is very close to the moon and far from the earth, so the moon seems big in the image. The second image is very far from both the earth and the moon, so the earth and moon appear like their actual relative sizes in the image. So yes, the earth DOES appear smaller in the second image, but the moon got smaller a lot faster just like your hand.," "DSCOVR basically had its camera zoomed in more. The EPIC camera on the spacecraft that took the image is specifically designed to observe the Earth from a distance, whereas the cameras on the Apollo missions were more general purpose cameras. To be more precise, in a camera the focal length of the lens determines the physical size of the image formed on the sensor of the camera. Then the physical size of the sensor determines the field of view of the camera, and the pixel resolution of the sensor determines the size of each pixel in the image. With analogue film there are no pixels but the film still has a resolution limit because of its chemistry and there's also a resolution limit imposed by the lens of the camera. Finally a large image can simply be cropped, although the DSCOVR image is in fact pretty much its full size as an image.

lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1: You can call what you're asking about a 'wealth tax', or 'capital tax'. These taxes are taxes not based on income you earned in a year, but some measure of how much you own. Some countries (Italy I believe is a prime example) tax ownership of foreign land. Some countries tax amounts owned by corporations [Canada did this until ~5-10 years ago depending on province]. Some countries strictly tax your wealth above a certain level (Switzerland, as has been mentioned, does this). One form of what you are referring to that does exist in the US is the 'Estate Tax'. This tax is a tax on the amount of wealth that a person owns, at the time they die. The threshold for when this tax applies has been very volatile over the last 20 years, but the threshold is generally in the multi-millions, and I believe the threshold sits somewhere around $5M. If these taxes start to crop up more and more (and I believe these taxes will), don't be shocked at the initial 'sticker price'. Theoretically a wealth tax could replace some of the current income tax in many countries without creating a strict increased tax burden on their people. For example: if you owe $10k in income tax this year, but a $2k capital tax is instituted next year, then you are still in the same position as long as your income tax is reduced to $8k. Whether these taxes are effective or preferable or not is really a question of economics, not personal finance, so I will not belabour that point. Note: if the wealth you have saved earns wealth (interest, or dividends, or maybe rent from a property you own), then those earnings are typically taxed alongside your wage income. Any 'wealth tax' or 'capital tax' as I've described above would be in addition to income tax on investment earnings. These taxes on wealth would apply beyond the income tax on earnings from wealth.
lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe: You could have both options exercised (and assigned to you) on the same day, but I don't think you could lose money on both options on the same day. The reason is that while options exercises are immediate, options assignments are processed after the markets close at the end of each day. See http://www.888options.com/help/faq/assignment.jsp for details. So you would get both options assignments at the same time, that night. The net effect should be that you don't own any stock (someone would put you the stock, then the stock would be called away) and you don't have the options anymore. You should have incoming money of $1500 selling the stock to the call exerciser and outgoing money of $1300 buying stock from the put exerciser, right? So you would have no more options but $200 more money in your account in the morning. You bought stock at 13 and sold stock at 15. This options position is an agreement to buy stock at 13 and sell stock at 15 at someone else's option. The way you lose money is if one of the options isn't exercised while the other option is exercised, i.e. if the stock is below 13 so nobody is going to opt to buy stock from you at 15, but they'll sell stock to you at 13; or the stock is above 15 so nobody is going to opt to sell stock to you at 13, but they'll buy stock from you at 15. You make money if neither option is exercised (you keep the premium you sold for) or both options are exercised (you keep the gap between the two options, plus the premium). Having both options exercised is surely rare, since early exercise is rare to begin with, and early exercise tends to happen when options are deep in the money; so you'd expect both options to be exercised if both options are deep in the money at some point. Having both options be exercised on the same day ... can't be common, but it's maybe most likely just before expiration with minimal time value, if the stock moves around quickly so both options are in the money at some point during the day.
lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96: The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how they will apply the payments. As Dilip notes in his answer, in the US, they will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must apply the rest above the minimum to the higher rate balance. In other countries, this will vary by law and custom. Do not assume it will pay off the higher balance, or proportionally, without asking. Let's take the following example. You owe $6000. $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate). If your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500 and your cash advance balance by $100. The average rate, then, is simply sum of the product of the rate times balance. So here, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15%. This is called a weighted average. If the bank applies the payment differently - such as to the lower rate first, or some specified part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate - then this will be misleading if you enter it into a calculator, because your average rate will rise over time as you pay off the purchase balance but don't pay off the cash advance balance, or may decrease if the opposite happens. The weighted average is probably reasonably close in the circumstance that you describe, even if you have rules applying the balance differently, so long as they don't 100% pay down the lower rate - so it may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations where it's not critical to be correct, just close. One approach using the online calculators that might be better, is to treat these like two separate cards. Many calculators exist for multiple balances. Then you can allocate payments differently to the two cards. This would allow you to see how long you will need until you've paid off the higher balance, for example, although it probably won't perfectly match things - unless you find a calculator that has this specific option available you probably will have to either live with a small error in your calculations or do the calculations by hand yourself manually on your own.

Many companies on the OTC are just starting off there because these companies don't meet the requirements to be listed on the NASDAQ or NYSE. Major exchanges like the NASDAQ and the NYSE only want the best companies to trade on their exchanges. The NASDAQ, for example, has three sets of listing requirements. A company must meet at least one of the three requirement sets, as well as the main requirements for all companies. These requirements include: Now don't assume that the OTC doesn't have requirements either, as this assumption is far from the truth as well. While there are no minimum level of revenue, profits or assets required to get listed on the OTC there are requirements for audited statements and ongoing filing and reporting to the SEC and NASD. Additionally there are several different levels of the OTC, including the OTCQX, the OTCCB and the OTC Pink, each with their own set of requirements. For more information about what it takes to be listed on OTC look here: http://www.otcmarkets.com/learn/otc-trading A company deciding to trade on the OTC is making the decision to take their company public, and these companies are investing to make it happen. Currently the fees to get listed on the OTC range from $30,000 to $150,000 depending on the firm you decide to go with and the services they offer as part as their package. Now, I know I wouldn't consider $30K or more to not be serious money! When I looked into the process of getting a company listed on the TSX the requirements seemed a lot more relaxed than those requirements of the major U.S. exchanges as well, consisting of an application, records submission and then a decision made by a TSX committee about whether you get listed. More information about the TSX here: http://apps.tmx.com/en/listings/listing_with_us/process/index.html I think the way that the OTC markets have gotten such a bad reputation is from these companies that you see pumping up OTC company stocks and getting massive amounts of people to buy without doing their due diligence and investigating the company and reading its prospectus. These companies get people to buy stocks, then when these people lose a bunch of money on an ill-informed investment decision these people blame it on the company being an OTC stock. Whether you decide to trade the OTC market or not, I wouldn't make a decision based on how many exchanges the company is listed on, but rather based on the research you do into the company and the requirements that company meets.

Of the many shows that have had a poisonous influence on British society over the past twenty years, Eastenders is the prime show. For two decades this show has celebrated the oaf, the thug, the wide-boy, the tart, the gobby, the violent, the sexually-incontinent, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious ...How many times has someone remarked that Eastenders "mirrors life"? Life on which planet, exactly? This show is written about "working-class" characters, as imagined by middle-class people who have taken a course in creative writing. Eager to show to their middle-class peers how familiar they are with the "working-class" they dream up the lumpen rabble that is the citizenry of Eastenders.This show has a poisonous influence on some minds less well-equipped than other minds to handle shows, and so we find members of the real population assuming the attitudes and demeanour of the inhabitants of Walford.Thus, it came to pass that Eastenders mirrors life; but only after life had been hoodwinked into mirroring Eastenders.Other soaps have followed in Eastenders' footsteps, filled to their stinking gunwhales with ugly, potato-faced, shaven-headed, pot-bellied characters, scowling at each other and issuing threats constantly. This is the proletariat as perceived by the writers who produce this soap. The writers will grow rich on the proceeds of such shows, and the writers will go on to enjoy the finer things of life in their rarified enclaves. Meanwhile, the burgeoning number of new, show-induced drones will proceed inexorably toward cultural bankruptcy.And there you have the new priests and the new creatures of the early 21st century. Much of this is due to the immeasurable power of that illuminated boxful of dancing pixels in the corner of your living-room. It's your fault, gentle reader: that boxful of pixels is what you chose as the only window through which to look out from your prison.

What do you think I should wear tomorrow?"
"What do you think of this outfit?"
"Would this necklace look good with these shoes?"
Many people ask these types of questions everyday. You may even be one of them. Many people think having multiple opinions rather than one opinion is always better. Why? Studies have shown that more than 50 percent of Americans ask for a second opinion before doing it. For example, have you ever been shopping and asked your friend if you should get fancy expensive shoes? And if they said no, you would ask someone else? Well you are not alone. This is very common according to a recent study conducted by Harvard University. Fashion is changing whether it be fast fashion, or street wear. People often ask for second opinions because they feel the need to ask for second opinions. Imagine yourself trying on an ugly over sized t-shirt. You may like it, and maybe your friend does too. But if you were to ask someone else like your dad to see if they would like it do you think they would? No! Absolutely not. Dads hate over sized ugly t-shirts. Asking for a second opinion is always a good idea. Whether it be positive feedback, or negative feedback. It shapes your mind to make the correct choice. This will not always be the case though. Some people refuse to listen, even if it is constructive negative feedback. A study found by George Mason University reports that after asking for a second opinion and the response is negative feedback, they will still continue to choose the opposite of the feedback they were given. Why are our mentalities like this? Humans have evolved over time to become the dominant species. Our brains in away think we are always right, and everyone is wrong. This is why some people have so much trouble respecting other people's opinions. They refuse to think they are wrong. The FBI reported that even serial killers asked for multiple opinions to see if they should kill their first victim. Although everyone said no, the serial killer continues to make the bad choice anyway. Although many people do ask for more opinions for feedback, what about the people that don't ask for opinions? Research found by the Virginia Department of Health has found out that those with depression, anxiety, and insomnia were 10 times less likely to ask for multiple opinions and advice. Due to over thinking, shyness, and embarrassment, they think they will only get negative feedback, which leads to them not even asking for opinions. This is another reason why depression is on the rise. People feel like they are trapped, that there is no one to help them, not even their close friends can help them. They are scared of getting judged and humiliated for asking for advice because they are scared of being wrong or appearing stupid. This is a common issue today that is still growing. Another study found by Virginia Tech discovered that people who typically do ask for advice almost everyday, almost always ask someone older due to them being wiser and having more knowledge in life than they do. People who ask for opinions ask older people for opinions because older people have more experience. Looking for feedback and asking for multiple opinions is always the best if you are trying to look for good advice, or wanting to make improvements to something in your life. Whether it be a school project, important office work, or trying on different clothes, there will always be room for improvement when you ask for opinions. So don't be afraid to ask multiple people for advice and feedback. Asking for opinions helps people make better choices in life.
