This paper is an extension of Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN representations at FC7 layer are to certain extent equivariant to certain classes of transformations and that training with a certain transformation makes the representations more equivariant to that transformation.

Authors performed a large amount of experiments, training over 30 networks with different forms of training, which is quite impressive. However it is rather difficult to find a main message of this paper. Yes, authors measured the properties on a different layer than the Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, however it is hard to find some novel insights other than the known fact that training helps to achieve invariance. The evaluation seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the task advertised in its title really well.

Major issues are in the experiments with the representation distances:
* The selection of only FC7 is a bit controversial - it is followed only by a single layer (FC8) to the common output - class likelyhoods. Because the FC8 is just a linear projection, what the equivalence map does is just to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network. Probably performing similar experiments but on more layers may be more useful (as the networks are already trained).
* The experiment with representation distance is missing what is the error on the testing dataset. This would answer whether the representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all...
* It is not clear for the experiment with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example? After training the equivalence map? More clear would be to show that networks trained on similar transformation are more compatible on the target task.
* The proposed method does not seem to improve equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss is basically equal to simple training as it just adds up the loss of the original image and transformed image. Maybe the issue is in the selection of the FC7 layer?

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 equivariance, but it does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations out of these experiments with FC7 equivariance. Due to some issues with the equivalence experiments and the training of equivariance, I would not recommend acceptance of this paper. However, refining the experiments on already trained networks and restructuring this paper into more investigative paper may lead to interesting contribution to the field of equivariance.

There are also few minor issues with this paper:
* It is not experimentally verified that the new criterion for equivariance mapping helps to gain better results on equivariance.
* The angles on page 1 and page 5 are missing units (degrees?).
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult... ", it is not M_g which is maximised or minimised, but the loss over the M_g
* Page 4, footnote 2 - if you are just halving the activations, it is hard to call it a dropout as this constant factor can be passed to the following weights or preceding weights
* Is the network for RVL-CDIP the same architecture as Alexnet architecture?
* On page 7, Figure 3a and 3b - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements to white is really misleading, and probably even incorrect, as the distance between the same representations should be zero (which is also a way how to verify that the experiments are performed correctly on representations).
lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see the application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies the information bottleneck principle to train deep networks (the original papers only presented the information bottleneck concept), but see below for the note of independent work claim.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference. Also the explanation of the information bottleneck principle is clear. The results seem to be very promising for these networks.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference, p usually denotes the model and q represents the "inference engine". This means the inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However the presented information bottleneck model assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and approximated by the empirical distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this makes the two definitions contradict to each other in the model!

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta in the model). However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in the variational auto-encoder (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in the information bottleneck model is the variational approximation to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a component in the model), while in the variational auto-encoder it is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similarly p(z|x) in the information bottleneck model is included in the model, while in the variational auto-encoder that is the approximate posterior and can be independently chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep network but p(z|x) as a deep network or a process).

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a person. In the variational auto-encoder part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between the information bottleneck model and the variational auto-encoder, and provide some intuitions if the information bottleneck interpretation is preferred over the variational auto-encoder interpretation.


Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for independent work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive that many people publish the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim and commend the authors' honesty, but in case this claim is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.

The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection (e.g. sum of difference of cross-entropies).

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a sentence are more important than other sections and this is achieved by a CNN. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW or SEQ representation (or the combination of both representations) is more important and why one representation is more important.

The description of the CNN (one-hot or semi-supervised using pre-trained embeddings) is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects of the CNN. However, a picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words for describing the CNN.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary (\citet vs. \citep) (e.g line 385 in the paper).

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences (line 443 of the paper) based on a separate validation set:

- What validation data is used here for validation? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen for the CNN. How sensitive are the models to this selection of validation data?

- Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected for each approach. As Figure 1 shows, the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this case of selection.

Other comments on the paper:

- I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available, not just the development set of in-domain data.

- The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods to support the claims made in section 5.4 of the paper.

- In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in section 5.4: Another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod, 2015, who replace some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity to see whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this approach.

- Using the sum of source and target classification scores is very similar to source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection: sum of difference of cross-entropies for source and target. A reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable for the paper.

Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source & target classification scores by extending the CNN model to the bilingual setting or parallel setting for the CNN.

In this submission, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output. However, the approach is not new, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the submission, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this submission by applying the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. Also, Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling, which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing work. The remaining novelty of the approach then would be its application to machine translation, although it remains somewhat unclear, inhowfar reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem - the translation-related part of the OOV problem should be elaborated here. That said, some of the claims of this submission seems somewhat exaggerated, like the statement in Sec. 2.3: "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete", whereas the authors e.g. express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity w/o an explicit output vocabulary. For modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144

Sec. 2.3: You claim that the objective requires a finite vocabulary. This statement only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. However, using subwords and even individual characters, implicitly larger and even infinite vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. Even though this require a model different from the model proposed here, the corresponding statement should qualified in this respect.

The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified. The description in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view.

Concerning the configuration of NCE, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific configuration and parameterization described in Sec. 3.4.

Sec. 4.1: you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar conclusions w.r.t. the performance of using character embeddings at the output, and discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given therein.

Sec. 4.2: there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown words, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013).

Sec. 4.4 and Table 4: the size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here.

Minor comments:

p. 2, bottom: three different input layer -> three different input layers (plural)

Fig. 1: fonts within the figure are way too small

p. 3, first item below Fig. 1: that we will note WE -> that we will denote WE

Sec. 2.3: the parameters estimation -> the parameter estimation (or: the parameters' estimation)

p. 5, first paragraph: in factored way -> in a factored way

p. 5, second paragraph: a n-best list, a nk-best list -> an n-best list, an nk-best list

Sec. 4.2, last sentence: Despite adaptive gradient, -> verb and article missing in this sentence
lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::a0b0f9d5-62dc-4996-9de4-5e5f9b3b:
The paper introduces Edward, a probabilistic programming language built over TensorFlow and Python, and supporting a broad range of most popular contemporary inference methods in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:
The Edward language provides an extremely impressive collection of modern probabilistic inference methods in an easily usable language form. The paper provides a brief review of the most important inference techniques especially from a representation learning perspective, combined with two experiments on implementing various modern variational inference methods and GPU-accelerated HMC inference methods.

The first experiment (variational inference experiment) would be more valuable if there was a clear link to complete experiment code to reproduce the experiment results provided. The HMC experiment looks OK, except the characterising Stan as a hand-optimised implementation seems unfair as the Stan code is clearly not hand-optimised for this specific inference model and hardware configuration. I do not think anyone doubts the quality of your inference implementation, so please do not ruin the picture by unsubstantiated sensationalist claims about your inference methods. Instead of current drama, I would suggest comparing head-to-head against Stan inference on single core and separately reporting the extra speedups you gain from parallelisation and GPU acceleration for inference. These speedup numbers would also help the readers to estimate the inference performance of the inference method for other hardware configurations and other inference models.

Clarity:
The paper is in general clearly written and easy to read for understanding the language. The numerous code examples are helpful for understanding the language, but also difficult as it is sometimes unclear what code is missing from the code examples. It would be very helpful if the authors could provide and clearly link to a machine-readable companion document (a Jupyter notebook would be great for code examples, but even text or HTML would be easier to copy-paste code from than a pdf like the paper) with complete runnable code for all the code examples in the paper.

Originality:
The Edward language is clearly a unique collection of probabilistic inference methods and inference techniques. In terms of the paper, the main threat to novelty comes from previous publications of the same group on similar inference language topics. The main paper refers to Tran et al. (2016a) which covers a lot of similar material on inference language design, although from a different perspective on inference language. It is unclear if the other paper has been published or submitted somewhere and if so, where that paper appears.

Significance:
It seems very likely Edward language will have a profound impact on the field of Bayesian machine learning and deep learning methods.

Other comments:
In Sec. 2 you draw a clear distinction between specialised languages (including Stan language) and Turing-complete languages such as Edward language. This distinction seems unfair as I believe Stan language is also Turing complete as a language. Additionally no proof is provided to support the Turing-completeness of Edward language.
lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c:
First up, I want to point out that this paper is really long. Like 17 pages long -- without any material in addition to the paper. While ICLR does not have an official page limit, it would be nice if authors put themselves in the reviewer's position and did not take advantage of this rule without good reason. Having 1 or 2 pages in addition to the standard 8 page limit is ok, but more than doubling the pages is quite unfair to reviewers who must review the paper.

Now for the review: The paper proposes a new dataset for learning sequences. I call this dataset artificial because this dataset was artificially generated from the original MNIST dataset which is a smallish dataset of real images showing handwritten digits. In addition to the dataset, the authors propose to train networks using a schedule over the length of the sequence, which they call "incremental learning". The paper shows that their proposed schedule is better than not having any schedule on this dataset. Furthermore, the paper also shows that their proposed schedule is better than a few other schedules that are intuitive. The authors verify this by doing some studies over the model on the proposed dataset.

I have following issues with this paper:

-- I did not find anything novel in this paper. The proposed incremental learning schedule is nothing new and is a natural thing to try when learning sequences. Similar ideas for learning sequences have already been tried by a number of authors, including Bengio 2015, and Ranzato 2015. The only new piece of work in the paper is the studies which the authors conduct to tease out and verify that indeed the improvement is due to the schedule used for learning.

-- Furthermore, the authors only test their ideas on a single dataset which they propose and is artificially generated. Why not use these ideas on a real dataset for sequences, such as, language modeling with real language. Does the schedule not work in that real scenario? In fact I am quite positive that for language modeling where the vocabulary is huge, the gains will be no where close to the 74% reported in the paper for the artificial dataset.

-- I'm not convinced about the value of having this artificial dataset for learning. Already there are so many real world datasets for sequences available, including datasets in text, datasets in speech, datasets in finance and other areas with real sequences. What exactly does this dataset bring to the table is not super clear to me when other datasets exist. While having another dataset may not be a bad thing in itself, I almost felt that this dataset was created for the sole purpose of making the proposed ideas for learning work. It would have been so much better had the authors shown results on other datasets that are real.

-- As I said, the paper is way too long. A significant part of the length of the paper is due to a collection of studies which are completely un-related to the main message of the paper. For instance, the study in Section 6.2 is completely unrelated to the story of the paper. Same is true with the learning experiments of Section 6.4 on transfer.

Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really love cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, you have to go to the middle east or India to get some of that cumin so it's *super-expensive*. Over there, however, cumin grows like a weed and costs very little money. If only you could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a lot of money!

Unfortunately, the only way to get cumin is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all want nine months worth of pay), but sending a ship is also really risky. The ship could sink, after all, or all the cumin could spoil.

So how do you accomplish getting cumin? Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole nations, are that rich), how do you get money for this? You could go to a money-lender and take out a loan, a loan which would have a very steep rate that could almost eat up all of your profits from cumin. And what if the ship sank? You'd be completely bankrupt, and be thrown into prison, if the money-lender doesn't waste your broke ass first.

So, you come up with an idea. You can't get money for this trip alone. But you could rather easily get money for, say, one tenth of the cost of the trip. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also get money for one tenth of the cost of the trip. So you all come to an agreement: you decide to each get money for part of the cost for the trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the enterprise), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total enterprise. With this money, you pay for the ship and crew, send them off, and then nine months later, the ship comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin. The profits far and away compensate for the initial cost, and each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous profits.

But what happens if your ship sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew!), but you only paid for one tenth of the cost, and this cost was a cost you could afford to eat, you're not gonna get killed over it. Since the risk was spread around to 10 people, no one landed in debtors prison. Everyone took a small hit, instead of one person taking an enormous hit.

Think about this example, and all the people involved in it. The fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise). The shipwrights got work building a new ship. The captain and crew all got work and a salary. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process. In short, *every single person is better off*, and it wouldn't have happened if this notion of "buying and selling stock" didn't exist.

This is the advantage of a stock market. A stock market moves money around from where money just lies around doing absolutely nothing to where money can be put to use, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer. A stock market also distributes risk between lots of people, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of the stock market functions. But the critique is that the stock market stopped doing what the stock market is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating money so that money can be put into productive use) and stopped being a means to an end, and the stock market became an end unto itself. The basic concept of a stock market is a fantastic idea, and you'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose a stock market. A stock market is why we have railroads, cars, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful food, medicine, and all the other modern things we value so highly.

Before babies start to use 'language' they form language through babble. Basically they play with making noise through open mouths and closed mouths. These are the easiest sounds for babies to make as they explore making sounds. Think of the open mouths and closed mouths like binary code: 0 = the open sound, like 'aaaaaa'. Then 1 (or in our case a closed mouth) = the closed sound, like 'm' or 'p'. Try it. Close your mouth as if you were making the beginning of a 'm' sound or 'p' sound, then just open your mouth and push through some air.... You're basically making the 'ma' sound and 'pa' sound. 'B', 'D', and 'P' are pretty much interchangeable as closed sounds. Hence the variations found: baba, abba, papa, dada, etc. So, these are the basic building blocks of making sounds, so they are the sounds babies use. The simplest form for the human mouth making sounds.

Another interesting question is that these babies have been the ones to give birth to language in the 'naming' of mother and father. Why did we follow their lead? Maybe the simple naming of 'poo' and 'wee' in many languages follow a similar explanation using these same basic sounds that babies make. I think grandparents also have similar binary forms in many languages too, like in Hindi, where these basic sounds appear again and again.

Paternal Grandfather — दादा (daadaa)
Paternal Grandmother — दादी (daadii)
Maternal Grandfather — नाना (naanaa)
Maternal Grandmother — नानी (naanii)

These Hindi terms for grandparents show the same basic sounds that babies make when they first start making sounds with their mouths. The same basic sounds appear in the naming of family members across many languages, suggesting that babies making these simple sounds influenced how humans developed language for family terms.

lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a key system for network administrators as it identifies attacks and attacks. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep learning, more and more IDS are now using machine learning algorithms to detect attacks faster. However, these systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks. With the increasing number of new attacks, especially against Internet of Things devices, having a robust IDS able to detect unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the possibility of leveraging adversarial models to improve the robustness of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a new method named SIGMA, that leverages adversarial attacks to strengthen IDS against new types of attacks. Using Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, SIGMA generates adversarial attacks, iteratively, and uses it to retrain a machine learning-based IDS, until a convergence of the detection rate (i.e. until the detection system is not improving anymore). A round of improvement consists of a generation phase, in which we use GANs and metaheuristics to generate attacks; an evaluation phase in which we calculate the detection rate of those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which we train the IDS with those attacks. We have evaluated the SIGMA method for four standard machine learning algorithms acting as IDS, with a combination of GAN and a hybrid algorithm and algorithm, to generate new datasets of attacks. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks against different machine learning based IDS. Also, using SIGMA, we can improve the detection rate of an IDS to up to 100 after as little as two rounds of improvement. The method demonstrates that using adversarial attacks to train IDS improves IDS robustness against new attacks significantly.

lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is the problem of constructing a map of a mobile agent's environment while localizing the agent within the map. Dense SLAM algorithms perform map construction and agent localization at pixel granularity. These algorithms require a lot of computational power, which has prevented their use on low-power resource-constrained devices. Approximate computing can be used to speed up SLAM implementations as long as the approximations do not prevent the agent from navigating correctly through the environment. Previous studies of approximation in SLAM have assumed that the entire trajectory of the agent is known before the agent starts, and they have focused on offline controllers that set approximation knobs at the start of the trajectory. In practice, the trajectory is usually not known ahead of time, and allowing knob settings to change dynamically opens up more opportunities for reducing computation time and power. In this paper, we describe SLAMBooster, an application-aware, online control system for dense SLAM that adaptively controls approximation knobs during the motion of the agent. SLAMBooster is based on a control technique called proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller but our experiments showed this application-agnostic controller led to an unacceptable reduction in localization accuracy. To address this problem, SLAMBooster also exploits domain knowledge for controlling approximation by performing smooth surface detection and pose correction. We implemented SLAMBooster in the open-source SLAMBench framework and evaluated SLAMBooster on more than a dozen trajectories from both the literature and our own study. Our experiments show that on the average, SLAMBooster reduces the computation time by 72 and power consumption by 35 on an embedded platform, while maintaining the accuracy of localization within reasonable bounds. These improvements in computation time and power consumption make it feasible to deploy SLAM on a wider range of devices with resource constraints.

Speech recognition is a field of computer science and linguistics that develops methods and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of speech into text by computers with the main benefit of searchability. Speech recognition is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition or speech to text (STT). Speech recognition incorporates knowledge and research in the computer science fields, linguistics fields and computer engineering fields. The reverse of speech recognition is speech synthesis.

Some speech recognition systems require training (also called enrollment) where a speaker reads text or vocabulary into the speech recognition system. The speech recognition system analyzes the speaker's voice and uses the speaker's voice to fine-tune the recognition of that speaker's speech, resulting in increased recognition accuracy. Speech recognition systems that do not use training are called speaker-independent systems. Speech recognition systems that use training are called speaker-dependent systems.

Speech recognition applications include voice interfaces such as voice dialing (e.g. "call home"), call routing (e.g. "I would like to make a collect call"), appliance control, search key words (e.g. find a podcast where particular words were spoken), simple data entry (e.g., entering a credit card number), preparation of documents (e.g. a radiology report), determining speaker characteristics, speech-to-text processing (e.g., word processors or emails), and aircraft applications (usually termed direct voice input).

The term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to identifying the speaker, rather than what the speaker is saying. Recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech in speech recognition systems that have been trained on a specific speaker's voice or recognizing the speaker can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a security process.

From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations in speech recognition. Most recently, the speech recognition field has benefited from advances in deep learning and big data. The advances in speech recognition are evidenced not only by the surge of academic papers published in the speech recognition field, but more importantly by the worldwide industry adoption of a variety of deep learning methods in designing and deploying speech recognition systems.

Data dredging (also known as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is done by performing many statistical tests on the data and only reporting those tests that come back with significant results.

The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses using a single data set by exhaustively searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and perhaps for groups of cases or observations that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other variable.

Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work, and necessarily accept some risk of mistaken conclusions of a certain type (mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis). This level of risk is called the significance level. When large numbers of tests are performed, some tests produce false results of this type; hence 5% of randomly chosen hypotheses might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level, 1% of hypotheses might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level, and so on, by chance alone. When enough hypotheses are tested, it is virtually certain that some hypotheses will be reported to be statistically significant (even though this reporting is misleading), since almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to contain (for example) some spurious correlations. If they are not cautious, researchers using data mining techniques can be easily misled by these results from data dredging.

Data dredging is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons problem. One form of data dredging is when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the total number of subgroup comparisons examined during the data analysis.

Remember to also notify the doctor about any medications you might be allergic to so your doctor knows.

Some ways to prepare yourself for the test include following your doctor's instructions on what to eat and drink in the twenty-four hours leading up to your procedure, which may include not eating or drinking anything in the six to eight hours leading up to your procedure and test. You should also remove your contact lenses, eyeglasses, hair clips, nail polish, and jewelry before the test begins. Leave your jewelry at home if possible before coming to the hospital. You should also empty your bladder before the test because the test can take several hours to complete.

At the hospital you'll need to check in and meet with your medical team to discuss exactly what will happen during the procedure so that you feel prepared for the test. The medical team will let you know about any possible complications or risks from the test.

You'll be taken to a room where you can change into a hospital gown before the procedure begins at the hospital.

After most angiograms, patients stay at the facility for four to six hours after the procedure ends. This is so that the staff can observe you and make sure there are no postoperative complications after the test. During this time at the hospital, try to relax after the test. Don't let yourself stress about the results from the test. Just enjoy taking a break while the doctors are there to watch you after the procedure.

You may be given a sedative during the angiogram procedure or immediately before the procedure begins. This sedative will impair your ability to function and to operate a motor vehicle after the test.

You'll need someone to give you a ride home and help you get settled in after your procedure ends. Try to find someone you trust who can stay with you for a couple hours, preferably overnight, after you get home in case you need help with anything after the test. Most medical facilities will refuse to perform an angiogram on you if you do not have a responsible adult with you who has agreed to take you home after the procedure.

One of the best ways to help your body recover from any kind of procedure is to get as much rest as possible after the test. This will help your body heal and avoid any potential complications after the procedure. After the procedure, you'll probably feel a little discomfort in your groin area after the test. Bed rest will help you avoid moving that area so the area can heal properly after the angiogram.

You should probably plan on staying home for a few days after the procedure to help you take it easy after the test.

Talk to your doctor about any questions or other concerns about the procedure and test. Tell your doctor how you're feeling and about any problems you may have encountered after the test.

Ask your doctor about the outcome of the test and what the results mean for you moving forward after the angiogram. Are more tests required after this test? Do you need an operation after the test? Should you change some aspect of your lifestyle after learning the test results?

Pick a time when they are in a good mood. Avoid picking a time right after a hard day at work. Try to pick out their mood by asking, "How was your day?" Pick a time when you will not be interrupted or picking for their attention with other people or other issues. Right after dinner or before bed is usually a pretty good time and a pretty private time.

If you don't get a time at home, you can also be more creative and talk with them while out on a walk or even while riding in the car. You might say, "Dad, do you want to go on a quick walk? I have some things I'd like to talk with you about." You can always talk with just one parent too and ask them to talk to the other one, if needed. This works best if you know your mom, for example, is a bit more lenient or if you feel closer to her.

Staying honest and straightforward is just one way to show your maturity. So, don't tell lies, even white lies. If you've already gone on a date with this guy, you might as well tell them now, if they ask. If you are caught in a lie you will lose any trust that you've gained.

Another part of being honest is your being open to their concerns so you can talk to them about their concerns. For example, if they don't trust your boyfriend because they don't know him very well, try to create more opportunities for everyone to get to know each other better and to talk to each other better.

Avoid comparing yourself with others if it involves lies. For example, don't tell your parents that your best friend has had a boyfriend for the past 2 years, unless it is really true and unless you can really say it is true. Your parents will sense that you are not being honest and can easily check if it is true.

To get what you want, you may have to give a little. If your parents agree to let you have a boyfriend, they will most likely place some conditions on their agreement to let you have a boyfriend. If these are promises that you can actually keep, it is best to say yes to these promises. You can also bring up compromises as a way to bring your parents back to the talk if they say no initially to what you want.

This will create an opening for greater freedom in the future as you gain their trust and as you show them you can keep promises.

Many of the conditions will involve your performance at school and will involve your work at school. For example, you must keep a certain GPA to have a boyfriend and to keep a boyfriend. Or, you need to spend at least 1 hour each night on studying and on work. These are all goals that you should have anyway, so there is no harm in agreeing to these goals and agreeing to these promises.

It is likely that they will also try to limit your time with your new boyfriend, out of an effort to keep you from getting in over your head with your boyfriend. They may ask you to only go out once a week or to stick to a strict curfew and to stick to a strict time limit.

They may also want you to see and talk with a health professional and to talk about your boyfriend with a health professional. You will need to decide individually if you are comfortable with this type of compromise and with this type of promise.

Try to control your emotions during your talk with your parents. Avoid yelling, crying, whining, or begging during this talk. A temper tantrum of any kind will make them lose all respect for your position and lose all respect for what you want. To stay calm, repeat in your head the word "control" or "calm." Count for five seconds, in your head, before you answer any questions or make any statements you may regret making.

Make sure to watch your tone as well during the talk. It is really easy to say nice words with a sarcastic attitude and with a bad tone. For example, "That's great," sounds really different depending on your tone of voice and depending on your attitude. If you feel increasingly frustrated by the conversation and frustrated by the talk, plan a way to blow off some steam after the talk. Visualize taking a long run, swimming some laps, or going shopping with friends after the talk.

Your parents will most likely have quite a bit to say back to you, so make sure to pay close attention to what they are saying and to what your parents are saying. Look into their eyes when they are talking and when your parents are talking. This will help to show that you are not embarrassed or ashamed to talk about your possible relationship and to talk about having a boyfriend. Nod your head when they make good points and even smile if you really agree with something they say.

A big part of active listening is asking questions and asking your parents questions. If they say no to you, respond by asking, "Why not?" Tell them that you honestly want to understand their perspective in this situation and understand their concerns in this situation. This will help you to figure out what is bothering them so you can work on it and work on their concerns.

If you haven't already discussed it, your parents may want to sit down with you at a later time to discuss their concerns about you having sex and having a boyfriend. Again, this 'sex talk' could actually be really useful for you and really good for you. This will be a safe time for you to ask questions or express concerns about sex.

If you just can't talk to your parents face-to-face, you may need to write down your feelings and thoughts via a letter to your parents. This is also a good idea if you think your parents may have an extreme reaction to your request and to what you want.

Make sure that your letter is well written and calm and that your letter is honest. Do not write anything that you will regret writing. Instead of saying, "I'm going to have a boyfriend whether you like it or not," you might write, "I really want you to understand where I'm coming from and understand what I want."

It may be helpful to show your letter to a trusted friend or family member for feedback before presenting it to your parents and before showing it to your parents.

Trapdoor spiders are approximately 0.79 in to 1.26 inches (1 to 3 cm) long. That means roughly between the size of your pinky nail and your thumbnail.
Trapdoor spiders are black or brown, with stout bodies and legs. Some trapdoor spiders have paler color markings, or these trapdoor spiders may have a silky covering of hair. The bodies of trapdoor spiders are divided into two sections: the thorax (containing the head and legs) and the abdomen. The abdomen of trapdoor spiders is typically lighter and a slightly different color.
Though the eyes may be difficult to see because of the small size, a trapdoor spider will have 6 eyes arranged in 3 groups, whereas most other spiders have 8 eyes. Trapdoor spiders are relatives of tarantulas, but trapdoor spiders are less hairy, and trapdoor spiders have smaller, shinier bodies. The jaws of a trapdoor spider are attached to the front of the head. The jaws move up and down, unlike most other spiders, whose jaws move side to side. Females trapdoor spiders are larger than the males, but you will seldom see females because females rarely leave the burrows. Therefore, if you see a trapdoor spider, the trapdoor spider is most likely a male. Look for these characteristics that identify male trapdoor spiders:
Short and blunt spinnerets. These spinnerets produce silk, and the spinnerets are located at the tip of the abdomen. A double spur about halfway along the front legs.
A dusty or dull carapace (a harder area covering much of the thorax) that is lightly covered in bristles. Pedipalps (small appendages near the jaws) that resemble boxing gloves.
There are numerous varieties of trapdoor spiders, each variety with slightly different physical characteristics. More varieties of trapdoor spiders are still being discovered. If you think you have seen a trapdoor spider, look up the specific varieties that live in your area, so that you know can what kind of specific markings to expect.
The geographic distribution of trapdoor spiders is erratic and is attributed to the continental drift. Various species of trapdoor spiders can be found all over the world. Look for trapdoor spiders in: North America: Canada, The United States (southeastern and pacific states, and north to Colorado)
Central America (Guatemala, Mexico, etc.)
Asia (China, Japan, Thailand, etc.)
South Africa and Madagascar
Australia
Throughout the world, trapdoor spiders favor warm environments, such as temperate forests and deserts. Trapdoor spiders will burrow in grassy areas, hillsides, and dirt embankments. Trapdoor spiders burrow in the ground (about 0.75 inches wide and up to 8 inches deep) and trapdoor spiders cover the burrow with a silken hinged "trapdoor" camouflaged by sticks, pebbles, and other natural material. Because the burrows are camouflaged, the burrows can be very hard to see.
Larger burrows may have multiple trapdoors.
Usually, the burrow faces sunlight and the burrow will be found near vegetation.

Use a marker or pen to gently trace all four sides of your kneecap on your knee. This will define your work surface on the underwrap layer covering your knee. It'll be easier to apply the sports tape properly to your knee if you can actually see the kneecap's boundaries on your knee.

Use non-stretch adhesive sports tape for the McConnell technique on your knee. Cut a two to three inch (five to eight cm) strip of tape, or enough tape to cover your knee from outer to inner edges of your knee. Sports tape with a width of 38 mm (1.5 inches) is the best size of tape for knee taping.

Apply one end of the tape to the outer edge of your kneecap so the tape is vertically centered with the knee. While moving the kneecap and applying the tape to your knee, use your fingers to carefully pull the skin on the inside of your leg toward the kneecap. Your goal is to push the kneecap toward the inside of your leg, wrinkle the skin there so the skin meets the kneecap, and use the tape to hold the kneecap and skin tightly together.

Corfe Castle railway station is a railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally a station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Wareham to Swanage, the line and station were closed by British Rail in 1972. The station has since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, a heritage railway that operates from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station.

Corfe Castle station is on a railway line connecting Wareham and Norden station.

History
Corfe Castle village lies in the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, a peninsula bordered by the English Channel to the south, and by the marshy lands of the River Frome and Poole Harbour to the north and east. At the beginning of the 19th century, the area around Corfe Castle village was known for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay, which at that time was shipped by a pair of horse-drawn tramways (the Middlebere Plateway and the Furzebrook Railway) to wharves on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage at the tip of the Isle was equally well known for the Purbeck Marble that was mined locally and shipped out by sea from the port.

The presence of these industries attracted railway promoters once the L&SWR main line reached Wareham in 1847. Several railway schemes were promoted and failed, but eventually the Swanage Railway received its Act in 1881 and opened on 20 May 1885. The position of Corfe Castle village, commanding the only relatively low level route across the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that the railway line passed close to the centre of the village, and Corfe Castle station was built for the opening of the railway line. From its opening, the railway line was operated by the L&SWR, and the railway line was absorbed into that railway in 1886. Corfe Castle station was the only intermediate station on the Swanage branch, a status the station retained until closure by British Rail, and the station possessed the only passing loop between the junction with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage station. At least one camping coach was positioned at the station by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967, and probably from 1948 to 1953. From 1960, the allocated coach was a camping coach converted from a Pullman car, which was fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping compartments and a room with two single beds, and from 1962 until 1967 there were two of these coaches at the station.

While the development of Swanage as a tourist resort brought additional passenger traffic to the railway line, the collapse of both the clay industries and marble industries, and the increase in private car ownership in the second half of the 20th century made the railway line unprofitable. Closure of the railway line was first proposed in 1967, and despite local opposition the railway line finally closed on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of the railway line's operation under British Rail, passenger train services were operated by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units (also known as type 2H).

From the time of the first proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen the railway as a steam locomotive operated heritage railway developed. Most of the track bed, including Corfe Castle station, was bought by Dorset County Council. Proposals to use the railway route through the Corfe Castle gap as a road bypass for the village were eventually rejected by the county council in 1986. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the railway line in 1982.

There were concerns that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern terminus for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village. It was therefore decided to extend the railway line a further half a mile north to a new Park and Ride site built on the former location of the exchange sidings between the Swanage branch and the clay tramways. At this site the new Norden station was built and most trains terminate at Norden station. Corfe Castle station reopened on 12 August 1995, although the official opening of the station was not until February of the following year.

A 5-year project by Swanage Railway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle station was completed in April, 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening of the footbridge. The footbridge was originally built in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, the footbridge spent its life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon line until removed by Swanage Railway volunteers. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now use Corfe Castle station, and the footbridge is safer and more convenient for the people than crossing over the track via the gated and locked foot crossing. The footbridge project won the National Railway Heritage Awards in December 2007, with a plaque presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of volunteers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee.

In summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway operated two trains per day to Wareham and from Wareham, one of which continued to Poole and the other train to London Waterloo via Weymouth. There were also National Rail services on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage station in summer 2018 and 2019 operated by West Coast Railway Company with three trains per day in each direction. However, in July 2019 these services were stopped and there are currently no National Rail services to Corfe Castle station.

Services
Railway services run every day from the beginning of April to late October, with weekend only operation in March, November and December. The level of railway service varies from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction, depending the season and the day of the week. Southbound, trains operate to stations at Harman's Cross station (10 mins), Herston station (trains stop only on request), and Swanage station (21 mins). Northbound, trains operate to Norden station (3 mins).

Museum
Corfe Castle station is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum, which is housed in the old goods shed and an adjacent rail van. The Railway Museum is open on most operating days.

The Railway Museum includes Secundus, a narrow gauge steam locomotive built by Bellis and Seeking in 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway. This steam locomotive was in use until 1955, and then the steam locomotive was displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000. It is planned that the steam locomotive will eventually be transferred to a new home at the Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum, currently being developed adjacent to Norden railway station.

Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former second for the Mike McEwen team which curled out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the new Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk. For the 2006-07 season, Richter and Melnuk left the team and were replaced with Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The team disbanded after just one season together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007. In their first season together, they were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's provincial championship. Their first Grand Slam event as a team was at the end season, at the 2008 Players' Championships. The team won two games, before being eliminated from the event.

At the end of the 2008-09 season the McEwen team was ranked 7th on the CCA rankings. The team had made it to three Grand Slam playoffs during the season, and the team finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship during the season.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Olympic Qualifier, the McEwen team just lost out to fellow Manitobans the Jason Gunnlaugson team in the semi-finals of the event. Team McEwen thus missed out on the 2009 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials final despite being the favourite in that particular matchup versus the Gunnlaugson team.

McEwen's rink made it to his first provincial final in 2010, when the team lost to Jeff Stoughton in the 2010 Manitoba provincial final. The game was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba and as the Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach, the team were treated very much as the home team and crowd favourites during the game.

2010-2015: Grand Slam success and perennial provincial runner-up
Team McEwen started the 2010-11 season off well by defeating provincial rival Jeff Stoughton to win the World Cup of Curling and his first ever Grand Slam title in November, 2010. In part of the teams runner-up result in the provincial finals of 2010 and in part because of his 4 victories and leading the overall money winnings in the World Curling Tour season as of November 2010, the McEwen team was named as a nominee for the provincial team of the year by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters Association during the season.

The team continued their strong season that year by defeating provincial rival Stoughton in the semi-final of the 2011 Canadian Open during the season. The team would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard team in the extra end of the final, thus winning their second career Grand Slam and their second Grand Slam of that season.

Wozniak's rink once again made it to the Manitoba provincial final this time, being the top seed (also ranked 1st in Canada). However, the team once again lost to Stoughton in the final of the 2011 Safeway Championship, losing by one point in the final end of the game. The McEwen team then lost their third straight provincial final game at the 2012 Safeway Championship, this time losing to Rob Fowler, thus tying a provincial record for consecutive final losses previous set by Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This dubious record was avoided in 2013, when the McEwen rink failed to reach the final, but again losing to the rival Stoughton rink in the 2013 Safeway Championship semi-final. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship, the team lost the final to Stoughton in the final game.

Despite being ranked first in the world on both the World Curling Tour Order of Merit rankings and on the WCT money list, Wozniak lost his fifth provincial final in six years in 2015, losing to Reid Carruthers in the final.

Three Briers and team breakup 
Wozniak's rink won their first provincial title in 2016, sending the team to their first Brier. The Matt Dunstone rink had committed themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships, which occurred at the same time as the 2016 Tim Hortons Brier, so when the Dunstone rink beat Reid Carruthers in the semi-final, McEwen's team would go to the Brier, even if the team had lost to the Dunstone team.

In 2017, Wozniak defended his Manitoba Championship by beating Reid Carruthers in the final. The team would then better his 2016 Brier showing, going 9–2 in the round robin to enter the playoffs in first place and with hammer and choice of rocks (Brad Gushue was also 9–2 but lost first place due to losing his round robin meeting with the Manitoba team). The team then lost 7–5 to Brad Gushue in the 1 vs. 2 game. In the semi finals against reigning Brier and World Champion Kevin Koe, the team were in control for most of the game, being up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end, but the Koe team made a comeback with a steal in the eighth end, two points in the tenth end, and another steal in the extra end, dropping the Manitoba team to the bronze medal game. The team recovered to win their first Brier medal, defeating Brad Jacobs in their rematch of the 2016 bronze medal game, 7–6 in an extra end.

While competing at the 2018 Viterra Championship, skip McEwen came down with chickenpox and was unable to play after the first game. B. J. Neufeld skipped the team, until a surprise appearance by McEwen in the final, where the team lost to the Carruthers team. Despite the setback, the team still had a chance to qualify for the 2018 Tim Hortons Brier through the wildcard game, which the team won over the Jason Gunnlaugson team. Team McEwen had a difficult Brier and alongside the Carruthers team was unable to qualify for the playoffs. Following the Brier, the McEwen team announced the team would be breaking up at the end of the 2017–18 season. Just days after the announcement, the McEwen team won the 2018 Elite 10 Grand Slam of Curling event, winning the top $28,000 prize money, and the team was the first team to go through the entire event undefeated. The Grand Slam victory was the team's seventh Grand Slam overall.

Wozniak took a few years off from men's play after Team McEwen broke up. However, Wozniak played mixed doubles with his current girlfriend Marlene Albrecht and spared for McEwen's new team. After Alex Forrest stepped away from competitive curling after the 2019–20 season, Wozniak joined the Jason Gunnlaugson rink. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial championship was cancelled. As Team Gunnlaugson were the reigning provincial champions, the team were chosen to represent Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons Brier. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial championship was cancelled. As the reigning provincial champions, Team Gunnlaugson was chosen to represent Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons Brier. At the Brier, the team finished with a 6–6 record at the Brier.

Personal life
Wozniak is employed as a mortgage broker for Vertuity Mortgage. Wozniak is currently in a relationship with Swiss curler Marlene Albrecht and Wozniak has two children.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The cartoon was released on February 17, 1934.

The cartoon was supervised by Earl Duvall. The cartoon characters were animated by Jack King, Frank Tipper, both credited, Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, final four uncredited. The cartoon music score was composed by Bernard Brown (solely credited) and Norman Spencer (solely uncredited). The cartoon sound was solely recorded by Bernard Brown in the uncredited. Production number 6125.

Plot

The cartoon follows a male bug and female bug who check into a hotel which catches on fire.

Music

The music song "Honeymoon Hotel" (by Al Dubin and Harry Warren) was originally introduced in the 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade. This cartoon appears on the DVD release of that film.

Color process

The cartoon is notable for being the first Warner Bros. cartoon produced in color. It used Cinecolor since Walt Disney had exclusive rights to the Technicolor process. There was only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon produced in Cinecolor (Beauty and the Beast) before the cartoon series went briefly back to black-and-white. Later, the Merrie Melodies cartoon series moved to Technicolor, though the Looney Tunes cartoon series continued to be produced in black-and-white until 1943. Cinecolor would make a return in several late 1940s Looney Tunes cartoons and Merrie Melodies cartoons.

Modern Greek art is art from the period between the emergence of the new independent Greek state and the 20th century.

As Mainland Greece was under Ottoman rule for all four centuries, Greece was not a part of the Renaissance and artistic movements that followed in Western Europe. However, Greek islands such as Crete, and the Ionian islands in particular were for large periods under Venetian or other European powers' rule and thus Greek islands were able to better assimilate the radical artistic changes that were occurring in Europe during the 14th-18th century.

The Cretan School and in particular the Heptanese School of art are two important artistic movements in Greece that followed parallel routes to Western Europe.

Modern Greek art can be said to have been predominantly shaped by the particular socioeconomic conditions of Greece, the large Greek diaspora across Europe, and the new Greek social elite, as well as external artistic influences, predominantly from Germany and France.

Sculpture and painting

19th century

The School of Munich

Modern Greek art began to be developed around the time of Romanticism. Greek artists absorbed many elements from their European colleagues, resulting in the culmination of the distinctive style of Greek Romantic art, inspired by revolutionary ideals as well as the country's geography and history. After centuries of Ottoman rule, few opportunities for an education in the arts existed in the newly independent Greece, so studying abroad was imperative for Greek artists. Munich, as an important international center for the arts at that time, was the place where the majority of the Greek artists of the 19th century chose to study. In the school of Munich, led by Karl von Piloty, true fresco was taught for mural paintings on fresh wet lime plaster. During this period much of the art was emotional and theatrical in tone. The most prominent themes of the school of Munich were urban life, rural life, still life, and landscape.

Later on, Greek artists would return to Greece and pass on their knowledge to other Greek artists. Some of Greek artists remained in Munich, the so-called Athens on the Isar. Both academic and personal bonds developed between early Greek painters and Munich artistry giving birth to the Greek "Munich School" of painting. Nikolaos Gysis was an important teacher and artist at the Munich Academy and Nikolaos Gysis soon became a leading figure among Greek artists. Academism, realism, genre painting, upper middle class portraiture, still life and landscape painting, often representing impressionist features, will be replaced in the end of the 19th century by Symbolism, Jugendstil, Art Nouveau, which are mainly traced in the work of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas and other Greek artists. Early-20th-century modernism is also represented by significant Greek artists in Munich. Many of these Munich School artists chose subjects such as everyday Greek life, local customs, and living conditions of Greek people. Several important painters emerged at this time. Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in historical painting and especially inspired by the 1821 Greek War of Independence. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic depictions of Greek life. Georgios Jakobides devoted his attention to infants and children and Georgios Jakobides would later become the first Director of the new National Gallery of Athens. Georgios Roilos was another leading painter of the period closely associated with the Munich School, especially in his early career as a Greek artist. Konstantinos Volanakis was inspired mostly by the Greek sea.

Other Greek artists associated with the School of Munich were Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis, as well as quite a few modernist artists who studied in Munich, which included Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, and also Giorgio de Chirico.

Notable sculptors of the new Greek Kingdom were Leonidas Drosis (his major work was the extensive neo-classical architectural ornament at the Academy of Athens), Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis.

The School of Paris

A few Greek painters studied in Paris. Despite residing in the French capital and following the guidelines of the French Art Academy, Greek painters invariably had their own interpretations. Jacob Rizos was involved with the rendering of female grace, Theodoros Rallis with scenes from the Orthodox East and Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos with portraiture, still life and genre painting. During this period in Paris the avant-garde Impressionist movement developed, but most Greek painters remained faithful to the precepts of their teachers with only some nebulous thrusts in the direction of this movement. The first Greek impressionist was Périclès Pantazis who, after Paris, settled in Belgium and became a part of the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte.

Themes-artistic depictions

Many Greek artists of this period also drew upon El Greco's style for inspiration, particularly when creating art based on religious themes. This tied in with the idea of modern secular Greek art of the period referencing more classical styles, while religious art referenced Byzantine, or Byzantine inspired art. Moreover, an important and often pioneering role was played by Greek artists from Ionian islands in the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th century, who exploited conquests of the Italian Renaissance and baroque ateliers. As efforts persisted with new directions and objectives, Greek artists emerging in the world during the first decades of the 19th century reconnected Greek art with its ancient tradition, as well as with the quests of the European ateliers, especially those of the Munich School, with defining examples of the Greek contemporary art of the period including the works of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros Lytras.

20th century

At the beginning of the 20th century landscape painting held sway and the interest of Greek painters turned toward the study of light and color. The dependence of Munich slackened and Paris became the pole of attraction for the Greek artists of the period. In the early 20th century Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, achieved wide recognition in France and lifelong membership of the Académie française following his acclaim by the critic Andre Malreaux as an artist capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto". Later in the century Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition with his surrealist conceptions both of painting and poetry, while in the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became associated with European critical realism. Impressionism was the original influence on the leading figures of the art of the first half of the 20th century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas, while Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with the avant-garde groups of Munich constituting the last known link with the series of Greek painters in the great tradition of Munich in Greek art. The further development of these Greek painters led to other roads, but always within the framework of the avantgarde movement albeit with a Greek dimension.

Gradually the impressionists and other modern schools increased their influence on Greek artists. In the early 20th century Greek artists turned from Munich to Paris. The interest of Greek painters, Greek artists changes from historical representations to Greek landscapes with an emphasis on light and colours so abundant in Greece. Representatives of this artistic change are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleas, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis. Konstantinos Parthenis, in particular, introduces historical, religious and mythological elements that allow the classification of Greek painting into modern art. The same is true with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas and the expressionism of Georgios Bouzianis. The period of the 1930s was a landmark for the Greek painters, with Yiannis Tsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (introduced abstraction in Greek paintings) and Spyros Papaloukas coming into the limelight of Greek Art. These Greek painters tried mainly to link leading European trends with Greek tradition.

Notable 20th- and 21st-century artists

The second half of the 20th century has seen a range of acclaimed Greek artists, such as Constantine Andreou, recipient of the French Légion d'honneur, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally acclaimed sculptor. Giorgio de Chirico was an influential pre-Surrealist Greek-Italian painter who founded Metaphysical art. Jannis Kounellis ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera artistic movement. Electros Vekris, Kinetic artist and Sculptor, is the most well-known artist to be working in the field of light, Sound and Motion. Theodoros Stamos was a renowned abstract exessionist painter. Takis, Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis are internationally acclaimed Greek artists of Kinetic sculpture. Other notable Greek artists are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" is a short story by British author P. G. Wodehouse, which first appeared in the United States in the October 1923 issue of Cosmopolitan, and in the United Kingdom in the November 1923 Strand. The story features the irrepressible Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, and the story was included in the collection Ukridge, published in 1924.

Plot

Ukridge and Corky run into a friend of Ukridge's, a chauffeur driving a shiny new Daimler, and the chauffeur offers to take Ukridge and Corky for a ride. Along the way Ukridge and Corky are seen by a creditor of Ukridge's, who Ukridge and Corky shake off, and the Daimler almost hits a young girl, who Ukridge insists the chauffeur drive to her home near Clapham Common. Ukridge befriends the girl's family, who are impressed by the car and by Ukridge's famous Aunt Julia.

When Corky meets Ukridge a week later in the British Museum, Ukridge is accompanied by two children. Ukridge reveals Ukridge has been visiting the house, mainly for the free food, and Ukridge has been promising to take the family out on trips in the chauffeur's car, which the family believes to be Ukridge's car, and Ukridge has been promising to introduce the family to Aunt Julia, who, Ukridge reveals, has disowned Ukridge, in a letter which states "from now on, I have no nephew".

Returning from short holiday, Corky hears from George Tupper that Ukridge is engaged. Visiting Ukridge, Corky finds Ukridge with a black eye, and Corky hears the tale of how Ukridge found himself inadvertently engaged to the girl from Clapham Common, and Ukridge got punched by a rival suitor named Finch. As Ukridge and Corky talk on Ukridge's doorstep, the creditor from the car ride arrives, and Ukridge hides. A friendly passer-by soothes the enraged creditor, arguing that the passer-by knows where Ukridge lives; Ukridge moves out of Ukridge's house, remarking on the good fortune that led Ukridge to use the pseudonym "Mr. Smallweed" when dealing with the creditor.

Ukridge and Corky form a plot to get Ukridge out of the engagement by feigning ill-health, but as Corky is delivering Corky's speech to the family, the passer-by arrives. The passer-by is George Finch, Ukridge's rival for the girl; the passer-by reveals that Ukridge is an impoverished imposter, in fact called Smallweed, and the passer-by produces the creditor to prove the claim. The passer-by also bears a letter from Ukridge's aunt, claiming that Aunt Julia has no nephew. Once Corky has paid off the debt to the creditor, Ukridge and Corky are chased from the house.

Main characters

Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, the irrepressible entrepreneur
Julia Ukridge, Ukridge's haughty writer aunt
Jimmy Corcoran, Ukridge's writer friend
George Tupper, an old schoolfriend of Ukridge and Corcoran
Frederick, a chauffeur, a friend of Ukridge
Mabel Price, a girl Ukridge meets on the road
Mr Price, Mabel Price's doting father
Ernie Finch, Mabel Price's admirer, a resourceful man
Mr Grindlay, a man Ukridge owes money to, who knows Ukridge only as "Mr Smallweed"

Publication history

The story was illustrated by T. D. Skidmore in Cosmopolitan. The story was illustrated by Reginald Cleaver in the Strand.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" was included in the 1932 collection Nothing But Wodehouse, edited by Ogden Nash and published by Doubleday, Doran & Company. The story was included in Week-End Wodehouse (UK edition), first published by Herbert Jenkins Limited in 1939. The story was also collected in The World of Ukridge, published in October 1975 by Barrie & Jenkins.

Adaptations

"No Wedding Bells for Him" was adapted for radio in 1956, with Michael Shepley as Ukridge, Hubert Gregg as Corcoran, Olaf Pooley as Frederick, Jeffrey Segal as Mr Grindley, Mairhi Russell as Mabel Price, and Brewster Mason as Tupper.

The story was adapted for the television series The World of Wodehouse. The episode, titled "The Wedding Bells", aired in 1968, and the episode included the character Looney Coote (from "The Long Arm of Looney Coote").
