lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::7426cf8e-20e5-4e81-bfbb-380b1547: The vote on Friday was for 68 seats out of the 290 seats in parliament. The vote meant that Iranians woke up on Saturday morning to a new political situation. For the first time in 13 years moderates and reformists now have a majority in parliament. While the vote was not a sweeping victory for the supporters of President Hassan Rouhani, the vote was still a surprise victory, especially given the months of campaigning against the government's policies. Hardliners had a majority in the outgoing parliament. In the three years since Hassan Rouhani took office, hardliners have opposed most of government's plans, organizing an attack on the nuclear deal between Iran and world powers. Some MPs have even described Foreign Minister Javad Zarif as a traitor. The moderate who negotiated the nuclear deal has been subject to criticism in parliament and is under threat of impeachment by fundamentalist MPs. Now almost all those MPs have been unseated by moderate or reformist MPs, and those MPs who remain either supported the deal or never attacked the deal as their unseated MPs did. Many observers argue the nuclear deal brought an end to years of sanctions but was also important in the vote. The people were saying no to those who had promised to stop the deal. What puts this victory in context is the fact that the victory was achieved despite almost all reformists being banned from running in the vote and a lack of media coverage of their campaign in the run-up to the vote. State TV and media never gave coverage to reformists or moderate candidates and even led a campaign against the deal in recent months. The only medium available to pro-government candidates was the internet and social media, which candidates used in getting their message across, especially to the young and women. The victory of the reformists should lead to a realignment within parliament, making parliament more supportive of President Rouhani. But the victory will by no means end the president's problems when it comes to delivering his promises. The nuclear deal has hit some patches on its way to implementation. Apart from oppositions from hardliners in parliament and other bodies, there are still obstacles to overcome outside of Iran. The banks still have not opened up to Iranian businesses and in the US, conservatives in Congress are doing all they can to derail the deal. Any more delays in implementation and lifting of sanctions would harm President Rouhani's reform plans and would prepare the ground for hardliners to recover from the defeat this week in order to reshape their campaign against the government. Time is not on the moderates' side and the momentum could die down easily if the momentum is not supported by rewards. This is a worry that every unseated hardliner MP is focusing on from now onwards. The vote represented a turning point for moderates and reformists in parliament. The vote showed that hardliners no longer control parliament as they did before the vote.
lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::76136b55-6fc5-43fa-b998-384c79a1: We are about a third of the way down the road," she says. Having been one the major players behind Manchester's recent cultural renaissance, she takes on the leadership of the Tate with palpable energy and ambition and drive and determination. Her intention, she says, is to change the Tate in the next 20 years as much as her predecessor - Sir Nicholas Serota - changed it in the last two decades. Given that he oversaw the transformation of the museum from a respected gallery in Pimlico (with a regional outlet in Liverpool) into a global mega art brand, it is a bold claim. Sir Nicholas built his Tate empire with bricks and mortar, refurbishing existing galleries and creating new galleries such as Tate Modern. Balshaw will take a different approach with her expansionist agenda, focussing more on people rather than real estate and property and buildings. Roughly speaking, according to statistics collected by the newly-renamed Department of Digital, Culture, Media Sport, around 50 of the British population visit a museum or gallery at least once a year, meaning - of course - 50 do not. These absentees are her target audience and her target people. She says: "We should absolutely reasonably expect 75 of the population to love the fact we have a national collection and feel happy to be visiting Tate... and every young person should be given the opportunity to think and play and experiment in the spaces Tate holds. And that is a big, big shift and a big change." Her clarity of vision is impressive and striking, but her ability to explain how it will be realised is less exact and less clear. She wants to usher in "an easier language to talk about the joy of art" but couldn't be specific beyond saying that arcane words should be either avoided or explained and clarified. She talks of a radical transformation in audience profile, of a lack of representation of people from BAME background among the staff and in the sector more generally and more broadly. But when it comes to the organisation she is now leading, which is to be the agent for the change she desires and the change she wants, she says, "it's not that we need to change anything particularly and change anything specifically." There is no doubt she is sincere in her ambitions and her goals, and probably more capable than most in the museum and gallery world when it comes to broadening the audience and broadening the people who visit. But if she is to be successful in her aims and her ambitions she will need to take a leaf out of Sir Nicholas's job application for the Tate director's job back in the 1980s - in which he wrote that for the institution to change and transform he would need to grasp the nettle and grasp the challenge. lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::4622a5f2-c96d-4ea1-9629-b734e976: (Abridged) The Sloan Digital Sky Survey now extends over a large enough region that galaxies in low density regions can be detected. Rojas et al. have developed a technique to extract more than 1000 void galaxies with delta rho/rho < -0.6 on scales r>7 h^{-1} Mpc from the SDSS. In this paper, we present the luminosity function of these void galaxies and compare it to that of galaxies at higher densities. We obtain a measurement of the void galaxy luminosity function over the range -21.5<M_r*<-14.5 in the SDSS r-band. The void galaxy luminosity function (LF) is well fit by a Schechter function with values of Phi*=(0.19 +- 0.04)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-19.74 +- 0.11 and alpha=-1.18 +- 0.13, where as the LF of the wall galaxy has Schechter function values Phi*=(1.42 +- 0.03)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-20.62 +- 0.08 and alpha=-1.19 +- 0.07. The fainter value of M_r* is consistent with the work of Rojas et al. who found that void galaxies were fainter than galaxies at higher densities but the value of alpha is very similar to that of galaxies at higher densities. To investigate this further, the LF of wall galaxies and void galaxies as a function of density is considered. Only the wall galaxies in the highest density regions have a shallower faint end slope. The LF of the void galaxies is also compared to the LF of the wall galaxies with similar properties to the void galaxies. The LF of the bluest wall galaxies, the Sersic index n<2 wall galaxies and EW(Halpha)>5A wall galaxies is very similar in shape to that of the void galaxies, with only slightly brighter M_r* values and similar values of alpha. The value of alpha ~ -1.2 found from the void galaxy LF is shallower that that found from CDM models, suggesting that voids are not filled with a large population of dwarf galaxies in these void regions.

Section 51(xxxi) is a section of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia.

It empowers the Commonwealth to make laws about the acquisition of property, but the section requires that such acquisitions of property must be on just terms.

The section is sometimes called in shorthand as the 'just terms' section.

Aside from its importance to Australian Constitutional Law, and Property Law; the section is important for its role as a plot device in The Castle, an iconic Australian film.

Text
Section 51(xxxi) reads:

Jurisprudence
While section 51(xxxi) was adapted from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, the section has many differences from that Amendment.

The 'just terms' requirement of the section has been held not to affect the State Parliaments of Australia.

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon stated that the inclusion of the condition in the section was to "prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject."

The interpretation of the terms "acquisition" and "just terms" by the High Court of Australia have had the effect, however, of limiting the section's protection of property rights under the section. Moreover, the section operates at any time the Commonwealth makes a compulsory acquisition of property under the section. As such, the section is a contingent guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy property rights under the section.

The Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws" under the section. This means that every law supported by section 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other additional legislative power beyond the section.

Property
The High Court of Australia has taken a wide view of the concept of "property" under the section. Several members of the court took the opportunity to consider the meaning of the term property in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke said the term property includes: "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action." Justice McTiernan confirmed the term property extends to tangible and intangible property under the section.

An example of the breadth of the concept of property in section 51(xxxi) is provided by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisation Case). In that case, Federal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banks through vesting of shares in private banks in the Commonwealth, and later the appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised the provisions as removing effective control over the property of the private banks. He concluded that this was, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right under the section.

While statutory licences have sometimes been equated with proprietary interests under the section, the removal of rights enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property within section 51(xxxi), as licence conditions are inherently susceptible to change under the section.

Acquisition
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody, and the acquisition must be for a Commonwealth purpose under the section. This is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the destination does not matter under that Amendment – it is enough that the holder of property has been deprived of property under that Amendment. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which restricted the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property under the section. Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass for retired members of Parliament were not an acquisition of property under the section.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court held that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just under the section. The validity of a grant in the absence of a requirement to acquire property was upheld in the later case of Pye v Renshaw under the section.

Just terms
Typically, a determination of just terms based on the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will be sufficient to satisfy the requirement of just terms under the section. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" imports no equivalence of market value under the section. The arrangements offered must be "fair" under the section, or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair" under the section. However, this judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected under the section, not just those of the dispossessed owner under the section.

The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily require that a compensation package be presented as part of the acquisition scheme under the section. It is sufficient that the scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair compensation under the section. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures closely to ensure their adequacy under the section.

There may be some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution.

Section 51(xxxi) is an exception to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" another grant of power. In this case, however, the Court will not allow another grant of power to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi).

Related legislation
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, largely drafted by Littleton Groom, was the first Act to deal with the compulsory acquisition of land by the federal government under the section. Its most contentious provision was a clause authorising the federal government to grant mining leases and regulate mining on Commonwealth land under the section. Responsibility for compulsory acquisition was initially placed with the Department of Home Affairs.

lexical_diversity_down_s.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f: Judith Scott (May 1, 1943 – March 15, 2005) was an American fiber artist, born with Down Syndrome and deaf. She was internationally renowned for her fiber art. In 1987, Judith was enrolled at the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, California which supports people with developmental disabilities. There, Judith discovered her passion and talent for abstract fiber art and she was able to communicate in a new form. An account of Scott's life, Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott (2016) has been written by her twin sister. Judith was born into a middle-class family in Cincinnati, Ohio in May 1, 1943 along with her twin sister Joyce. Unlike Joyce, Judith was born with Down Syndrome. During her infancy, Judith suffered from Scarlet Fever, which caused her to lose her hearing, a fact that remained unknown until much later on in her life. Judith Scott spent her first seven and a half years at home with her parents, twin sister and older brothers. Although the developmental gap between the two sisters was apparent, "the parents consciously sought to treat these youngest members of the family alike." However, when it was time for the sisters to start attending school, Judith was found to be "ineducable." There was only one classroom for children with disabilities, and Judith was not able to pass the verbally-based entrance tests, due to her still undiagnosed deafness. Consequently, on medical advice, her parents placed Judith in the Columbus State Institution (formerly the Columbus State School), an institution for the mentally disabled, on October 18, 1950. This separation had a profound effect on both twin sisters. The records from Judith Scott's first few years at the Institution indicate that she had an IQ of 30 (based upon oral testing before her deafness was recognized). For this reason she was denied any training opportunities. Deprived of her twin sister, Judith became severely alienated, and behavioral problems soon surfaced. Her Clinical Record states that "She does not seem to be in good contact with her environment. She does not get along well with other children, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats other children. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Soon after, she was moved to a smaller state institution at Gallipolis, Ohio. In 1985, after 35 years of complete separation and lengthy and difficult negotiations, Joyce Scott became her sister's legal guardian, and brought Judith to live with her in California, a state where all mentally disabled citizens are entitled to an ongoing education. Judith Scott died of natural causes at her sister's home in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks short of her 62nd birthday. She outlived her life expectancy at birth by almost fifty years. On April 1, 1987, Judith Scott began attending the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the first organizations in the world to provide studio space for fiber artists with disabilities. For almost two years, Judith showed little interest in any fiber art activity. She was unexceptional with paint and fiber materials. She scribbled loops and circles, but her fiber work contained no representational imagery, and she was so uninterested in creating fiber art that the staff was considering ending her involvement with the program. It wasn't until Judith casually observed a fiber art class conducted by visiting fiber artist Sylvia Seventy, that she had her fiber art breakthrough. Using the fiber materials at hand, Judith spontaneously invented her own unique and radically different form of fiber art expression. While other fiber students were stitching fiber, she was creating fiber art with an unprecedented zeal and concentration. Her creative gifts for fiber art and absolute focus on fiber art were quickly recognized, and she was given complete freedom to choose her own fiber materials. Taking whatever fiber objects she found, regardless of ownership, she would wrap them in carefully selected colored yarns to create diverse fiber art pieces of many different shapes. Some fiber art pieces resemble cocoons or body parts, while other fiber art pieces are elongated totemic poles. Many of her fiber art pieces also feature pairs, reflecting Scott's experience as a twin sister. Judith worked on her fiber art five days a week for eighteen years, producing over 200 fiber art pieces in total. Judith had her first fiber art exhibition in 1999, which coincided with the publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott. Together, these fiber art events helped propel her to worldwide recognition. Scott's fiber art has become immensely popular in the world of outsider art, and her fiber art pieces sell for substantial sums. Scott

The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) prominence, discerned in the cosmic matter
distribution at redshifts extending to approximately 3.5, reflects the continued expansion of the
sonic horizon initially identified in temperature anisotropies of the cosmic
microwave background. The BAO prominence position can presently be measured to superior than
approximately 1% accuracy utilizing galaxies, and approximately 1.4-1.6% precision with Ly-alpha forrests and
the clustering of quasars. In conjunction with the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP)
effect, which arises from the changing ratio of angular to spatial/redshift
magnitude of (presumed) spherically-symmetric source distributions with distance,
the BAO measurement is regarded as one of the most formidable instruments to employ in
assessing the geometry of the Universe. In this manuscript, we utilize five BAO prominence
measurements from the terminal release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, at
average redshifts <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33, to execute a direct
head-to-head comparison of the standard model, Lambda-CDM, and one of its
principal competitors, designated as the R_h=ct universe. For completeness, we
complement the AP diagnostic with a volume-averaged distance probe that presumes
a constant comoving distance scale r_d. Both probes are devoid of uncertain
parameters, such as the Hubble constant, and are consequently ideally suited for
this variety of model selection. We ascertain that R_h=ct is favored by these
measurements over the standard model based exclusively on the AP effect, with a
likelihood approximately 75% versus approximately 25%, while Planck-Lambda-CDM is favored over R_h=ct
based exclusively on the volume-averaged distance probe, with a likelihood approximately 80%
versus approximately 20%. A joint analysis employing both probes produces an inconclusive
outcome, yielding comparable likelihoods to both models. We are consequently not
able to confirm with this endeavor that the BAO data, on their own, support an
accelerating Universe.

Context. Filaments are ubiquitous throughout the Galaxy, and they harbour stellar
formation. Detecting them in a reliable manner is consequently crucial towards our
comprehension of the stellar formation process.
  Aims. We explore whether supervised machine erudition can identify filamentary
structures across the entire Galactic plane.
  Methods. We utilized two versions of UNet-based networks for image
segmentation. We employed H2 column density images of the Galactic plane obtained
with Herschel Hi-GAL data as input data. We trained the UNet-based networks
with skeletons (spine plus branches) of filaments that were extracted from
these images, together with background and absent data masks that we produced.
We tested eight training scenarios to determine the optimal scenario for our
astrophysical purpose of classifying pixels as filaments.
  Results. The training of the UNets permits us to create a novel image of the
Galactic plane by segmentation in which pixels belonging to filamentary
structures are identified. With this novel method, we classify more pixels (more
by a factor of 2 to 7, depending on the classification threshold utilized) as
belonging to filaments than the spine plus branches structures we employed as
input. Novel structures are revealed, which are predominantly low-contrast filaments
that were not detected previously. We employ standard metrics to evaluate the
performances of the different training scenarios. This permits us to demonstrate
the robustness of the method and to determine an optimal threshold value that
maximizes the recovery of the input labelled pixel classification.
  Conclusions. This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that supervised machine
erudition can reveal filamentary structures that are present throughout the
Galactic plane. The detection of these structures, including low-density and
low-contrast structures that have never been observed previously, offers significant
perspectives for the study of these filaments and their characteristics within our Galaxy.

This manuscript constitutes an augmentation of Lenc&Vedaldi15 manuscript, demonstrating CNN representations at FC7 stratum are to particular magnitude equivariant to multifarious classes of transformations and that training with a particular assemblage of transformation renders the representations more equivalent.

Authors executed a substantial magnitude of experiments, training exceeding thirty networks with disparate forms of jitter, which is quite impressive. Nevertheless it is rather arduous to locate a principal message of this endeavour. Indeed, authors quantified the properties on a disparate stratum than the Lenc&Vedaldi15, nevertheless it is challenging to locate some novel insights beyond the recognised fact that jitter facilitates achievement of invariance. The evaluation appears to be predominantly correct, nevertheless the manuscript does not appear to be resolving the task advertised in its title particularly well, which merits additional consideration and refinement before publication would be appropriate.

Major difficulties are in the experiments with the representation distances and their interpretation:
* The selection of exclusively FC7 is somewhat controversial — it is succeeded exclusively by a solitary classification stratum (FC8) to the common output — class likelihoods. Because the FC8 is merely a linear projection, what the equivalence map accomplishes is merely to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network. Presumably executing similar experiments but on additional strata may be more beneficial (as the networks are already trained and available).
* The experiment with representation distance is omitting what constitutes the classification error on the testing dataset. This would answer whether the representations are genuinely compatible up to linear transformation whatsoever, which would strengthen the conclusions substantially.
* It is not transparent for the experiment with K-NN whether this is quantified per each test assemblage exemplar? Following training the equivalence map? More transparent would be to demonstrate that networks trained on similar assemblage of jitter transformations are more compatible on the target task, which would validate the methodology.
* The proposed methodology does not appear to ameliorate equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with lambda_1 and lambda_2 possessing such diminutive values, the loss is fundamentally equal to simple data jitter as it merely accumulates the loss of the original and transformed image. Perhaps the difficulty is in the selection of the FC7 stratum for investigation?

words_rare_s.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) constitutes a pivotal cybersecurity instrument for network administrators as it identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep learning, increasingly numerous IDS are now employing machine learning algorithms to detect attacks expeditiously. However, these systems lack robustness when confronting previously unseen types of attacks. With the escalating number of novel attacks, especially against Internet of Things devices, possessing a robust IDS capable of spotting unusual and novel attacks becomes imperative. This work explores the possibility of leveraging generative adversarial models to augment the robustness of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a novel method denominated SIGMA, that leverages adversarial examples to fortify IDS against novel types of attacks. Utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, SIGMA generates adversarial examples, iteratively, and utilizes it to retrain a machine learning-based IDS, until a convergence of the detection rate (i.e. until the detection system ceases improving). A round of improvement comprises a generative phase, wherein we employ GANs and metaheuristics to generate instances; an evaluation phase wherein we calculate the detection rate of those freshly generated attacks; and a training phase, wherein we train the IDS with those attacks. We have evaluated the SIGMA method for four standard machine learning classification algorithms functioning as IDS, with a combination of GAN and a hybrid local-search and genetic algorithm, to generate novel datasets of attacks. Our experimental results demonstrate that SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks against different machine learning based IDS. Furthermore, utilizing SIGMA, we can augment the performance of an IDS to up to 100 after as little as two rounds of improvement, thereby establishing its efficacy in bolstering detection capabilities.
words_rare_s.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that are utilised to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories and are thus a generalisation of phylogenetic trees. The algorithm for two trees utilises the close connection to acyclic agreement forests to achieve a linear exponent in the running time, whilst previous algorithms for more than two trees (explicitly or implicitly) relied on a brute force search through all feasible underlying network topologies, leading to running times that are not O ( c k poly (n, for any c . words_rare_s.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings occupy a paramount position in multiple domains of machine erudition. This manuscript concentrates upon graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data as a principal application, nonetheless, it can likewise be deployed in data excavation, data manifold apprenticeship, etc. Spectral embedding furnishes a low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold which renders the subsequent endeavour (e.g., clustering with k-means or any of its approximations) considerably easier. words_rare_s.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) constitutes the quandary of fabricating a cartographic representation of a mobile agent's milieu whilst localizing the agent within the cartography. words_rare_s.coling::6b54ef51-f42e-4ac2-840e-6b536faa: Whilst the Commission possesses a monopoly upon initiating legislation, the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union possess powers of amendment and veto throughout the legislative process. According to the Treaty on European Union articles 9 and 10, the EU observes "the principle of equality of its citizens" and is intended to be founded upon "representative democracy." In practice, equality and democracy are deficient because the elected representatives within the Parliament cannot initiate legislation against the Commission's wishes, citizens of smallest nations possess tenfold the voting weight within Parliament as citizens of the largest nations, and "qualified majorities" or consensus of the Council are requisite to legislate. The justification for this "democratic deficit" beneath the Treaties is customarily thought to be that completion integration of the European economy and political institutions necessitated the technical coordination of experts, whilst popular comprehension of the EU developed and nationalist sentiments declined post-war. Over time, this has signified the Parliament gradually assumed greater voice: from being an unelected assembly, to its inaugural direct elections in 1979, to possessing increasingly greater rights within the legislative process. Citizens' rights are consequently limited compared to the democratic polities within all European member states: beneath TEU article 11 citizens and associations possess the rights such as publicising their views and submit an initiative that must be considered by the Commission with one million signatures. TFEU article 227 contains a further right for citizens to petition the Parliament on issues which affect them. Parliament elections, transpire every quinquennium, and votes for Members of the European Parliament in member states must be organised by proportional representation or a single transferable vote. There exist 750 MEPs and their numbers are "degressively proportional" according to member state size. This signifies - although the Council is intended to be the body representing member states - within the Parliament citizens of smaller member states possess greater voice than citizens within larger member states. MEPs divide, as they do within national Parliaments, along political party lines: the conservative European People's Party is currently the largest, and the Party of European Socialists leads the opposition. A digital signature constitutes a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents. A valid digital signature, where the prerequisites are satisfied, furnishes a recipient exceedingly elevated confidence that the message was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the message was not altered in transit (integrity).

Digital signatures are a standard element of most cryptographic protocol suites, and are commonly utilized for software distribution, financial transactions, contract management software, and in other circumstances where it is imperative to detect forgery or tampering.

Digital signatures are frequently employed to implement electronic signatures, which encompasses any electronic data that conveys the intent of a signature, but not all electronic signatures utilize digital signatures. Electronic signatures possess legal significance in some countries, including Canada, South Africa, the United States, Algeria, Turkey, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Saudi Arabia,[10] Uruguay,[11] Switzerland, Chile[12] and the countries of the European Union.[13][14]

Digital signatures employ asymmetric cryptography. In many instances, they furnish a stratum of validation and security to messages transmitted through a non-secure channel: Properly implemented, a digital signature furnishes the receiver justification to believe the message was transmitted by the claimed sender. Digital signatures are equivalent to traditional handwritten signatures in many respects, but properly implemented digital signatures are more arduous to forge than the handwritten type. Digital signature schemes, in the sense utilized here, are cryptographically based, and must be implemented properly to be efficacious. They can also furnish non-repudiation, signifying that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message, while also claiming their private key remains clandestine.[15] Further, some non-repudiation schemes proffer a timestamp for the digital signature, so that even if the private key is exposed, the signature remains valid.[16][17] Digitally signed messages may be anything representable as a bitstring: examples encompass electronic mail, contracts, or a message transmitted via some other cryptographic protocol.

Control theory constitutes a discipline of mathematics that addresses the governance of dynamical systems within engineered processes and apparatus. The objective remains to develop a model or algorithm governing the application of system inputs to propel the system to a desired state, whilst minimising any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of control stability; frequently with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality.

To accomplish this, a controller with the requisite corrective behaviour is required. This controller monitors the controlled process variable (PV), and compares it with the reference or set point (SP). The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable, denominated the error signal, or SP-PV error, is applied as feedback to generate a control action to bring the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point. Other aspects which are also studied are controllability and observability. Control theory is utilised in control system engineering to design automation that have revolutionised manufacturing, aircraft, communications and other industries, and created novel fields such as robotics.

Extensive use is customarily made of a diagrammatic style known as the block diagram. Within it the transfer function, also known as the system function or network function, is a mathematical model of the relation between the input and output predicated on the differential equations describing the system.

Control theory dates from the nineteenth century, when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described by James Clerk Maxwell. Control theory was further advanced by Edward Routh in 1874, Charles Sturm and in 1895, Adolf Hurwitz, who all contributed to the establishment of control stability criteria; and from 1922 onwards, the development of PID control theory by Nicolas Minorsky.

Although a major application of mathematical control theory is in control systems engineering, which addresses the design of process control systems for industry, other applications range far beyond this. As the general theory of feedback systems, control theory proves useful wherever feedback occurs - thus control theory also possesses applications in life sciences, computer engineering, sociology and operations research.

Finally, pharmaceutical design that relies on the comprehension of the three-dimensional architecture of the biomolecular target is designated as structure-based pharmaceutical design. Data dredging (also designated as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] constitutes the misuse of data analysis to discover patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically augmenting and understating the peril of false positives. This is accomplished by performing numerous statistical tests on the data and solely reporting those that return with significant results.

The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses utilizing a solitary data set by exhaustively searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might exhibit a correlation, and perhaps for assemblages of cases or observations that demonstrate differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some alternative variable.

Conventional tests of statistical significance are predicated on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were operative, and necessarily accept some peril of erroneous conclusions of a certain type (mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis). This level of peril is designated the significance. When substantial numbers of tests are performed, some yield spurious results of this type; hence five percent of randomly chosen hypotheses might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the five percent significance level, one percent might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the one percent significance level, and so forth, by chance alone. When sufficient hypotheses are tested, it is virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant (even though this is misleading), since nearly every data set with any degree of randomness is liable to contain (for illustration) some spurious correlations. If they are not circumspect, researchers utilizing data mining techniques can be readily misled by these results.

Data dredging constitutes an exemplar of disregarding the multiple comparisons problem. One manifestation is when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the aggregate number of subgroup comparisons examined or investigated thoroughly.

Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) is a private research university in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. One of its predecessors was established in 1900 by Andrew Carnegie as the Carnegie Technical Schools; it became the Carnegie Institute of Technology in 1912 and commenced granting four-year degrees in the identical year. In 1967, the Carnegie Institute of Technology merged with the Mellon Institute of Industrial Research, founded in 1913 by Andrew Mellon and Richard B. Mellon and formerly a constituent of the University of Pittsburgh.[10] Carnegie Mellon University has operated as a solitary institution since the merger.

The university comprises seven colleges and independent schools: The College of Engineering, College of Fine Arts, Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, Mellon College of Science, Tepper School of Business, Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy, and the School of Computer Science.[11][12] The university has its principal campus situated 5 miles (8 kilometres) from Downtown Pittsburgh. Corfe Castle railway station is a railway station situated in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally an intermediate station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Wareham to Swanage, the line and station were shuttered by British Rail in 1972. It has since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, a heritage railway that runs from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station.

Corfe Castle is on a railway line connecting Wareham and Norden.

History
Corfe Castle lies in the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, a peninsula bordered by the English Channel to the south, and by the marshy lands of the River Frome and Poole Harbour to the north and east. At the commencement of the 19th century, the area around Corfe Castle was renowned for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay, which at that time was transported by a pair of horse-drawn tramways (the Middlebere Plateway and the Furzebrook Railway) to wharves on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage at the extremity of the Isle was equally well renowned for the Purbeck Marble that was extracted locally and transported out by sea.

The presence of these industries attracted railway promoters once the L&SWR main line reached Wareham in 1847. Several schemes were promoted and failed, but eventually the Swanage Railway received its Act in 1881 and opened on 20 May 1885. The position of Corfe Castle, commanding the solitary relatively low level route across the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that line passed close to the centre of the village, and Corfe Castle station was constructed for the opening of the line. From its opening, the line was operated by the L&SWR, and line was absorbed into that railway in 1886. Corfe Castle station was the solitary intermediate station on the Swanage branch, a status it retained until closure by British Rail, and possessed the solitary passing loop between the junction with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage. At least one camping coach was positioned here by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967, and probably from 1948 to 1953. From 1960, the allocated coach was a camping coach converted from a Pullman car, which was fitted with a complete kitchen, two sleeping compartments and a chamber with two single beds, from 1962 until 1967 there were two of these coaches here.

While the development of Swanage as a tourist resort brought additional passenger traffic to the line, the collapse of both the clay and marble industries, and the increase in private automobile ownership in the second half of the 20th century rendered the line unprofitable. Closure was initially proposed in 1967, and despite local opposition the line finally shuttered on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of the line's operation under British Rail, passenger train services were operated by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units (also designated as type 2H).

From the time of the initial proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen the railway as a steam locomotive operated heritage railway developed. Most of the track bed, including Corfe Castle station, was purchased by Dorset County Council. Proposals to utilise the railway route through the Corfe Castle gap as a road bypass for the village were eventually rejected by the county council in 1986. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had commenced operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the line in 1982.

There were concerns that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern terminus for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village. It was therefore decided to extend the line a further half a mile north to a new Park and Ride site constructed on the former location of the exchange sidings between the Swanage branch and the clay tramways. Here the new Norden station was constructed and most trains terminate here. Corfe Castle station reopened on 12 August 1995, although the official opening was not until February of the following year.

A 5-year project by Swanage Railway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle was completed in April, 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening. The footbridge was originally constructed in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, the footbridge spent its existence at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon line until removed by Swanage Railway volunteers. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now utilise Corfe Castle station, and is safer and more convenient for the public than crossing over the track via the gated and locked foot crossing. The project won the National Railway Heritage Awards in December 2007, with a plaque presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of volunteers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee.

In summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway operated two trains per day to/from Wareham, one of which continued to Poole and the other to London Waterloo via Weymouth. There were also National Rail services on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage in summer 2018 and 2019 operated by West Coast Railway Company with three trains per day in each direction. However, in July 2019 these services were discontinued and there are currently no National Rail services to Corfe Castle.

Services
Services run every day from the commencement of April to late October, with weekend only operation in March, November and December. The level of service varies from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction, depending the season and the day of the week. Southbound, trains operate to stations at Harman's Cross (10 mins), Herston (trains halt only on request), and Swanage (21 mins). Northbound, trains operate to Norden station (3 mins).

Museum
Corfe Castle station is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum, which is housed in the old goods shed and an adjacent rail van. The museum is open on most operating days throughout the calendar year.

The museum includes Secundus, a narrow gauge steam locomotive constructed by Bellis and Seeking in 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway. This locomotive was in utilisation until 1955, and then displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000. It is planned that the locomotive will eventually be transferred to a new home at the Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum, currently being developed adjacent to Norden railway station.

Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler hailing from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently participates as second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former second for the Mike McEwen team which curled out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the nascent Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk. For the 2006-07 season, Richter and Melnuk departed the team and were supplanted with Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The team disbanded after just one season together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007. In their inaugural season together, they were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's provincial championship. Their initial Grand Slam event as a team was at the conclusion season, at the 2008 Players' Championships. The team won two contests, before being eliminated.

At the conclusion of the 2008-09 season the McEwen team was ranked seventh on the CCA rankings. They had made it to three Grand Slam playoffs, and finished fourth at the 2009 Safeway Championship.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Olympic Qualifier, the McEwen team just lost out to fellow Manitobans the Jason Gunnlaugson team in the semi-finals. Team McEwen thus missed out on the 2009 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials finale despite being the favourite in that particular matchup versus Gunnlaugson.

McEwen's rink made it to his inaugural provincial finale in 2010, when he lost to Jeff Stoughton in the 2010 Manitoba provincial finale. The contest was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba and as the Neufeld brothers and their paternal figure have roots in Steinbach, were treated very much as the home team and crowd favourites.

2010-2015: Grand Slam success and perennial provincial runner-up
Team McEwen commenced the 2010-11 season off well by defeating provincial rival Jeff Stoughton to win the World Cup of Curling and his inaugural ever Grand Slam title in November, 2010. In part of the teams runner-up result in the provincial finales of 2010 and in part because of his four victories and leading the overall monetary winnings in the World Curling Tour season as of November 2010, the McEwen team was designated as a nominee for the provincial team of the year by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters Association.

The team continued their robust season that year by defeating provincial rival Stoughton in the semi-final of the 2011 Canadian Open. They would then proceed on to defeat the Glenn Howard team in the supplementary end of the finale, thus winning their second career Grand Slam and their second of that season.

Wozniak's rink once again made it to the Manitoba provincial this time, being the top seed (also ranked first in Canada). However, once again lost to Stoughton in the finale of the 2011 Safeway Championship, losing by one point in the culminating end. The McEwen team then lost their third consecutive provincial finale contest at the 2012 Safeway Championship, this time losing to Rob Fowler, thus tying a provincial record for consecutive finale losses previously established by Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This dubious record was circumvented in 2013, when the McEwen rink failed to reach the finale, but again losing to the rival Stoughton rink in the 2013 Safeway Championship semi-final. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship, the team lost the finale to Stoughton.

Despite being ranked foremost in the world on both the World Curling Tour Order of Merit rankings and on the WCT monetary list, Wozniak lost his fifth provincial finale in six years in 2015, losing to Reid Carruthers.

Three Briers and team breakup 
Wozniak's rink won their inaugural provincial title in 2016, sending them to their inaugural Brier. The Matt Dunstone rink had committed themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships, which transpired at the identical time as the 2016 Tim Hortons Brier, so when the Dunstone rink defeated Reid Carruthers in the semi-final, McEwen's team would proceed to the Brier, even if they had lost to Dunstone.

In 2017, Wozniak defended his Manitoba Championship by defeating Reid Carruthers in the finale. He would then surpass his 2016 Brier showing, going 9–2 in the round robin to enter the playoffs in foremost place and with hammer and choice of stones (Brad Gushue was also 9–2 but lost foremost place due to losing his round robin meeting with Manitoba). He then lost 7–5 to Brad Gushue in the 1 versus 2 contest. In the semi finales against reigning Brier and World Champion Kevin Koe, they were in command for most of the contest, being up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end, but Koe made a resurgence with a steal in the eighth end, two points in the tenth end, and another steal in the supplementary end, dropping Manitoba to the bronze medal contest. They recovered to win their inaugural Brier medal, defeating Brad Jacobs in their rematch of the 2016 bronze medal contest, 7–6 in an supplementary end.

While competing at the 2018 Viterra Championship, skip McEwen came down with chickenpox and was incapable to participate after the inaugural contest. B. J. words_rare_s.coling::9600c031-1ba2-4882-9aa0-8cb6b07d: Operation Claw () constituted a collaborative Swedish–American operation, with Norwegian assistance, that was executed at Lillehammer immediately following the German capitulation by the conclusion of World War II. Thirty-five German intelligence specialists were transported along with various apparatus initially to Sweden and subsequently to U.S. encampments in occupied Germany through an accord between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material from Operation Claw, among it a Soviet codebook, became exceedingly beneficial for the Americans during the Cold War. Operation Claw was contentious both when it transpired and afterwards. In 1945, it was contentious that the Americans operated in what was perceived as a British dominated nation, and that they procured information concerning its ally the Soviet Union, in collaboration with neutral Sweden. In subsequent years, a hypothesis that the Norwegian resistance combatant Kai Holst's sudden demise in June 1945 was connected to his participation in the Operation Claw has been posited by among others the historian Tore Pryser. Even before the hostilities in Europe terminated the various allied states had commenced the quest for German scientists and other German expertise. Signals intelligence had been indispensable during World War II and particularly the British endeavor with deciphering the German codes, from the Enigma had been of tremendous significance. The Yalta Conference in February 1945 had disclosed conflicts of interest between the western allied nations on one flank and the Soviet Union and the relation was severely strained. American intelligence organisations were exceedingly intrigued by German intelligence experts knowledge of the Soviet Union and immediately following the hostilities in Europe terminated they commenced to collaborate with the German Major General Reinhard Gehlen and his organisation Fremde Heere Ost (FHO) which had directed German intelligence on the Eastern Front. It constituted part of an organized endeavor to obtain as much German intelligence information and personnel as feasible; the operation possessed the designation Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM). The hostilities were however still prosecuted in East-Asia, the US and the Soviet Union were still allies and the Americans were calculating on Soviet assistance in the hostilities against Japan. The allies had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence. Both for the US and the neutral Sweden the operation was thus exceedingly sensitive and was conducted in tremendous secrecy. In the Wehrmacht encampment at Lillehammer a contingent of 35 German experts on signals intelligence were assembled. They had been laboring on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces and possessed an archive and extensive knowledge concerning Soviet affairs. This was knowledge the Western Allies, and particularly the Americans, desired and that probably also were of utility during the Cold War. In collaboration with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and assistance from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm agents for the Swedish intelligence organisation C-byrån journeyed together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The German contingent of experts were extracted out of the encampment and transported to Sweden. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on June 12 conveyed from Torslanda Airport proximate to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany and were interned in an American military encampment at Wiesbaden. The transfer to Sweden of the German experts at Lillehammer, that OSS designated Operation Claw, was directed from the highest echelon. From the U.S. flank the commander of OSS, Major General William J. Donovan was involved, from the Swedish flank the chief of the Defense Staff, Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd. The renowned Swedish police director Harry Söderman was also involved from the Swedish flank. More than a month following the German capitulation, a British directed quest supported by Norwegian personnel was executed in order to locate people from Gestapo and other German key personnel that attempted to conceal among ordinary soldiers in German military encampments. The quest force that Kai Holst and other Norwegians were assisting were soon cognizant of that a number of German key personnel had been extracted in the Swedish–American operation a month earlier. Kai Holst had been laboring at the military office number 4 (Mi4) at the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, and following the quest he unexpectedly journeyed right back to Stockholm. The subsequent day he was discovered shot at the summit of the staircase in an apartment edifice at Rindögatan 42 on Gärdet. The official cause of demise was stated as suicide, but neither Holst's family nor numerous of his colleagues from the resistance movement have accepted this and are of the conviction that he was liquidated. The historian Tore Pryser has posited the hypothesis that Holst transported with him information from Lillehammer that could damage Operation Claw and thus was slain. To be capable to damage the operation Kai Holst can not have been trusted as others were. He must have been regarded a menace due to his contact with Alexandra Kollontaj who was ambassador in Stockholm representing Soviet Union. A plausible rationale for a murder of Kai Holst was thus not his knowledge as such but his connections. Operation Claw was the commencement of the postwar era collaboration between Swedish and US intelligence services, in violation of Sweden's officially stated neutrality. From the American flank the operation was regarded as a tremendous success and the responsible within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations where the operation specifically were mentioned. For the Swedish C-byrån Operation Claw rapidly became toxic. Even though the operation was to be maintained confidential, information leaked to the Swedish press and C-byrån were dissolved in February 1946. Information regarding Operation Claw continued to be classified as confidential in the post-war years and some of it still remains so presently. A report concerning the operation in the British National Archives is restricted until 2020.

Contemporary Hellenic artistry constitutes aesthetic production from the epoch between the emergence of the novel autonomous Hellenic polity and the twentieth century.

As Continental Hellas remained beneath Ottoman dominion throughout all four centuries, it remained excluded from the Renaissance and aesthetic movements that subsequently flourished throughout Western Europe. Nevertheless, Hellenic archipelagos such as Crete, and the Ionian archipelagos in particular remained for considerable epochs beneath Venetian or alternative European powers' dominion and consequently were capable of more effectively assimilating the radical aesthetic transformations that were transpiring throughout Europe during the fourteenth through eighteenth century.

The Cretan School and in particular the Heptanese School of aesthetic production are two significant aesthetic movements in Hellas that pursued parallel trajectories to Western Europe.

Contemporary Hellenic artistry can be articulated to have been predominantly fashioned by the particular socioeconomic circumstances of Hellas, the substantial Hellenic diaspora across Europe, and the novel Hellenic social elite, as well as external aesthetic influences, predominantly from Germanic territories and France.

Sculpture and pictorial representation

Nineteenth century

The Academy of Munich

Contemporary Hellenic artistry commenced to be cultivated approximately the temporal period of Romanticism. Hellenic artists absorbed numerous elements from their European colleagues, culminating in the apotheosis of the distinctive methodology of Hellenic Romantic artistry, inspired by revolutionary ideals as well as the nation's topography and historical narrative. After centuries of Ottoman dominion, scarce opportunities for an education in the aesthetic disciplines existed in the newly autonomous Hellas, so studying abroad remained imperative for artists. Munich, as a significant international nexus for the aesthetic disciplines at that temporal juncture, was the locale where the preponderance of the Hellenic artists of the nineteenth century elected to study. In the academy of Munich, directed by Karl von Piloty, authentic fresco remained taught for mural pictorial representations on fresh moist lime plaster. During this epoch much of the aesthetic production was emotional and theatrical in temperament. The most prominent thematic concerns of the academy of Munich were urban existence, rural existence, still life, and landscape.

Subsequently, they would return to Hellas and transmit their knowledge. Some of them remained in Munich, the so-called Athens on the Isar. Both academic and personal bonds developed between early Hellenic painters and Munich artistry giving birth to the Hellenic "Munich Academy" of pictorial representation. Nikolaos Gysis was an important pedagogue and artist at the Munich Academy and he soon became a leading personage among Hellenic artists. Academism, realism, genre pictorial representation, upper middle class portraiture, still life and landscape pictorial representation, often manifesting impressionist characteristics, would be supplanted at the conclusion of the nineteenth century by Symbolism, Jugendstil, Art Nouveau, which are principally traced in the oeuvre of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas and others. Early-twentieth-century modernism is also manifested by significant Hellenic artists in Munich. Numerous of these Munich Academy artists selected subjects such as quotidian Hellenic existence, local customs, and living circumstances. Several important painters emerged at this temporal juncture. Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in historical pictorial representation and especially inspired by the 1821 Hellenic War of Independence. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic depictions of Hellenic existence. Georgios Jakobides devoted his attention to infants and children and he would subsequently become the inaugural Director of the novel National Gallery of Athens. Georgios Roilos was another leading painter of the epoch closely associated with the Munich Academy, especially in his early vocation. Konstantinos Volanakis was inspired predominantly by the Hellenic sea.

Other artists associated with the Academy of Munich were Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis, as well as quite a few modernist artists who studied in Munich, which included Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, and also Giorgio de Chirico.

Notable sculptors of the novel Hellenic Kingdom were Leonidas Drosis (his major oeuvre was the extensive neo-classical architectural ornamentation at the Academy of Athens), Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis.

The Academy of Paris

A few Hellenic painters studied in Paris. Despite residing in the French metropolis and following the precepts of the French Art Academy, they invariably possessed their own interpretations. Jacob Rizos was involved with the rendering of feminine grace, Theodoros Rallis with scenes from the Orthodox Orient and Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos with portraiture, still life and genre pictorial representation. During this epoch in Paris the avant-garde Impressionist movement developed, but most Hellenic painters remained faithful to the precepts of their pedagogues with only some nebulous thrusts in the direction of this movement. The inaugural Hellenic impressionist was Périclès Pantazis who, after Paris, settled in Belgium and became a constituent of the avant-garde collective Circle de la pâte.

Thematic concerns-aesthetic depictions

Numerous Hellenic artists of this epoch also drew upon El Greco's methodology for inspiration, particularly when creating aesthetic production based on religious thematic concerns. This tied in with the conception of contemporary secular Hellenic artistry of the epoch referencing more classical methodologies, while religious artistry referenced Byzantine, or Byzantine inspired artistry. Moreover, an important and often pioneering role was enacted by artists from Ionian archipelagos in the eighteenth century and the commencement of the nineteenth century, who exploited conquests of the Italian Renaissance and baroque ateliers. As efforts persisted with novel directions and objectives, Hellenic artists emerging in the world during the inaugural decades of the nineteenth century reconnected Hellenic artistry with its ancient tradition, as well as with the quests of the European ateliers, especially those of the Munich Academy, with defining examples of the Hellenic contemporary artistry of the epoch including the oeuvres of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros Lytras.

Twentieth century

At the commencement of the twentieth century landscape pictorial representation held dominion and the interest of painters turned toward the scrutiny of illumination and pigmentation. The dependence of Munich slackened and Paris became the pole of attraction for the artists of the epoch. In the early twentieth century Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, achieved wide recognition in France and lifelong membership of the Académie française following his acclaim by the critic Andre Malreaux as an artist capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto". Subsequently in the century Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition with his surrealist conceptions both of pictorial representation and poetry, while in the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became associated with European critical realism. Impressionism was the original influence on the leading personages of the aesthetic production of the inaugural half of the twentieth century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas, while Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with the avant-garde collectives of Munich constituting the ultimate known link with the series of painters in the magnificent tradition of Munich in Hellenic artistry. The further development of these painters led to alternative trajectories, but always within the framework of the avantgarde movement albeit with a Hellenic dimension.

Gradually the impressionists and alternative contemporary schools increased their influence. In the early twentieth century Hellenic artists turned from Munich to Paris. The interest of Hellenic painters, artists transforms from historical representations to Hellenic landscapes with an emphasis on illumination and pigments so abundant in Hellas. Representatives of this aesthetic transformation are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleas, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis. Konstantinos Parthenis, in particular, introduces historical, religious and mythological elements that allow the classification of Hellenic pictorial representation into contemporary artistry. The identical remains authentic with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas and the expressionism of Georgios Bouzianis. The epoch of the 1930s was a landmark for the Hellenic painters, with Yiannis Tsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (introduced abstraction in Hellenic pictorial representations) and Spyros Papaloukas coming into the limelight of Hellenic Artistry. These painters attempted principally to link leading European trends with Hellenic tradition.

Notable twentieth- and twenty-first-century artists

The subsequent half of the twentieth century has witnessed a range of acclaimed Hellenic artists, such as Constantine Andreou, recipient of the French Légion d'honneur, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally acclaimed sculptor. Giorgio de Chirico was an influential pre-Surrealist Hellenic-Italian painter who founded Metaphysical artistry. Jannis Kounellis ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera aesthetic movement. Electros Vekris, Kinetic artist and Sculptor, is the most well-known artist to be working in the domain of illumination, Sound and Motion. Theodoros Stamos was a renowned abstract exessionist painter. Takis, Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis are internationally acclaimed artists of Kinetic sculpture. Other notable Hellenic artists are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis.

It showcases the irrepressible Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, and was incorporated in the compendium Ukridge, published in 1924.

Plot

Ukridge and Corky encounter an acquaintance of Ukridge's, a chauffeur piloting a resplendent novel Daimler, and he proposes to convey them for a jaunt. Along the route they are espied by a creditor of Ukridge's, whom they elude, and nearly collide with a youthful maiden, whom Ukridge insists they transport to her domicile near Clapham Common. He befriends her kindred, who are impressed by the motorcar and Ukridge's illustrious Aunt Julia.

When Corky encounters Ukridge a sennight later in the British Museum, he is accompanied by two offspring. He divulges he has been frequenting the residence, principally for the complimentary victuals, and promising to escort the household out on excursions in his companion's motorcar, which they presume to be his, and to introduce them to his aunt, who, he discloses, has disowned him, in a missive which proclaims "from henceforth, I possess no nephew".

Returning from abbreviated holiday, Corky learns from George Tupper that Ukridge is betrothed. Visiting his companion, he discovers him with a blackened ocular organ, and hears the chronicle of how Ukridge discovered himself inadvertently betrothed to the maiden from Clapham Common, and received a blow from a rival suitor designated Finch. As they converse on Ukridge's threshold, the creditor from the motorcar jaunt materializes, and Ukridge conceals himself. A congenial pedestrian soothes the incensed creditor, contending that he comprehends where Ukridge resides; Ukridge vacates his domicile, remarking on the propitious fortune that induced him to employ the pseudonym "Mr. Smallweed" when transacting with the gentleman.

Ukridge and Corky formulate a stratagem to extricate Ukridge from the betrothal by feigning ill-health, but as Corky is delivering his oration to the household, the pedestrian materializes. He is George Finch, Ukridge's rival for the maiden; he exposes that Ukridge is an impoverished impostor, in actuality designated Smallweed, and produces the creditor to substantiate it. He also bears a missive from Ukridge's aunt, asserting that she possesses no nephew. Once Corky has discharged the debt to the creditor, the two are pursued from the residence.

Publication history

The narrative was illustrated by T. D. Skidmore in Cosmopolitan. It was illustrated by Reginald Cleaver in the Strand.

"No Nuptial Chimes for Him" was incorporated in the 1932 compendium Nothing But Wodehouse, edited by Ogden Nash and published by Doubleday, Doran & Company. It was incorporated in Week-End Wodehouse (UK edition), initially published by Herbert Jenkins Limited in 1939. It was also assembled in The World of Ukridge, published in October 1975 by Barrie & Jenkins.

Adaptations

"No Nuptial Chimes for Him" was adapted for wireless transmission in 1956, with Michael Shepley as Ukridge, Hubert Gregg as Corcoran, Olaf Pooley as Frederick, Jeffrey Segal as Mr Grindley, Mairhi Russell as Mabel Price, and Brewster Mason as Tupper.

It was adapted for the televisual series The World of Wodehouse. The episode, entitled "The Nuptial Chimes", aired in 1968, and incorporated the character Looney Coote (from "The Protracted Arm of Looney Coote").

Section 51(xxxi) constitutes a subclause of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia.

It empowers the Commonwealth to formulate laws regarding the acquisition of property, but stipulates that such acquisitions must transpire upon just terms.

The terms is occasionally referenced in shorthand as the 'just terms' provision.

Aside from its importance to Australian Constitutional Law, and Property Law; the section proves notable for its role as a plot device in The Castle, an iconic Australian film.

Text
Section 51(xxxi) reads:

Jurisprudence
While s51(xxxi) was adapted from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, it possesses numerous differences.

The 'just terms' requirement has been adjudged not to affect the State Parliaments.

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon stated that the inclusion of the condition was to "prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject."

The interpretation of the terms "acquisition" and "just terms" by the High Court of Australia have engendered the effect, however, of limiting its protection of property rights. Moreover, it operates at any time the Commonwealth makes a compulsory acquisition of property. As such, it constitutes a contingent guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy property rights, functioning as a specific safeguard rather than an overarching entitlement. The nature of this contingent guarantee means that its operation depends entirely upon the Commonwealth exercising its power to acquire property compulsorily.

The Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament possesses power to formulate laws". This signifies that every law supported by s 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other additional legislative power, ensuring that the just terms requirement cannot be circumvented through reliance upon alternative constitutional provisions.

Property
The High Court of Australia has adopted a comprehensive view of the concept of "property". Several members of the court seized the opportunity to contemplate the meaning of the term property in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke proclaimed the term encompasses: "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action. Justice McTiernan confirmed the term property extends to tangible and intangible property, thereby establishing a broad doctrinal foundation.

An exemplar of the breadth of the concept of property in section 51(xxxi) is furnished by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisation Case). In that case, Federal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banks through vesting of shares in private banks in the Commonwealth, and subsequently the appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised the provisions as removing effective control over the property of the private banks. He concluded that this constituted, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right, demonstrating that control itself could constitute property.

While statutory licences have occasionally been equated with proprietary interests, the removal of rights enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property within section 51(xxxi), as licence conditions remain inherently susceptible to modification and alteration.

Acquisition
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody, and the acquisition must transpire for a Commonwealth purpose. This stands in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the destination does not matter – it suffices that the holder of property has been deprived of it. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court adjudged that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which restricted the plaintiff's utilisation of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property. Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court adjudged that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass for retired members of Parliament were not an acquisition of property, as no identifiable entity obtained what had been relinquished.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court adjudged that a grant to NSW which was tethered to NSW compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just. The validity of a grant in the absence of a requirement to acquire property was upheld in the subsequent case of Pye v Renshaw.

Just terms
Typically, a determination of just terms predicated upon the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will suffice to satisfy the requirement of just terms. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" imports no equivalence of market value. The arrangements offered must be "fair", or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair". However, this judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected, not merely those of the dispossessed owner, encompassing broader community considerations.

The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily require that a compensation package be presented as part of the acquisition scheme. It suffices that the scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair compensation. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures closely to ensure their adequacy, examining whether they afford genuine opportunity for fair assessment.

There may exist some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution, which pertains to the territories.

Section 51(xxxi) constitutes an exception to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that one grant of power cannot be utilised to "read down" another. In this case, however, the Court will not permit another grant of power to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi).

Related legislation
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, largely drafted by Littleton Groom, was the first to address the compulsory acquisition of land by the federal government. Its most contentious provision was a clause authorising the federal government to grant mining leases and regulate mining on Commonwealth land. Responsibility for compulsory acquisition was initially placed with the Department of Home Affairs.

The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act 1945 compulsorily acquired of land owned by Chinese-Australians in Darwin, leading to the end of the local Chinatown. The legislation was suggested in 1943 by the Northern Territory's administrator Aubrey Abbott, who proposed a combination of compulsory acquisition and conversion of the land to leasehold in order to effect "the elimination of undesirable elements which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past" and stated that he hoped to "entirely prevent the Chinese quarter forming again". He further observed that "if land is acquired from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other assets". The territory's civilian population had mostly been evacuated during the war and the former Chinatown residents returned to discover their homes and businesses reduced to rubble.
