During her infancy, Judith suffered from Scarlet Fever, which caused her to lose her auditory capacity, a fact that remained unknown until much later on in her existence. Judith Scott spent her first seven and a half years at her domicile with her parents, twin sister and older brothers. Although the developmental gap between the two girls was apparent, "the parents consciously sought to treat these youngest members of the family alike." However, when it was time for the girls to commence attending school, Judith was found to be "ineducable." There was only one classroom for children with disabilities, and Judith was not able to pass the verbally-based entrance examinations, due to her still undiagnosed deafness. Consequently, on medical advice, her parents placed Judith in the Columbus State Institution (formerly the Columbus State School), an institution for the mentally disabled, on October 18, 1950. This separation had a profound effect on both twins. The records from Judith Scott's first few years at the Institution indicate that she had an intelligence quotient of 30 (based upon oral testing before her deafness was recognized). For this reason she was denied any training opportunities. Deprived of her twin, Judith became severely alienated, and behavioral difficulties soon surfaced. Her Clinical Record states that "She does not seem to be in satisfactory contact with her environment. Soon after, she was moved to a smaller state institution at Gallipolis, Ohio. In 1985, after thirty-five years of complete separation and lengthy and difficult negotiations, Joyce Scott became her sister's legal guardian, and brought Judith to reside with her in California, a state where all mentally disabled citizens are entitled to an ongoing education. Judith Scott expired of natural causes at her sister's domicile in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks short of her sixty-second birthday. She outlived her existence expectancy at birth by almost fifty years. On April 1, 1987, Judith Scott commenced attending the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the first organizations in the world to provide studio space for artists with disabilities. She scribbled loops and circles, but her compositions contained no representational imagery, and she was so uninterested in creating that the staff was contemplating terminating her involvement with the program. Utilizing the materials at hand, Judith spontaneously invented her own unique and radically different form of artistic expression. While other students were stitching, she was sculpting with an unprecedented zeal and concentration. Her creative gifts and absolute focus were quickly recognized, and she was given complete freedom to select her own materials. The trustworthy prediction of the time-related behavior of complicated systems is key in
many scientific fields. This strong interest is however blocked by
modeling problems: often, the controlling equations describing the physics of the
system under consideration are not available or, if known, their solution
might require a computer time that does not work with the prediction time
limits. Not surprisingly, coming close to complicated systems in a general
mathematical format and teaching it from scratch from available observations has
become common practice in the age of machine learning, as shown by the
many successful examples based on deep neural networks. However,
the ability to apply the models more widely, edges of guarantee and the impact of data are
often overlooked or examined mainly by depending on earlier knowledge of the
physics. We tackle these problems from a different viewpoint, by taking on a
curriculum learning strategy. In curriculum learning, the dataset is structured
such that the training process starts from simple samples towards more difficult
ones in order to help coming together and the ability to apply more widely. The concept has been
developed and successfully applied in robotics and control of systems. Here, we
apply this concept for the learning of difficult moving systems in a
step-by-step way. First, using insights from the ergodic theory, we judge
the amount of data enough for ahead-of-time guaranteeing a faithful model of the
physical system and carefully look into the impact of the training set and
its structure on the quality of long-term predictions. Based on that, we
consider entropy as a measurement of how complicated the dataset is; we show how an
informed design of the training set based on the study of the entropy
greatly improves the resulting models in terms of the ability to apply more widely, and
provide insights on the amount and the choice of data required for an effective
data-driven modeling approach that works well.

We study a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a topological
crystalline insulator (TCI) protected by rotation symmetry. The model is built
by stacking two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers which transform
under matching representations of the rotation group, for example $p_\pm$ orbitals.
Despite its clear similarity to the Kane-Mele model, it does not host stable
gapless surface states. However the model shows topological responses
including the appearance of measured broken charge bound to rotational
defects (disclinations) and the pumping of angular momentum in response to
threading an elementary magnetic flux, which are described by a mutual
Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective
gauge field matching to the rotation symmetry. In addition, we show that
although the filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier
representation, this problem is removed upon the addition of suitable
atomic orbitals, which means fragile topology. As a result, the response of
the model can be found by representing it as a combination of atomic
orbitals with positive and negative whole number amounts. Following the
study of the model, which serves as a typical example of 2D TCIs
protected by rotation, we show that all TCIs protected by point group
symmetries which do not have protected surface states are either atomic
insulators or fragile phases. Notably, this means that gapless surface
states exist in free electron systems if and only if there is a stable Wannier
problem. We then use size reduction to map the problem of
sorting 2D TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D) problem
which is then used to obtain the complete non-interacting sorting of
such TCIs as well as the reduction of this sorting in the presence of
interactions.
words_common_s.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). This allows some of the work of creative content creation to be passed from humans to machines. The approach was tested in the area of chess problem creation. We used it to automatically create many sets of chess problems based on features taken and put together from chess problems and tournament games by humans, famous paintings, computer-made abstract art, photographs of people, and classical music tracks. The quality of these created chess problems was then judged automatically using an existing and carefully-tested computer-based chess beauty model. They were also judged by human experts in the area. The results show that features collected and put together from chess and other areas using the DSNS approach can indeed be used to automatically create chess problems of reasonably high beautiful quality. In particular, a low quality chess starting point (i.e. tournament game sequences between weak players) used together with actual photographs of people was able to produce three-move chess problems of similar quality or better to those created using a high quality chess starting point (i.e. published creations by human experts), and more quickly as well. Why information from a foreign area can be brought in and useful in this way remains an open question for now. The DSNS approach is, in theory, able to grow and usable to any area in which objects have features that can be shown using real numbers.

The baryon sound wave (BAO) peak, seen in the cosmic matter
spread at distances back in time up to about 3.5 billion years, shows the continued growth of the
sound boundary first identified in temperature differences of the cosmic
microwave background. The BAO peak position can now be measured to better than
about 1% accuracy using galaxies, and about 1.4-1.6% correctness with Ly-alpha forests and
the grouping of quasars. In combination with the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP)
effect, which comes from the changing ratio of angle to space or distance
size of (assumed) ball-shaped source spreads with distance,
the BAO measurement is viewed as one of the most powerful tools to use in
checking the shape of the Universe. In this paper, we use five BAO peak
measurements from the final release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, at
average distances back in time of 0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33, to carry out a direct
head-to-head comparison of the standard model, Lambda-CDM, and one of its
main competitors, known as the R_h=ct universe. For completeness, we
add to the AP test with a volume-averaged distance measure that assumes
a constant shared distance scale r_d. Both measures are free of uncertain
numbers, such as the Hubble constant, and are therefore perfectly suited for
this kind of model selection. We find that R_h=ct is preferred by these
measurements over the standard model based only on the AP effect, with a
likelihood about 75% versus about 25%, while Planck-Lambda-CDM is preferred over R_h=ct
based only on the volume-averaged distance measure, with a likelihood about 80%
versus about 20%. A joint study using both measures produces an unclear
outcome, giving comparable likelihoods to both models. We are therefore not
able to confirm with this work that the BAO data, on their own, support a
speeding up Universe.

Context. Thread-like shapes are everywhere in the Galaxy, and they contain star
formation. Finding them in a dependable way is therefore important towards our
understanding of the star formation process.
  Aims. We look at whether guided machine learning can find thread-like
shapes across the whole flat disk of the Galaxy.
  Methods. We used two versions of UNet-based networks for image
separation into parts. We used H2 column thickness images of the flat disk of the Galaxy obtained
with Herschel Hi-GAL data as input data. We trained the UNet-based networks
with backbones (center line plus branches) of thread-like shapes that were pulled out from
these images, together with background and missing data covers that we made.
We tested eight training situations to decide the best situation for our
space science purpose of sorting pixels as thread-like shapes.
  Results. The training of the UNets allows us to create a new image of the
flat disk of the Galaxy by separation into parts in which pixels belonging to thread-like
shapes are found. With this new method, we sort more pixels (more
by a number of 2 to 7, depending on the sorting level used) as
belonging to thread-like shapes than the center line plus branches shapes we used as
input. New shapes are shown, which are mainly low-difference thread-like shapes
that were not found before. We use standard measurements to judge the
performances of the different training situations. This allows us to show
the strength of the method and to decide a best level value that
makes the most of the recovery of the input marked pixel sorting.
  Conclusions. This early demonstration study shows that guided machine
learning can show thread-like shapes that are present throughout the
flat disk of the Galaxy. The finding of these shapes, including low-thickness and
low-difference shapes that have never been seen before, offers important
views for the study of these thread-like shapes.

I mean, not really. Actually, not at all. If Labour win this year, will it affect me? I don't really think so. I'll continue doing what I do and people will continue to hate the government until a couple of terms later National come back in, and it still has no real effect on my daily life. So, therefore, I am of the opinion that I really don't give a shit, and it's not worth my time researching to try and give a shit, therefore I should leave the voting to people who know somewhat what they're talking about. And that's fine, and it's a generally accepted attitude here, but recently there has been a whole lot of making people feel guilty about voting, with campaigns with sayings like "It's only democracy if you vote, idiot," and I've even seen some extreme ones with a picture of the earth dying (something about climate change) and just a huge block letter "VOTE" next to it. If I were to mention I wasn't planning on voting to half of my friends, they'd be fine with it, but the other half would fucking grill me alive, saying that I'm "not helping my country's future." And this guilt makes people feel that they need to vote, and they obviously don't know who for, so they are easily open to being tricked. Just yesterday I saw a flyer in one of my lectures with a breakdown on each party's policies. Except it wasn't a breakdown, in fact it had colour-coded which policies were good (whose opinion) and it basically stacked up left to right that right is evil and left is good. The green party also came in and offered free bus passes outside of peak hours for university students, which is the most stupid policy in the world, because it achieves nothing in the real world, but it gets a bunch of voters changed over. I'm sure the right wing is doing it too, but the left is more obvious to me as a university student. So in conclusion - people should not be encouraged to vote, they should be encouraged not to vote, if they do not know what they're talking about. People will vote for all the wrong reasons and politics becomes open to extreme tricking of voters. The only reason the electoral commission is making people feel guilty about voting is because they are all interested in politics, and don't understand that a lot of people just quite simply don't care. It's like forcing the entire country to watch the rugby (and honestly, the All Blacks losing would have a bigger effect on me than a change in government). Hello, users of CMV! words_common_s.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: The truth is that I am actually undecided on this issue, but I will start on the side against gay marriage for two reasons: 1. I lean less towards my starting side and it seems much more weak and unpopular, so speaking up for a weaker position I feel less strongly about helps to practice my argument speaking skills. 2. I believe that the burden of proof is on the side in favor of gay marriage (as I will explain), so I started on the other side. First, please watch [this video] (it's only two minutes). Due to this argument, I feel that the burden of proof is on the people that wish to change the requirements for the institution of marriage (I do not have problems with changing it itself, but I am just saying that changing it requires good reason). When people answer the question "Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?" with "Why not?," this is really just the teapot mistake (trying to shift the burden of proof). I do not believe equality is a good argument. It is true that people with different sexual direction deserve equal rights to life, liberty, freedom, and the pursuit of happiness as detailed by the constitution. However, the whole equality thing is a red herring in this particular instance. Marriage is not a kind of special benefit or a right that must be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around having children, and homosexual relationships, which may be loving and committed, by definition cannot produce children. There are also heterosexual marriages which cannot produce children, such as old or unable to have children couples, but if you watched the video, you'll understand why it's not the same; just because there are exceptions to the norm, doesn't mean you can extend the definition to a non-norm, as the norms are not defined by their exceptions. This "equality" is not the same as women voting or black people being free. Many times the requirements are presented as (a posed question): "If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?" Marriage requirements have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love for that matter. If your requirements are two individuals who have romantic or sexual love, then incest is fair game. Some will argue that incest is different because within the family, there are power issues, and also genetic problems. There can be power issues within any relationship, whether heterosexual, homosexual, or between family members. There is no reason to base marriage laws on this. Also, family member couples don't have to have children, can adopt, or may be unable to have children or homosexual. One may argue that incest should be a valid form of marriage as well as homosexuality. You can try to argue this point if you want, but please include valid reasoning as the burden of proof is on you. The "why would you care?" argument is wrong; Just because a suggestion does not affect anyone badly, doesn't mean we can change institutions at whim. Even under utilitarianism, this argument doesn't work. Gay people can have fulfilling long-term romantic and sexual relationships without calling it marriage. Changing marriage for the happiness of a group is similar (in logic, not emotionally) to giving in to lobbyist demands so that they will be happier. Most arguments for gay marriage are appeals to emotion or popularity. The term "gay rights" was designed to make it sound like we have holding camps for them. Even the term "homophobe" was created to make the opposition look bad. Just because this issue is popular in our current time, and many of the opponents are religious fundamentalists who use straw man arguments, doesn't make the "more reasonable side" correct. If there was a movement to make family member marriage legal and it was popular, with videos and websites online that praised the struggle of such couples, most people would be for that as well. Why is one sexual difference (and I mean to use that term with complete respect and absolutely no bad meaning, suggestion, or implication) more "marriageable" than another? View changed. In all fairness, I was already seventy-five percent there when I wrote this.
words_common_s.coling::bd4df89c-701f-407b-9fc6-2c51aa5b: I'm talking about the type of blame spoken again and again by certain users of rpolitics, certain members of OWS, and [Gawker's Hamilton Nolan]. It is a way of thinking I will restate roughly as follows: The simple fact that we live in a system where some people can gather vastly more money than others is, itself, wrong; if you do gather wealth under this system, you are quite possibly a bad person. Hedge fund managers are sitting around spending tens of millions of on preserved sharks in containers...don't they know that a tiny bit of their daily earnings would make a huge difference in others' lives? Would be enough to pay off the average redditor's student loans, for example? Every time I've heard this terrible argument, I've heard it from people fighting for causes or internet writers who come from the middle- (or, perhaps, working-class) level of an advanced Western economy. Here's the thing, though: you, too, have vastly more money and things than most people worldwide. If you could save 100 by not buying a better smartphone, by walking home in the rain instead of taking a cab, by eating cheap beans or rice for a few weeks or by skipping that new piece of clothing you wanted, you could give that 100 to save the lives of dozens of kids who would otherwise die of a disease spread by mosquitoes. Is your comfort, ease and fun more important than other peoples' lives? And, by the way, I will not allow excuses to the effect of: "but groups giving to the poor might not use the money in the right way; gifts of money could have bad effects on local business in the long run..." As a starting point of this CMV, we must agree that if wealth could be shared out again, that sharing would, indeed, help the people receiving it. We must further agree that if the average American wanted to give in a truly helpful manner towards a worthy cause, he'd be able to do so. I don't think these are wild things to believe. So, my view is that people who speak out against "the rich," purely on the ground that they're rich, are dishonest for ignoring their own compared-to-others money situation in the world. If they believe others' wealth should be shared out again to reduce the gap between rich and poor, they are dishonest for not sharing their own wealth to reduce the gap between rich and poor. Now, I don't give much to groups helping the poor. But nor do I see people richer than me as naturally evil human beings. I can see the choice shown by my decisions, which is: I'd rather buy a better plane seat than save 500 lives in a poor developing country. For this reason, if some billionaire would rather buy a nicer yacht than sell all his property to push for government control of all wealth, I don't really blame him. words_common_s.coling::4b504a77-e4f6-447f-996a-b39d54b5: (CNN) The leader of Yemen's Houthi rebels promised not to back down on Sunday as a top Saudi military official claimed weeks of airstrikes had greatly weakened the Shiite group. "Our fighters will not leave from the main cities or the government buildings," rebel leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi said in a televised address. "Anyone who thinks we will surrender is dreaming." His comments came after more than three weeks of Saudi-led coalition bombings aimed at pushing back the Houthis, who rushed into the capital of Sanaa in January and forced out President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi from power. Hadi still claims he's Yemen's lawful leader and is working with the Saudis and other friends to return to his country. Since mid-March, more than 700 people have been killed in violence that shows no sign of slowing, according to numbers from the World Health Organization. The Houthis say they have the support of the country's people behind them. "It's the right of the Yemeni people to stand against the attacks in all possible ways as long as the attacks continue," Al-Houthi said Sunday. "After our people move and act against the attacks and killing of children and women, we do not want to hear any voices and cries." But there are signs of some breaking apart among forces loyal to former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh, many of whom have fought alongside the rebels. Gen. AbdulRahman AlHalili, who leads more than 10,000 troops, has now joined himself with Hadi, military sources said Sunday. Meanwhile, Saudi Brig. Gen. Ahmed Asiri said Sunday that airstrikes had destroyed the Houthis' central command by hitting their communications. The rebels, he said, are now holding a protective stance in surrounded areas. Since it began the campaign known as Operation Decisive Storm on March 26, the Saudi-led coalition has launched 2,300 airstrikes, Asiri said. After hours at sea, chaos and desperation in Yemeni city. CNN's Don Melvin and Christine Theodorou contributed to this report.
words_common_s.coling::ef2146c2-c9fe-4563-b26a-b39f1bb9: This is the very loud moment a mother of six boys finds out she's finally having a girl after the seventh time trying. Video shows Cher Lair from Apex, North Carolina, cutting into a cake at her gender reveal party with family gathered around. She did not know the sex of her baby and gave the scan results to a baker. As she lifts up a slice of pink cake, she can hardly believe her eyes and goes on to scream out in excitement. After falling back in surprise, she then gets down on her knees again and again breathing hard and saying: 'Oh my God.' People standing nearby can be heard cheering and clapping in the background as they watch the scene happen. Lair told WTVD-TV that she and her husband, Stephen, had given up on ever having a daughter. 'At first, on baby three and four I'm thinking, "They'll be a girl at some point. They can't all be boys." 'But after four and five and six, you're kind of thinking, "Yeah, they can, she said. Caught on camera: This is the very loud moment a mother of six boys finds out she's finally having a girl, the seventh time trying. Big moment: Video shows Cher Lair from Apex, North Carolina, cutting into a cake at her gender reveal party with family gathered around. Catch her if you can: As she lifts up a slice of pink cake, she can hardly believe her eyes and goes on to scream out in excitement. The mother-of-six found out she was expecting a little lady on Monday. A friend, who was told the child's sex, helped out to bake the pink-colored chocolate cake. Lair says that she's nervous about a girl entering such a 'boy house' but she's excited to doing 'mommy-daughter' things. 'I want to take her to Cinderella, for foot care treatments and hand care treatments, and shop for a prom dress,' she added. Boy household: Lair said that she and her husband, Stephen, had given up on ever having a daughter. Very happy: Lair is set to have her seventh child in August - right now there is no word on possible names. To this day the video of Lair's gender reveal reaction has been watched more than 100,000 times with many viewers giving it the thumbs up. One person who left a comment wrote: 'That is an great video. 'This little girl is going to be so lucky to have six big brothers to look after her...congrats!' Lair is set to have her seventh child in August. Right now there is no word on possible names.
words_common_s.coling::a1534ce8-2639-4c7c-b509-3d430b55: Hit rap group of three Migos have been arrested on the first part of their U.S. tour after police found drugs and guns inside their van during a college show. Rappers Quavious Marshall, 24, Kirschnick Ball, 20, and Kiari Cephus, 23, were walked off the Georgia Southern University campus during the middle of their performance on Saturday night and taken into police keeping. According to NBC News, all of the band members have been refused bail - meaning they might not be able to carry out their coming tour dates. Migos were next supposed to perform at the Ksu Meeting Center in Georgia before traveling on to a number of other states including Wisconsin, Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania and New York. From left to right: Hip hop rappers Quavious Marshall, 24, Kirschnick Ball, 20, and Kiari Cephus, 23, have been arrested on the first part of their U.S. tour after drugs and guns were found in their van. Police said that they thought the music stars had drugs when 'a very strong smell' of marijuana was noticed coming from their two tour buses. When Migos left to perform at Georgia Southern University's Hanner Fieldhouse arena over the weekend, police took the chance to carry out a search. Many guns, marijuana and another unknown drug were found inside the vehicles, officials said. They added that the things they found 'were deeply worrying' as they had been brought to a university-paid event where over a thousand students were gathered together. In the spotlight: According to NBC News, all of the band members have been refused bail - meaning they might not carry out their coming tour dates. Bad habits? Migos pose with friends for a group photo, posted to social media. The three band members - best known for their 2013 single Versace and their 2014 track Fight Night - were arrested after leaving the stage. They are reported to face charges of drug ownership; ownership of guns in a school safety area; and ownership of guns during the doing of a crime. It wasn't known early Monday if they had lawyers. Phone calls and emails to the group's management team by the Associated Press were not quickly returned. About a dozen other suspects - all people riding in the two vans - were also taken into police keeping following the concert. Information about them and the charges they face were not quickly available. The arrests took place during the school's yearly spring concert. Migos - which formed as a group in 2009 - had an agreement with Georgia Southern to perform at the event, the sheriff's office said.
words_common_s.coling::49a2d576-81e8-4b16-889d-beb4a986: A teenager has died after falling off the roof of a six-story Bronx building as he ran away from police officers who were answering complaints of a group smoking marijuana and hanging around. Hakeem Kuta, 17, was on life support and died Saturday morning after receiving injuries from the fall that happened on Thursday night, said the New York Police Department. Police said Kuta, junior at Bronx Envision Academy, appeared to have made a mistake about a ledge while backing away from coming cops. Scroll down for video. Hakeem Kuta (above) fell six stories from the roof of the Bronx building on Thursday. Police were answering complaints of a group of teens smoking marijuana and hanging around in the lobby when Kuta and the five others ran when police officers arrived (above scenes from where he fell). The 17-year-old jumped over a three-foot high wall (pictured above) before he fell six stories from the building. Officers had chased Kuta and five other teenagers up the stairs after complaints that they were smoking marijuana in the lobby of the building located on Valentine Avenue in Mott Haven, said spokesman Stephen Davis. When the officers got to the roof, some teens jumped to another roof and ran away, however Kuta and his 14-year-old companion, who has not been named, were trapped in by a dividing wall. Police said Kuta then jumped over a three-foot high wall without knowing there was a gap between the buildings. His friend tried to help by desperately holding onto his jacket as Kuta hung 60 feet from the ground above an alleyway, according to ABC 7. When officers got the roof, some teens jumped and ran away. However, Kuta and his 14-year-old companion were trapped in by a dividing wall. Hakeem was taken to St Barnabas Hospital (above) where he was listed in critical condition. He died around 11am on Saturday. Officer Edmundo Rivera grabbed onto the companion to keep him from falling over the edge, but the friend lost his hold on Kuta who fell from the roof, dropping six stories to the pavement. Police ran to where he fell in the courtyard and Kuta was then taken to St. Barnabas Hospital where he was listed in critical condition. He died around 11am on Saturday. His father Munir Kuta, 42, an immigrant from Ghana said his son stayed out of trouble and does not do drugs, according to the New York Daily News. 'It's not so easy,' he said. 'He was a nice kid.' Authorities said there most likely would not have been any arrests as they only wanted the teens to stop smoking marijuana, according to ABC 7. No tickets were given out, although marijuana was found in the lobby. Kuta's father, Munir, an immigrant from Ghana said his son stayed out of trouble. He said: 'He was a nice kid'. No tickets were given out, although marijuana was found in the lobby (above the building on Valentine Avenue).

words_common_s.coling::6d5e183d-832b-4aa4-a6e2-563f2423: A Chinese policewoman fought off a large-knife-carrying criminal with her bare hands, even though she received several wounds in the process. The man in his twenties, who was holding two knives, stabbed her in the shoulder after she faced him while on patrol, reported the People's Daily Online. Scroll down for video. Chinese social media users praised 'tough girl' Cao Yu for her incredible bravery. The 22-year-old faced the man, who was waving around a large knife in a public square in south west China. She continued to fight with him as he used the 60 centimetre-long large knife, receiving further wounds to both hands, before her work partners turned up to bring the man under control. The young policewoman, who was found 'bleeding all over', is now getting better in hospital after the horrible event. Ms Cao said: 'I couldn't just let the man hurt innocent people.' The 60 centimetre-long knife that caused terrible cuts on the unarmed 22-year-old policewoman. The criminal also held another small knife. She added in an interview with a local television station: 'I was trying to take over the large knife and slow him down until another officer came to help me. 'There were a lot of tourists walking around the square, and I needed to make sure that they were safe.' The man is thought to have robbed a person passing by when Ms Cao saw him. Bloodied: The wounds on Cao Yu's shoulder and right hand after she was struck with the large knife. Mr Cao is getting medical treatment in the local hospital after fighting off the robber. Jiao Chun, one of the policemen who arrived on the scene, said: 'Our work partners asked him to drop his large knife but he didn't. He kept saying that he wanted to rob someone for more money.' Are we too shorthanded to send an armed and well-trained policeman to fight the bad guy?'

words_common_s.coling::65648d18-be4d-475d-bcab-2fbcdb8a: They are really two different questions (start ELI5 mode): Bridge: The Atlantic is really really big. Based on where you cross, it could even be bigger than the USA. On top of that, it's wet and it gets storms which both can cause quite a bit of damage to concrete and steel which would be used to make the bridge. The ocean is too deep to sink the support posts down to hold up the bridge. It's too stormy and full of waves so that a floating type bridge would just shake itself to pieces. It's also big and empty and very few people would really want to drive across it because it would be very boring and they wouldn't be able to carry enough fuel for the trip. (Adult version: we can't sink support posts to hold steady the bridge and current building materials won't stand up to the forces of a floating bridge. Looking after it would be an absolute nightmare due to the wearing away of salt water and air. You could only put in fuel on the crossing if fuel were shipped out to the middle of the ocean, which basically defeats the purpose) Tunnel: The Atlantic is very very deep. All of that water on top of the ocean floor means that there's lots of pressure at the bottom. Kind of like how your ears hurt when you dive deeply at the pool but multiply it by 10,000. All of that pressure means that if they tried to dig a tunnel then it would have to absolutely never ever spring a leak or the walls would fall down and everyone would drown. On top of that, you'd need really really big fans to make sure that there was enough air for everyone down there. You would also have the same problem with fuel. (Adult version: the real problem would be at the joins of the pre-made tunnel sections which would go into the tunnel hole. There's no way that they'd be able to be made strong enough to stand up to the pressure and even small leaks at that pressure would go through materials like a movie laser. On top of that, moving air through the tunnel would be a huge issue. You would have thousands of kilometers of dead air that would have to be moved around somehow or you'd never make it through. As above, fuel as well),Nope. words_common_s.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418: There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common ones: Division by zero: You may remember from early school math that you can't divide a number by zero. The result is not defined. Well, if a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. Access breaking the rules: A program is only allowed to get into certain parts of memory. Other parts are not allowed. If a program tries to get into part of memory that is not allowed, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. Stuck waiting: Let's say you and your friend Billy are playing with blocks. You have the red block, and Billy has the blue block. You want to switch blocks, so you tell Billy that you will give him the red block after he gives you the blue block. Billy tells you that he will give you the blue block after you give him the red block. Both of you will sit there forever waiting for the other person to hand over their block, and you will never get anything done. That is a stuck waiting situation, and when it happens inside a program, the program stops working and there is nothing you can do except kill it and start it again. Not handled mistake: Sometimes a program will have a special sort of error checking built into it. When an error is found, part of the program throws a mistake signal, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the mistake signal and deal with it. If a mistake signal gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a box will pop up letting you know that a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will stop. All of these situations are caused by "bugs" in the program. "Bugs" are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or don't think about every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more "bugs" than other programs. Why? Maybe because the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test it as well as they should have, or because the program is so hard to understand that it is difficult to deal with every possible situation that might happen. Think of a program as "a way to do things" - a common example given is how to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. Your first program might read: get bread get peanut butter get jelly get knife put peanut butter on one slice put jelly on other slice put bread together SERVE If you run out of peanut butter, you're stuck halfway through the steps without anywhere left to go - that's a crash. A more hard program would describe how a pizza restaurant works - there's more ingredients, more ways to put them together, you have a lot of different workers coming and going at the same time a bunch more things that can go wrong. There's things that can go wrong you can fix things that can't be fixed - things that can't be fixed (or people are too lazy to fix) are crashes.
words_common_s.coling::37e384a6-d2b8-444e-ac7f-d4288c17: Sometimes if say there aren't that many athletes to fill up a whole race in one category, they will run similar categories together. If you look at cycling the categories are people with upper body disabilities, people with one limb disability that can peddle with both legs, people with a leg injury where they only peddle with one leg, and people with both legs affected. If the CP affects the legs on an athlete they would be put in the last category, just as someone else with another disability that affects both of an athletes legs. The athletes must be looked at by people around the world, which requires an examination of how the disability affects the athlete. This helps make sure that people can't trick the system and get placed in a category for more disabled athletes. The whole point is making sure everyone gets a fair chance to compete while still being able to hold actual races with enough people in them.

words_common_s.coling::a9b058a8-5ce8-448f-820a-6ffba640: Because of the camera's field of view (FOV). If you're a big first person shooter game player (or you know about cameras) you're probably familiar with FOV. If we think about what we can see as a cone starting at our eye and opening out like [this] (URL0) then FOV is the angle between the two outside lines. In shooter games FOV is often made bigger by top players to gain an advantage, since it lets you see more of your surroundings. [Here] (URL1) is a quick example of increasing a game's FOV I googled up. The image on the left has the FOV made bigger to 65 degrees compared to the usual setting of 45 degrees on the left. With the larger FOV you can see more on the left and right. But you'll also notice that the 2 trailer things look like they're farther away even though the player is standing in the same place - that's because as you increase the FOV you also change how the light from distant objects is going to come together on your 2D surface. Basically a larger FOV means that objects seem to decrease in size faster as they get farther away. The opposite is also true, if you decrease the FOV then it increases the size that you see of far away objects since they now come together on a larger part of the view area. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61deg. It makes it very good at collecting light from far away objects because it is pointed at a very small cone. It also means that the distance between the Earth and the Moon doesn't have the same effect on how big they look compared to each other as it does when taken with a regular camera or human eyes.," "Hold your hand in front of your face. It's probably about as big as your computer screen. Keep your hand in the same spot and move your head backwards. Your hand now appears smaller than the computer screen. There's a certain distance where your hand and the computer screen get smaller together, at the same rate. This is because the distance between you and those two things becomes a lot greater than the distance between those two things. How big something looks based on the angle depends on distance, and the comparison of distances. Basically, the first image is very close to the moon and far from the earth, so the moon seems big. The second image is very far from both the earth and the moon, so they appear like their actual sizes compared to each other. So yes, the earth DOES appear smaller in the second image, but the moon got smaller a lot faster just like your hand.," "DSCOVR basically had its camera zoomed in more. The EPIC camera on the spacecraft that took the image is made just for watching the Earth from a distance, whereas the cameras on the Apollo trips were more general purpose. To be more clear, in a camera the distance from the lens to the point where it focuses determines the physical size of the image formed on the part that captures the image. Then the physical size of the part that captures the image determines the field of view, and the number of tiny dots per inch on the part that captures the image determines the size of each tiny dot in the image. With old-style film there are no tiny dots but the film still has a sharpness limit because of its makeup and there's also a sharpness limit created by the lens. Finally a large image can simply be cut down to a smaller section, although the DSCOVR image is in fact pretty much its full size.
words_common_s.coling::1770be09-c92d-43e3-ab15-7b7318ca: For starters, I'm sure you understand that there are many different kinds of radiation.... light is radiation.... and that you're talking about the kind that splits atoms right? The kind bombs and power plants are based on yes? You're going to have to describe what an atom is. An atom is the basic building block of everything in the world. They are made of protons, neutrons, and electrons. Different numbers or mixes of these result in different atoms. Most atoms are stable, they don't change.... but some aren't. The ones that aren't will LOOK FOR being stable by getting rid of protons, neutrons, and electrons over time. These are sent away very quickly, which is what makes them dangerous. They are like tiny little bullets that hit other things at the atom level. If they crash into another atom, they hit it with enough force to send that atom's protons, neutrons, and so on flying around..... like a pool ball hitting a big group of pool balls.," "In simple terms, what happens is that certain basic materials are not stable, and to get more stable, they let go of bits and energy, known as being radioactive. This happens because there are too many bits in the atom for it to be stable. It's like a crowded elevator. Since there are so many people, everyone is not comfortable, and some people will just leave the group instead of sticking together to go all the way to the top. In the end enough people will leave, and the elevator will be comfortable again. This is how lead is made; it's uranium that has let go of enough bits to make it 'stable', or comfortable enough for the bits to stay together without losing anyone.,Radiation is different types of kind of light, going from radio waves to X-rays and beyond. Some atoms are radioactive, which means they fall apart, and when they do, fast-moving bits fly off. One kind of bit that flies off are gamma rays, which is a form of light, and so radiation. When scientists first found out about being radioactive, they didn't fully understand the different kinds of light, so there was a lot of confusion over what was radiation, what was being radioactive, and what was both. That's why some people still use "radiation" when they mean "being radioactive." So, to look back over this: radiation - different kinds of light being radioactive - bits that fly off of radioactive atoms gamma rays - both!
words_common_s.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1: You can call what you're asking about a 'wealth tax', or 'capital tax'. These are taxes not based on income you earned in a year, but some measure of how much you own. Some countries (Italy I believe is a good example) tax ownership of foreign land. Some countries tax amounts owned by businesses [Canada did this until around 5-10 years ago depending on province]. Some countries directly tax your wealth above a certain level (Switzerland, as has been mentioned, does this). One form of what you are talking about that does exist in the US is the 'Estate Tax'. This is a tax on the amount of wealth that a person owns, at the time they die. The limit for when this tax applies has been very unstable over the last 20 years, but it is usually in the multi-millions, and I believe sits somewhere around $5M. If these taxes start to show up more and more (and I believe they will), don't be surprised at the first 'sticker price'. In theory a wealth tax could replace some of the current income tax system in many countries without creating a direct increased tax burden on their people. That means: if you owe $10k in income tax this year, but a $2k capital tax is started next year, then you are still in the same position as long as your income tax is reduced to $8k. Whether these taxes are useful or better or not is really a question of money study, not personal finance, so I will not spend more time on that point. Note: if the money you have saved earns money (interest, or payments, or maybe rent from an apartment you own), then those earnings are usually taxed alongside your wage income. Any 'wealth or capital tax' as I've described it above would be in addition to income tax on money earned from savings and property.
words_common_s.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe: You could have both choices used (and given to you) on the same day, but I don't think you could lose money on both on the same day. The reason is that while uses are immediate, giving them to you happens after the markets close at the end of each day. See http://www.888options.com/help/faq/assignment.jsp for details. So you would get both given to you at the same time, that night. The final result should be that you don't own any stock (someone would make you take the stock, then it would be taken away) and you don't have the choices anymore. You should have money coming in of $1500 selling the stock to the call user and money going out of $1300 buying from the put user, right? So you would have no more choices but $200 more cash in your account in the morning. You bought at 13 and sold at 15. This choices position is an agreement to buy at 13 and sell at 15 at someone else's choice. The way you lose money is if one of the choices isn't used while the other is, meaning if the stock is below 13 so nobody is going to choose to buy from you at 15, but they'll sell to you at 13; or above 15 so nobody is going to choose to sell to you at 13, but they'll buy from you at 15. You make money if neither is used (you keep the payment you sold for) or both are used (you keep the gap between the two, plus the payment). Having both used is surely unusual, since early use is unusual to begin with, and tends to happen when choices are deep in the money; so you'd expect both to be used if both are deep in the money at some point. Having both be used on the same day cannot be common, but it's maybe most likely just before they run out with very little time value left, if the stock moves around quickly so both choices are in the money at some point during the day.
words_common_s.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96: The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how they will use the payments. As Dilip notes in his answer, in the US, they will likely use the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must use the rest above the minimum to the higher rate balance. In other countries, this will change by law and custom. Do not think it will pay off the higher balance, or in equal parts, without asking. Let's take the following example. You owe $6000. $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate). If your bank uses payments to both balances in equal parts, then a payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500 and your cash advance balance by $100. The average APR, then, is simply the total of the product of the APR times balance. So here, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15%. This is called a weighted average, which means each part is counted based on its size. If the bank uses the payment in a different way - such as to the lower rate first, or some stated part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate - then this will be wrong if you enter it into a calculator, because your average APR will go up over time as you pay off the purchase balance but don't pay off the cash advance balance, or may go down if the opposite happens. The weighted average is probably fairly close in the situation that you describe, even if you have rules using the balance in a different way, so long as they don't 100% pay down the lower rate - so it may be the easiest choice for you in terms of rough guesses (where it's not important to be correct, just close). One way using the online calculators that might be better, is to treat these like two separate loans or cards. Many calculators exist for multiple balances. Then you can give out funds in different ways to the two 'cards'. This would let you see how long you will need until you've paid off the higher balance, for example, although it probably won't perfectly match things - unless you find a site that has this exact choice available you probably will have to either live with a small error in your numbers or do the math by hand.
words_common_s.coling::9e189795-5152-41d4-9713-20ef5189: Wyoming is a good state for this. It is cheap and yearly following of rules is small. Although Delaware has the best advertising effort, so people know about it, the truth is that there are over 50 states and areas in the United States with their own competing business creation laws to bring in money (as well as their own law-making groups that change those laws), so you just have to read the laws to find a state that is good for you. What I mean is that whatever Delaware does to get in the news about its easy business laws, has been copied and done even better by other states by this point in time. And regarding Delaware's special business court, all other states in the country can also lean on Delaware court decisions, so this benefit is not unique to Delaware. Wyoming is cheaper than Delaware for small presence in the United States, requires less information then Delaware, and is also tax free. A "registered agent" can get you set up and you can find one to help you with the address problem. This should only cost $99 - $200 over the state fees. An LLC does not need to have an address in the United States, but many registered agents will let you use their address, just ask. Many kinds of businesses still require a bank account for local and world trade. Many don't require any financial go-between any more to receive payments. But if you do need this, then opening a bank account in the United States will be more difficult. Again, the registered agent or lawyer can get a Tax Identification Number for you from the IRS, and this will be needed to open a US bank account. But it is more likely that you will need an employee or stand-in director in the United States to go in person to a bank and open an account. This person needs to be mentioned in the Operating Agreement or other official form on the business creation documents. They will simply walk into a bank with your articles of business creation and operating agreement showing that they are allowed to act on behalf of the business and open a bank account. They then quit their position, and this is a private document between the LLC and the employee. But you will be able to receive and accept payments and reach the world financial system now. A lot of companies that work across many countries set up smaller owned companies in a number of countries this way.
words_common_s.coling::df393828-70be-448f-bbdb-11367e15: I cannot say this strongly enough, so I'll just say it again: Don't plan your money around your credit score. Don't even think about your credit score at all. Plan a budget and stick to it. Make sure you include short and long term savings in your budget. Pay your bills on time. Use credit in a smart way. Do all of these things, and your credit rating will take care of itself. Don't try to plan your money around raising it. On the subject of zero percent loans in particular, my rule of thumb is to only ever use them when I have enough money saved up to buy the thing completely, and even then only if my budget will still balance with the added cost of paying back the loan. Other people have other rules, including not taking such loans at all, and you should come up with a rule that works for you, but you should have a rule. One rule you shouldn't have is "do whatever will make your credit score better" because you shouldn't plan your money around your credit score. All things thought about, I think the most important thing in your situation is to make sure that you don't let the starting low rate trick you into making purchases you wouldn't otherwise make. You're not really getting free money; you're just moving around the time frame for payment, and only within a limited window at that. Also, be sure to read the fine print in the credit agreement; they can be filled with traps and problems. In particular, if you don't clear the balance by the end of the starting rate period, you can sometimes have interest charges added looking backward to the date of purchase. Make sure you know your terms and conditions completely and totally. It sounds like you're just getting started, so best of luck, and remember that Rome wasn't built in a day. Being patient can be the most helpful tool in your personal money management collection of tools. P.S. Don't plan your money around your credit score.
words_common_s.coling::b21c6524-7e1a-4589-933c-d0152005: The idea that companies listed OTC are not serious is far from the truth. Many companies on the OTC are just starting off there because they don't meet the needs to be listed on the NASDAQ or NYSE. Major stock exchanges like the NASDAQ and the NYSE only want the best companies to trade on their exchanges. The NASDAQ, for example, has three sets of listing needs. A company must meet at least one of the three need sets, as well as the main rules for all companies. These include: Now don't think that the OTC doesn't have rules either, as this is far from the truth as well. While there are no minimum level of income, profits or property needed to get listed on the OTC there are needs for checked financial statements and ongoing filing and reporting to the SEC and NASD. Also there are several different levels of the OTC, including the OTCQX, the OTCCB and the OTC Pink, each with their own set of needs. For more information about what it takes to be listed on OTC look here: http://www.otcmarkets.com/learn/otc-trading A company deciding to trade on the OTC is making the decision to take their company public, and they are putting money in to make it happen. Right now the fees to get listed on the OTC range from thirty thousand dollars to one hundred and fifty thousand dollars depending on the firm you decide to go with and the services they offer as part as their package. Now, I know I wouldn't consider thirty thousand dollars or more to not be serious money! When I looked into the process of getting a company listed on the TSX the needs seemed a lot more easy than those of the major United States markets as well, made up of an application, records submission and then a decision made by a TSX committee about whether you get listed. More information about the TSX here: http://apps.tmx.com/en/listings/listing_with_us/process/index.html I think the way that the OTC markets have gotten such a bad name is from these "Get Rich on Penny Stock" companies that you see pushing up OTC company stocks and getting huge amounts of people to buy without doing their careful checking and looking into the company and reading its information document. Then when they lose a bunch of money on a poorly-informed money choice they blame it on the company being an OTC stock. Whether you decide to trade the OTC market or not, I wouldn't make a decision based on how many exchanges the company is listed on, but rather based on the careful study you do into the company.

words_common_s.coling::a3c20aed-e22b-4f5a-ac3a-784b5d94: This soap is worse than bad: it's poisonous. Of the many television shows that have had a damaging influence on British society over the past twenty years, Eastenders is the top example. For two decades this show has celebrated the fool, the thug, the cheater, the loose woman, the loud-mouth, the violent, the sexually out-of-control, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious ...How many times has someone or other said that Eastenders "mirrors life"? Life on which planet, exactly? It's written about "working-class" characters, as imagined by middle-class people who have taken a course in creative writing. Eager to show to their middle-class friends how familiar they are with the "working-class" they dream up the lowest mob that is the population of Eastenders.This has a poisonous effect on some minds less well-prepared than others to handle fiction, and so we find members of the real population taking on the attitudes and behavior of the people of Walford.Thus, it came to pass that Eastenders mirrors life; but only after life had been tricked into mirroring Eastenders.Other soaps have followed in EE's footsteps, filled to their stinking edges with ugly, potato-faced, shaven-headed, pot-bellied characters, scowling at each other and making threats constantly. This is the working class as seen by the writers who produce this trash. The writers will grow rich on the money from such output, and will go on to enjoy the finer things of life in their special separated areas. Meanwhile, the growing number of new, TV-created robots will move steadily toward cultural emptiness.And there you have the new priests and the new creatures of the early 21st century. Much of this is due to the huge power of that lit boxful of dancing dots in the corner of your living-room. It's your fault, gentle reader: that's what you chose as the only window through which to look out from your prison.

words_common_s.coling::7c3f2a9c-bdfc-4800-8191-0036c8ce: This movie stars Ben Kingsley as Frank, a hit man for some Russian criminals based out of Buffalo. After he falls asleep in his car during a would-be hit, his mob boss uncle sends him to San Francisco, where he is to attend drinking problem meetings and get a job as a dead body preparer's helper. words_common_s.coling::c0381ae0-3b9c-40a4-bc53-f4a76564:
This paper builds on Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN pictures at FC7 layer are to some degree similar in behavior to different kinds of changes and that training with a particular group of changes makes the pictures more equal.

Authors did a large amount of tests, training over 30 networks with different forms of random changes, which is quite impressive. However it is rather difficult to find a main message of this work. Yes, authors measured the features on a different layer than the Lenc&Vedaldi15, however it is hard to find some new understandings other than the known fact that random changes help to reach sameness. The checking seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the task advertised in its title really well.

Major problems are in the tests with the picture distances:
* The choice of only FC7 is a bit controversial - it is followed only by a single sorting layer (FC8) to the common output - class chances. Because the FC8 is just a straight line change, what the sameness map does is just to move again the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the starting network. Probably doing similar tests but on more layers may be more useful (as the networks are already trained).
* The test with picture distance is missing what is the sorting error on the testing data set. This would answer whether the pictures are actually matching up to straight line change at all...
* It is not clear for the test with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example? After training the sameness map? More clear would be to show that networks trained on similar group of random change types are more matching on the target task.
* The suggested method does not seem to improve sameness in behavior in a steady way on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss is basically equal to simple data random changes as it just adds up the loss of the starting and changed image. Maybe the problem is in the choice of the FC7 layer?

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 sameness in behavior, but it does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations out of these tests. Due to some problems with the sameness tests and the fine adjusting of sameness in behavior, I would not recommend acceptance of this paper. However, making better the tests on already trained networks and changing the structure of this paper into more searching work may lead to interesting addition to the field.

There are also few smaller problems:
* It is not checked through tests that the new rule for sameness mapping helps to gain better results.
* The angles on page 1 and 5 are missing units (degrees?).
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult... ", it is not M_g which is made biggest or smallest, but the loss over the M_g
* Page 4, footnote 2 - if you are just cutting in half the activations, it is hard to call it a dropout as this constant factor can be passed to the following or earlier weights
* Is the network for RVL-CDIP the same building design as Alexnet?
* On page 7, Figure 3a+3b - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements to white is really misleading, and probably even wrong, as the distance between the same pictures should be zero (which is also a way how to check that the tests are done correctly).
words_common_s.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck rule and am very happy to see its use with deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that uses IB to train deep networks (the original papers only presented the idea), but see below for the note of separate work claim.

The working out of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational guessing. Also the explanation of the IB rule is clear. Trial results seem to be very promising and show good outcomes.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing and hard to follow. In variational guessing or information making larger, p usually means the model and q represents the "guessing engine". This means the choice of guessing method is separate to the building process. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and guessed by the real distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense or in what way? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this makes the two definitions go against each other and creates problems!

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta). However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in VAE (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different and not the same! For example, r(z) in VIB is the variational guess to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a part in the model), while in VAE it is the earlier distribution which is actually defined in the building process. Similarly p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model, while in VAE that is the guess posterior and can be separately chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep NN but p(z|x) as a deep NN or a Gaussian process).

In summary, I think the presentation for the building process is unclear and needs work. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the VAE part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between VIB and VAE, and provide some gut feelings if the VIB understanding is preferred over the other approach.

Typos and mistakes:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for separate work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented a separate work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive that many people publish the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim and praise the authors' honesty, but in case this is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.
words_common_s.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-area sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to earlier work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection (e.g. sum of difference of cross-entropies).

The reason to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a text/sentence are more important than others and this is achieved by a CNN. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW or SEQ (or the combination of both) representation is more important and why.

The written description of the CNN (one-hot or semi-supervised using pre-trained embeddings) is clear, detailed, and points out the important parts. However, a picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not needed (\citet vs. \citep) (e.g line 385).

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of deciding the number of selected in-area sentences (line 443) based on a separate validation set:

- What validation data is used here? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen. How sensitive are the models to this?

- Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected. As Figure 1 shows, the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this case.

Other comments:

- I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-area data is available, not just the development set.

- The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods to support the claims made in section 5.4.

- In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in 5.4: Another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod, 2015, who replace some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity to see whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this.

- Using the sum of source and target classification scores is very similar to source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection: sum of difference of cross-entropies. A reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable.

Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source & target classification scores by extending the CNN model to the bilingual/parallel setting.
words_common_s.coling::4e7728dc-010d-47cb-95f2-16525a71:
In this paper, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is followed that keeps word-level representations both in the context, and sometimes also in the output. However, the approach is not new, compare (Kim et al. 2015) as mentioned in the paper, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this paper by using the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. Also, Jozefowicz et al. provide a side-by-side discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling, which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing work. The remaining new contribution of the approach then would be its use to machine translation, although it remains somewhat unclear, how much reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem - the translation-related part of the OVV problem should be explained in more detail here. That said, some of the claims of this paper seems somewhat overstated, like the statement in Section 2.3: "making the notion of vocabulary no longer needed", while the authors for example express doubts concerning the understanding of difficulty measure without an clear output vocabulary. For example modeling of especially common word forms still can be expected to help, as shown in for example arXiv:1609.08144
Section 2.3: You claim that the goal requires a limited vocabulary. This statement only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. However, using smaller word pieces and even single characters, quietly larger and even unlimited vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood measure. Even though this require a model different from the one put forward here, the matching statement should be made more specific in this respect.
The way character representations are used for the output should be made clearer. The description in Section 2.4 is not clear enough in my view.
Concerning the setup of NCE, it would be helpful to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific setup and settings described in Section 3.4.
Section 4.1: you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar results with respect to the performance of using character representations at the output, and discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given in that work.
Section 4.2: there are ways to calculate and understand difficulty measure for unknown words, compare (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013).
Section 4.4 and Table 4: the size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here and made available for readers to understand the complete picture.
Smaller comments:
page 2, bottom: three different input layer should be three different input layers (plural)
Figure 1: text styles within the figure are way too small
page 3, first item below Figure 1: that we will note WE should be that we will denote WE
Section 2.3: the parameters estimation should be the parameter estimation (or: the parameters' estimation)
page 5, first paragraph: in factored way should be in a factored way
page 5, second paragraph: a n-best list, a nk-best list should be an n-best list, an nk-best list
Section 4.2, last sentence: Despite adaptive gradient, needs verb and article missing
words_common_s.coling::a0b0f9d5-62dc-4996-9de4-5e5f9b3b:
The paper introduces Edward, a chance-based programming language
built over TensorFlow and Python, and supporting a broad range of most
popular current methods in chance-based machine learning.
Quality:
The Edward library provides an extremely impressive collection of
modern chance-based reasoning methods in an easily usable form.
The paper provides a brief review of the most important techniques
especially from a representation learning viewpoint, combined with
two experiments on putting into action various modern changeable reasoning
methods and GPU-speeded-up HMC.
The first experiment (changeable reasoning) would be more valuable if
there was a clear link to complete code to reproduce the results
provided. The HMC experiment looks OK, except the describing Stan
as a hand-improved version seems unfair as the code is clearly
not hand-improved for this specific model and hardware setup.
I do not think anyone doubts the quality of your version, so
please do not ruin the picture by unsupported attention-grabbing
claims. Instead of current drama, I would suggest comparing
head-to-head against Stan on single core and separately reporting the
extra speedups you gain from running things at the same time and GPU. These numbers
would also help the readers to estimate the performance of the method
for other hardware setups.
Clarity:
The paper is in general clearly written and easy to read. The many
code examples are helpful, but also difficult as it is sometimes
unclear what is missing. It would be very helpful if the authors could
provide and clearly link to a machine-readable companion document (a Jupyter
notebook would be great, but even text or HTML would be easier to
copy-paste from than a pdf like the paper) with complete runnable code
for all the examples.
Originality:
The Edward library is clearly a unique collection of chance-based
reasoning methods. In terms of the paper, the main threat to newness
comes from previous publications of the same group. The main paper
refers to Tran et al. (2016a) which covers a lot of similar material,
although from a different viewpoint. It is unclear if the other
paper has been published or submitted somewhere and if so, where.
Significance:
It seems very likely Edward will have a deep impact on the field
of Bayesian machine learning and deep learning.
Other comments:
In Sec. 2 you draw a clear distinction between specialised languages
(including Stan) and Turing-complete languages such as Edward. This
seems unfair as I believe Stan is also Turing complete. Additionally
no proof is provided to support the Turing-completeness of Edward. The authors should be more careful about making such claims without backing them up properly.

First up, I want to point out that this paper is really long. Like 17 pages long -- without any extra material. While ICLR does not have an official page limit, it would be nice if authors put themselves in the reviewer's shoes and did not take unfair advantage of this rule. Having 1 or 2 pages in addition to the usual 8 page limit is ok, but more than doubling the pages is quite unfair.

Now for the review: The paper puts forward a new artificial dataset for sequence learning. I call it artificial because it was artificially created from the original MNIST dataset which is a smallish dataset of real images of handwritten digits. In addition to the dataset, the authors put forward to train returning networks using a schedule over the length of the sequence, which they call "step-by-step learning". The experiments show that their suggested schedule is better than not having any schedule on this data set. What is more, they also show that their suggested schedule is better than a few other natural schedules. The authors check this by doing some removal studies over the model on the suggested dataset.

I have following issues with this paper:

-- I did not find anything novel in this paper. The suggested step-by-step learning schedule is nothing new and is a natural thing to try when learning sequences. Similar idea have already been tried by a number of authors, including Bengio 2015, and Ranzato 2015. The only new piece of work is the removal studies which the authors carry out to pull out and check that indeed the improvement in performance is due to the curriculum used.

-- What is more, the authors only test their idea on a single dataset which they put forward and is artificially created. Why not use it on a real sequential dataset, such as, language modeling. Does the method not work in that situation? In fact I am quite positive that for language modeling where the word list size is huge, the performance gains will be no where close to the 74% reported in the paper.

-- I'm not convinced about the value of having this artificial dataset. Already there are so many real world sequential dataset available, including in text, speech, finance and other areas. What exactly does this dataset bring to the table is not super clear to me. While having another dataset may not be a bad thing in itself, I almost felt that this dataset was created for the sole purpose of making the suggested ideas work. It would have been so much better had the authors shown experiments on other datasets.

-- As I said, the paper is way too long. A big part of the length of the paper is due to a collection of experiments which are completely unrelated to the main message of the paper. For instance, the experiment in Section 6.2 is completely unrelated to the story of the paper. Same is true with the transfer learning experiments of Section 6.4. These parts could have been removed or shortened to make the paper easier to read and more focused on the central points.
