Corfe Castle railway station is a railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally a middle station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Wareham to Swanage, the line and station were closed by British Rail in 1972. It has since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, a historic railway that runs from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station.

Corfe Castle is on a railway line connecting Wareham and Norden.

History
Corfe Castle lies in the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, a long narrow piece of land bordered by the English Channel to the south, and by the wet muddy lands of the River Frome and Poole Harbour to the north and east. At the beginning of the 19th century, the area around Corfe Castle was known for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay, which at that time was shipped by a pair of horse-drawn track railways (the Middlebere Plateway and the Furzebrook Railway) to loading docks on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage at the tip of the Isle was equally well known for the Purbeck Marble that was dug out locally and shipped out by sea.

The presence of these businesses attracted railway builders once the L&SWR main line reached Wareham in 1847. Several plans were put forward and failed, but eventually the Swanage Railway received its Act in 1881 and opened on 20 May 1885. The position of Corfe Castle, commanding the only fairly low level route across the hilly backbone of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that line passed close to the centre of the village, and Corfe Castle station was built for the opening of the line. From its opening, the line was run by the L&SWR, and line was taken into that railway in 1886. Corfe Castle station was the only middle station on the Swanage branch, a status it kept until closure by British Rail, and had the only passing loop between the meeting point with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage. At least one camping coach was placed here by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967, and probably from 1948 to 1953. From 1960, the given coach was a camping coach changed from a Pullman car, which was fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping rooms and a room with two single beds, from 1962 until 1967 there were two of these coaches here.

While the development of Swanage as a tourist town brought additional passenger traffic to the line, the collapse of both the clay and marble businesses, and the increase in private car ownership in the second half of the 20th century made the line not able to make money. Closure was first put forward in 1967, and despite local opposition the line finally closed on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of the line's running under British Rail, passenger train services were run by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units (also known as type 2H).

From the time of the first idea of closure, a campaign to reopen the railway as a steam engine run historic railway developed. Most of the track bed, including Corfe Castle station, was bought by Dorset County Council. Plans to use the railway route through the Corfe Castle gap as a road bypass for the village were eventually turned down by the county council in 1986. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started running a steam service at the Swanage end of the line in 1982.

There were worries that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern end point for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village. It was therefore decided to extend the line a further half a mile north to a new Park and Ride site built on the former location of the exchange sidings between the Swanage branch and the clay track railways. Here the new Norden station was built and most trains end here. Corfe Castle station reopened on 12 August 1995, although the official opening was not until February of the following year.

A 5-year project by Swanage Railway workers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle was completed in April, 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening. The footbridge was originally built in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, the footbridge spent its life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon line until removed by Swanage Railway workers. The footbridge can fit the people who now use Corfe Castle station, and is safer and more easy for the public than crossing over the track by way of the gated and locked foot crossing. The project won the National Railway Historic Awards in December 2007, with a sign presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of workers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee.

In summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway ran two trains per day to and from Wareham, one of which continued to Poole and the other to London Waterloo by way of Weymouth. There were also National Rail services on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage in summer 2018 and 2019 run by West Coast Railway Company with three trains per day in each direction. However, in July 2019 these services were stopped and there are currently no National Rail services to Corfe Castle.

Services
Services run every day from the beginning of April to late October, with weekend only running in March, November and December. The level of service changes from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction, depending the season and the day of the week. Southbound, trains run to stations at Harman's Cross (10 mins), Herston (trains stop only on request), and Swanage (21 mins). Northbound, trains run to Norden station (3 mins).

Museum
Corfe Castle station is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum, which is housed in the old goods shed and a nearby rail van. The museum is open on most running days.

The museum includes Secundus, a narrow track steam engine built by Bellis and Seeking in 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway. This engine was in use until 1955, and then displayed in the now closed Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000. It is planned that the engine will eventually be moved to a new home at the Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum, currently being developed next to Norden railway station.

Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former second for the Mike McEwen team which curled out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the new Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk. For the 2006-07 season, Richter and Melnuk left the team and were replaced with Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The team broke up after just one season together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007. In their first season together, they were a runner-up at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's area championship. Their first Grand Slam event as a team was at the end season, at the 2008 Players' Championships. The team won two games, before being knocked out.

At the end of the 2008-09 season the McEwen team was ranked 7th on the CCA rankings. They had made it to three Grand Slam playoffs, and finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Olympic Qualifier, the McEwen team just lost out to fellow Manitobans the Jason Gunnlaugson team in the second-to-last round. Team McEwen thus missed out on the 2009 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials final despite being the favourite in that particular matchup vs Gunnlaugson.

McEwen's rink made it to his first area final in 2010, when he lost to Jeff Stoughton in the 2010 Manitoba area final. The game was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba and as the Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach, were treated very much as the home team and crowd favourites.

2010-2015: Grand Slam success and always the area runner-up
Team McEwen started the 2010-11 season off well by beating area rival Jeff Stoughton to win the World Cup of Curling and his first ever Grand Slam title in November, 2010. In part of the teams runner-up result in the area finals of 2010 and in part because of his 4 wins and leading the total money winnings in the World Curling Tour season as of November 2010, the McEwen team was named as a possible choice for the area team of the year by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters Association.

The team continued their strong season that year by beating area rival Stoughton in the second-to-last round of the 2011 Canadian Open. They would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard team in the extra end of the final, thus winning their second career Grand Slam and their second of that season.

Wozniak's rink once again made it to the Manitoba area this time, being the top seed (also ranked 1st in Canada). However, once again lost to Stoughton in the final of the 2011 Safeway Championship, losing by one point in the final end. The McEwen team then lost their third straight area final game at the 2012 Safeway Championship, this time losing to Rob Fowler, thus matching a area record for back-to-back final losses previously set by Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This questionable record was avoided in 2013, when the McEwen rink failed to reach the final, but again losing to the rival Stoughton rink in the 2013 Safeway Championship second-to-last round. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship, the team lost the final to Stoughton.

Despite being ranked first in the world on both the World Curling Tour Order of Merit rankings and on the WCT money list, Wozniak lost his fifth area final in six years in 2015, losing to Reid Carruthers.

Three Briers and team breakup
Wozniak's rink won their first area title in 2016, sending them to their first Brier. The Matt Dunstone rink had promised themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships, which happened at the same time as the 2016 Tim Hortons Brier, so when the Dunstone rink beat Reid Carruthers in the second-to-last round, McEwen's team would go to the Brier, even if they had lost to Dunstone.

In 2017, Wozniak defended his Manitoba Championship by beating Reid Carruthers in the final. He would then better his 2016 Brier showing, going 9–2 in the round robin to enter the playoffs in first place and with hammer and choice of rocks (Brad Gushue was also 9–2 but lost first place due to losing his round robin meeting with Manitoba). He then lost 7–5 to Brad Gushue in the 1 vs. 2 game. In the second-to-last rounds against current Brier and World Champion Kevin Koe, they were in control for most of the game, being up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end, but Koe made a comeback with a steal in the eighth end, two points in the tenth end, and another steal in the extra end, dropping Manitoba to the bronze medal game. They recovered to win their first Brier medal, beating Brad Jacobs in their rematch of the 2016 bronze medal game, 7–6 in an extra end.

While competing at the 2018 Viterra Championship, skip McEwen came down with chickenpox and was unable to play after the first game. B. J. Neufeld skipped the team, until a surprise appearance by McEwen in the final, where they lost to Carruthers. Despite the setback, they still had a chance to qualify for the 2018 Tim Hortons Brier through the wildcard game, which they won over Jason Gunnlaugson. Team McEwen had a difficult Brier and alongside Carruthers was unable to qualify for the playoffs. Following the Brier, the McEwen team announced they would be breaking up at the end of the 2017–18 season. Just days after the announcement, the McEwen team won the 2018 Elite 10 Grand Slam of Curling event, winning the top $28,000 prize money, and was the first team to go through the entire event unbeaten. The Grand Slam win was the team's seventh total.

Wozniak took a few years off from men's play after Team McEwen broke up. However, he played mixed doubles with his current girlfriend Marlene Albrecht and filled in for McEwen's new team. After Alex Forrest stepped away from competing in curling after the 2019–20 season, Wozniak joined the Jason Gunnlaugson rink. Due to the COVID-19 sickness spread in Manitoba, the 2021 area championship was called off. As Team Gunnlaugson were the current area champions, they were chosen to represent Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons Brier. Due to the COVID-19 sickness spread in Manitoba, the 2021 area championship was called off. As the current area champions, Team Gunnlaugson was chosen to represent Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons Brier. At the Brier, they finished with a 6–6 record.

Personal life
Wozniak is working as a home loan broker for Vertuity Mortgage. He is currently in a relationship with Swiss curler Marlene Albrecht and has two children.

words_common_s.coling::9600c031-1ba2-4882-9aa0-8cb6b07d: Operation Claw () was a joint Swedish–American operation, with Norwegian support, that was carried out at Lillehammer shortly after the German surrender by the end of World War II. Thirty-five German intelligence experts were moved along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied Germany through an agreement between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material from Operation Claw, among it a Soviet codebook, became very useful for the Americans during the Cold War. Operation Claw was controversial both when it happened and afterwards. In 1945, it was controversial that the Americans operated in what was seen as a British controlled country, and that they got information about its ally the Soviet Union, in cooperation with neutral Sweden. In later years, a theory that the Norwegian resistance fighter Kai Holst's sudden death in June 1945 was related to his involvement in the Operation Claw has been put forward by among others the historian Tore Pryser. Even before the war in Europe ended the various allied states had begun the search for German scientists and other German knowledge. Signals intelligence had been extremely important during World War II and especially the British work with breaking the German codes, from the Enigma had been of huge importance. The Yalta Conference in February 1945 had shown conflicts of interest between the western allied nations on one side and the Soviet Union and the relation was badly strained. American intelligence organizations were very interested in German intelligence experts knowledge of the Soviet Union and immediately after the war in Europe ended they began to work together with the German Major General Reinhard Gehlen and his organization Fremde Heere Ost (FHO) which had led German intelligence on the Eastern Front. It was part of an organized effort to get as much German intelligence information and workers as possible; the operation had the name Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM). The war was however still fought in East-Asia, the US and the Soviet Union were still allies and the Americans were counting on Soviet help in the war against Japan. The allies had chosen Norway as part of the British area of influence. Both for the US and the neutral Sweden the operation was thus very sensitive and was done in great secrecy. In the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer a group of 35 German experts on signals intelligence were gathered. They had been working on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces and had an archive and wide-ranging knowledge about Soviet affairs. This was knowledge the Western Allies, and especially the Americans, wanted and that probably also were of use during the Cold War. In cooperation with the American intelligence organization Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and support from the Norwegian office in Stockholm agents for the Swedish intelligence organization C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence experts to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The German group of experts were taken out of the camp and moved to Sweden. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on June 12 flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany and were held in an American military camp at Wiesbaden. The transfer to Sweden of the German experts at Lillehammer, that OSS called Operation Claw, was directed from the highest level. From the U.S. side the leader of OSS, Major General William J. Donovan was involved, from the Swedish side the chief of the Defense Staff, Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd. The famous Swedish police director Harry Söderman was also involved from the Swedish side. More than a month after the German surrender, a British led search supported by Norwegian workers was carried out in order to find people from Gestapo and other German key workers that tried to hide among ordinary soldiers in German military camps. The search force that Kai Holst and other Norwegians were helping were soon aware of that a number of German key workers had been removed in the Swedish–American operation a month earlier. Kai Holst had been working at the military office number 4 (Mi4) at the Norwegian office in Stockholm, and after the search he suddenly traveled right back to Stockholm. The next day he was found shot at the top of the staircase in an apartment building at Rindögatan 42 on Gärdet. The official cause of death was stated as suicide, but neither Holst's family nor many of his colleagues from the resistance movement have accepted this and are of the opinion that he was killed. The historian Tore Pryser has put forward the theory that Holst brought with him information from Lillehammer that could damage Operation Claw and thus was killed. To be able to damage the operation Kai Holst can not have been trusted as others were. He must have been thought of as a threat due to his contact with Alexandra Kollontaj who was ambassador in Stockholm representing Soviet Union. A possible reason for a murder of Kai Holst was thus not his knowledge as such but his connections. Operation Claw was the beginning of the after-the-war time cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence services, in breaking of Sweden's officially stated neutrality. From the American side the operation was viewed as a great success and the people responsible within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with medals where the operation in particular were mentioned. For the Swedish C-byrån Operation Claw quickly became poisonous. Even though the operation was to be kept secret, information leaked to the Swedish press and C-byrån were ended in February 1946. Information about Operation Claw continued to be marked as secret in the years after the war and some of it still remains so today. A report about the operation in the British National Archives is restricted until 2020.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The short was released on February 17, 1934.
The film was looked after by Earl Duvall. The characters were brought to life by Jack King, Frank Tipper, both given credit, Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, final four not given credit. The music was written by Bernard Brown (the only one given credit) and Norman Spencer (the only one not given credit). The sound was the only thing recorded by Bernard Brown in the not given credit. Production number 6125.
Plot
The cartoon follows a male and female bug who check into a hotel which catches on fire.
Music
The song "Honeymoon Hotel" (by Al Dubin and Harry Warren) was first brought out in the 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade. This short appears on the DVD release of that film.
Color process
The film is well known for being the first Warner Bros. cartoon made in color. It used Cinecolor since Walt Disney had the only rights to the Technicolor process. There was only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon made in Cinecolor (Beauty and the Beast) before the series went briefly back to black-and-white. Later, the Merrie Melodies moved to Technicolor, though the Looney Tunes continued to be made in black-and-white until 1943. Cinecolor would make a return in several late 1940s Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts.

Modern Greek art is art from the time period between the appearance of the new independent Greek state and the 20th century.

As Mainland Greece was under Ottoman rule for all four centuries, it was not a part of the Renaissance and art movements that followed in Western Europe. However, Greek islands such as Crete, and the Ionian islands in particular were for large periods under Venetian or other European powers' rule and therefore were able to better take in the extreme art changes that were happening in Europe during the 14th-18th century.

The Cretan School and in particular the Heptanese School of art are two important art movements in Greece that followed side-by-side routes to Western Europe.

Modern Greek art can be said to have been mainly shaped by the particular social and economic conditions of Greece, the large Greek diaspora across Europe, and the new Greek social elite, as well as outside art influences, mainly from Germany and France.

Sculpture and painting

19th century

The School of Munich

Modern Greek art began to be developed around the time of Romanticism. Greek artists took in many elements from their European colleagues, resulting in the highest point of the distinctive style of Greek Romantic art, inspired by revolutionary ideals as well as the country's geography and history. After centuries of Ottoman rule, few opportunities for an education in the arts existed in the newly independent Greece, so studying abroad was absolutely necessary for artists. Munich, as an important international center for the arts at that time, was the place where the majority of the Greek artists of the 19th century chose to study. In the school of Munich, led by Karl von Piloty, true fresco was taught for wall paintings on fresh wet lime plaster. During this period much of the art was emotional and dramatic in tone. The most well-known themes of the school of Munich were urban life, rural life, still life, and landscape.

Later on, they would return to Greece and pass on their knowledge. Some of them remained in Munich, the so-called Athens on the Isar. Both academic and personal bonds developed between early Greek painters and Munich art skill giving birth to the Greek "Munich School" of painting. Nikolaos Gysis was an important teacher and artist at the Munich Academy and he soon became a leading figure among Greek artists. Academism, realism, genre painting, upper middle class portrait making, still life and landscape painting, often representing impressionist features, will be replaced in the end of the 19th century by Symbolism, Jugendstil, Art Nouveau, which are mainly found in the work of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas and others. Early-20th-century modernism is also represented by important Greek artists in Munich. Many of these Munich School artists chose subjects such as everyday Greek life, local customs, and living conditions. Several important painters appeared at this time. Theodoros Vryzakis worked in historical painting and especially inspired by the 1821 Greek War of Independence. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic pictures of Greek life. Georgios Jakobides devoted his attention to babies and children and he would later become the first Director of the new National Gallery of Athens. Georgios Roilos was another leading painter of the period closely connected with the Munich School, especially in his early career. Konstantinos Volanakis was inspired mostly by the Greek sea.

Other artists connected with the School of Munich were Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis, as well as quite a few modernist artists who studied in Munich, which included Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, and also Giorgio de Chirico.

Notable sculptors of the new Greek Kingdom were Leonidas Drosis (his major work was the extensive neo-classical building decoration at the Academy of Athens), Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis.

The School of Paris

A few Greek painters studied in Paris. Despite living in the French capital and following the guidelines of the French Art Academy, they always had their own understandings. Jacob Rizos was involved with the rendering of female grace, Theodoros Rallis with scenes from the Orthodox East and Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos with portrait making, still life and genre painting. During this period in Paris the avant-garde Impressionist movement developed, but most Greek painters remained faithful to the teachings of their teachers with only some unclear pushes in the direction of this movement. The first Greek impressionist was Périclès Pantazis who, after Paris, settled in Belgium and became a part of the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte.

Themes-artistic pictures

Many Greek artists of this period also drew upon El Greco's style for inspiration, particularly when creating art based on religious themes. This tied in with the idea of modern non-religious Greek art of the period looking back to more classical styles, while religious art looked back to Byzantine, or Byzantine inspired art. Moreover, an important and often leading role was played by artists from Ionian islands in the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th century, who took advantage of achievements of the Italian Renaissance and baroque workshops. As efforts continued with new directions and goals, Greek artists appearing in the world during the first decades of the 19th century reconnected Greek art with its ancient tradition, as well as with the searches of the European workshops, especially those of the Munich School, with defining examples of the Greek contemporary art of the period including the works of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros Lytras.

20th century

At the beginning of the 20th century landscape painting held control and the interest of painters turned toward the study of light and color. The need for Munich lessened and Paris became the center of attraction for the artists of the period. In the early 20th century Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, achieved wide recognition in France and lifelong membership of the Académie française following his praise by the critic Andre Malreaux as an artist capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto". Later in the century Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition with his surrealist ideas both of painting and poetry, while in the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became connected with European critical realism. Impressionism was the original influence on the leading figures of the art of the first half of the 20th century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas, while Nikiphoros Lytras connected himself with the avant-garde groups of Munich making up the last known link with the series of painters in the great tradition of Munich in Greek art. The further development of these painters led to other roads, but always within the framework of the avantgarde movement although with a Greek dimension.

Slowly the impressionists and other modern schools increased their influence. In the early 20th century Greek artists turned from Munich to Paris. The interest of Greek painters, artists changes from historical pictures to Greek landscapes with a focus on light and colours so plentiful in Greece. Representatives of this art change are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleas, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis. Konstantinos Parthenis, in particular, brings in historical, religious and mythological elements that allow the classification of Greek painting into modern art. The same is true with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas and the expressionism of Georgios Bouzianis. The period of the 1930s was a landmark for the Greek painters, with Yiannis Tsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (introduced abstraction in Greek paintings) and Spyros Papaloukas coming into the limelight of Greek Art. These painters tried mainly to link leading European trends with Greek tradition.

Notable 20th- and 21st-century artists

The second half of the 20th century has seen a range of praised Greek artists, such as Constantine Andreou, recipient of the French Légion d'honneur, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally praised sculptor. Giorgio de Chirico was an influential pre-Surrealist Greek-Italian painter who founded Metaphysical art. Jannis Kounellis ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera art movement. Electros Vekris, Kinetic artist and Sculptor, is the most well-known artist to be working in the field of light, Sound and Motion. Theodoros Stamos was a well-known abstract expressionist painter. Takis, Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis are internationally praised artists of Kinetic sculpture. Other notable Greek artists are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" is a short story by British author P. G. Wodehouse, which first appeared in the United States in the October 1923 issue of Cosmopolitan, and in the United Kingdom in the November 1923 Strand. It features the unstoppable Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, and was included in the collection Ukridge, published in 1924.

Plot
Ukridge and Corky run into a friend of Ukridge's, a driver for hire driving a shiny new Daimler, and he offers to take them for a ride. Along the way they are seen by a person Ukridge owes money to, who they shake off, and almost hit a young girl, who Ukridge insists they drive to her home near Clapham Common. He makes friends with her family, who are impressed by the car and Ukridge's famous Aunt Julia.

When Corky meets Ukridge a week later in the British Museum, he is with two children. He shows that he has been visiting the house, mainly for the free food, and promising to take the family out on trips in his friend's car, which they believe to be his, and to bring them to meet his aunt, who, he shows, has turned her back on him, in a letter which states "from now on, I have no nephew".

Returning from short holiday, Corky hears from George Tupper that Ukridge is engaged. Visiting his friend, he finds him with a black eye, and hears the tale of how Ukridge found himself without meaning to engaged to the girl from Clapham Common, and got punched by a man who also wants her named Finch. As they talk on Ukridge's doorstep, the person he owes money to from the car ride arrives, and Ukridge hides. A friendly person walking by calms down the angry person he owes money to, pointing out that he knows where Ukridge lives; Ukridge moves out of his house, talking about the good fortune that led him to use the false name "Mr. Smallweed" when dealing with the man.

Ukridge and Corky form a plan to get Ukridge out of the engagement by pretending to be sick, but as Corky is delivering his speech to the family, the person walking by arrives. He is George Finch, Ukridge's competitor for the girl; he shows that Ukridge is a poor person pretending to be someone else, in fact called Smallweed, and brings in the person he owes money to for proof. He also brings a letter from Ukridge's aunt, saying that she has no nephew. Once Corky has paid off the debt to the person he owes money to, the two are chased from the house.

Main characters
Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, the unstoppable businessman
Julia Ukridge, his proud writer aunt
Jimmy Corcoran, Ukridge's writer friend
George Tupper, an old friend from school of Ukridge and Corcoran
Frederick, a driver for hire, a friend of Ukridge
Mabel Price, a girl Ukridge meets on the road
Mr Price, her loving father
Ernie Finch, her admirer, a clever man
Mr Grindlay, a man Ukridge owes money to, who knows him only as "Mr Smallweed"

Publication history
The story was drawn in pictures by T. D. Skidmore in Cosmopolitan. It was drawn in pictures by Reginald Cleaver in the Strand.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" was included in the 1932 collection Nothing But Wodehouse, put together by Ogden Nash and published by Doubleday, Doran & Company. It was included in Week-End Wodehouse (UK edition), first published by Herbert Jenkins Limited in 1939. It was also collected in The World of Ukridge, published in October 1975 by Barrie & Jenkins.

Versions in other forms
"No Wedding Bells for Him" was changed for radio in 1956, with Michael Shepley as Ukridge, Hubert Gregg as Corcoran, Olaf Pooley as Frederick, Jeffrey Segal as Mr Grindley, Mairhi Russell as Mabel Price, and Brewster Mason as Tupper.

It was changed for the television series The World of Wodehouse. The episode, titled "The Wedding Bells", aired in 1968, and included the character Looney Coote (from "The Long Arm of Looney Coote").

" "Tired" I grinned, been driving out here for years but this is the first time I've seen anyone out here on the back roads, let alone try and get a ride. "I'm not afraid and I'd really not be stood in the middle of a freezing wood in a sundress on an October evening." "Fair enough" I shrugged, leaning over and opening the car door. As she dropped into the passenger seat putting her feet up on the front panel, my guesses were right. There was enough light from the inside lighting to show the bruises on her ankles, and the faded pale skin of scar tissue where she had bled out. This woman wasn't living. Or at least she didn't have the right to be complaining and leaving muddy boot prints on the inside of my car, when those boots should probably be in an evidence locker next to her body in the place where they keep dead bodies. "The boots? "I nodded. Were you camping up here? "Something like that" she nodded "I've been away from the city too long though" "My husband thought we needed to get away." "We had been growing apart and I think he wanted to bring us back together." "errrr" I said quietly. I haven't had the best luck in love and the last thing I needed was to make angry a dead woman who had clearly been murdered by her husband on their 'bringing us back together' trip. "And your leaving without him?" "He left without me!" she looked at me angrily! "why do you think I was trying to get a ride?" "He took the car keys" "I guess that makes sense "I replied, dropping down a gear and opening the speed control on the straight part. "So how far out are we?" she asked turning back to me. "About twenty minutes outside Oxford" "Not long now" "what do you mean? not long now" As she said it she turned away from me and looked out of the front window. She stared into the light as if in slow motion the car broke apart around us. Broken glass sprayed across the seats and my head spun round with a crack. The air was filled with the hissing of the engine and the loud sound of the truck's horn as the driver was bent over his wheel. "Hey Guy" "Hey Smart One" The dead girl poked me. "You still with us?" I turned my head to her and watched her face as my neck was clearly broken. "Your new to this aren't you" I said. "huh?" she replied "You asked why I could see you" "That's the thing." "I'm already dead."
words_common_s.coling::3acbf3b4-cdc2-42b4-9b2c-839dd8bb: I fought the demon's mental walls one by one, taking hold of their messy form and bending them into the stable shapes of the Solomon Keys I had spent the last three years studying. At last I came to the last one, this one was far more difficult but carried within it the mark of its name. IT fought and cried, and screamed and tried to push me back by imagining every terrible thing it would do to me and then showing it in high quality into my own mind. But I pushed those terrible pictures aside as if turning down the sound of a commercial on the TV and started my attack against its walls. One by one I pulled apart the secret writing of its lines and loosened his hold on them enough for them to freely go back to their natural shape. As the last three lines locked into place the entire thing hummed with a beautiful singing sound that I knew meant the Key had worked. At that moment I reached out and turned it with my mind even as I spoke the name out loud into its mind. It suddenly became as calm as a hindu cow and all fighting stopped. It now had me on its back, talking quietly into its ear, directing its movement and voices. This had been my plan all along, after reading the options written in stone, and suggested in the magic book I had found buried beneath it, understanding of old things made by the angry good people..... understanding that included how demons could be destroyed. "Now, creature," I told it without feeling "stop your crying, we have work to do. I plan to become the Punishment of Hell before this night is through."
words_common_s.coling::b27b582c-94a8-4076-8b94-e286cb9f: Who knew the Meeting for People Named Brian would be such a bloodbath? I did. My name is Mark Stanson. Attacks everywhere. It was only after we sent the third person to the mental hospital that would not stop asking for someone named Brian that I decided to look into it further. I realized more of the mob had started walking my way. As I reached for my handgun a cold wet hand grabbed me from behind. "What?! NO MARK. MY NAME IS MARK!" But it was too late. I was soon surrounded by them. In the confusion, my bloody badge fell to the floor. As I closed my eyes the last thing I saw was my name. Marcus Brian Stanson.

"Human new ideas seem like they are only driven through fighting and breaking things. I had always thought of fighting wars being like Darwin's ideas in nature: the strong should live, the weak do not. If Darwin is right, how did these peace lovers ever grow from the early mud? "I can not answer for the past. Our family members who came before us were violent, greedy creatures." That seemed good enough. Zor't seemed to think on it a moment, before he followed it up with a surprising response. "Since we made contact, our measuring tools lead us to believe that a large amount of your materials have been moved to weapon-making sites. Why is this so?" "I know nothing of what you speak. It would go against the rule set forth by the Council. Perhaps you've read your measuring tool information wrong." Zor't seemed to be sharply angry from the hint that they'd read the information wrong. "Mr. Hartigan, we do not read information wrong. This is not big-headed pride, it is truth. You have moved an worrying amount of your materials towards weapon making, at great danger to the poorer among you, who now go hungry and fight outside this very building. We at the Council not only hate violence, but are unable altogether of causing it. This is a terrible wrong action and will be reasons for your keeping out from the Council, and I will see to it personally." Boy, Zor't can get heated about his peace-loving. Too bad the long-haired peaceful types couldn't get voted in, or maybe Zor't would have it his way. I almost feel sorry for him. Unable to cause violence..... "That's all I needed to hear. Thank you Councillor." As the bullet entered the space, the gun barrel rose to meet Zor't's face. As the firing pin hit the explosive charge, he closed his eyes and seemed at peace, prepared for the end. Was it acceptance? Was it being brave? Or was it something else..... Can fear exist without violence?..... hmm. That's a question for thinkers and scientists, not people who handle relations between groups like myself. Now, let's show the Council how violent humans can be to get what we want.
words_common_s.coling::7a28bc6c-3b1e-4ac2-a169-10374ef5: Kevin could hear the front door unlocking from his spot in the main bathroom. Perhaps "main" was an overly nice word for the much used and only toilet in the two room city apartment, but it did connect to the bedroom, and that was by being the only bedroom in the house the main one. The toilet seat caught Kevin's right cheek as he leaned toward the bathroom door, working hard to follow the steps that were now almost certainly moving through the entry. He tried to remember who had an extra key. His girlfriend. The cleaning woman he had hired once who promised never to return again. His mom. His pet sitter. After a moment of quiet thinking, Kevin decided that the steps in the hallway belonged to none of these key holders. There was a stranger in the house. A wave of fear started a following wave of belly pain, bending Kevin over for the eighth time that day. His mouth was full of spit and the taste of salt, as if his entire body was getting ready to throw up, but there was nothing left in him at this point. Whatever remained of the Evil Food Item he hadn't decided if it was the January eggnog or last night's shwarma was already on its way to the nearest city waste treatment building. He wished it the worst of chemical deaths. The footsteps were in the kitchen now, joined by the sound of opening drawers and cupboards. Kevin hoped they'd miss the fancy bottle opener he'd gotten from his trip to Norway. Even though it reminded him of his least favorite ex, it had become an important tool at house parties. It was also a perfect way to start telling stories about travel, which he found very effective on college aged types. The loud storm of slamming drawers moved strongly toward the bedroom. Kevin tried not to become tight with worry. But it wasn't long before the loud sounds stopped. A still quiet began to build in the house. The stranger's voice: "Ummm..... hello?" Kevin: " ..... hi." And then, quickly. "Please don't come in here." Waiting hung heavy as Kevin's "smell." "I didn't think there was anyone home." "Yeah." Kevin said in a high voice. A shake of stomach pain turned itself into spit. "Ugh. I..... I'm just..... if you could not take my stuff." "Are you okay, man? I've never smelled anything like..... I mean, I'm sorry. This isn't how it usually works. Are you dying or something?" "Probably." "Do you need me to call 9-1-1? I can do that. After I leave, I mean." "Yeah. I might." "So uh..... good bye? Good luck?" "Wait!" The steps had begun to move away, back toward the door. "Wait! Wait!" "What?" "Can you leave the bottle opener? Please? It's just the one thing." "Ummm..... sure. Yeah. No problem, man." "Thanks." The door clicked shut. Kevin threw up.
words_common_s.coling::bb048a1e-39f8-4c80-9db0-70176b1c: Grace Files The Department Break-Room is always a fun place. Its workers, like me, all share one little gift from the Chief Boss: Living forever. So long as we continue to do our jobs, we're given all the time we could ever want or need. A large piece, usually a bit less than three quarters of it, is spent working. Mostly because there are so many people running around the world dying at any given moment. Even with the help of being outside of Time and Space, we Reapers still have a bit of trouble handling all the people who are dying. Of course, we can all still take off a quarter of our forever to hang out on Earth or around the Department's Campus, and that leads to another fun thing that living forever causes: you get people from everywhere and every time you can think of. One of the older reapers was around when the Aztec Kingdom was basically a handful of guys with a crazy idea using a sharp plant, a snake, and an eagle. Another of us was on the Senate Floor when Gaius Julius Caesar was killed. You get a lot of weird meetings when you mix in so many people. For example, you get Roman sitting in front of a big screen TV watching a Chariot Race from back when the Kingdom was at its top point. The Aztec is talking with a Norseman about the good points of hanging as compared to cutting the heart out as a method of religious killing. Some of the Americans, such as myself, are talking about college sports around a water cooler, and the younger members of our staff are setup in the area we call " The Arcade. " After all those people... there's the guy at the bar. He's the oldest of the Reapers. We don't even know the guy's name, since he hasn't bothered telling anyone and his records are covered up. He doesn't get out much, but we've all seen him walking around the Department. Never seen him in the Break Room though, much less at the bar. We've got every drink thought up, at least up until the present day out on Earth. I took a seat next to him. " Evening, " I said without thinking too much about the guy understanding me since Language walls don't exist for Reapers, we hear everything in our native language. Everyone hears us in their native language as well, which leads to all kinds of craziness in the modern world... or when we talk to people in Ancient Greece or Rome. " Evening, " the Eldest said. His voice sounded deep, and old. " What are you drinking to, " I asked. " Death, " the Eldest said. I didn't laugh, and neither did he. " Whose? " I asked. " Millions, " he said. I nodded in reply. Reapers may be able to live forever, and we may have a lot of not-quite-natural powers, but we're all still human at our center. Our minds are just like the minds of the people we reap, and doing our job is rough. I'd honestly call it the hardest job in the world... having to be there when someone's dying. Seeing the sad families of those who slip away to cancer, or other sicknesses, and having to deliver a bitter kindness to spare someone the pain. That's not even thinking about the bad things you get when you walk into a fighting area to get back the dead, or have to get back someone who fell to complete sadness and gave up on living... Anyway, there isn't a Reaper on staff who hasn't gotten sad over that, over not being able to help the dying beyond giving them the bitter kindness that is death. We're all human, and we all still have our fellow feeling and care. I figured that the Eldest had managed to go through that. " You talked to the Helpers about it? " I asked. The Helpers aren't Reapers for the most part. They're among the Dead, the people who live in whatever comes next. They're also people who come into the Department on their own to help us out with our mental problems. I know I spend a lot of time talking to ' em. " No... " the guy said, " at least... not this hundred years. " " Which deaths have you down? " I asked. " Brother killing brother... " the Reaper said, " It... it reminds me of myself a bit too much. " I nodded. Reapers come in all forms. Some of us are like me, and we took the job offer to get someone else a better life after death than they would have had otherwise. Some are here working to get themselves into something halfway decent. The Eldest was clearly among the latter. " So, " I said, " You thought about asking that those tasks be sent to other Reapers? " " Can't... " he said, " It's part of my... my punishment. " " Ouch, " I said, and I truly meant it. When it comes to Reapers like the Eldest, they have something called a Punishment which is made to change them to a state where they would be all right in the Life After Death they're due to be sent to. It's a set of duties they must finish, or be sent on ahead of time to one of the... less wanted final resting places. If they're lucky, they just get reborn as someone new. If they're unlucky, they're meant to get thrown into Pain and Suffering. " It's just... " He said, " I've seen so many of them. Every time I go out... I don't see the person I'm sent for. I see someone... someone I knew back before I was a Reaper... and I see myself standing over them. " I saw a tear roll down the Eldest's face at those words, and I remained quiet. " Damn it... " the Eldest said, " I need to get back to work... need to get out of here... " " Luck, " I said, " and think about setting up a meeting time. We don't need you going off on your own and breaking rules. That usually results in a lot of paperwork for the rest of us. " The Eldest made a small laugh at that, and nodded in my direction as he got up to leave. It was only once he'd left the room that I noticed that I still didn't have his name.
words_common_s.coling::78c59284-8d42-44bc-9994-350a50f2: Mr Ashley failed to appear before a business select committee about working terms and conditions at the company's warehouse in Derbyshire. In a letter, he accuses MPs of "abusing parliamentary procedures" in order to "create a media circus at Westminster." Chris Bryant MP said the House could "force" Mr Ashley to attend a meeting. The row follows a BBC investigation into the work practices at the company's warehouse in Shirebrook. Updates on this story and more from Derbyshire The Newcastle United FC owner was given a deadline of 21 March to respond to a letter from MP Iain Wright - who chairs the Business, Innovation and Skills (BIS) select committee - following his no-show. The letter said the committee kept the right to "take the matter further" should he not attend future dates. In response, Mr Ashley said: "I was disgusted to learn that you have taken a stance that is deliberately unfriendly and confrontational. "By refusing to visit Sports Direct to see things with your own eyes, you are missing out on a genuine opportunity to gain a detailed and balanced understanding of the matters you wish to discuss. "I believe you are abusing parliamentary procedure in an attempt to create a media circus in Westminster, which is not in the best interests of any of the people who work at Sports Direct." It is thought that no one has been charged with contempt of Parliament since the 1950s. Mr Bryant said in the Commons on Thursday: "Mr Ashley may be the 22nd richest man in Britain, but he is running a modern day sweatshop and this House will get to the truth." The committee is due to meet on Tuesday to discuss the next steps following Mr Ashley's letter and response to their concerns.

words_common_s.coling::54bd7a63-4df1-4ef1-979a-2ae688d3: Media playback is not supported on this device The takeover, which would include the Rodney Parade ground, has already been approved by the WRU and Dragons boards. It needs to be accepted by 75 per cent of Newport RFC shareholders next month. Dragons chief executive Stuart Davies agreed the decision was very important, adding: "It is a hugely important moment in the history of Newport RFC, the Dragons and Rodney Parade." He warned that holding company Rodney Parade Ltd faced going into closure of a deal was not agreed. The shareholders have been given a document providing information on the main issues. It also includes an open letter from Tony Brown, one of the two main money backers, supporting the deal. Rugby union has been played at Rodney Parade since 1877, and the ground is used by the Dragons area side, Newport RFC and League Two football club Newport County. The place is in need of updating, with the pitch suffering from water-logging problems that have led to football and rugby matches being given up or put off. The deal on offer would see: Davies described the Dragons current money position - set out in the documents sent to shareholders - as "not healthy" and suggested a refusal to go ahead with the takeover could lead to the end of rugby at Rodney Parade. "It all points to one thing. Rugby stops and the ground stops." "It's an old place known the world over and the protection of the place has been at the heart of this," he said. "It's an extremely important evening and we have done everything we can to make sure everything is understood and more importantly the results of it not being supported. "When you read through the letter and see the accounts you understand what our trading position is. "Our money situation is not healthy so the letter clearly sets out in the event a "no vote" the directors are likely to call in an administrator or receiver and that leads to events where the ground has to be sold for best price to protected creditors. "It all points to one thing. Rugby stops and the ground stops." Newport RFC chairman Will Godfrey said the WRU's offer of PS3.75m for the ground showed its value as a sports ground. "The problem you have got is that you either treat it as a building site or a sporting place," he said. "There is limited demand for a sporting place so when we worked out the value we consider that to be a fair price for a sporting place. "Some of the buildings here are pretty old and people coming are going to look at them and say is a further investment going to bring back a return?" Major supporter Brown said in his letter to shareholders he had at first put in PS4m into Newport Rugby Club after his connection started in 1997 which was turned into shares and written off when he at first left the board. After returning to the board, Brown claims he and Martyn Hazell put in an extra PS5.5m to 'keep the Newport Gwent Dragons and Newport running.' He said the deal on offer was "the product of two years of many difficult board meetings and hard decisions being taken to develop it to this point, once we accepted that the current business model was not working and would in the end fail. "Both Martyn and myself are over 80 and worried to cut back on our duties. "Before doing so, we have looked at many different options while trying to make sure a successful Dragons, a safe Newport RFC, protection of the place and the continuation of professional rugby in Gwent at Rodney Parade. "The WRU became our preferred option rather than a choice of last way out, and I believe they are doing this with the best of plans. "They are best placed to make a success of the Dragons, and make sure rugby for all continues at Rodney Parade."
words_common_s.coling::7426cf8e-20e5-4e81-bfbb-380b1547: The vote held on Friday was for 68 seats out of the 290 in parliament. It meant that worried Iranians woke up on Saturday morning to an all new political situation. For the first time in 13 years the people who want change and the people in the middle now have a majority in parliament. While it was not a complete victory for the supporters of President Hassan Rouhani, it was still a surprise win, especially given the months of heavy campaigning against the government's policies. The people who want strict religious control had a majority in the outgoing parliament. In the three years since Hassan Rouhani took office, they have bitterly opposed most of government's plans, organising a fierce attack on the nuclear deal between Iran and world powers. Some MPs have even gone so far as to describe Foreign Minister Javad Zarif as a traitor. The popular middle-ground politician who talked out the nuclear deal has regularly been subject to harsh criticism in parliament and is under constant threat of removal by the strict religious MPs. Now almost all those MPs have been removed by middle-ground or reform-minded counterparts, and those who remain either supported the deal or at least never attacked it as loudly as their removed friends. Many people who watch politics argue the nuclear deal not only brought an end to years of harsh international punishments but was also the deal-breaker in the elections. The people were saying no to those who had promised to stop the deal. What puts this victory in a more meaningful context is the fact that it was achieved despite almost all well-known reform-minded people being banned from running in the elections and a complete lack of news coverage of their campaign in the run-up to the elections. State TV and news never gave equal coverage to the reform-minded or middle-ground candidates and even led a campaign against the deal in recent months. The only way available to pro-government candidates was the internet and social media, which they used to the maximum in getting their message across, especially to the young and women. The triumph of the people who want reform should lead to a major shift within parliament, making it more supportive of President Rouhani. But it will by no means end the president's problems when it comes to delivering his election promises. The nuclear deal has hit some rough patches on its way to being put into action. Apart from local oppositions from strict religious people in parliament and other unelected bodies, there are still a lot of obstacles to overcome outside of Iran. The international banks still have not opened up to Iranian businesses and in the US, the people who want strict control in Congress are doing all they can to wreck the deal. Any more delays in its being put into action and following lifting of punishments would harm President Rouhani's economic reform plans and would prepare the ground for the strict religious people to recover from the this week's defeat in order to reshape their campaign against the government. Time is not on the side of the middle-ground people and the new forward movement could die down easily if it is not supported by economic rewards. This is a worry that every removed strict religious MP is focusing on from now onwards.
words_common_s.coling::76136b55-6fc5-43fa-b998-384c79a1: We are about a third of the way down the road," she says. Having been one the major players behind Manchester's recent cultural rebirth, she takes on the leadership of the Tate with clear energy and drive. Her plan, she says, is to change the Tate in the next 20 years as much as her former boss - Sir Nicholas Serota - changed it in the last two decades. Given that he watched over the change of the museum from a respected gallery in Pimlico (with a local branch in Liverpool) into a global huge art brand, it is a bold claim. Sir Nicholas built his Tate empire with bricks and stone, fixing up existing galleries and creating new places such as Tate Modern. Balshaw will take a different approach with her growth plan, thinking more on people rather than real property. Roughly speaking, according to numbers collected by the newly-renamed Department of Digital, Culture, Media Sport, around 50 of the British population visit a museum or gallery at least once a year, meaning - of course - 50 do not. These people who stay away are her target group. She says: "We should definitely reasonably expect 75 of the population to love the fact we have a national collection and feel happy to be visiting Tate... and every young person should be given the chance to think and play and try things out in the spaces Tate holds. And that is a big, big shift." Her clear sense of what she wants is impressive, but her ability to explain how it will be done is less exact. She wants to bring in "an easier language to talk about the joy of art" but couldn't be clear beyond saying that difficult words should be either avoided or explained. She talks of a big change in audience makeup, of a lack of people from BAME background among the staff and in the field more generally. But when it comes to the group she is now leading, which is to be the force for the change she desires, she says, "it's not that we need to change anything particularly." There is no doubt she is honest in her goals, and probably more able than most in the museum and gallery world when it comes to reaching more of the audience. But if she is to be successful in her aims she will need to take a lesson out of Sir Nicholas's job request for the Tate director's job back in the 1980s - in which he wrote that for the place to change he would need to grasp the nettle and take firm action to make real changes happen in meaningful ways. words_common_s.coling::6670f84e-b3ea-4cdf-98af-e79e2579: Luiz, 27, joined the Blues from Benfica for PS21.3m in January 2011. "The move is now dependent on David Luiz agreeing personal terms with PSG and passing a medical," a statement on Chelsea's official website read. The Brazilian has three years left on the five-year contract he signed at Stamford Bridge in September 2012. He said on Twitter: "Thanks CFC for this time of great partnership. I'm thankful for all! It's a new challenge and together we'll go even further. Allez Paris!" Luiz has been the target of interest from Barcelona in the last two summers, but French champions PSG - despite recently failing Uefa's financial fair play (FFP) rules - will break the transfer record for a defender to get his services. Luiz is not part of manager Jose Mourinho's first-choice main defensive pairing and his exit would provide money to strengthen in other areas, especially as Chelsea themselves only narrowly followed FFP rules. Atletico Madrid striker Diego Costa is among those linked with a move to Stamford Bridge. Because of FFP, Chelsea cannot afford to spend heavily on incoming players unless they get back similar amounts from outgoings - which they could, and did, in the earlier years of owner Roman Abramovich's time in charge. The new financial restrictions, coupled with Mourinho's plans from a footballing view, are now at the front of the club's thinking and also explain the PS37.1m sale of midfielder Juan Mata to Manchester United in January. All 12 of Luiz's goals for the Blues came in his first two-and-a-half seasons and although he played 34 games during the 2013-14 campaign, Mourinho likes John Terry and Gary Cahill at centre-half better and Luiz is not seen as a long-term option in midfield. Chelsea have high hopes for 21-year-old Czech Tomas Kalas and 19-year-old Englishman Nathaniel Chalobah as defensive options. The Blues also spent PS12m on St Etienne centre-back Kurt Zouma in January.

words_common_s.coling::aa7ddd1b-2f96-496d-ba44-14337121: After our last great Mlife spa time (Vdara's ESPA), we decided to try another place (our goal is to try all Mlife spas at least once.) words_common_s.coling::be76162e-6297-4c2c-be8b-8be691cc: This is clearly the kind of place where you drink beer, wearing sweatpants, on the days when you can't be bothered to put makeup on. It's certainly not a white wine drink or fancy cocktail sort of place. What's great about this place is how cheap it is. As part of the Scream Pubs family you get drinks prices starting from as little as PS1.80, and if you're hungry then PS4-5 will make sure you leave with a full stomach. There are two pool tables too, although they are quite close together which means you usually end up on both the giving and receiving end of a pool stick in the back every few minutes at least. In the downstairs area there are also loads of tv screens for watching sport, although the terrible music they play will clearly make you wish you'd stayed at home to watch the football in your own living room: the jukebox is set up to always play the songs that are least picked, meaning the really terrible ones that no-one ever pays for, to make people put money into it to do everyone a favour and change the song. And there are lots of other things that may well put you off coming here. For starters, given that it's below ground means it's dark, dirty and generally a bit sad. Add to this the fact that this place hasn't seen a makeover in far too long, and you end up with a mix of dark and gloomy combined with worn out and dirty. But the very worst thing about here is the condition of the bathrooms. Without wanting to sound hard to please, I like my toilets to have a) toilet paper and b) a lock on the door. But when you've spent so long waiting in line for one of the only 3 bathrooms (one of which will usually be out of order) you tend to just put up with it anyway!
words_common_s.coling::1c1fb589-36fc-45ac-bccc-1e9cced6: It's like Buffalo Wild Wings without the wings. Well, yeah, and more beer. Just a little bit. words_common_s.coling::8d68dd4d-1de2-4490-8a68-ccd52f7f: Usually the low advertised rates are for term life insurance. This type of life insurance has an end date, and is usually used to protect during times of higher expenses.... for example, one might buy a term policy that ends when the kids finish college or house mortgage is paid off, to make sure than an early death doesn't prevent the kids from going to college or forcing a surviving spouse to sell the house. But if you live until that point in time, the policy ends without payment. So say the average buyer is in their 30's and covers into their 50's or 60's.... most will live, so only a small number pay out and the ones that don't help cover the ones that do.', "The chances of a payment are so small and the number of people paying is so large. For example let's say 100 people buy a 100 life insurance plan for 10 and 1 person dies. The insurance company gets 100 10 1000 The insurance company pay 100 to the dead persons family leaving them with 900 The insurance company can also put the 900 in other things and earn money from the investment. Now raise the numbers of people buying insurance and lower the percentage of people making claims and the possible profits for the insurance company are huge. The insurance company is also very careful to keep out people who are more likely to make an insurance claim. Life insurance is difficult or impossible to get if you have a life threatening condition, car insurance gets harder the worse your driving record is, and so on and so forth.," "It isn't. The payments are figured out based on probability and odds. Also the length of the term and a large number of other factors come into play. Make no mistake; the insurance business is in it for profit. Just like a casino, if you put a quarter in a slot machine, you may win thousands.
words_common_s.coling::4622a5f2-c96d-4ea1-9629-b734e976:
(Shortened) The Sloan Digital Sky Survey now covers a large enough
area that galaxies in low density surroundings can be found. Rojas et al.
have created a method to pull out more than 1000 void galaxies with delta
rho/rho < -0.6 on scales r>7 h^{-1} Mpc from the SDSS. In this paper, we
show the brightness function of these galaxies and compare it to that of
galaxies at higher densities. We get a measurement of the void galaxy
brightness function over the range -21.5<M_r*<-14.5 in the SDSS r-band. The
void galaxy brightness function (LF) is well fit by a Schechter function with
values of Phi*=(0.19 +- 0.04)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-19.74 +- 0.11
and alpha=-1.18 +- 0.13, while the LF of the wall galaxy has Schechter
function numbers Phi*=(1.42 +- 0.03)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-20.62
+- 0.08 and alpha=-1.19 +- 0.07. The dimmer value of M_r* is in agreement with
the work of Rojas et al. who found that void galaxies were dimmer than galaxies
at higher densities but the value of alpha is very close to that of galaxies
at higher densities. To look into this further, the LF of wall and void
galaxies as a function of density is thought about. Only the wall galaxies in the
highest density areas have a less steep faint end slope. The LF of the void
galaxies is also compared to the LF of the wall galaxies with matching
features to the void galaxies. The LF of the bluest, Sersic index n<2 and
EW(Halpha)>5A wall galaxies is very close in shape to that of the void
galaxies, with only slightly brighter M_r* values and matching values of alpha.
The value of alpha around -1.2 found from the void galaxy LF is less steep than that
found from CDM models, pointing to the idea that voids are not filled with a large
group of dwarf galaxies.
words_common_s.coling::f05692cf-092b-40e0-9f4a-d3f7ccd6: I know I'm going to get trouble for this but, oh well here goes... Hungry, I go out into the mean hot wet weather that is Scottsdale in rainy season, looking for food on a Sunday afternoon. After a couple of closed on Sunday letdowns, I decided to go looking at the always-disappointing Schlotskys Deli on Scottsdale. Lo and behold, shiny new Capriottis and Everything Bagel came in to save the neighborhood. Great.... No wait, hold my calls, I'm not done. I walk in and the place is about eighty-five degrees in the restaurant.... Terrible. I walk up to the register to order and asked the very pregnant sweating girl how long ago did they take over Schlotskys. She rolled her eyes, looked down, and said two months, what would you like to order? I ordered. Then she asked for my name to tag my order. I told her my name. Another giant eye roll and a (forget it, who cares) shrug. She says I can't spell. Because I don't normally care whether my name is spelled or said correctly, even though, on this very rare time, I had said it sound by sound for her, I just blew it off. But then, right on the cash register screen facing me, was her spelling.... corney. I laughed. She made a noise.... What? She says. I'm just laughing at how you spelled my name. Then she smiles in a mean way and says it works. And walked away without even looking at me. OK, kind of rude. I walk down to where the food comes out, and the young guy making my sandwich is also sweating (no kidding) and wiping the sweat off with the back of his wrist. Whatever.... it's Scottsdale. The other kid working was on his lunch break. I could tell that by how he blew past me full speed, across the store, awkwardly holding a plastic cup and slid three feet to a stop in front of an available table to eat at, and dropped his rear end down. I hope he chose something without caffeine. Look, I know they're young, I know it's hot here, I know other guy is jumpy and uncoordinated, I know she's pregnant, I can even guess that she may not like her job, life, self.... None of those things take away the fact that you, those workers, went out and got yourself a job in the food serving business.... Serving others, food. Part of serving is being polite. Another part is being professional. Where the heck are the adults to control these young people and teach them how to represent your business? Shame on you. Oh, the sandwich was wonderful! Thank you, sweaty tall kid.
words_common_s.coling::da2d8730-7c13-4b32-befb-c2bbe666:
Section 51(xxxi) is a part of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia.

It gives the Commonwealth the power to make laws about the taking of property, but says that such takings must be on just terms.

The terms is sometimes called in short as the 'just terms' rule.

Apart from its importance to Australian Constitutional Law, and Property Law; the section is well known for its role as a story piece in The Castle, a famous Australian film.

Text
Section 51(xxxi) reads:

Case Law
While s51(xxxi) was taken from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, it has many differences.

The 'just terms' rule has been held not to affect the State Parliaments.

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon said that the adding of the condition was to "prevent random uses of the power at the cost of a State or a person."

The understanding of the terms "taking" and "just terms" by the High Court of Australia have had the result, however, of limiting its protection of property rights. What is more, it works at any time the Commonwealth makes a forced taking of property. As such, it is a possible guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy property rights.

The Commonwealth may only take property on just terms for a "purpose in relation to which the Parliament has power to make laws". This means that every law supported by s 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other extra lawmaking power.

Property
The High Court of Australia has taken a wide view of the idea of "property". Several members of the court took the chance to think about the meaning of the term property in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke said the term includes: "every kind of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, non-physical inherited rights such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and rights to sue. Justice McTiernan said the term property extends to physical and non-physical property.

An example of the width of the idea of property in section 51(xxxi) is given by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisation Case). In that case, Federal law planned the taking of private banks through placing of shares in private banks in the Commonwealth, and later the naming of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon described the rules as removing real control over the property of the private banks. He decided that this was, in the basic sense, a taking of a property right.

While legal permits have sometimes been treated the same as property interests, the removal of rights enjoyed under a legal permit does not usually amount to a taking of property within section 51(xxxi), as permit conditions are naturally open to change.

Taking
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been taken by somebody, and the taking must be for a Commonwealth purpose. This is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the end place does not matter – it is enough that the holder of property has been removed from it. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which limited the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth taking any property. In the same way in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring payments and life Gold Pass for retired members of Parliament were not a taking of property.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court held that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW by force taking property was invalid as a taking of property upon terms which were not just. The validity of a grant in the lack of a need to take property was supported in the later case of Pye v Renshaw.

Just terms
Usually, a decision of just terms based on the market value of the property at the time of taking will be enough to satisfy the need of just terms. Unlike the "just payment" need in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" brings in no sameness of market value. The plans offered must be "fair", or such that a lawmaking body could reasonably see them as "fair". However, this judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected, not just those of the removed owner.

The need of "just terms" does not always require that a payment package be presented as part of the taking plan. It is enough that the plan provides good processes for deciding fair payment. However, the Court may look at such processes closely to make sure they are good enough.

There may be some takings of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported only by section 122 of the Constitution.

Section 51(xxxi) is a different case to the norm for understanding of the parts of section 51, that one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" another. In this case, however, the Court will not allow another grant of power to be read so broadly as to get around the specific limit to the power granted by section 51(xxxi).

Related law
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, largely written by Littleton Groom, was the first to deal with the forced taking of land by the federal government. Its most argued about rule was a part allowing the federal government to grant mining leases and control mining on Commonwealth land. Responsibility for forced taking was at first placed with the Department of Home Affairs.

The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act 1945 by force took land owned by Chinese-Australians in Darwin, leading to the end of the local Chinatown. The law was put forward in 1943 by the Northern Territory's head man Aubrey Abbott, who put forward a combination of forced taking and change of the land to leasehold in order to bring about "the removal of unwanted people which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past" and said that he hoped to "completely prevent the Chinese area forming again". He further noted that "if land is taken from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other property". The territory's civilian population had mostly been moved away during the war and the former Chinatown residents returned to find their homes and businesses reduced to broken remains.
