words_common_s.coling::c7e45e24-dc16-40b2-9030-8200e20e: They're not free though are they. Both users no matter where they are need an internet connection. Even if you both used free wifi the wifi is free to bring in business and is still being paid for. The fact that it appears free is down to it using the internet which has no borders. For traditional voice and text it needs your provider paying the provider in the other country for their service to deliver the call or text. Although usually the fees are hugely increased. Bottom line you pay either way just in a different way. Phone systems were built a long time ago, when talking to people in other countries was really expensive - that set an example. Usually phone companies were national businesses that controlled everything, often with legal protection from other companies trying to compete. So they would charge high fees to other telephone companies trying to hand calls into their country. They could do this because there was no other choice and fees for calling other countries weren't worried about by most people (in reality these fees were like the extra money that the telephone company was allowed in payment for providing an affordable national calling network). Then the internet came along. Many internet providers started as small competitive new companies offering service over phone lines (dial up). That meant they were eager to freely connect with content providers as it made them more able to compete (by providing better service to their customers), even when they were far apart they could get cheap connections as they'd have access to a "telephone hotel" with lots of companies competing to offer connections between cities and towns and other places. So internet access has become very cheap, phone providers haven't kept up. Note: this should also provide you with a good background on net neutrality. As the United States moves to a single company controlling the network (you could dial into any dial up provider but most Americans only have one or two high speed cable choices) internet providers are trying to move back to the old model where they had much more power over what they charged customers. In countries with more open networks (for example in New Zealand you can choose any fiber provider in your local exchange, normally a few dozen choices) this isn't such a problem. You're already a phone company customer (trying to earn more). Skype is still hoping to make you a customer (earn anything).
words_common_s.coling::8986a229-067f-4f9d-8d01-514889d3:
If there is an available course plan for the Biology class, read it carefully to know the rules, materials needed, and any other important information before going to the first Biology class. It is a good idea to look over it before going to class each day to make sure nothing is forgotten. One way of remembering the course plan is to mark it with bright colors, draw lines under important parts, and write notes on it.


Use different note-taking methods such as drawing lines under words, marking with bright colors, drawing a picture such as a star next to something important, drawing a box around important sentences or parts, and taking notes either on a separate sheet of paper or the back of the course plan. These tips will make sure everything is remembered.
Make sure it is okay with the teacher before marking up the course plan. If needed, make a copy with a machine that makes copies so there are multiple copies. It is a good idea to keep one unmarked and the other with notes so if anything changes, new notes can be made on the second copy.
Students without copy machines at home have a few different choices for copying the course plan. One is to go to the nearest library that has a copy machine and bring the course plan along. Usually it costs no more than twenty cents for each page to copy. Another choice is for students with smartphones or tablets with a camera built into the device. Put an app made for copying documents on the device. These kinds of apps allow users to take a picture of a document and it will change it to PDF, DOC, and other different document types. If these choices are not available, do not wait or worry to ask the school if they have a copy machine or if the Biology teacher can copy the course plan. They will be happy to help.

Most science classes including Biology will require students to pay a lab fee. This fee goes towards giving the students lab materials needed for experiments and activities. Usually the teacher will give students at least the first week of class to pay this fee. Most of the time it is given back, meaning when students have finished the course the money is given back to them. If anything has been damaged by a student, most likely this fee will not be given back to them. Be careful of lab materials, both dangerous and safe ones.


Usually pencils or pens and paper to take notes are required in most classes. Even if it is not required by the teacher, it is a very good idea to bring them and take notes anyway. This will help remember information and allow students to look over what they learned in class.
Learn good note-taking skills to be even more successful. Look at "Part 2 of 3: Taking Notes" for more information.

This gets students ready for class faster and so they are not looking around in their school bag when it is actually time to use them. Only skip this if the teacher tells the students not to take anything out until they say so. This is also a good time to quickly look over yesterday's homework and notes to be sure nothing is missing.
words_common_s.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f: Judith Scott (May 1, 1943 – March 15, 2005) was an American fiber sculptor, born with Down Syndrome and deaf. She was known around the world for her art. In 1987, Judith was signed up at the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, California which supports people with brain development problems. There, Judith found her love and skill for abstract fiber art and she was able to share her thoughts in a new form. A story of Scott's life, Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott (2016) has been written by her twin sister. Judith was born into a middle-class family in Cincinnati, Ohio in May 1, 1943 along with her non-identical twin sister Joyce. Unlike Joyce, Judith was born with Down Syndrome. During her baby years, Judith got sick from Scarlet Fever, which caused her to lose her hearing, a fact that stayed unknown until much later on in her life. Judith Scott spent her first seven and a half years at home with her parents, twin sister and older brothers. Although the development gap between the two girls was clear, "the parents on purpose tried to treat these youngest members of the family alike." However, when it was time for the girls to start going to school, Judith was found to be "not able to be taught." There was only one classroom for children with problems, and Judith was not able to pass the word-based entry tests, due to her still not known deafness. Because of this, on medical advice, her parents placed Judith in the Columbus State Institution (before called the Columbus State School), a place for the mentally disabled, on October 18, 1950. This separation had a deep effect on both twins. The records from Judith Scott's first few years at the Institution show that she had an IQ of 30 (based upon spoken testing before her deafness was found). For this reason she was not given any training chances. Cut off from her twin, Judith became very separated from others, and behavior problems soon came up. Her Clinical Record states that "She does not seem to be in good contact with her world around her. She does not get along well with other children, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats other children. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Soon after, she was moved to a smaller state place at Gallipolis, Ohio. In 1985, after 35 years of complete separation and long and difficult talks, Joyce Scott became her sister's legal guardian, and brought Judith to live with her in California, a state where all mentally disabled citizens have the right to an ongoing education. Judith Scott died of natural causes at her sister's home in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks short of her 62nd birthday. She lived longer than her life expectancy at birth by almost fifty years. On April 1, 1987, Judith Scott began going to the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the first groups in the world to provide studio space for artists with problems. For almost two years, Judith showed little interest in any artistic activity. She was not special with paint. She drew loops and circles, but her work had no pictures of real things, and she was so not interested in creating that the staff was thinking about ending her time with the program. It wasn't until Judith without planning watched a fiber art class taught by visiting artist Sylvia Seventy, that she had her artistic big step forward. Using the materials at hand, Judith suddenly came up with her own special and very different form of artistic way of showing herself. While other students were sewing with needles, she was making sculptures with a never before seen energy and focus. Her creative gifts and complete focus were quickly seen, and she was given complete freedom to choose her own materials. Taking whatever objects she found, no matter who owned them, she would wrap them in carefully picked colored yarns to create different sculptures of many different shapes. Some look like cocoons or body parts, while others are long thin standing poles. Many of her works also have pairs, showing Scott's life as a twin. Judith worked on her art five days a week for eighteen years, making over 200 pieces in total. Judith had her first showing in 1999, which happened at the same time as the printing of John MacGregor's book called Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott. Together, these events helped push her to worldwide being known. Scott's work has become very popular in the world of outsider art, and her pieces sell for large amounts of money. Scott is now called a modern artist, no longer just an outsider. Her art is held in the permanent collections of many museums, including: Museum of Modern Art (Manhattan, New York), the American Visionary Art Museum (Baltimore, Maryland), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Museum of American Folk Art (Manhattan, New York), Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art (Chicago, Illinois), Irish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin, The Oakland Museum, Oakland, CA. L'Aracine Musee D'Art Brut (Paris, France), Art Brut Connaissance & Diffusion Collection (Paris and Prague), Collection de l'art brut (Lausanne, Switzerland). Below is a list of select important showings for Judith Scott. 2018 – Judith Scott: Touchdown, Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California 2014-15 – Bound and Unbound, Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn, New York 2009 – Judith Scott: Looking Back, Ricco Maresca Gallery, New York City, New York 2002 – Cocoon: Judith Scott, Ricco-Maresca Gallery, New York City, New York 2019 – Memory Palaces: Inside the Collection of Audrey B. Heckler, American Folk Art Museum, New York City, New York 2019 – The Doors of Perception, Put Together by Javier Téllez in working together with the Outsider Art Fair, Frieze Art Fair, New York City, New York 2019 – Flying High: Women Artists of Art Brut, Bank Austria Kunstforum, Vienna 2018 – Outliers and American Vanguard Art, National Gallery of Art, Washington DC 2017 – Forget Me Not: Judith Scott, Zuckerman Museum of Art, Kennesaw, Georgia 2017 – Viva Arte Viva, the 57th Venice Biennale, Venice, Italy 2015 – Collection ABCD, La Maison Rouge, Paris, France 2013 – Create, Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California 2013 – Create, Boca Raton Museum of Art, Boca Raton, Florida 2013 – Extreme Art, The Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, Ridgefield, Connecticut 2012 – Rosemarie Trockel: A Cosmos, New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York City, New York 2011 – World Transformers, Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt, Frankfurt, Germany 2000 – Visions, American Visionary Art Museum, Baltimore, Maryland 2005 – Creative Growth, The Ricky Jay Broadside Collection, Yerba Buena Center for the Arts, San Francisco, California

After the talk below, I looked at earlier work by the authors (MUS-ROVER) on which this paper was built. On one hand, this was very helpful for me to better understand the current paper. On the other hand, this was very needed for me to better understand the current paper.

Overall, while I think that I like this work, and while I am familiar with the JSB chorales, with chance-based ways of doing things, with n-grams, etc, I did find the paper quite hard to follow at different parts. The heavy use of symbols did not help the clearness.

I think the ideas and ways of doing things are good, and certainly worth publishing and worth following up on. I am not sure that, in the paper's current form, ICLR is a right place. (By the way, the problem is not the use as I think that music uses can be very right, nor is the problem always with the way of doing things... see my next idea..). I get the sense that a long-form journal piece would actually give the authors the space needed to fully explain these ideas, provide clearer running examples where needed, provide the needed background for the right readership, provide the needed background on the earlier system, perhaps showing results on a second group of data to show how general the way of doing things is, etc. A short meeting paper just seems to me to be too packed a format for giving this work the description it deserves. If it were possible to focus on just one part of this system, then that might work, but I do not have good ideas for exactly how to do that.

If the paper were changed in big ways (though I cannot offer details for how to do this within the right page count), I would think about raising my score. I do think that the effort would be better spent in turning this into a long (and clearer) journal piece to send in.
